lessons.title: Iterators & Generators
lessons.interviewAnswer: An iterable can produce an iterator; an iterator owns traversal state and implements `__next__`, raising `StopIteration` when exhausted. A generator function is convenient syntax for building an iterator: calling it returns a generator object, and each `yield` suspends the frame until the next request. Generators support streaming and bounded-memory composition, but they are normally one-pass and lazy errors occur during consumption rather than construction.
keyPoints: Iterable creates an iterator
Iterator owns state
yield suspends a frame
Laziness changes timing
One pass requires explicit ownership
lessons.why: Data and ML systems repeatedly cross boundaries where eager materialization is too expensive: reading compressed records, decoding images, paginating APIs, generating training batches, or streaming model outputs. The iteration protocol provides a common pull-based interface for these cases. Correctness failures are subtle because construction can succeed while work later fails during consumption. A generator may be accidentally exhausted during logging, consumed twice by two downstream stages, or leave a file or cursor open when a caller stops early. Interviews probe iterables and generators because a strong answer connects language protocol, memory behavior, timing, and cleanup rather than saying only that `yield` saves memory.
lessons.intuition: Think of an iterator as a paused computation with one public request: give me the next item. The consumer pulls; the producer runs only far enough to answer and then pauses. A list is a completed shipment, while a generator is a production line. The line can keep working with a small in-process inventory, but the factory and its inputs remain active until production finishes or closes. This model explains why a generator is lazy, why it is usually one-pass, why errors appear when `next` is called, and why early termination needs deliberate cleanup.
lessons.deepDive: The full explanation is organized into the structured sections below.
lessons.workedExample: Stream validated records into complete and final partial batches while keeping only one batch in memory.

commonMistakes.mistake: A generator stores no data and always uses constant memory.
commonMistakes.correction: Its suspended frame retains locals, and downstream operations may buffer or materialize. State is bounded only when every pipeline stage has a proven bound.

commonMistakes.mistake: An iterable and iterator are the same thing.
commonMistakes.correction: An iterable can usually create fresh iterators; an iterator owns an active traversal and is normally single-use.

commonMistakes.mistake: Code in a generator runs when the function is called.
commonMistakes.correction: Calling creates the generator object. Most body code, validation, I/O, and exceptions occur when consumption begins.

followUps.question: Why can `itertools.tee` consume substantial memory?
followUps.answer: It must buffer values already consumed by the faster branch but not yet consumed by the slower branch. The buffer grows with the distance between consumers.

followUps.question: When is a list better than a generator?
followUps.answer: Use a list when the result is small, must be traversed repeatedly, needs indexing or length, or when eager validation and resource release make the boundary clearer.

followUps.question: What does `yield from` add beyond a small loop?
followUps.answer: It delegates the complete generator protocol, forwarding values, send/throw/close behavior, and capturing the subgenerator's return value.

lessons.production: Specify replayability, ordering, resource ownership, cancellation, retry, and partial-result semantics for streaming interfaces. Keep database cursors, files, and HTTP responses open only across a clearly scoped consumption block. Bound every queue or accumulator, monitor processed counts and iterator age, and test early termination. For training pipelines, make sharding, shuffle buffers, random seeds, and epoch boundaries explicit; a Python generator alone does not provide distributed determinism or recovery.
lessons.description: Iterators and generators are Python's protocol for producing values one at a time. They let callers consume a sequence without requiring the producer to materialize every result first, which is valuable for large files, database pages, preprocessing pipelines, and streams. This chapter separates an iterable—the object that can create an iterator—from an iterator—the stateful object that returns the next value. It then explains how generator functions suspend at `yield`, how one-pass consumption changes correctness, how `yield from` delegates, and how cleanup and exceptions behave. Laziness is not automatically faster and it does not make an unbounded computation safe by itself: the surrounding pipeline can still buffer, retain references, repeat expensive work, or hold a resource open. You will learn to design a small iterator, batch a stream without losing records, test exhaustion and edge cases, and decide when a concrete list is clearer. The central skill is reasoning about ownership and timing: who advances the iterator, when work happens, how errors surface, and which resource remains live while iteration is suspended.
learningObjectives: Distinguish iterable, iterator, generator function, and generator object using the Python iteration protocol.
Trace suspension, resumption, exhaustion, exception propagation, and delegation through a generator pipeline.
Build and verify a bounded-memory batching iterator while identifying retention and cleanup failure modes.

deepSections.title: The iterable and iterator protocols
deepSections.body:
`iter(obj)` asks an iterable for an iterator, normally through `obj.__iter__()`. `next(iterator)` calls `iterator.__next__()`. A successful call returns one value; exhaustion is signaled by raising `StopIteration`, not by returning a special sentinel that might also be valid data. A container such as a list is iterable and can create independent iterator objects. An iterator is also iterable: its `__iter__` method conventionally returns itself, because it already represents one active traversal.

This distinction predicts behavior. Two calls to `iter(a_list)` can traverse independently. Two names referring to the same iterator share one cursor and divide the values between them. `for` loops, comprehensions, `sum`, `list`, `any`, `zip`, and many library functions consume this protocol. A custom iterator normally separates reusable configuration in the iterable from mutable cursor state in the iterator. Returning `self` from a reusable container's `__iter__` can accidentally make nested iteration interfere.

An iterator's contract includes exhaustion stability in practical code: after `StopIteration`, future `next` calls should remain exhausted. Consumers should not catch broad exceptions and reinterpret them as normal exhaustion. Empty input, partial consumption, and repeated `iter` calls are essential tests because they reveal whether ownership and state are designed correctly.

deepSections.title: Generator functions, suspension, and control flow
deepSections.body:
A function containing `yield` is a generator function. Calling it creates a generator object without executing the body to completion. The first `next` starts execution; reaching `yield value` returns that value and suspends the frame, preserving local variables, instruction position, and active exception-handling state. The next request resumes immediately after that yield. Falling off the end or executing `return` exhausts the generator.

This is state-machine behavior expressed with ordinary-looking code. A batching generator can retain one partial batch between calls. A tree traversal can retain its stack in suspended frames. The convenience does not eliminate state; it makes the state implicit in the frame. That can complicate debugging if the generator captures a large object, mutable external variable, open transaction, or lock. Inspect data flow and lifecycle exactly as you would for an explicit stateful object.

Generators can receive values with `send`, receive exceptions with `throw`, and be terminated with `close`, which raises `GeneratorExit` inside the frame. These features enable coroutines but are rarely needed for straightforward data iteration. Prefer a simple pull interface until bidirectional control is genuinely required. Never yield from a `finally` block during close. Keep cleanup in `finally` or, more clearly, place resource ownership outside the generator in a context manager.

deepSections.title: Delegation and pipeline composition
deepSections.body:
`yield from subiterator` delegates iteration rather than spelling `for item in subiterator: yield item`. It forwards values and also handles the full generator protocol, including sent values, thrown exceptions, close, and the subgenerator's return value. For simple flattening, the important benefit is that the code states delegation directly. Recursive traversals and staged parsers often become clearer when each function owns one layer and delegates the next.

Generator expressions compose naturally: `valid = (parse(line) for line in lines if line.strip())`. Each stage is lazy, so backpressure is implicit in a synchronous pull pipeline: downstream work requests the next item only when ready. That does not provide distributed-stream backpressure, parallelism, checkpointing, or replay. A slow operation still blocks the caller. An async iterator extends the idea for asynchronous waits, but it is a distinct protocol using `__aiter__`, `__anext__`, and `async for`.

Composition can hide repeated work. Iterating the same generator twice does not recompute; the second pass sees only what remains. Recreating a generator expression may recompute expensive parsing. `itertools.tee` supplies independent-looking iterators by buffering values needed by the slower consumer, so memory can grow with their distance. State whether the source is replayable, regenerate it deliberately, or materialize at a boundary when multiple passes are part of the algorithm.

deepSections.title: Memory, resources, and failure timing
deepSections.body:
A generator reduces peak memory only when every stage keeps bounded state. Calling `list(generator)` materializes the output. Sorting generally needs all values. Grouping an unbounded stream in a dictionary still grows without bound. A closure or suspended local can retain a large array even if only small values are yielded. Measure allocations across the complete pipeline rather than comparing one generator object with one list object.

Laziness moves computation and failures to iteration time. Validation performed inside the generator does not run when the generator is created. If a service returns a generator and then closes the database session, consumption later fails. If a caller reads only the first few values, code after the last reached yield may never run unless the generator is explicitly closed or finalized. Deterministic resource cleanup belongs in a `with` statement whose scope covers consumption, or in an object with an explicit close lifecycle.

Generators are useful across API boundaries only when the consumption contract is clear. Document whether the iterator is single-use, whether order is stable, what exceptions can occur mid-stream, whether partial results are meaningful, and who closes it. Add cancellation and timeout behavior for network-backed sources. For retryable pagination, distinguish retrying one page from restarting the entire one-pass traversal, because replay can duplicate already emitted records.

lessons.math: If a source contains n items and batching retains at most b items, the batching layer uses O(b) auxiliary space rather than O(n). Total processing remains O(n) plus the work performed per item. This bound fails when a downstream stage materializes, sorts, tees with a lagging consumer, or accumulates unbounded keyed state.

workedExamples.title: Batch a one-pass event source without losing the tail
workedExamples.setup: An API client yields events page by page. Training accepts batches of at most 128 events, and the final incomplete batch must be processed exactly once.
workedExamples.walkthrough: The batching generator owns one list. It appends each validated event and yields the list when its size reaches the limit, then replaces the list rather than mutating the yielded object. After source exhaustion it yields a non-empty tail. Tests flatten the batches and compare them with the input, assert every batch size is within the bound, cover empty input, and demonstrate that the returned generator is exhausted after one pass. If the API can fail between pages, the source layer owns retries and resume tokens; the batching layer should not silently replay previously emitted events.
workedExamples.conclusion: The design has bounded batching state and explicit one-pass semantics, but end-to-end recovery still depends on checkpointing at the source or sink boundary.

exercises.prompt: Explain why `iter([1, 2]) is iter([1, 2])` is not a useful independence test and state what should be tested instead.
exercises.solution: Those are two different list objects. Store one list, call `iter` twice, and confirm the two iterator objects advance independently while yielding equal values.

exercises.prompt: Write the invariants for a batching generator with maximum size b.
exercises.solution: Every input appears once and in order; every emitted batch has 1 through b items; empty input emits nothing; the concatenated batches equal the input; auxiliary batch state never exceeds b.

exercises.prompt: A generator reading a file works in one function but fails with 'I/O operation on closed file' after being returned. Why?
exercises.solution: The function returned a lazy computation from inside a `with open(...)` block. The file closed before the caller consumed it. Consume within the context or expose a context-managed iterator whose lifetime includes iteration.

lab.useIt:
from itertools import chain, islice
source = (n * n for n in range(10))

lab.verifyIt:
data = list(range(10))
out = list(batches(iter(data), 3))
assert [len(x) for x in out] == [3, 3, 3, 1]

list(g)

lessons.title: Decorators & Context Managers
lessons.interviewAnswer: A decorator is a callable transformation applied when a function or class is defined; `@d` above `f` is essentially `f = d(f)`. A context manager implements enter and exit around a `with` block so setup and cleanup have one lexical scope, including exception paths. Good decorators preserve metadata with `functools.wraps` and keep behavior explicit. Good context managers release resources deterministically and suppress exceptions only by deliberate contract.
keyPoints: Decoration transforms at definition time
Wrapper runs at call time
wraps preserves metadata
with guarantees an exit call
Composition order changes semantics
lessons.why: Cross-cutting concerns otherwise spread across every call site. A timing decorator can standardize latency measurement; a transaction context can make commit and rollback boundaries visible. Frameworks also rely on decorators for registration and dependency declarations. Because the syntax is compact, its behavior can become invisible. A retry decorator around a non-idempotent call may duplicate writes. A cache may retain user data. A context manager may catch an exception and return a truthy value, silently converting failure into success. Interviews use these features to test first-class functions, closures, protocols, and exception flow. Production engineering demands the additional question: what behavior is hidden, and can operators observe and reverse it?
lessons.intuition: A decorator is a function-building function: it receives a callable and binds a replacement name. The replacement may call the original, but it does not have to. A context manager is a two-sided bracket: enter establishes an invariant, and exit restores or releases it. The block is inside the bracket even when it raises. Decorators change what a callable means across calls; context managers change the environment for one visible block. That distinction helps choose the clearer abstraction.
lessons.deepDive: The full explanation is organized into the structured sections below.
lessons.workedExample: Combine a metadata-preserving timing decorator with a context manager that records success or failure without suppressing the exception.

commonMistakes.mistake: `@decorator` runs the wrapper only when the function is called.
commonMistakes.correction: The decorator expression and transformation run during definition; the returned wrapper usually runs later at invocation.

commonMistakes.mistake: `functools.wraps` makes a decorator behaviorally transparent.
commonMistakes.correction: It preserves metadata and the wrapped link, but the wrapper can still change exceptions, results, concurrency, timing, or side effects.

commonMistakes.mistake: A context manager always swallows exceptions after cleanup.
commonMistakes.correction: Exceptions propagate unless `__exit__` deliberately returns truthy or a generator-based manager catches and does not re-raise them.

followUps.question: In which order do stacked decorators execute?
followUps.answer: They transform bottom-up and invoke from the outermost returned wrapper inward. Write `a(b(f))` to reason about the order.

followUps.question: Why is `ExitStack` useful?
followUps.answer: It acquires a dynamic number of resources and registers callbacks as acquisition succeeds, then unwinds completed acquisitions in reverse order even when a later acquisition fails.

followUps.question: When can a retry decorator be unsafe?
followUps.answer: When the operation has non-idempotent side effects, the error is permanent, attempt budgets compound across layers, or cancellation and deadlines are not propagated.

lessons.production: Version and document decorator semantics because changing wrapper order can change authorization, caching, metrics, and retries without altering call sites. Bound and expose cache state, redact logged arguments, propagate trace and cancellation context, and separate logical-request metrics from attempt metrics. Keep resource scopes short, unwind partial acquisition, surface cleanup failures, and test rollback. Provide a kill switch or direct underlying callable for rollback where cross-cutting behavior can affect availability.
lessons.description: Decorators and context managers both add cross-cutting behavior around core code, but they solve different lifecycle problems. A decorator transforms a function or class at definition time, often returning a wrapper that performs work before and after a call. A context manager establishes a runtime context for a lexical block and guarantees an exit path for normal completion and exceptions. This chapter builds both mechanisms from ordinary Python objects, then covers function metadata, descriptors and methods, decorator factories, exception suppression, composition order, and resource ownership. These tools appear throughout data and AI systems in tracing, retry, caching, authorization, device or precision scopes, transactions, locks, and temporary configuration. They also create risk: a wrapper can change signatures, duplicate retries, hide failures, or capture sensitive arguments; a context manager can suppress an exception accidentally or hold a scarce resource while slow work runs. You will learn to keep transformations transparent, make cleanup deterministic, test success and failure paths, and decide when an explicit helper is more readable than syntax-level abstraction.
learningObjectives: Trace decorator application and invocation, including factories, stacked order, closures, and method binding.
Implement class-based and generator-based context managers with correct cleanup and exception behavior.
Evaluate wrappers and resource scopes for metadata, observability, retry, security, and failure-semantics risks.

deepSections.title: Decorator evaluation, closures, and stacked order
deepSections.body:
For `@decorator` followed by `def train(...):`, Python creates the function object, evaluates the decorator expression, calls the decorator with the function, and binds `train` to the returned object. A decorator factory such as `@retry(attempts=3)` is evaluated first; it returns the actual decorator. Configuration therefore belongs to one closure, the original function to another, and per-call arguments to the wrapper. Confusing these times can create shared mutable state or expensive work during module import.

A wrapper typically accepts `*args, **kwargs`, performs behavior, and calls the wrapped function. That broad signature is convenient at runtime but can obscure inspection and static tooling. `functools.wraps` copies identifying attributes and establishes `__wrapped__`, allowing introspection to reach the original callable. It does not prove semantic transparency: a wrapper can still change return types, exception behavior, synchronization, or timing. Preserve type information with `ParamSpec` and `TypeVar` when a public typed decorator matters.

Stacked decorators apply bottom-up: `@a` above `@b` produces `a(b(function))`. Calls then enter `a`, enter `b`, call the function, exit `b`, and exit `a`. Order changes behavior. Caching outside authorization can expose results across callers if cache keys omit identity; retries outside metrics can count one logical request while metrics inside retries count attempts. Write the intended order as an explicit composition during design and test observable outcomes.

deepSections.title: Methods, descriptors, and class decoration
deepSections.body:
Functions stored on a class participate in Python's descriptor protocol. Access through an instance creates a bound method that supplies the instance as the first argument. A decorator that returns a normal function preserves this common behavior; a callable wrapper object may need descriptor support to bind correctly. This is why a wrapper can work for a free function but fail as a method. Prefer function wrappers unless a class is justified, and test instance, class, and static methods separately.

`classmethod`, `staticmethod`, and `property` are themselves descriptor-producing transformations. Their order relative to custom decorators matters because one layer may receive a descriptor rather than a plain callable. Class decorators receive the completed class and return the binding replacement. They are useful for registration or dataclass-like transformation, but metaclasses or explicit registration may be clearer when inheritance behavior is central.

Closures retain referenced objects. A decorator-level dictionary used as a cache can keep arguments and results alive indefinitely. A lock captured once serializes every instance even if per-instance locking was intended. State may need bounded eviction, weak references, synchronization, or placement on an instance. Treat every stateful decorator as a small service: define keying, lifetime, concurrency, observability, and invalidation rather than hiding them behind `@cache` or a custom name.

deepSections.title: The context-manager protocol and exception flow
deepSections.body:
The `with expression as target` statement evaluates the expression, calls its `__enter__`, binds the returned value, executes the body, and then calls `__exit__`. On normal completion, the exit arguments describe no exception. On failure they contain the exception type, value, and traceback. If `__exit__` returns a truthy value, the exception is suppressed; otherwise it propagates after cleanup. Suppression should be narrow and documented because an accidental `return True` can hide data corruption or failed writes.

A class-based context manager makes state and protocol methods explicit. `contextlib.contextmanager` lets a generator express the same lifecycle: code before the single `yield` enters, the yielded value is bound, and `finally` code exits. The generator must yield exactly once. Catch only exceptions the manager is responsible for, and re-raise unexpected errors. `closing`, `suppress`, `nullcontext`, and redirection helpers cover common narrow patterns. `ExitStack` dynamically composes a variable number of managers and unwinds them in reverse acquisition order, which is safer than hand-built cleanup lists.

Asynchronous context managers use `__aenter__`, `__aexit__`, and `async with` when setup or teardown must await. A synchronous manager should not block an event loop with slow network cleanup. Context management gives deterministic lexical cleanup; it does not automatically bound how long a block holds a connection, file, GPU context, temporary environment mutation, or lock.

deepSections.title: Designing safe cross-cutting behavior
deepSections.body:
Use a decorator when behavior should consistently follow a callable wherever it is invoked and the transformation remains understandable. Use a context manager when ownership has a visible begin and end. Use an ordinary helper when explicit calls communicate the control flow better. Retries, transactions, and caching often deserve named policy objects because their semantics are richer than a thin wrapper.

Retries require an allowlist of transient failures, bounded attempts, backoff, jitter, time budgets, and idempotency. Timing requires a monotonic clock and must record exceptions as well as successes. Logging must redact secrets and avoid serializing full tensors or datasets. Authorization must run before cache lookup unless cache isolation is proven. A transaction manager must distinguish commit, rollback, cleanup failure, and nested transaction behavior. A temporary-configuration manager must restore the previous value even if setup partially fails.

Tests should inspect preserved name, documentation, signature, and `__wrapped__`; call with positional and keyword arguments; verify return and exception propagation; and exercise stacked order. For context managers, assert acquisition and release on success, body failure, and setup failure. Verify whether an intended exception is suppressed and that all other exceptions escape. Instrument wrappers so operators can distinguish original calls from attempts, cache hits, and cleanup failures.

lessons.math: If decorators a and b wrap f, `@a` above `@b` gives g = a(b(f)); invocation follows a_enter → b_enter → f → b_exit → a_exit. For a retry policy with at most k attempts, worst-case call count is k, so non-idempotent side effects can be multiplied by k unless an idempotency mechanism prevents duplication.

lessons.title: NumPy Vectorization & Broadcasting
lessons.interviewAnswer: Vectorization expresses operations over whole arrays so NumPy can execute tight compiled loops instead of one Python operation per element. Broadcasting compares shapes from the trailing dimensions; dimensions are compatible when equal or when one is 1, with missing leading dimensions treated as 1. It often avoids copying the smaller input, but the output or intermediates can still be large. Correct NumPy code reasons explicitly about shape, axis, dtype, and whether indexing returns a view or copy.
keyPoints: Shape is part of the type
Broadcast from trailing axes
Ufuncs run compiled element loops
Basic slicing usually views
Intermediates and dtype dominate failures
lessons.why: Array operations are the substrate of data preprocessing, scientific computing, and tensor frameworks. Shape bugs can silently normalize across the wrong axis, mix samples, or create a pairwise matrix instead of a feature-wise operation. Dtype bugs can overflow integers or lose precision. View/copy confusion can mutate upstream data or keep gigabytes alive. Performance advice that stops at 'avoid loops' can make matters worse by allocating an n-by-n intermediate. Interviews probe broadcasting because it reveals whether a candidate can reason dimensionally. Production code needs the same skill plus memory accounting, numerical validation, and a fallback when vectorization exceeds the machine's budget.
lessons.intuition: An ndarray is a typed block of values plus a shape and a stride recipe for locating each logical element. A universal function walks compatible arrays using those recipes. Broadcasting pretends a size-one dimension repeats so the loop can reuse values; it does not normally tile the input first. Imagine placing shape labels above every expression and aligning them from the right. If one aligned label is neither equal nor 1, the operation is invalid. If it is 1, that value is reused along the larger dimension.
lessons.deepDive: The full explanation is organized into the structured sections below.
lessons.workedExample: Standardize each feature of an n-by-d matrix with `(X - mean) / scale`, where both statistics have shape `(d,)` or `(1, d)`.
lessons.code:
import numpy as np
X=np.random.randn(100000,20)
mean=X.mean(axis=0); std=X.std(axis=0)
Z=(X-mean)/std

commonMistakes.mistake: Broadcasting duplicates the smaller array in memory before every operation.
commonMistakes.correction: Broadcasting normally reuses values through iteration/stride logic, but the result and intermediate expressions can still allocate large arrays.

commonMistakes.mistake: Every vectorized expression is faster and more memory efficient than a loop.
commonMistakes.correction: Large temporaries, poor locality, conversion, or an O(n²) output can dominate. A chunked loop around compiled kernels can be safer.

commonMistakes.mistake: Slicing and indexing either always copy or always view.
commonMistakes.correction: Basic slicing generally views; advanced integer/boolean indexing copies. Reshape and related operations depend on layout.

followUps.question: Why does `keepdims=True` help?
followUps.answer: It retains reduced axes with size one, preserving dimensional intent and making subsequent broadcasting align explicitly.

followUps.question: How can a tiny slice keep a huge allocation alive?
followUps.answer: A basic slice is a view whose base owns the buffer. Keeping the view keeps that base reachable; copy the small slice if independent lifetime is desired.

followUps.question: How do you catch semantically wrong but broadcast-compatible code?
followUps.answer: Name and assert dimensions, use non-square test shapes, preserve axes with `keepdims`, and verify invariants over the intended axes.

lessons.production: Validate shape, dtype, units, finiteness, and feature order at boundaries. Fit normalization only on training data, version the statistics, and reproduce them in serving. Estimate output and temporary bytes before pairwise operations, monitor peak resident memory, and chunk when necessary. Make mutation and ownership explicit, avoid depending on accidental contiguity, and benchmark representative arrays. Use stable numerical formulations and tolerance-based assertions rather than exact floating-point equality.
lessons.description: NumPy performance comes from representing homogeneous n-dimensional data in an `ndarray` and applying compiled array operations over that data. Vectorization moves element loops out of Python; broadcasting aligns compatible shapes without conceptually writing repeated values. Neither technique removes the need to reason about memory. An expression can allocate several full-size temporaries, a broadcast can create an enormous result, and a small slice can retain a large base array. This chapter develops a shape-first model covering dimensions, axes, strides, dtypes, universal functions, reduction, broadcasting, basic versus advanced indexing, and copies versus views. You will trace a standardization example, derive output shapes from the trailing-dimension rules, and verify memory sharing rather than guessing. The production goal is to write numerical code that is correct before it is clever: explicit about shapes, dtype precision, missing or invalid values, memory budget, and numerical checks. When vectorized code becomes opaque or produces a huge intermediate, chunking, a compiled loop, or a clearer algorithm can be the better engineering choice.
learningObjectives: Predict ndarray result shapes using axes, reductions, and the trailing-dimension broadcasting rules.
Distinguish views from copies using indexing category, strides, base ownership, and memory-sharing checks.
Design vectorized numerical work that controls dtype, temporaries, invalid values, and memory growth.

deepSections.title: Array model: shape, axes, dtype, and strides
deepSections.body:
An `ndarray` describes homogeneous elements with `shape`, `ndim`, `dtype`, and strides. Shape `(n, d)` might mean n observations and d features, but NumPy does not know those semantics. Axis numbers are positional: reducing axis 0 removes or retains the first dimension depending on `keepdims`; reducing axis 1 works across columns for each row in this convention. Always state what an axis means before writing the expression.

The dtype determines element representation and operation behavior. Fixed-width integer arithmetic can overflow. Integer division promotes according to NumPy's type rules; reductions may use a wider accumulator for some dtypes but this should not be guessed. Float32 halves element storage relative to float64 and is common in ML, yet it has less precision and range. Mixed dtypes invoke promotion rules that can change memory and results. Inspect result dtype in critical paths and choose accumulation precision deliberately.

Strides specify byte jumps along each axis. A transpose can often be a new array object with the same underlying buffer and different shape/strides. Such a non-contiguous view may be cheap to create but less friendly to a downstream library requiring contiguous storage. Contiguity, alignment, and memory order affect data movement; they do not change the mathematical shape. Optimize only after measuring the actual kernel and copy boundary.

deepSections.title: Universal functions, reductions, and vectorization
deepSections.body:
A universal function such as `np.add` or `np.exp` applies a compiled elementwise loop and supports broadcasting, dtype resolution, and optional output buffers. Vectorized expressions reduce Python interpreter overhead and can exploit optimized low-level loops. Reductions such as `sum`, `mean`, or `max` combine an axis and therefore change shape. `keepdims=True` retains reduced axes with size one, often making the next broadcast explicit and less error-prone.

Vectorization can allocate temporaries. `(x - mean) / std` may create a subtraction result and a division result; boolean masks and fancy indexing can allocate more. In-place operations or an `out` parameter can reduce allocations only when aliasing, dtype casting, and error behavior are safe. Mutating input to save memory is a semantic change, not a free optimization. Libraries such as numexpr, Numba, or compiled extensions can fuse or compile suitable work, but each adds constraints and should follow profiling.

Not all loops are bad. A Python loop around a large vectorized kernel can control peak memory. An algorithm with sequential dependence cannot be made elementwise by syntax. A clear loop compiled with an appropriate tool may outperform a maze of temporary arrays. Compare end-to-end time and peak memory on representative shapes, including data conversion, not a tiny isolated expression.

deepSections.title: Broadcasting rules and shape derivation
deepSections.body:
Compare operand shapes from the rightmost dimension moving left. Missing leading dimensions behave as size one. Each aligned pair is compatible if the sizes are equal or one is 1. The result size is the larger compatible size. For `X` with shape `(n, d)` and feature means `(d,)`, alignment treats the means as `(1, d)`, so subtraction produces `(n, d)`. A column vector `(n, 1)` and row vector `(1, d)` produce `(n, d)`.

Use explicit singleton dimensions to communicate intent: `x[:, None]` changes `(n,)` to `(n, 1)`. Pairwise differences `x[:, None] - x[None, :]` yield `(n, n)`. This is mathematically correct and can be catastrophically large. A conceptual broadcast view may use stride zero for a repeated dimension, but the elementwise operation's output usually requires storage. Estimate output bytes as the product of result dimensions times item size before constructing pairwise or multi-axis expressions.

Broadcasting errors are useful because incompatible shapes stop execution. More dangerous are compatible but semantically wrong shapes, such as subtracting an `(n,)` vector from an `(n, d)` matrix when n happens to equal d. Name dimensions, assert shapes at boundaries, use `keepdims`, and test non-square examples so accidental alignment cannot hide.

deepSections.title: Views, copies, and indexing semantics
deepSections.body:
Assignment creates another name for the same array object. Basic slicing normally creates a new array object that views the same data, so mutation can affect the original. Advanced indexing with integer or boolean arrays creates a copy. Reshape returns a view when compatible with the memory layout but may copy when necessary. Transpose usually returns a view with permuted strides. The exact base chain can be indirect, so use `np.shares_memory` for a definite sharing check and inspect ownership when debugging.

A view can retain its base buffer. Keeping 100 elements sliced from a massive temporary can keep the massive allocation alive; copying the small result can lower long-term memory. Conversely, an unintended advanced-index copy in a hot path can double peak memory. Write ownership boundaries deliberately: copy when an independent artifact is required, keep a view when shared mutation and lifetime are controlled, and mark arrays read-only when that expresses the contract.

Boolean masks introduce another alignment surface. The mask shape must correspond to indexed axes, and selecting values often flattens or changes shape. Chained indexing can operate on a temporary copy. Prefer one explicit indexing operation, confirm the result shape, and test whether writes are intended to modify the source. These practices matter when feature matrices are shared across training, evaluation, and cached preprocessing.

lessons.math: For operands with aligned dimensions a_i and b_i, broadcasting is valid when a_i = b_i, a_i = 1, or b_i = 1; the result dimension is max(a_i, b_i). An output with shape (s_1, ..., s_k) and dtype item size q requires approximately q·∏s_i bytes, excluding temporaries and allocator overhead.

lab.goal: Derive broadcast shapes, standardize safely, and verify numerical invariants and memory sharing.
lab.useIt:
import numpy as np
X = np.array([[1., 10.], [3., 10.], [5., 10.]])
mean = X.mean(axis=0, keepdims=True)
scale = X.std(axis=0, keepdims=True)
safe_scale = np.where(scale == 0, 1.0, scale)
Z = (X - mean) / safe_scale
lab.verifyIt:
assert broadcast_shape((3, 1, 5), (4, 5)) == (3, 4, 5)
assert Z.shape == X.shape
assert np.isfinite(Z).all()
assert np.allclose(Z[:, 0].mean(), 0.0)
assert np.allclose(Z[:, 0].std(), 1.0)
assert np.allclose(Z[:, 1], 0.0)
view = X[:, :1]
copy = X[:, [0]]
assert np.shares_memory(X, view)
assert not np.shares_memory(X, copy)

lessons.title: pandas: Merge, GroupBy, Missing Data
lessons.interviewAnswer: For pandas work, first define each table's grain and key cardinality. Use `merge` for relational joins and validate the intended one-to-one or many-to-one relationship; use groupby aggregation when rows collapse and transform when results must align with original rows. Treat missing values according to their meaning, not with a universal fill. Use explicit `.loc` assignment under current Copy-on-Write semantics, and test row counts, uniqueness, dtypes, match rates, and edge cases.
keyPoints: Grain before operations
Join cardinality is a contract
Aggregate and transform differ
Missingness has meaning
Validate shape, keys, and dtypes
lessons.why: Most tabular model failures begin before training: duplicated joins overweight entities, inconsistent categories break serving, timestamps leak the future, or silent dtype changes alter comparisons. pandas is permissive because exploratory work benefits from flexibility; a production pipeline must supply the missing constraints. Interviews use merge and groupby questions to test relational reasoning, not memory of method names. The high-value answer predicts how many rows can appear, which keys may be unmatched, how nulls propagate, and how the result will be verified. Current Copy-on-Write behavior also makes old advice about ambiguous chained assignment obsolete; explicit single-operation assignment is the durable habit.
lessons.intuition: Treat every DataFrame as a relation with a sentence describing one row. A customer table says one row per customer; an orders table says one row per order. A join combines those sentences and its output grain follows the key relationship. Groupby partitions rows by a key, then aggregation produces one row per group while transformation broadcasts a group result back to member rows. A missing value is a state in the data-generating process, not an instruction to call `fillna(0)`.
lessons.deepDive: The full explanation is organized into the structured sections below.
lessons.workedExample: Aggregate orders to customer grain, validate the customer dimension as unique, then left-join and fill only the structural no-order aggregates.
lessons.code:
agg=(orders.groupby('customer_id',as_index=False)
          .agg(total_spend=('amount','sum'),
               n_orders=('order_id','nunique')))
features=customers.merge(agg,on='customer_id',how='left')

commonMistakes.mistake: A left join always preserves the number of left rows.
commonMistakes.correction: It preserves left records but duplicate matches on the right can multiply each record. Enforce the intended cardinality with `validate`.

commonMistakes.mistake: `groupby().count()` counts group rows.
commonMistakes.correction: `count` counts non-missing values per selected column; `size` counts rows, and `nunique` counts distinct non-missing values by default.

commonMistakes.mistake: Fill every missing numeric value with zero.
commonMistakes.correction: Zero is valid only when the missing mechanism means measured absence. Unknown, not applicable, censored, and structurally unmatched states need distinct policies.

followUps.question: What is the difference between groupby aggregate and transform?
followUps.answer: Aggregation reduces groups to summaries; transform returns values aligned with the original rows, usually one result per input row.

followUps.question: How do you diagnose unexpected rows after a merge?
followUps.answer: Inspect key multiplicities on both sides, use `validate` and `indicator`, compare row and unique-key counts, and examine high-multiplicity keys before changing data.

followUps.question: What changed with Copy-on-Write?
followUps.answer: Derived objects behave independently for mutation while pandas may share storage internally until write; chained assignment cannot update the original and explicit `.loc` assignment is required.

lessons.production: Version schemas and transformation code together. Record input/output rows, unique keys, duplicate rates, merge match categories, null rates, invalid parses, reconciliation totals, and memory. Fit temporal and statistical transforms only on allowed training history. Fail closed on violated key contracts instead of dropping duplicates. Make jobs idempotent, partition outputs deterministically, preserve lineage, and provide rollback to the previous data version. Move to SQL, DuckDB, Spark, or another engine when data size, concurrency, or governance exceeds an in-memory process.
lessons.description: pandas makes labeled tabular transformations concise, but correctness depends on contracts that the syntax does not infer for you. A merge can multiply rows because keys are duplicated. A groupby can drop missing keys or return a differently indexed result. A fill operation can change dtype, encode an invalid statistical assumption, or leak future information. This chapter treats a DataFrame transformation as a relational and statistical program: define row grain, key cardinality, schema, missingness policy, and expected output before calling an API. It covers label versus position indexing, Copy-on-Write mutation semantics in current pandas, database-style joins, groupby aggregation and transformation, nullable dtypes, and validation patterns. The worked example builds customer features from orders while preserving customers with no orders and detecting duplicate dimension keys. You will learn to measure row counts and match rates, distinguish structural absence from unknown measurement, test edge cases, and recognize when pandas is no longer the right execution engine. The goal is a reproducible data contract, not a clever chain of method calls.
learningObjectives: Specify DataFrame row grain, keys, dtypes, and missing-value semantics before a transformation.
Predict merge cardinality and groupby result shape, then enforce those expectations with validation.
Write mutation-safe pandas code and test transformations for duplicates, nulls, schema drift, and leakage.

deepSections.title: Schema, indexing, and mutation
deepSections.body:
A DataFrame has labeled axes and columns with dtypes. The index can be meaningful, but many pipelines are clearer with domain keys as ordinary columns and a simple index. `.loc` selects by labels and boolean conditions; `.iloc` selects by integer position. Label slices can include the stop label, unlike ordinary Python positional slicing. Never assume current row order is a business key. Sort explicitly when order matters and assert uniqueness when a label is intended to identify one record.

Schema includes more than names: dtype, nullability, allowed categories, timezone, units, and row grain. Object dtype can hide mixed Python values. Nullable integer, boolean, and string dtypes preserve missingness without forcing every column into float or generic object representation. Conversion should be deliberate and invalid parsing should produce a measured error or explicit missing value according to policy.

Copy-on-Write is the current pandas 3.x model: derived objects behave as copies from the user's perspective, while data may be shared internally until a write. Chained assignment cannot reliably update the original and should be replaced by one `.loc[row_mask, column] = value` operation. This is clearer across versions and makes the mutation target visible. Avoid `inplace=True` as a performance belief; it does not guarantee zero allocation or clearer ownership.

deepSections.title: Merges, cardinality, and row multiplication
deepSections.body:
A merge matches key values using inner, left, right, or outer semantics. The crucial property is cardinality. If key k appears a_k times on the left and b_k times on the right, an inner match contributes a_k times b_k rows for that key. Duplicate keys therefore multiply records. This can be correct for a many-to-many relationship but is disastrous when a dimension table was expected to have one row per entity.

Use `validate='one_to_one'`, `'one_to_many'`, or `'many_to_one'` to make the relationship executable. Use `indicator=True` during validation to measure left-only, right-only, and matched records. Normalize key dtype and representation before joining; string `'001'`, integer 1, case differences, whitespace, and timezone mismatches are domain problems rather than merge tricks. Decide how null keys behave and whether they are legal.

Choose output columns and suffix policy explicitly. Joining entire wide tables can duplicate unused data and inflate memory. Measure input/output row counts, unique keys, and match rates. A left join used for feature enrichment should usually preserve the left row count under a many-to-one contract. If it does not, stop rather than deduplicating afterward: post-join deduplication hides which record was chosen and may corrupt measures.

deepSections.title: GroupBy: aggregation, transformation, filtration, and application
deepSections.body:
GroupBy follows split-apply-combine, but the kind of apply determines output shape. Aggregation reduces each group to scalar or summary rows. Transformation returns a result aligned to the original group rows, enabling within-group centering or percentage-of-total features. Filtration retains or removes whole groups according to a predicate. General `apply` offers flexibility but can be slower and can produce difficult index behavior; prefer named aggregations, vectorized transforms, and built-in operations when they express the task.

Grouping keys become index levels by default in many aggregations; `as_index=False` can keep them as columns. `sort`, `observed`, and `dropna` affect ordering, categorical combinations, and missing-key groups. Do not rely on defaults when these semantics matter. A categorical groupby may represent unobserved categories depending on configuration. A missing group key may be excluded unless requested.

Named aggregation makes output schema explicit: `total=('amount','sum')`. Distinguish row count, non-null count, and distinct count: `size`, `count`, and `nunique` answer different questions. Null amounts may be skipped by a sum, and all-null groups need a business rule. Test a tiny table where these counts differ so an accidental substitution cannot pass.

deepSections.title: Missing data, temporal correctness, and validation
deepSections.body:
pandas represents missingness through sentinels such as `NaN`, `NaT`, and `pd.NA`, with behavior influenced by dtype. Use `isna` rather than equality comparisons. Arithmetic and reductions may propagate or skip missing values according to operation parameters. A fill value is an assumption: zero may mean measured absence, category 'unknown' may combine distinct mechanisms, and mean imputation changes variance and relationships. Preserve an indicator when missingness itself may carry information, while checking whether that signal will exist at serving time.

Dropping missing rows changes the population. Forward filling assumes ordering and persistence; using it across entity boundaries or after random sorting is wrong. Time-series interpolation and feature construction must use only information available at the prediction timestamp. Fit imputation values on training data and apply them to validation and production. Record null rates by source and important slice so upstream changes are visible.

Validate transformations with assertions or a schema tool: required columns, dtypes, uniqueness, ranges, row-count relationships, match rate, null budget, and time boundaries. Compare aggregates before and after joins when amounts should be conserved. Keep representative duplicate, unmatched, all-null, empty, and timezone cases in tests. For large data, inspect memory usage, select columns early, use appropriate dtypes, process partitions, or move to a query engine when the workload no longer fits one process.

lessons.math: For join key k with multiplicities a_k and b_k, an inner join emits Σ_k a_k b_k matched rows. A many-to-one enrichment requires b_k ≤ 1 and should preserve the left row count for a left join. Group aggregation emits at most one summary row per observed group, while transform preserves the original row alignment.

workedExamples.title: Build customer spend features with explicit join and missingness policy
workedExamples.setup: Customers are one row per customer. Orders are one row per order; some customers have none, some order amounts are invalid, and duplicate customer rows are an upstream error.
workedExamples.walkthrough: Validate customer IDs as unique and order IDs according to retry policy. Parse amounts, quarantine invalid records, aggregate valid orders by customer with named totals and distinct counts, then left-merge into customers with `validate='one_to_one'` because both sides are now customer grain and `indicator=True` for coverage. A missing aggregate for a left-only customer structurally means no matched order and may become zero; a missing amount inside a matched order is a measurement-quality problem and must not be silently treated as zero. Assert left row preservation, uniqueness, nonnegative counts, and reconciliation of aggregate totals.
workedExamples.conclusion: Aggregation before joining makes the output grain explicit, and separate missingness policies prevent 'no order' from being confused with 'unknown amount'.

exercises.prompt: A key occurs twice on the left and three times on the right. How many matched rows does that key create?
exercises.solution: Six rows: each of the two left rows pairs with each of the three right rows.

exercises.prompt: Choose aggregate or transform for subtracting each department's mean salary from every employee salary.
exercises.solution: Use transform for the group mean because the mean must align back to every original employee row.

exercises.prompt: A feature job's row count grows after enriching events with account attributes. What do you inspect first?
exercises.solution: Check duplicate account keys and enforce a many-to-one merge. Do not deduplicate the expanded output because that hides the incorrect dimension grain.

lab.goal: Build a contract-checked customer feature table and verify key uniqueness, row preservation, reconciliation, and missingness policy.
lab.useIt:
import pandas as pd
customers = pd.DataFrame({'customer_id': [1, 2, 3]})
orders = pd.DataFrame({'order_id': [10, 11, 12], 'customer_id': [1, 1, 2], 'amount': [5., 7., 3.]})
agg = orders.groupby('customer_id', as_index=False).agg(total_spend=('amount', 'sum'), n_orders=('order_id', 'nunique'))
features = customers.merge(agg, on='customer_id', how='left', validate='one_to_one', indicator=True)
features[['total_spend', 'n_orders']] = features[['total_spend', 'n_orders']].fillna(0)

assert customers['customer_id'].is_unique

lessons.title: Testing ML / Data Code
lessons.interviewAnswer: Test ML and data systems in layers: unit-test deterministic transforms and edge cases; validate schemas and invariants on representative data; test numerical properties with justified tolerances; regression-test model outputs or metrics on frozen slices; and integration-test serialization, feature parity, and serving paths. Control randomness and external dependencies, but do not replace production monitoring. A good test names the risk it catches and fails with enough evidence to diagnose it.
keyPoints: Test risks, not implementation trivia
Tiny adversarial fixtures
Approximate numerical invariants
Separate code, data, and model checks
Monitoring covers what tests cannot
lessons.why: Data code often runs successfully while producing incorrect data. Models can satisfy shape checks while degrading a minority slice. Serialization or preprocessing differences can make offline evaluation irrelevant to serving. A suite therefore needs semantic assertions: row and key contracts, absence of leakage, finiteness, monotonicity, invariance, and metric thresholds with uncertainty. Interviews probe testing because production ML combines conventional software failure with data drift and statistical variation. A precise answer distinguishes deterministic tests from noisy evaluation and explains why tests before deployment and monitoring after deployment are complementary controls.
lessons.intuition: A test is a small experiment against a claim. Unit tests isolate a deterministic claim; integration tests check contracts between parts; model evaluations estimate behavior over a dataset; monitoring observes the real environment. Use the narrowest experiment that can falsify the risk. A tiny table containing a duplicate key, null, unseen category, boundary timestamp, and constant column often teaches more than a large random fixture whose failure is hard to understand.
lessons.deepDive: The full explanation is organized into the structured sections below.
lessons.workedExample: Test a fitted column standardizer for shape, finite output, constant columns, training-only statistics, and a serialization round-trip.

commonMistakes.mistake: High line coverage means the ML system is well tested.
commonMistakes.correction: Coverage only reports execution. It does not prove assertions cover leakage, data contracts, numerical properties, model slices, or integration boundaries.

commonMistakes.mistake: Set one global seed and every result becomes deterministic.
commonMistakes.correction: Seeds control specific random streams; parallel hardware, libraries, data order, and external services can remain nondeterministic.

commonMistakes.mistake: Mock every dependency in unit tests and integration is covered.
commonMistakes.correction: Mocks can drift from real contracts. Use local fakes for speed plus contract and integration tests against actual boundaries.

followUps.question: How do you test a model when exact predictions legitimately change?
followUps.answer: Test stable invariants and signatures, then compare approved metrics and slices on versioned data with justified tolerances or uncertainty rather than exact arrays everywhere.

followUps.question: Where should monkeypatch be applied?
followUps.answer: Patch the symbol where the code under test looks it up. Prefer explicit dependency injection when the dependency is part of the design.

followUps.question: What is a metamorphic test?
followUps.answer: It checks a known relationship between transformed inputs and outputs when an exact expected result is hard to specify, such as permutation invariance or monotonicity.

lessons.production: Gate releases with fast deterministic tests, schema and lineage checks, artifact compatibility, frozen-slice evaluation, and limited end-to-end paths. Separate slow/GPU suites while ensuring they run before release. Store failure seeds and version every input artifact. After deployment, use shadow or canary comparisons, monitor data and model slices, enforce latency/error budgets, and rehearse rollback. Convert incidents into regression tests and operational monitors with clear owners.
lessons.description: Testing data and machine-learning software requires more than checking a few expected numbers. A useful suite separates deterministic transformation behavior, data contracts, numerical properties, model behavior, component integration, and end-to-end system paths. It also controls nondeterminism without pretending stochastic systems are bit-for-bit stable. This chapter develops a risk-based test strategy using plain assertions and pytest concepts: arrange-act-assert, fixtures with scoped cleanup, parametrization, temporary resources, monkeypatching at the lookup site, approximate comparisons, property and metamorphic checks, golden artifacts, and model regression tests. You will learn why test data should be tiny but adversarial, how to avoid leakage between tests, how to choose tolerances, and how to keep slow or flaky external dependencies out of unit tests. The worked example tests a normalization transform against shape, finiteness, constant-column, and training-statistic invariants. The production perspective connects local tests to schema validation, shadow evaluation, canaries, monitoring, rollback, and incident reproduction. The aim is evidence about failure risk, not a high coverage percentage detached from behavior.
learningObjectives: Map risks in data, numerical, model, and system behavior to the cheapest reliable test layer.
Use fixtures, parametrization, dependency seams, approximate assertions, and metamorphic properties without shared-state leakage.
Design regression and integration checks that remain deterministic, interpretable, and useful during deployment and rollback.

deepSections.title: A risk-based test portfolio
deepSections.body:
Unit tests cover pure parsing, feature calculations, shape transformations, loss helpers, and decision rules. They should be fast, deterministic, and local. Contract tests validate interfaces: schema, dtype, units, nullability, ordering, model signature, and serialized format. Integration tests exercise real boundaries such as database adapters, object storage, a feature service, or model loading. A small number of end-to-end tests verify the critical path in an environment close to production.

Data validation is not simply another unit assertion. It evaluates a dataset or batch against constraints and distribution expectations. Model regression tests use a frozen dataset and artifact to detect unintended changes in predictions, metrics, calibration, latency, or size. They should not freeze improvement: thresholds and reviewed golden changes distinguish intended updates from accidents. Slice tests expose failures hidden by an aggregate metric.

Prioritize by impact, likelihood, and detectability. Test leakage, label alignment, join cardinality, preprocessing parity, and rollback before cosmetic formatting. Coverage can reveal unexecuted code but does not prove behavioral adequacy. Mutation testing or deliberate fault injection can show whether assertions actually notice a broken branch. Every production incident should yield the cheapest reproducible test or monitor that would have detected it.

deepSections.title: Fixtures, parametrization, and dependency control
deepSections.body:
pytest discovers test functions and rewrites plain `assert` statements to provide useful failure detail. Parametrization runs one behavior across explicit cases, making boundaries visible without copy-paste. Parameters are passed as-is, so mutable values can leak changes between cases; create fresh objects when mutation is part of the test. Give cases readable IDs so failures identify the scenario.

Fixtures provide explicit setup dependencies and can yield a value, then perform teardown. Scope controls lifetime: function scope maximizes isolation; broader scopes can speed expensive stable setup but increase coupling and contamination risk. Prefer small composable fixtures over a global environment. Temporary-path fixtures avoid collisions, and cleanup must run on failures. Use factories when each test needs multiple independently configured objects.

Monkeypatch the name looked up by the code under test, not the function's original definition in an unrelated module. Better still, inject clocks, random generators, clients, and repositories through explicit seams. Fake deterministic boundaries locally; keep separate contract/integration tests against real services. An over-mocked test can pass while components cannot work together. Assert observable results and important interactions, not every internal call sequence, so refactoring does not create noise.

deepSections.title: Numerical, stochastic, and model behavior tests
deepSections.body:
Floating-point results should usually be compared with absolute and relative tolerances tied to scale, dtype, and algorithm, not an arbitrary large epsilon. Assert shape, dtype, finiteness, and domain bounds before value closeness. Test constant inputs, empty permitted inputs, large magnitude, missing values, and near-boundary decisions. Numerical algorithms often have properties stronger than fixtures: normalized probabilities sum to one, a distance is nonnegative and symmetric, a permutation-equivariant transform changes correspondingly, or increasing a threshold cannot increase the accepted set.

Property-based tests generate inputs across a domain; metamorphic tests verify relationships when an exact oracle is difficult. They supplement carefully selected examples. Fix a random seed for reproducibility, pass an explicit generator, and store failure seeds. A fixed seed does not make GPU kernels, distributed reductions, or external models universally deterministic. Define acceptable variability and separate a deterministic smoke check from a statistical evaluation repeated over enough examples or seeds.

Model tests can verify signature, serialization round-trip, preprocessing parity, prediction range, known examples, slice metrics, and comparison with an approved baseline. A single metric threshold may be noisy or encourage overfitting to the test set. Record dataset version, confidence or uncertainty, and multiple safety-critical metrics. Never use the test suite's frozen evaluation set to repeatedly tune the model without accounting for adaptive overfitting.

deepSections.title: Maintaining tests across the ML lifecycle
deepSections.body:
A test should be independent, deterministic within its stated contract, and diagnostic. Name the behavior and scenario. Arrange only the data needed, perform one meaningful action, and assert invariants with messages or rich comparisons. Avoid time sleeps, live network calls, global random state, and dependence on test order. Quarantine is not a permanent solution for flakiness; classify whether the cause is a race, nondeterminism, environment, timeout, or an invalid assertion and fix the source.

Golden files are useful for complex structured outputs when reviewed diffs are meaningful. Normalize volatile IDs and timestamps and avoid blindly accepting snapshots. Large model artifacts do not belong in every unit test; use a tiny deterministic substitute plus separate artifact compatibility tests. Mark slow, GPU, and external integration suites and run them at an appropriate CI stage. Cache dependencies without sharing mutable outputs.

Deployment adds checks tests cannot simulate completely: shadow comparisons, canary metrics, feature distribution and missingness monitoring, latency and error budgets, human review, and rollback drills. Link a release to code, data, feature, configuration, and model versions so a regression is reproducible. Alerts require ownership and playbooks. Testing reduces known risk; monitoring detects environmental change and unknown failure modes.

lessons.math: For floating results x and y, a common closeness rule is |x-y| ≤ atol + rtol·|y|, with tolerances justified by dtype and scale. For a metric estimate p over n independent binary outcomes, sampling uncertainty is on the order of sqrt(p(1-p)/n); therefore tiny evaluation sets cannot support narrow regression thresholds.

workedExamples.title: Verify a normalization component beyond one expected array
workedExamples.setup: A transformer fits per-feature mean and scale on training rows, maps constant columns safely, then is serialized for serving.
workedExamples.walkthrough: Use a tiny non-square matrix with one varying and one constant column. Assert fitted statistic shapes, unchanged sample/feature shape, finite output, zero mean and unit standard deviation only for the varying training feature, and zeros for the centered constant feature. Transform a validation row using stored training statistics and assert fit state does not change. Parametrize float32 and float64 with appropriate tolerances. Round-trip the artifact and compare outputs. Add invalid-shape and non-finite-policy cases.
workedExamples.conclusion: The suite checks mathematical properties, state ownership, leakage prevention, dtype behavior, error paths, and serving compatibility rather than one happy-path snapshot.

exercises.prompt: Why should floating-point tests use both relative and absolute tolerances?
exercises.solution: Relative tolerance scales with magnitude, while absolute tolerance handles expected values near zero where a purely relative bound becomes ineffective.

exercises.prompt: Design three cases for a many-to-one feature join.
exercises.solution: Include a normal match, an unmatched left record with explicit missing policy, and a duplicated right key that must fail cardinality validation.

exercises.prompt: A unit test patches `requests.get`, but the module imported `get` directly and still calls the network. Why?
exercises.solution: The module looks up its own imported name. Patch that lookup site or inject a client into the function.

Provides production-oriented context for model evaluation, deployment validation, monitoring, and iteration.

import numpy as np
