lessons.description: Mean squared error and mean absolute error summarize regression residuals using different cost geometries. This chapter derives MSE, RMSE and MAE, proves that squared loss targets a conditional mean while absolute loss targets a conditional median, and explains convexity, gradients, subgradients, outlier influence and units. It covers weighted and grouped aggregation, multioutput targets, log-scale evaluation, inverse transforms, missing targets, heteroskedasticity, tail metrics, confidence intervals, baselines and asymmetric alternatives such as pinball loss. Worked examples show one outlier reversing model preference and explain why back-transforming a log forecast requires care. The lab implements weighted MSE, RMSE and MAE, compares with scikit-learn, verifies inequalities and demonstrates the mean-versus-median optimum. Production guidance fixes the evaluation contract, monitors residual slices and target delay, and prevents metric-definition drift. The goal is to choose an error measure that represents the actual prediction estimand and cost rather than declaring one metric universally robust. It also explains how paired comparisons keep competing models on the same evidence.
learningObjectives: Compute and interpret weighted MSE, RMSE and MAE on a declared target scale.
Derive their conditional mean and median population optima.
Diagnose outlier, grouping, transform and aggregation effects on model rankings.
Design a regression scorecard with baselines, uncertainty, tails and operational slices.

deepSections.title: Loss functions select different point summaries
deepSections.body: For one feature profile x, a point predictor chooses a single number for a distribution of possible Y. Expected squared loss has derivative 2(a-E[Y|x]), so the conditional mean is optimal when the expectation exists. Absolute loss has a subgradient based on probability mass below and above a, making a conditional median optimal. These targets differ under skew. Training a flexible model on MSE therefore estimates a mean-like function; training on MAE estimates a median-like function. RMSE is the square root of an aggregate MSE and does not create a new per-observation objective. If the action requires a high service quantile, neither mean nor median is enough; pinball loss targets a conditional quantile. If overprediction and underprediction costs differ, use an asymmetric decision loss and report each side separately.

deepSections.title: Squaring changes influence and units
deepSections.body: The derivative of squared loss grows with residual magnitude, so large misses dominate optimization and evaluation. Absolute loss has constant-magnitude subgradients away from zero, reducing but not eliminating outlier influence. A valid rare catastrophe should not be dismissed as an outlier when its cost is important; a corrupted label should be repaired through data lineage rather than hidden by MAE. MSE is in squared target units and harder to communicate; RMSE restores units but remains sensitive to large errors. MSE and RMSE preserve model ordering only when computed on exactly the same weighted evaluation set. Normalized metrics can aid cross-series comparison but introduce denominators and failure modes. Always report the target scale, any clipping or transform, and whether errors were aggregated before or after inverse transformation.

deepSections.title: The averaging unit defines the population
deepSections.body: A row-weighted average estimates performance over rows. If one customer has hundreds of events and another has one, it estimates an event-weighted rather than customer-weighted outcome. Choose weights from the deployment decision and sampling design, then divide by their sum. For time series, aggregate over horizon, series and time deliberately; macro and volume-weighted results answer different questions. Multioutput regression similarly needs target-specific units or weights. Missing labels should not be silently treated as zero; define censoring and target-availability rules. Compute uncertainty over independent entities or time blocks, not naive rows. A paired bootstrap or fold comparison preserves that models are evaluated on the same units. Report confidence intervals and the distribution of paired error differences, not only separate standard errors.

deepSections.title: One mean cannot describe an error distribution
deepSections.body: Compare against a constant mean or median, seasonal naive forecast and current production system. Plot residual sign, magnitude and quantiles against prediction, target, time and important slices. MSE can improve while 95th-percentile absolute error worsens; MAE can improve while rare catastrophic misses grow. Decompose squared error by bias and spread descriptively and examine calibration of conditional means or quantiles when relevant. R-squared and percentage metrics answer other questions and can disagree. Freeze the scorecard before model selection to avoid metric shopping. If many slices are inspected, distinguish exploratory findings from confirmatory thresholds and consider multiplicity. Preserve individual residuals or sufficient aggregates with privacy controls so incidents can be traced without retaining unnecessary sensitive outcomes.

deepSections.title: Metric definitions are versioned production code
deepSections.body: Version target query and cutoff, inclusion criteria, prediction horizon, units, inverse transform, weights, clipping, missing-label policy, aggregation and baseline. Unit-test hand examples and invariants such as nonnegativity, RMSE squared equals MSE and exact predictions score zero. Monitor label coverage and delay before interpreting metric movement. Report rolling MSE, MAE, tail absolute error, signed bias, subgroup results and decision cost with independent-unit uncertainty. A target-definition or weight change creates a new metric series and should not be spliced silently. Backfill late labels by prediction cohort. Gate promotion on prespecified thresholds and retain the prior model and score report for rollback. Avoid optimizing a proxy indefinitely after business cost or population changes.

workedExamples.title: One outlier reverses preference
workedExamples.body: Model A residuals are [0,0,0,8], giving MAE 2 and MSE 16. Model B residuals are [3,3,3,3], giving MAE 3 and MSE 9. MAE prefers A because most predictions are exact; MSE prefers B because it avoids the large miss. The decision depends on whether that eight-unit miss carries disproportionate cost.

workedExamples.title: Log-scale accuracy is not original-scale accuracy
workedExamples.body: A model predicts log revenue and achieves low MSE there. Exponentiating the conditional log mean estimates a median-like original-scale quantity under lognormal noise, not the original conditional mean. Evaluate predictions after the intended back-transform and, if estimating a mean, account for the residual distribution rather than applying exp mechanically.

Why can MAE have many minimizing constants?
exercises.solution: For an even sample, any value between the two middle order statistics can be a median and minimize total absolute deviation.

exercises.prompt: How should repeated patient visits be aggregated?
exercises.solution: If the target claim is patient-level performance, compute patient-level summaries or weights and uncertainty by patient rather than treating visits as independent equal units.

lessons.title: Precision, Recall & F1
lessons.interviewAnswer: Classification metrics start from the decision and the evaluation population. Accuracy is the fraction correct, but it hides which class is harmed and can look excellent under imbalance. A confusion matrix separates false positives and false negatives. Precision asks, among predicted positives, how many were positive; recall or sensitivity asks, among actual positives, how many were found; specificity measures rejection of negatives. F-beta combines precision and recall with a declared trade-off, while balanced accuracy and macro averaging prevent large classes from dominating. For probabilistic models I also evaluate log loss, Brier score and calibration because threshold metrics discard probability quality. I freeze label semantics, positive class, threshold, averaging rule, sample unit and abstention policy, then report uncertainty and operational slices. No single classification metric is universally sufficient.
keyPoints: The confusion matrix is the accounting identity behind thresholded classification metrics.
Precision depends on prevalence as well as model behavior; recall and specificity condition on actual class.
Micro, macro, weighted and per-class averages answer different population questions.
Threshold metrics evaluate a decision rule; proper probability scores evaluate the forecast before thresholding.
Undefined denominators, abstentions, repeated entities and delayed labels require explicit policies.
lessons.why: A classifier rarely makes a cost-free symmetric decision. Fraud review has limited capacity, medical screening values missed disease differently from unnecessary follow-up, and content moderation may allow abstention. Accuracy compresses all of those consequences into one count. Even precision and recall are not intrinsic constants: precision changes when deployment prevalence changes, and both depend on the threshold and population. Multiclass averaging can quietly move the weight from examples to classes. Probability quality matters when scores drive ranking, pricing or later decisions. A defensible evaluation therefore begins with the action, constructs a complete confusion matrix, preserves per-class and per-slice evidence, and adds calibrated probability metrics and decision cost where appropriate.
lessons.intuition: Imagine 1,000 cases with ten positives. Predicting every case negative is 99% accurate and operationally useless if finding positives is the purpose. The confusion matrix exposes the zero true positives. Precision looks from the alert queue inward; recall looks from all positives outward. Changing the threshold changes both queues. A metric is a particular view of this flow, so choose the view that matches who acts and who bears each error.
lessons.deepDive: Rigorous classification evaluation links confusion counts, conditioning direction, averaging, probability quality and downstream utility. It treats the label and unit of analysis as data contracts, distinguishes threshold selection from final estimation, and reports uncertainty over independent entities. Multiclass, multilabel and selective systems require additional bookkeeping rather than automatic reuse of a binary headline score.
lessons.math: For positive label 1, precision=TP/(TP+FP), recall=TP/(TP+FN), specificity=TN/(TN+FP), accuracy=(TP+TN)/N, and F_beta=(1+beta^2)PR/(beta^2 P+R). Balanced accuracy is the unweighted mean of class recalls in binary classification. Micro averaging pools confusion counts before division; macro averaging computes each class metric then averages. Log loss is -N^-1 sum_i [y_i log p_i+(1-y_i)log(1-p_i)], and Brier loss is N^-1 sum_i(p_i-y_i)^2. Confidence intervals must reflect the independent sampling unit.
lessons.code:
from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix,accuracy_score,precision_score,recall_score,f1_score
cm=confusion_matrix(y,pred,labels=[0,1]); sk=(accuracy_score(y,pred),precision_score(y,pred),recall_score(y,pred),f1_score(y,pred))

commonMistakes.misconception: High accuracy proves a useful classifier.
commonMistakes.correction: Accuracy can be dominated by a common class. Inspect confusion counts, class-specific metrics and decision utility.

commonMistakes.misconception: Precision is a fixed property of the model.
commonMistakes.correction: It changes with threshold, prevalence and population composition.

commonMistakes.misconception: Macro and micro F1 are interchangeable summaries.
commonMistakes.correction: Macro weights classes equally; micro pools decisions and gives common classes more influence.

commonMistakes.misconception: A good F1 score means probabilities are trustworthy.
commonMistakes.correction: F1 evaluates one threshold and says nothing directly about calibration or proper probability quality.

followUps.question: When is balanced accuracy useful?
followUps.answer: When class frequencies are unequal and equal class recall is the intended weighting; still report each class recall and support.

followUps.question: How do you handle precision when there are no predicted positives?
followUps.answer: Treat it as undefined, expose the zero denominator and counts, and choose an explicit reporting policy rather than silently interpreting zero as evidence.

followUps.question: Why can micro F1 equal accuracy?
followUps.answer: In single-label multiclass classification every error contributes one false positive and one false negative, so pooled micro precision and recall reduce to the fraction correct.

lessons.production: Version labels, eligibility, prediction horizon, positive class, sample unit, threshold, weights, averaging and abstention. Unit-test confusion counts, swapped labels and zero denominators. Report counts and support with accuracy, per-class recall and precision, chosen aggregates, probability scores, calibration, operational cost and uncertainty over independent entities. Track prevalence and score drift because predictive values can change without model-code changes. Backfill by prediction cohort as delayed outcomes arrive. Select thresholds away from the final test set, gate releases on prespecified critical slices and capacity constraints, and retain the previous policy and model for rollback.
lessons.workedExample: Among 1,000 transactions, ten are fraudulent. Predicting all as legitimate yields TN=990, FN=10, TP=FP=0 and accuracy 99%. Recall is 0, and precision is undefined because no alerts exist. The counts reveal that the system performs no detection work.

lab.goal: Implement confusion counts and core binary metrics, compare them with scikit-learn, and verify denominator and label invariants.
lab.verifyIt:
assert m['tp']==2 and m['fp']==1 and m['fn']==1 and m['tn']==4
assert np.allclose([m['accuracy'],m['precision'],m['recall'],m['f1']],sk)
assert cm.tolist()==[[m['tn'],m['fp']],[m['fn'],m['tp']]]
assert metrics(y,y)['accuracy']==1 and metrics(y,y)['f1']==1
all_negative=np.zeros_like(y); assert np.isnan(metrics(y,all_negative)['precision'])

lessons.description: Classification metrics translate predictions into evidence about errors, probability quality and decision consequences. This chapter derives accuracy, precision, recall, specificity, negative predictive value, F-beta, balanced accuracy, Matthews correlation and multiclass averaging from the confusion matrix. It explains why prevalence and threshold alter predictive values, why accuracy can fail under imbalance, and how micro, macro, weighted and per-class reporting answer different questions. It separates hard-label evaluation from log loss, Brier score and calibration, covers top-k and multilabel settings, and treats abstention as an explicit outcome. Worked examples show a 99%-accurate useless classifier and a prevalence shift that changes precision without changing sensitivity or specificity. The lab implements binary counts and metrics, verifies them against scikit-learn, and checks invariants. Production guidance versions label definitions, positive-class orientation, thresholds, missing-label and abstention policies, evaluates independent entities and operational slices, and connects metrics to review capacity and error costs. Denominators and raw counts remain visible so small or undefined cells cannot masquerade as certainty.
learningObjectives: Derive binary classification metrics from confusion counts and explain their conditioning direction.
Select per-class, micro, macro and weighted summaries for a declared evaluation population.
Separate thresholded decision quality from ranking and probability-forecast quality.
Build a production scorecard that handles prevalence, abstention, uncertainty and operational cost.

deepSections.title: Start with complete error accounting
deepSections.body: A binary confusion matrix cross-tabulates actual and predicted labels into TP, FP, FN and TN. Every hard-label metric is a transformation of these four counts, so inspecting the counts prevents denominator mistakes. Recall conditions on actual positives and answers coverage; specificity conditions on actual negatives. Precision conditions on predicted positives and describes alert purity; negative predictive value does the same for predicted negatives. Accuracy weights the two correct cells by their observed prevalence. Balanced accuracy instead averages class recalls, giving each class equal weight. Matthews correlation uses all four cells and remains informative in many imbalanced settings, but its interpretation is less direct for operations. Always state which label is positive: swapping it changes precision, recall and the meaning of harm. When predictions or outcomes can be unknown, deferred or abstained, add explicit states rather than forcing them into negative. Report denominators alongside ratios, since 90% precision from nine of ten alerts is different evidence from 900 of 1,000.

deepSections.title: Prevalence and threshold change the operating point
deepSections.body: Sensitivity and specificity describe class-conditional behavior on a fixed distribution, while predictive values also depend on prevalence. Through Bayes' rule, precision equals sensitivity times prevalence divided by the overall predicted-positive rate. A screening test moved from a high-risk clinic to a general population can therefore keep the same sensitivity and specificity yet lose precision sharply. A score threshold creates the predicted labels; lowering it usually increases recall and false positives, while raising it usually increases precision and specificity. The right threshold depends on false-negative cost, false-positive cost, capacity and sometimes benefit per true positive. Select it using training or validation data, then estimate final performance on untouched data. Re-choosing a threshold on the test set leaks outcome information. If prevalence or costs change in production, re-evaluate expected utility rather than assuming an old F1 optimum remains valid.

deepSections.title: Averaging defines whose performance counts
deepSections.body: For multiclass classification, one-vs-rest counts can be computed for every class. Macro averaging gives every class equal weight and highlights rare-class failures; weighted macro weights by class support and can resemble majority performance; micro averaging pools decisions and is dominated by common examples. In single-label multiclass problems, micro precision, recall and F1 equal accuracy, so reporting all four creates no new evidence. Multilabel tasks add multiple decisions per example; sample averaging emphasizes people or documents, while label averaging emphasizes labels. Hierarchical taxonomies may need distance-aware costs because confusing two sibling species is not equivalent to crossing a broad category. Top-k accuracy is appropriate only when the interface truly presents k candidates. Preserve the full confusion matrix and per-class support, then add an aggregate whose weighting matches the deployment claim. Slice by relevant cohorts without using tiny noisy cells as definitive rankings.

deepSections.title: Scores, probabilities and decisions are different objects
deepSections.body: A classifier may rank examples well yet produce poorly calibrated probabilities, or be calibrated on average while ranking weakly. Hard-label metrics observe only one threshold and discard confidence. Log loss is a strictly proper score that heavily penalizes confident wrong probabilities; Brier loss is squared probability error and is easier to decompose, though its value reflects prevalence and refinement as well as calibration. Reliability diagrams diagnose calibration but require careful binning and uncertainty. ROC and precision-recall curves describe threshold sweeps, not probability calibration. Evaluate the artifact needed by the consumer: ranking metrics for a queue, proper scores and calibration for risk estimates, and threshold metrics plus utility for an automated action. Post-hoc calibration must be fitted without touching the final test set. Never call an arbitrary score a probability unless its empirical meaning has been checked.

deepSections.title: Make the scorecard a versioned decision contract
deepSections.body: Freeze label query, observation window, prediction horizon, positive class, eligibility rules, sample unit, threshold, weighting, abstention behavior and averaging. Test confusion counts on hand-calculated fixtures and define zero-denominator behavior rather than accepting library defaults silently. Compare with naive, current-production and policy baselines. Compute uncertainty by patient, customer, session or another independent entity; ordinary row bootstraps are optimistic when entities repeat. Monitor label coverage and delay, prevalence, score distribution, confusion counts, per-class metrics, probability scores, calibration and decision cost. Capacity metrics such as precision among the top K may be more actionable than unconstrained recall. Backfill metrics by prediction cohort when labels mature. Promotion gates should be prespecified across critical slices, and rollback should remain possible when costs, calibration or data quality deteriorate.

workedExamples.title: Accuracy hides a failed detector
workedExamples.body: Among 1,000 transactions, ten are fraudulent. Predicting all as legitimate yields TN=990, FN=10, TP=FP=0 and accuracy 99%. Recall is 0, and precision is undefined because no alerts exist. The counts reveal that the system performs no detection work.

workedExamples.title: Prevalence changes precision
workedExamples.body: With 90% sensitivity, 90% specificity and 50% prevalence, precision is 0.9. At 1% prevalence, the same class-conditional rates give precision 0.009/(0.009+0.099), about 8.3%. Deployment population matters even when the test mechanism is unchanged.

lessons.title: ROC-AUC vs PR-AUC
lessons.interviewAnswer: ROC and precision-recall curves evaluate a ranking across thresholds, but they emphasize different consequences. ROC plots true-positive rate against false-positive rate; its area is the probability that a randomly chosen positive receives a higher score than a randomly chosen negative, with tie handling. PR plots precision against recall and directly exposes alert purity, so it is usually more informative when positives are rare and false-positive volume matters. ROC AUC is prevalence-invariant under fixed class-conditional score distributions, whereas precision and PR baselines change with prevalence. Average precision is a non-interpolated weighted mean of precisions over recall increments and is not identical to every trapezoidal PR area. Neither curve selects an operating threshold or proves calibration. I compare curves on the same untouched examples, add uncertainty over independent units, report partial or capacity-constrained regions, and choose a threshold using costs and constraints outside the final test set.
keyPoints: ROC summarizes TPR versus FPR; PR summarizes precision versus recall over score thresholds.
ROC AUC has a pairwise ranking interpretation but may hide large absolute false-positive volume.
The no-skill PR precision baseline is prevalence, so PR results do not transport unchanged across populations.
Average precision and trapezoidal PR AUC use different interpolation assumptions and should be named precisely.
Curves evaluate ranking, not probability calibration, business utility or a deployed threshold by themselves.
lessons.why: Many classification systems emit a score and defer the action threshold to a policy. A single precision or recall value cannot reveal whether one model is better across plausible policies. ROC and PR curves trace the available trade-offs, but careless summaries can mislead. At low prevalence, a small false-positive rate can still create an overwhelming review queue, while ROC AUC averages over thresholds the business would never use. PR precision changes with prevalence and is sensitive to false-positive volume, but its area depends on a convention. Curves also ignore calibration and error cost. Good evaluation therefore preserves threshold-level counts, focuses on the feasible operating region, quantifies paired uncertainty, and connects the chosen operating point to capacity or expected utility.
lessons.intuition: Sort examples from highest score to lowest and move a threshold down the list. Each positive encountered increases recall; each negative contaminates the alert set and lowers precision. ROC instead divides false positives by all negatives, which can make contamination look small when negatives are enormous. The curves are two projections of the same ranked list. Their usefulness depends on which denominator matches the decision.
lessons.deepDive: Threshold curves summarize discrimination without committing to one cutoff. Their axes, baselines, interpolation and averaging conventions determine the question being answered. Robust comparison keeps examples paired, reports clinically or operationally relevant regions, handles ties and sample weights explicitly, and separates ranking from probability estimation and threshold optimization.
lessons.math: At threshold t, TPR(t)=TP(t)/(TP(t)+FN(t)), FPR(t)=FP(t)/(FP(t)+TN(t)), precision(t)=TP(t)/(TP(t)+FP(t)), and recall(t)=TPR(t). ROC AUC equals P(S+>S-)+0.5P(S+=S-) under standard tie handling. Average precision is sum_n (R_n-R_{n-1})P_n over successive thresholds in scikit-learn's non-interpolated definition. The random-ranking ROC baseline is 0.5; expected PR precision is prevalence pi. Partial AUC restricts the FPR range but requires a stated normalization convention.
lessons.workedExample: Suppose one million cases contain 1,000 positives. At 90% TPR and 1% FPR, the model finds 900 positives but flags about 9,990 negatives. Precision is only 900/(900+9,990), about 8.3%, despite the visually small FPR.

commonMistakes.misconception: ROC AUC is the probability the classifier is correct.
commonMistakes.correction: It is a pairwise ranking probability, not classification accuracy or calibrated confidence.

commonMistakes.misconception: PR AUC and average precision are always identical.
commonMistakes.correction: They can use different interpolation rules; name and document the exact summary.

commonMistakes.misconception: ROC is immune to class imbalance and therefore sufficient.
commonMistakes.correction: Its rates omit absolute false-positive volume; inspect feasible regions and PR or capacity metrics.

commonMistakes.misconception: The threshold with best test-set F1 is deployable evidence.
commonMistakes.correction: That reuses final labels for policy selection and gives an optimistic estimate.

followUps.question: Why is ROC AUC invariant to a monotonic score transform?
followUps.answer: The transform preserves every pairwise ordering and threshold ranking; only the numerical threshold values change.

followUps.question: When should partial AUC be used?
followUps.answer: When only a constrained FPR or TPR region is operationally possible, with the range and normalization stated in advance.

followUps.question: Can high AUC coexist with poor calibration?
followUps.answer: Yes. AUC depends on order, while calibration asks whether probability values match observed frequencies.

lessons.production: Version label query, positive class, score direction, eligibility, sample weights, tie handling, curve implementation and prediction cohort. Preserve threshold-level counts, compare models on paired untouched examples and compute uncertainty over independent entities. Report full curves only with operational summaries such as recall at a false-positive cap, precision at capacity, expected queue volume and cost. Select thresholds outside the final test set. Monitor prevalence, scores, queue size, confusion counts and calibration separately, backfill delayed labels by cohort, and trigger rollback when review capacity or critical error limits are breached.

lab.goal: Build ROC and precision-recall points from ranked scores, verify standard areas, and demonstrate invariance and prevalence behavior.
lab.buildIt:
import numpy as np
y=np.array([1,0,1,0,1,0]); s=np.array([.95,.80,.70,.60,.40,.10])
def ranked_points(y,s):
    order=np.argsort(-s,kind='stable'); yy=np.asarray(y)[order]; p=yy.sum(); n=len(yy)-p
    tp=np.cumsum(yy==1); fp=np.cumsum(yy==0)
    recall=tp/p; fpr=fp/n; precision=tp/(tp+fp)
    return fpr,recall,precision
fpr,tpr,precision=ranked_points(y,s)
roc_auc=float(np.trapz(np.r_[0,tpr],np.r_[0,fpr]))
ap=float(np.sum(np.diff(np.r_[0,tpr])*precision))
lab.useIt:
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score,average_precision_score,roc_curve,precision_recall_curve
sk_roc=roc_auc_score(y,s); sk_ap=average_precision_score(y,s); sk_fpr,sk_tpr,_=roc_curve(y,s)
lab.verifyIt:
assert abs(roc_auc-sk_roc)<1e-12
assert abs(ap-sk_ap)<1e-12
assert abs(roc_auc_score(y,np.exp(s))-sk_roc)<1e-12
assert abs(roc_auc_score(1-y,-s)-sk_roc)<1e-12
y_more_neg=np.r_[y,np.zeros(20,dtype=int)]; s_more_neg=np.r_[s,np.linspace(.94,.41,20)]
assert average_precision_score(y_more_neg,s_more_neg)<sk_ap
assert np.all(np.diff(sk_fpr)>=0) and np.all(np.diff(sk_tpr)>=0)

lessons.description: ROC and precision-recall analysis evaluates how a classifier ranks positives above negatives across possible thresholds. This chapter derives both curves from a sorted score list, explains their axes and baselines, and gives ROC AUC its pairwise probability interpretation. It shows why a seemingly tiny false-positive rate can overwhelm a rare-event system, why precision-recall curves expose alert purity, and why PR baselines move with prevalence. It distinguishes average precision from trapezoidal PR area, discusses ties, interpolation, sample weights, multiclass averaging, partial AUC and precision at a capacity limit. Worked examples calculate threshold points and translate rates into review counts. The lab builds curves from scratch, verifies AUC and average precision against scikit-learn, checks score-order invariance, and demonstrates the prevalence effect. Production guidance evaluates paired predictions on untouched cohorts, attaches cluster-aware uncertainty, focuses on feasible operating regions, checks calibration separately, and selects thresholds from costs or constraints without reusing final-test labels. Every reported point stays connected to its threshold, confusion counts and expected operational volume.
learningObjectives: Construct ROC and precision-recall points from ranked scores and threshold confusion counts.
Interpret ROC AUC, average precision, baselines and prevalence effects without overclaiming.
Compare models in an operationally feasible region using paired uncertainty and capacity constraints.
Separate ranking evaluation from calibration, threshold selection and downstream utility.

deepSections.title: Both curves come from one ranked list
deepSections.body: Start with continuous scores where larger means more positive. Sort examples descending and sweep the threshold from above the maximum to below the minimum. When the sweep admits a positive, TP increases and FN decreases; admitting a negative increases FP and decreases TN. ROC records FPR and TPR after each distinct score, while PR records recall and precision. Tied scores must enter together because no threshold can separate them; arbitrary within-tie ordering invents resolution. Include endpoint conventions explicitly. Sample weights replace counts with weighted masses and change the target population. Scores need only preserve order for the curve, so any strictly increasing transformation leaves ROC and PR points unchanged. Reversing score direction, mishandling the positive label or computing curves from hard labels destroys most ranking information. Keep threshold arrays alongside points so a candidate operating region can be translated back to an implementable rule.

deepSections.title: ROC measures class-conditional ranking
deepSections.body: ROC compares sensitivity with the fraction of negatives falsely accepted. Its diagonal represents random ordering, and AUC integrates TPR over FPR. The pairwise interpretation is valuable: AUC is the probability a random positive outranks a random negative, with half credit for a tie. It is not the probability a prediction is correct, does not identify a threshold and does not encode prevalence or costs. Because FPR divides by all negatives, a value such as 1% can still mean ten thousand false alerts in a million-negative population. Full AUC also averages regions that may be unusable. In screening or fraud, report TPR at a maximum FPR, a standardized partial AUC, or false positives at the actual population scale. Two ROC curves can cross, so the preferred model depends on the allowed region rather than the global area alone.

deepSections.title: Precision-recall exposes alert purity
deepSections.body: PR places recall on the horizontal axis and precision on the vertical axis. Precision directly answers how much of the selected queue is relevant, making the curve sensitive to class prevalence and false-positive volume. A random ranking has expected precision equal to prevalence, not a universal horizontal value. That is useful in one deployment population but complicates comparison across datasets with different prevalence. Average precision commonly weights precision by each increase in recall without linearly interpolating across gaps. Trapezoidal integration can be optimistic because straight lines between PR points may represent unattainable behavior; always name the implementation. Precision at K, recall at K and lift can be more direct when capacity fixes the queue length. At recall zero, precision conventions vary. Report counts and threshold or K with every selected point rather than treating a curve coordinate as context-free.

deepSections.title: Compare paired rankings, not isolated decimals
deepSections.body: Evaluate candidate models on exactly the same untouched examples. AUC or AP differences are paired statistics because the scores share labels and units; confidence intervals should resample independent entities or suitable time blocks while keeping predictions paired. Naive row bootstraps understate uncertainty for repeated customers, images from the same subject or temporally correlated events. Rare positives can make PR estimates extremely variable, so show the number of positives and interval bands or bootstrap distributions. Use cross-validation predictions only when every score is produced out of fold, and do not pool incompatible folds without considering calibration and population differences. For multiclass tasks, choose one-vs-rest or one-vs-one and state macro, weighted or micro aggregation. A global curve can hide a harmful subgroup; slice analysis needs sufficient support and a prespecified interpretation to avoid noisy metric shopping.

deepSections.title: A curve is an input to policy, not the policy
deepSections.body: The deployed threshold follows expected benefit, false-positive and false-negative costs, review capacity, service-level constraints and sometimes fairness or safety requirements. Choose it on training or validation data, then lock it for final estimation. If the score is used as probability, assess calibration with proper scores and reliability diagnostics separately; strong ranking can coexist with biased probabilities. Re-estimate expected counts under production prevalence, since PR precision can fall after a population shift even when class-conditional ranking is stable. Monitor score distributions, prevalence, threshold-level confusion counts, queue size and delayed labels by prediction cohort. A policy may include multiple thresholds for accept, review and reject, each requiring explicit coverage and risk. Version score direction, positive label, tie rule, weights, curve implementation and selected threshold, and keep a rollback policy when workload or harm breaches limits.

workedExamples.title: A small FPR creates a large queue
workedExamples.body: Suppose one million cases contain 1,000 positives. At 90% TPR and 1% FPR, the model finds 900 positives but flags about 9,990 negatives. Precision is only 900/(900+9,990), about 8.3%, despite the visually small FPR.

workedExamples.title: Manual ranking points
workedExamples.body: Scores [0.9,0.8,0.7,0.1] with labels [1,0,1,0] yield precisions 1, 1/2, 2/3 and 1/2 as the queue grows, with recalls 1/2, 1/2, 1 and 1. Thresholds expose exactly where the negative enters the queue.

exercises.solution: Two percent in expectation; the PR baseline follows prevalence.

exercises.prompt: Why might partial ROC AUC be more useful than full AUC?
exercises.solution: It restricts evaluation to the false-positive range the system can actually tolerate instead of averaging unusable thresholds.

exercises.prompt: A monotonic transform changes scores from logits to exponentials. What happens to AUC?
exercises.solution: Nothing, provided order and ties are preserved; the thresholds change but the ranking does not.

lessons.title: Train/Validation/Test & Cross-validation
lessons.interviewAnswer: Cross-validation estimates how a complete training procedure generalizes by repeatedly fitting it on training folds and scoring held-out folds. The splitter must reproduce the deployment unit and direction: shuffled K-fold for approximately IID units, GroupKFold when entities repeat, blocked or rolling splits for future prediction, and stratification when class support is needed. Every learned step—including imputation, scaling, encoding, feature selection, resampling and calibration—must be fitted inside each training fold, normally through a pipeline. CV estimates a procedure, not one already-fitted model. Fold scores are correlated because training sets overlap, so their standard deviation is not a simple confidence interval. I use out-of-fold predictions for paired diagnostics, keep an untouched final test set when selection is extensive, and use nested CV when the same data drive hyperparameter or model search and unbiased performance estimation.
keyPoints: The resampling unit and temporal direction must match the future generalization claim.
All data-dependent transformations belong inside the fold-specific training pipeline.
Cross-validation evaluates a training procedure; the final model is refit on all development data afterward.
Fold scores are dependent and can hide example weighting differences; preserve out-of-fold predictions and fold sizes.
Model selection and performance estimation are distinct tasks; nested CV or a final test set separates them.
lessons.why: A single train-test split can be noisy, especially with limited data, but more folds do not automatically make evaluation valid. Randomly splitting repeated patients leaks identity information. Shuffling time lets future patterns train a past prediction. Preprocessing the whole dataset before splitting gives validation rows influence over the fitted transformation. Trying many configurations and reporting the best CV score turns validation into training. Cross-validation is therefore a simulation design, not a checkbox. It must recreate which observations will be new, what information exists at prediction time, how the model is retrained, and which choices are tuned. A well-designed procedure provides reusable out-of-fold predictions, honest comparisons and diagnostics while reserving independent evidence for the final claim.
lessons.intuition: Treat each fold as a miniature deployment rehearsal. At the fold boundary, pretend the held-out units do not yet exist. Fit every learned artifact on the remaining data, make predictions once, and record them. If the rehearsal allows a future timestamp, a sibling row from the same patient, or a global feature statistic to cross the boundary, it is testing an easier world than production.
lessons.deepDive: Cross-validation design is governed by exchangeability, grouping, time, prevalence and selection. Splitters encode the target population; pipelines encode the training algorithm; scoring and aggregation encode the estimand. Reliable inference tracks out-of-fold predictions and independent units, uses repeated or nested designs only for their intended purpose, and avoids interpreting dependent fold variation as ordinary sampling uncertainty.
lessons.math: For folds I_k partitioning observations, a size-weighted CV loss is sum_k sum_{i in I_k} L(y_i,f^{-k}(x_i))/N, where f^{-k} is trained without fold k. The unweighted mean of fold means gives each fold equal weight and differs when sizes vary. K-fold training sets overlap, so fold losses are correlated. Leave-one-out has low training-set bias but can have high estimator variance and high cost. Repeated K-fold varies random partitions; nested CV uses outer folds for estimation and inner folds for selecting a procedure.
lessons.workedExample: A dataset has ten visits per patient. Row-wise K-fold puts visits from one patient in both train and validation, allowing identity-like features to inflate performance. GroupKFold assigns every visit for a patient to one fold and estimates generalization to unseen patients.
lessons.code:
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_validate,cross_val_predict
factory=make_pipeline(StandardScaler(),LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))
result=cross_validate(factory,X,y,cv=cv,scoring='accuracy',return_train_score=False)
lib_oof=cross_val_predict(factory,X,y,cv=cv,method='predict')

commonMistakes.misconception: Cross-validation automatically prevents leakage.
commonMistakes.correction: Only a correct splitter and fold-local fitting of every learned step prevent boundary violations.

commonMistakes.misconception: The standard deviation of K fold scores is a confidence interval.
commonMistakes.correction: Fold scores are dependent because training sets overlap and validation composition varies.

commonMistakes.misconception: More folds are always better.
commonMistakes.correction: They change training-size bias, validation variance and cost; group and time structure matters more than K.

commonMistakes.misconception: The best CV score is an unbiased final estimate.
commonMistakes.correction: Selection adapts to CV noise. Use untouched evidence or nested CV for estimation.

followUps.question: When should GroupKFold be used?
followUps.answer: When multiple rows share a unit whose information will be absent for a new deployment unit and groups must not cross train-validation boundaries.

followUps.question: Why put scaling in a pipeline?
followUps.answer: The scaler's mean and variance must be learned only from each training fold; a pipeline enforces that fit-transform boundary.

followUps.question: What is the difference between cross_val_score and cross_val_predict?
followUps.answer: The first returns fold scores; the second constructs out-of-fold predictions for compatible use cases and is not automatically an estimate of every pooled metric.

lessons.production: Version raw eligibility, prediction cutoff, groups, time boundaries, random seed, fold assignments, pipeline, search space, metric and aggregation. Assert group disjointness, temporal order and one out-of-fold prediction per eligible unit. Log transformer fit counts, fold support, errors, compute and candidate failures. Compare models on identical splits and paired independent-unit losses. Reserve final evidence or use genuine nested CV when selection is extensive. Refit the selected complete procedure on all development data, preserve the final test set, and deploy the exact feature and preprocessing contract with rollback artifacts.

lab.goal: Build leakage-safe K-fold evaluation with a preprocessing pipeline, verify library agreement, and construct complete out-of-fold predictions.
lab.buildIt:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.model_selection import KFold
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score
X,y=make_classification(n_samples=120,n_features=6,random_state=7)
cv=KFold(n_splits=5,shuffle=True,random_state=11); oof=np.full(len(y),np.nan); fold_scores=[]
for train,valid in cv.split(X):
    model=make_pipeline(StandardScaler(),LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))
    model.fit(X[train],y[train]); oof[valid]=model.predict(X[valid]); fold_scores.append(accuracy_score(y[valid],oof[valid]))
pooled=accuracy_score(y,oof)
lab.verifyIt:
assert not np.isnan(oof).any() and len(oof)==len(y)
assert np.array_equal(oof,lib_oof)
assert np.allclose(fold_scores,result['test_score'])
fold_sizes=np.array([len(v) for _,v in cv.split(X)]); assert abs(pooled-np.average(fold_scores,weights=fold_sizes))<1e-12
for train,valid in cv.split(X): assert set(train).isdisjoint(valid)

lessons.description: Cross-validation is a controlled simulation of training and deployment, not merely repeated random splitting. This chapter derives the out-of-fold estimate, distinguishes observation-weighted from fold-weighted aggregation, and explains the bias, variance and computational trade-offs of holdout, K-fold, repeated K-fold and leave-one-out evaluation. It selects splitters for IID observations, stratified classification, repeated entities, spatial groups and temporal forecasting, including why stratification can reduce observed fold variability. It shows how pipelines keep imputation, scaling, encoding, feature selection, resampling and calibration inside each training fold. Worked examples expose patient leakage and unequal fold weighting. The lab performs manual pipeline-based K-fold evaluation, verifies scikit-learn results and confirms that every row receives exactly one out-of-fold prediction. Production guidance versions split manifests and seeds, records fold-level artifacts and failures, compares paired predictions, separates model selection from estimation, and refits the chosen procedure on all eligible development data without touching the final test set. The emphasis is faithful rehearsal of the actual future novelty rather than maximizing a convenient resampling score.
learningObjectives: Choose a splitter whose held-out unit and temporal direction match deployment.
Construct leakage-safe fold pipelines and complete out-of-fold predictions.
Aggregate fold evidence with the correct observation, group or time weighting.
Separate tuning, comparison and final estimation using nested or held-out evaluation.

deepSections.title: Choose the splitter from the generalization claim
deepSections.body: Ordinary shuffled K-fold assumes observational units are sufficiently exchangeable. Each unit appears in one validation fold and K-1 training folds, allowing efficient reuse of limited data. Stratified K-fold approximately preserves class proportions, preventing folds with no rare positives and stabilizing some metrics; however, that engineering convenience can make folds more homogeneous and shrink apparent variability. When rows share a patient, household, device, document or experiment, hold out whole groups so memorized group signatures cannot cross the boundary. For a claim about new groups, GroupKFold is more relevant than row-level K-fold. For future prediction, preserve order with expanding or rolling windows and a gap when labels or features overlap the horizon. Spatial data may require geographic blocking. The correct splitter can yield a lower score because it asks the harder, correct question. Document the target deployment population and which source of novelty each split represents.

deepSections.title: Fit every learned operation inside each fold
deepSections.body: A transformation uses validation information whenever its state is estimated before splitting. Global means used for imputation, vocabulary selection, scaling parameters, target encodings, univariate feature selection, PCA components, oversampling, probability calibration and threshold selection all leak if learned from the full dataset. A pipeline receives raw fold data, fits transformations and estimator only on the training subset, and applies the frozen chain to validation rows. Pure deterministic row-local transformations that use no learned state can be performed earlier, but keeping them in the pipeline improves reproducibility. Target-derived features need especially strict out-of-fold construction, sometimes with an inner split inside each training fold. Cache carefully because artifacts are fold-specific. Verify the pipeline by recording fitted sample counts or transformer statistics and confirming validation IDs never contribute. Feature availability time matters even when the software pipeline is correct.

deepSections.title: Out-of-fold predictions preserve the most useful evidence
deepSections.body: Store one prediction for every eligible observation from a model that did not train on it. These out-of-fold predictions support pooled metrics, residual plots, slice analysis and paired comparison. For decomposable losses, pooling observation losses yields an observation-weighted estimate. Averaging fold metrics weights folds equally; this differs when fold sizes or group composition vary. Nonlinear metrics such as AUC do not always decompose, and pooling scores across folds can be affected by fold-specific score scales. Report fold sizes, per-fold results and the selected aggregate. For group-level claims, aggregate or resample by group. Cross-validation predictions should not be presented as predictions from the final refitted artifact. After procedure selection, fit that procedure on all development data, version its artifacts, and estimate its final performance using evidence not used to make the choice.

deepSections.title: More folds do not create independent experiments
deepSections.body: Increasing K trains each fold model on more data and reduces the pessimism caused by smaller training sets, but validation folds become smaller and computation rises. Leave-one-out is nearly unbiased for training size yet can be unstable and expensive. Repeated K-fold samples partition variability, but repeated scores share observations and training data. The standard deviation across fold scores describes split variation under that design; dividing it by square root K is not generally a valid confidence interval because folds are dependent. Prefer paired bootstrap or domain-appropriate cluster and block resampling on out-of-fold losses, while acknowledging model-training variability if it matters. Use the same splits for candidate models so comparisons are paired. Inspect fold-specific failures rather than celebrating a narrow mean. Learning curves across training sizes can diagnose whether more data or lower variance is likely to help.

deepSections.title: Selection consumes validation evidence
deepSections.body: Every choice informed by CV—features, algorithm, hyperparameters, threshold, metric, even a promising random seed—adapts to its noise. The best of many candidates is optimistically biased. An untouched final test set estimates the fully selected process once. With limited data, nested CV places the entire search in each outer training fold and evaluates the selected result on the outer holdout. The inner score selects; the outer scores estimate. Do not tune globally and then call outer CV nested. Freeze the search space and primary metric in advance, log failed trials and compute cost, and include preprocessing in the searched pipeline. Once evidence supports a procedure, refit it on all eligible development data and deploy with the same feature contract. Keep split manifests immutable so leakage investigations and paired comparisons can be reproduced.

workedExamples.title: Visits are not independent patients
workedExamples.body: A dataset has ten visits per patient. Row-wise K-fold puts visits from one patient in both train and validation, allowing identity-like features to inflate performance. GroupKFold assigns every visit for a patient to one fold and estimates generalization to unseen patients.

workedExamples.title: Fold and observation means differ
workedExamples.body: One fold has loss 0 on 10 rows and another loss 1 on 90 rows. The unweighted fold mean is 0.5, while pooled observation loss is 0.9. Neither is universally correct; the claimed weighting must be stated.

exercises.prompt: Why does global median imputation leak?
exercises.solution: Validation values influence the median applied to their own fold. Fit the imputer separately on each training fold.

exercises.prompt: Which splitter fits forecasting next month from past months?
exercises.solution: An ordered expanding or rolling time split, possibly with a gap matching label and feature overlap.

exercises.prompt: What does an out-of-fold prediction guarantee?
exercises.solution: That the row was not in that model's training fold; it does not by itself guarantee group, time or feature-lineage safety.

lessons.title: Data Leakage
lessons.interviewAnswer: Data leakage occurs when model training or evaluation uses information that would not be available for the same prediction in production, or when the validation boundary is contaminated. Target leakage includes post-outcome fields and features computed with future data. Train-test contamination includes fitting imputers, encoders, scalers, feature selectors or oversampling on all rows. Entity leakage places related rows in both sides; temporal leakage trains on the future or uses revised snapshots. Selection leakage arises when the test set repeatedly guides choices. I prevent leakage by defining a prediction timestamp and label horizon, documenting feature availability and lineage, splitting raw data by entity and time before learned transforms, fitting a complete pipeline inside each fold, using point-in-time joins, and reserving final evidence. I also run adversarial checks: remove suspicious features, shift cutoffs, inspect near-perfect proxies, and reproduce every feature from only the allowed historical snapshot.
keyPoints: Availability is defined at the prediction event, not by whether a column exists in today's warehouse.
Split raw independent units before fitting transformations, resampling, selection or calibration.
Point-in-time correct joins need event time, ingestion time, revision policy and label windows.
Repeated entities, duplicates and near-duplicates can contaminate validation without explicit target columns.
A test set ceases to be independent when repeated inspection changes modeling decisions.
lessons.why: Leakage is dangerous because it often produces the cleanest metrics and the strongest-looking feature. A hospital discharge code predicts an outcome that was decided before discharge; a fraud chargeback status is known weeks after authorization; a customer aggregate rebuilt from today's complete table includes future activity for historical predictions. Random splits can place duplicates or later visits from the same person on both sides. Even ordinary preprocessing leaks when validation rows contribute vocabulary, category statistics or feature selection. The resulting model may pass software tests yet fail immediately online. Preventing leakage requires a temporal and causal data contract plus evaluation boundaries, not merely dropping columns whose names contain the target.
lessons.intuition: Freeze time at the instant a prediction must be made. Cover every database field, model artifact and human decision created after that instant. If the remaining inputs cannot be reconstructed exactly from the historical snapshot, the offline example is cheating. Then isolate the future unit—customer, patient, device, geography or time block—so the model cannot recognize a related copy.
lessons.deepDive: Leakage is an information-boundary violation spanning labels, features, entities, preprocessing, selection and infrastructure. Point-in-time semantics distinguish event occurrence from database arrival and later revision. Prevention combines data lineage, raw-data splitting, fold-local pipelines, immutable evaluation sets and deployment-parity replay. Detection uses suspicious performance, ablations, availability audits and time-forward shadow evaluation, but absence of a symptom is not proof of safety.
lessons.workedExample: A readmission model includes a billing code finalized after discharge. Historical rows show excellent accuracy because the code reflects care delivered during the outcome window. At discharge-time prediction the final code does not exist, so the feature must be removed or reconstructed from codes available by the cutoff.
lessons.code:
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
availability={'signal_0':True,'signal_1':True,'signal_2':True,'post_outcome':False}
allowed=[i for i,name in enumerate(availability) if availability[name]]
model=make_pipeline(StandardScaler(),LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)).fit(X_leaky[tr][:,allowed],y[tr])
pipeline_auc=roc_auc_score(y[te],model.predict_proba(X_leaky[te][:,allowed])[:,1])

commonMistakes.misconception: Removing the target column eliminates leakage.
commonMistakes.correction: Post-outcome proxies, future aggregates, repeated entities and globally fitted transforms can still reveal forbidden information.

commonMistakes.misconception: A pipeline fixes every leakage problem.
commonMistakes.correction: It controls fitted transformations but cannot repair invalid timestamps, target-derived source fields or the wrong splitter.

commonMistakes.misconception: If a feature exists in the warehouse, it was historically available.
commonMistakes.correction: Warehouses contain late arrivals and revisions; reconstruct event and ingestion time at each prediction cutoff.

commonMistakes.misconception: The test set remains independent because labels are hidden from the model code.
commonMistakes.correction: Human choices informed by repeated test results also adapt to those labels.

followUps.question: Is normalization before splitting always serious leakage?
followUps.answer: It lets validation distribution influence fitted statistics. The magnitude varies, but the correct and reproducible design fits normalization within training folds.

followUps.question: How do you detect duplicate leakage in images or text?
followUps.answer: Use stable IDs and exact hashes first, then domain-appropriate perceptual hashes or embedding similarity with human review across partitions.

followUps.question: What is point-in-time correctness?
followUps.answer: Every historical feature value matches what the production system could have known by that prediction event, including arrival latency and revision state.

lessons.production: Version the prediction timestamp, label horizon and maturity, feature availability and revision table, point-in-time queries, raw snapshot, entity groups, duplicate policy, split manifest and complete pipeline. Assert feature-time cutoffs, entity disjointness and fold-local transformer fitting. Audit strongest features and simple baselines, run label-shuffle and suspicious-feature ablations, scan cross-split duplicates and replay historical features from source snapshots. Restrict final-test access and record every evaluation. Monitor offline-online feature parity and cohort performance; quarantine uncertain lineage and retain a known-safe model for rollback.

lessons.math: Let T_p be prediction time and A_j be the time feature j becomes available with its production value. A valid feature satisfies A_j<=T_p under the deployed latency and revision policy. A label for horizon h may use events in (T_p,T_p+h] but cannot feed features. For transformation theta=g(D), validation is clean only if theta is fitted from D_train rather than D_train union D_valid. For grouped data, train and validation entity-ID sets must be disjoint. For temporal evaluation, max training information time must precede each validation prediction cutoff, including any embargo needed for overlapping labels.

lab.goal: Create and detect a post-outcome target proxy, enforce an availability allowlist, and verify clean train-test boundaries.
lab.buildIt:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score
rng=np.random.default_rng(4); n=600
x=rng.normal(size=(n,3)); y=(x[:,0]+rng.normal(scale=1.5,size=n)>0).astype(int)
post_outcome=y+rng.normal(scale=.02,size=n); X_leaky=np.c_[x,post_outcome]
tr,te=train_test_split(np.arange(n),test_size=.3,random_state=5,stratify=y)
def auc(X):
    m=LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000).fit(X[tr],y[tr]); return roc_auc_score(y[te],m.predict_proba(X[te])[:,1])
leaky_auc=auc(X_leaky); clean_auc=auc(x)
lab.useIt:
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
availability={'signal_0':True,'signal_1':True,'signal_2':True,'post_outcome':False}
allowed=[i for i,name in enumerate(availability) if availability[name]]
model=make_pipeline(StandardScaler(),LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)).fit(X_leaky[tr][:,allowed],y[tr])
pipeline_auc=roc_auc_score(y[te],model.predict_proba(X_leaky[te][:,allowed])[:,1])
lab.verifyIt:
assert set(tr).isdisjoint(te) and len(set(tr)|set(te))==n
assert allowed==[0,1,2]
assert leaky_auc>.99
assert abs(pipeline_auc-clean_auc)<1e-12 and clean_auc<leaky_auc-.1
y_shuffled=rng.permutation(y); m=LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000).fit(x[tr],y_shuffled[tr]); shuffled_auc=roc_auc_score(y_shuffled[te],m.predict_proba(x[te])[:,1]); assert abs(shuffled_auc-.5)<.15
lab.shipIt: Turn availability metadata and cutoff assertions into CI gates, persist split IDs and snapshots, and require historical feature replay plus suspicious-feature ablation before release.

lessons.description: Data leakage is any violation of the information or evaluation boundary that makes offline performance easier than deployment. This chapter distinguishes target, temporal, entity, duplicate, preprocessing, feature-selection, resampling and test-set selection leakage. It defines prediction time, feature availability, event time, ingestion time, label horizon and revision policy, then shows how point-in-time joins reconstruct what the system actually knew. It explains why splitting raw independent units must precede imputation, scaling, encoding, target statistics, feature selection, calibration and oversampling. Worked examples expose a post-outcome hospital field and a historical aggregate rebuilt with future transactions. The lab creates an explicit target proxy, demonstrates its inflated validation AUC, removes it through an availability allowlist and verifies split disjointness. Production guidance maintains feature lineage and cutoff manifests, scans duplicates and proxies, replays features from historical snapshots, restricts final-test access, monitors online parity and keeps rollback paths when suspicious drift or impossible offline-online gaps appear. Every release should carry evidence that its inputs were reproducible at their original prediction cutoffs.
learningObjectives: Classify target, temporal, entity, transformation and selection leakage from concrete pipelines.
Specify prediction-time availability and point-in-time join semantics for every feature.
Design raw-data splits and fold-local pipelines that preserve entity and temporal boundaries.
Audit suspicious performance using lineage, ablations, duplicates and historical replay.

deepSections.title: Define what was knowable at prediction time
deepSections.body: Begin with a prediction event: an entity, timestamp and action. Each feature needs an event timestamp, an ingestion or processing timestamp, source lineage, expected latency and revision rule. A value that occurred before prediction but arrived afterward was unavailable. A value later corrected in the warehouse may differ from the value originally served. Labels require a start, horizon and maturity delay; outcome-window events cannot enter predictors. Static-looking fields may encode post-outcome workflow, such as closure reason, treatment completion or account recovery status. Human actions can also leak: a field recording that an investigator opened a case may be downstream of an earlier risk score. Create a feature availability table and reconstruct training rows with as-of joins from immutable snapshots or bitemporal data. Querying the latest dimension table for every historical row is not point-in-time correct.

deepSections.title: Leakage crosses more boundaries than target columns
deepSections.body: Direct target leakage uses the outcome or a deterministic derivative. Proxy leakage uses a post-outcome code, timestamp or workflow state strongly coupled to the label. Temporal leakage lets future observations, centered windows or revised data affect a past prediction. Entity leakage shares the same person, device, document family or experiment across train and validation. Duplicate leakage shares exact or near-identical content, including augmented variants. Transformation leakage fits imputers, scalers, encoders, vocabulary, PCA or feature selectors globally. Resampling leakage generates synthetic points before splitting, allowing validation information to influence training neighbors. Selection leakage occurs when many model, metric or threshold choices adapt to the test set. Pretraining contamination can place evaluation examples in a foundation model corpus. Name the boundary and adversary explicitly; leakage is relative to the deployment claim.

deepSections.title: Split first, then learn inside the boundary
deepSections.body: Start from raw eligible records and assign groups or chronological cohorts before computing learned transformations. In each fold, fit imputation, scaling, category handling, target encoding, feature selection, dimensionality reduction, resampling, model, calibration and threshold only on the training partition. Apply the frozen chain to validation. Target encoding usually requires an additional out-of-fold construction within training data so a row does not encode its own label. Time aggregates must include only events visible before each row's cutoff, often with a safety lag for ingestion. Keep label-building code physically separate from feature-building code and restrict permissions where possible. For repeated decisions, define whether evaluation targets new events for known entities or entirely new entities; the split differs. Validate uniqueness and near-duplicate hashes before training.

deepSections.title: Suspicious success deserves an information audit
deepSections.body: Near-perfect performance on a hard problem, a single dominant feature, a large gap between random and time-forward splits, and severe online degradation are leakage signals. They are not proofs, and ordinary-looking scores do not prove safety. Inspect feature names, provenance and availability timestamps. Train a simple model and rank univariate associations; manually explain the strongest predictors. Ablate suspicious fields and compare time-forward or group-held-out results. Shuffle labels to test whether preprocessing still extracts signal; performance should collapse to chance. Search exact and perceptual duplicates across partitions. Replay feature computation from a historical snapshot and compare with stored online features. Shift prediction cutoffs earlier to see whether purported features disappear correctly. Review joins for many-to-many explosions, future-effective dimension values and label-derived filters. Record the audit evidence with the model release.

deepSections.title: Leakage prevention continues after deployment
deepSections.body: Version the prediction contract, source queries, feature definitions, availability rules, split manifest, training snapshots and final-test access. CI can assert that feature timestamps precede cutoffs, entity and duplicate sets are disjoint, transformations fit only expected row IDs and label tables are inaccessible to feature jobs. Compare offline batch features with online logged features on the same prediction events. Monitor missingness, freshness, feature distributions and offline-online score gaps. Delayed labels should be backfilled by prediction cohort; joining them must not rewrite historical feature values. Limit repeated test-set dashboards for active development and rotate or supplement benchmarks when they become selection targets. If a feature's provenance becomes uncertain, quarantine it, evaluate an ablation and keep the last known-safe model available for rollback.

workedExamples.title: Post-outcome workflow field
workedExamples.body: A readmission model includes a billing code finalized after discharge. Historical rows show excellent accuracy because the code reflects care delivered during the outcome window. At discharge-time prediction the final code does not exist, so the feature must be removed or reconstructed from codes available by the cutoff.

workedExamples.title: Latest-table time travel
workedExamples.body: A churn feature joins each monthly customer row to today's account status. Closed accounts are marked closed even for months when they were active. An as-of join using the historical effective interval preserves the status known at each prediction month.

exercises.prompt: Why is a seven-day centered rolling average invalid for a real-time prediction today?
exercises.solution: The centered window includes future days. Use a trailing window ending before the prediction cutoff.

exercises.prompt: When should all visits for a patient be grouped?
exercises.solution: When the deployment claim is performance on unseen patients or identity-related information would make row-level validation easier than production.

exercises.prompt: How can a final test set leak without entering model training code?
exercises.solution: Repeated human inspection can guide features, algorithms and thresholds, adapting development to its labels.

lessons.title: Class Imbalance
lessons.interviewAnswer: Class imbalance means class frequencies and error costs are uneven; it does not by itself make learning impossible. I first preserve the natural prevalence in validation and use precision-recall, per-class recall, calibrated probabilities, capacity metrics and expected cost instead of accuracy alone. During training I may use class or sample weights, minority oversampling, majority undersampling, focal-style losses or anomaly methods, but every resampling step stays inside the training fold. Weights change the optimization target and resampling changes the effective prior, so raw probabilities may need correction or calibration on natural-prevalence data. Threshold selection is a separate decision problem based on false-positive cost, missed-positive cost and capacity. I also check rare-positive uncertainty, duplicates, temporal drift and subgroup support. The goal is not a balanced training table; it is reliable performance and utility on the real deployment population.
keyPoints: Imbalance describes prevalence; the actual problem depends on overlap, label quality, sample size and error cost.
Keep validation and test data at deployment prevalence unless estimating a deliberately reweighted population.
Class weights and resampling affect training, while thresholding affects the deployed action; they are not interchangeable.
Oversampling must occur within training folds, and synthetic points must never use validation neighbors.
Probability calibration must be assessed after weighting or resampling on data with the intended prevalence.
lessons.why: A classifier can achieve excellent accuracy by ignoring a rare class, yet a rare class may carry nearly all operational value. The opposite mistake is to force equal classes everywhere and accidentally evaluate a fictional population. Oversampling duplicates evidence rather than creating new independent cases; undersampling discards information about negatives; weights alter the loss; and all can distort probability estimates. When only dozens of positives exist, metrics are highly uncertain and a few duplicates or mislabeled cases can dominate. A rigorous approach separates four questions: what population will arrive, what training objective helps learn its boundary, what score quality is achieved, and what decision threshold maximizes value under constraints.
lessons.intuition: If one fire alarm occurs among a thousand normal events, predicting normal always is accurate but useless. Copying the one alarm many times makes the optimizer notice it, but does not create new knowledge about the diversity of fires. Evaluation must return to the original stream, where even a small false-positive rate may flood operators. Training emphasis and deployment prevalence are different levers.
lessons.deepDive: Imbalanced learning combines sampling design, loss weighting, ranking, calibration and decision policy. Balanced objectives can help the boundary but redefine the effective class prior. Valid evaluation uses untouched natural-prevalence cohorts, rare-event uncertainty and operational counts. Data collection, label review and hard-negative mining often matter more than increasingly elaborate resampling.
lessons.math: For N observations and K classes with class count n_c, scikit-learn's balanced weight is w_c=N/(K n_c), making each class contribute equal total weight before other sample weights. Weighted empirical risk is sum_i w_{y_i} L_i / sum_i w_{y_i}. If training prior pi_s differs from deployment prior pi_t and class-conditional distributions are stable, posterior odds can be adjusted by multiplying training odds by [pi_t/(1-pi_t)]/[pi_s/(1-pi_s)]. This label-shift correction fails when class-conditional features also change. Precision depends on deployment prevalence through Bayes' rule.
lessons.workedExample: A stream has one million negatives and 1,000 positives. At 80% recall and 1% FPR, it finds 800 positives but creates 10,000 false alerts, so precision is about 7.4%. The operational bottleneck is visible only after multiplying rates by prevalence and volume.

commonMistakes.misconception: Always oversample until classes are 50/50.
commonMistakes.correction: The useful ratio depends on optimizer, overlap and cost; evaluation must still represent the deployment population.

commonMistakes.misconception: Class weighting and lowering the threshold are equivalent.
commonMistakes.correction: Weighting changes fitting and possibly ranking; thresholding changes the action on a fixed score.

commonMistakes.misconception: SMOTE creates additional independent evidence.
commonMistakes.correction: Synthetic points derive from existing examples and assumptions; uncertainty still reflects original independent cases.

commonMistakes.misconception: ROC AUC solves imbalance evaluation.
commonMistakes.correction: It can hide alert volume and says nothing about probability calibration or the selected operating point.

followUps.question: When is undersampling useful?
followUps.answer: When majority data are enormous or redundant and a representative or hard-negative subset reduces cost without losing boundary information.

followUps.question: Why can class weights damage calibration?
followUps.answer: They change the effective loss contribution and class prior, so fitted scores need not represent natural-prevalence posterior probabilities.

followUps.question: How should rare-class uncertainty be reported?
followUps.answer: Show counts and cluster-aware intervals or bootstrap distributions, with label maturity and duplicate dependence made explicit.

lessons.production: Version the natural evaluation cohort, label maturity, independent unit, class and sample weights, resampling algorithm, random seed, calibration set and threshold policy. Fit all sampling inside training folds and keep augmented families together. Report rare-class counts, PR and capacity metrics, probability scores, calibration, workload and decision cost with cluster-aware uncertainty. Monitor prevalence, predicted-positive volume, delayed outcomes, reviewer yield and feedback-selection bias. Recalibrate or retune policy on separate evidence when prevalence or costs move, canary changes, and retain the previous model and threshold for rollback.
