lab.goal: Implement a multi-metric forecast scorecard, verify standard losses, and expose percentage-error and scaling behavior.
lab.buildIt:
import numpy as np
y_train=np.array([10.,12.,11.,13.,12.,14.,13.,15.,14.,16.,15.,17.])
y=np.array([0.1,10.,12.,20.,25.]); pred=np.array([0.3,9.,15.,18.,24.])
e=y-pred; mae=float(np.mean(np.abs(e))); rmse=float(np.sqrt(np.mean(e**2))); bias=float(np.mean(e)); mape=float(np.mean(np.abs(e/y))); wape=float(np.sum(np.abs(e))/np.sum(np.abs(y)))
scale=np.mean(np.abs(y_train[1:]-y_train[:-1])); mase=mae/scale
def pinball(actual,forecast,q):
    err=actual-forecast; return float(np.mean(np.maximum(q*err,(q-1)*err)))
q90=pinball(y,pred+2,.9)
lab.useIt:
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error, mean_squared_error, mean_pinball_loss
official_mae=float(mean_absolute_error(y,pred)); official_rmse=float(np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y,pred))); official_q90=float(mean_pinball_loss(y,pred+2,alpha=.9))
lab.verifyIt:
assert np.isclose(mae,official_mae) and np.isclose(rmse,official_rmse)
assert np.isclose(q90,official_q90)
assert np.isclose(wape,np.sum(np.abs(e))/np.sum(np.abs(y)))
assert abs(e[0])<abs(e[2]) and abs(e[0]/y[0])>abs(e[2]/y[2])
assert mape>.4  # the near-zero actual makes percentage error dominate this example
assert scale>0 and np.isclose(mase,mae/scale)
assert abs(bias)<mae and all(v>=0 for v in (mae,rmse,mase,wape,q90))
lab.shipIt: Generate immutable forecast-level metric ledgers, compute training-only scales and paired baselines, publish horizon and cohort scorecards, and alert on bias, negative skill and calibration failures.

lessons.description: Forecasting metrics translate forecast errors into model-selection and operating decisions. This chapter connects MAE and RMSE to median and mean targets, explains signed bias and error distributions, and distinguishes per-observation averages from aggregate ratios. It derives MASE and RMSSE using training-only naive or seasonal-naive denominators and analyzes MAPE, sMAPE and WAPE failures around zeros, negatives, intermittency and changing scale. It covers horizon, origin, series, regime and business weighting; macro versus micro aggregation; baseline skill; paired model comparisons; temporal dependence and block-aware uncertainty. It separates point, quantile, interval and distributional evaluation, introducing pinball loss, empirical coverage, sharpness, interval score, log score and CRPS without treating calibration alone as sufficient. Worked examples show ranking reversal and percentage-error instability. The lab implements a forecast scorecard, verifies core values against scikit-learn, and demonstrates why MAPE explodes near zero while MASE remains interpretable. Production guidance versions metric definitions, denominators and cohorts, delays scoring until labels mature, and monitors bias, negative skill and interval miscalibration by operational slice.
learningObjectives: Select point and probabilistic losses that align with the forecast output and downstream decision.
Compute MAE, RMSE, MASE, RMSSE, WAPE, bias, pinball and interval scores correctly.
Design horizon- and series-aware aggregation with explicit business weights and paired uncertainty.
Diagnose zero denominators, metric gaming, delayed labels and misleading pooled improvements.

deepSections.title: Loss functions choose what the forecast means
deepSections.body: A point forecast is incomplete until its target functional is named. Squared loss is optimized by the conditional mean, while absolute loss is optimized by a conditional median. They coincide only for special symmetric distributions. If shortage and overage costs differ linearly, the optimal forecast is a quantile determined by the cost ratio, not automatically the mean. RMSE has the same units as the target but is not the typical error; its square emphasizes tails, data faults and rare peaks. MAE is more robust and directly additive across units, yet may underweight catastrophic misses. Report signed mean error or cumulative bias separately because absolute scores can hide chronic underforecasting. Never train a median model and judge it as though it estimates the mean without explaining the mismatch. Translate domain cost into an explicit loss curve when possible, and keep statistical scores as diagnostics so a temporary price table does not erase general forecast quality.

deepSections.title: Scale-free does not mean assumption-free
deepSections.body: MAPE divides each error by the realized value. It is undefined at zero, unstable near zero, unsuitable for arbitrary-zero scales and asymmetric because the same absolute miss has different percentage penalties depending on the outcome. sMAPE changes the denominator but remains unstable and has competing definitions. WAPE pools absolute errors before dividing by total actual volume. It is useful as an aggregate volume-relative summary for nonnegative targets, but large series dominate and the denominator can drift across evaluation windows. MASE scales MAE by an in-sample naive error, making one mean the model matches the chosen naive benchmark. RMSSE does the squared analogue and was used in hierarchical retail evaluation. The denominator must use only the training era available at each origin; computing it on test outcomes leaks scale information. For seasonal data use a seasonal-naive difference with the declared period. Constant histories can give zero denominators, requiring an explicit exclusion, epsilon policy or alternative score rather than silent infinities.

deepSections.title: Keep the forecast ledger before aggregating
deepSections.body: Store one record per series, origin, target timestamp and horizon with prediction, outcome, baseline, weight and regime labels. First inspect loss by horizon because uncertainty and action value change with lead time. Then inspect series-level distributions: macro averaging gives each series equal influence, while micro or volume weighting gives high-exposure rows more influence. Both can be legitimate and should be reported together. Declare whether weights reflect revenue, units, service levels or decision frequency, and keep them fixed before comparing models. Overall means can hide a model that improves routine periods while failing holidays, cold starts or high-value products. Compute paired loss differences on exactly the same eligible forecast events. Confidence intervals should resample independent series when entities are independent, contiguous temporal blocks when errors cluster over time, or both in a hierarchical bootstrap. Row-level iid standard errors are usually too optimistic.

deepSections.title: Probability forecasts need truthful and diagnostic evaluation
deepSections.body: A nominal 90 percent interval that covers 90 percent of outcomes may still be uselessly wide. Coverage measures calibration but not concentration; sharpness measures width but must be judged subject to calibration. Interval score rewards narrow intervals and penalizes misses according to the nominal alpha. Quantile or pinball loss is proper for a requested quantile and supports asymmetric decisions. CRPS evaluates the entire univariate predictive distribution and resembles an integrated quantile loss. Log score strongly penalizes assigning tiny density to what occurs and is sensitive to density tails and numerical flooring. Proper scores discourage a forecaster from improving expected score by reporting a distribution other than its belief. Evaluate calibration by horizon, series scale and regime, inspect probability integral transform or quantile coverage patterns, and distinguish aleatoric forecast spread from model or data uncertainty. Joint path forecasts require additional multivariate or scenario checks because good marginals do not guarantee realistic temporal trajectories.

deepSections.title: A metric specification is a versioned production interface
deepSections.body: Write a metric card containing error sign convention, units, transform inversion, missing-label policy, denominator window, seasonal period, horizon weights, series weights, clipping, eligibility and baseline version. Mature labels before scoring and distinguish preliminary from revised outcomes. Monitor numerator and denominator separately so an apparent MASE improvement is not caused by a more volatile scaling era. Alert on sustained signed bias, negative baseline skill, tail error, service-level breach and interval undercoverage, not only average loss. Segment data-quality incidents from model misses but retain both views because the user experiences the combined system. Use shadow forecasts for paired comparisons, predeclare promotion thresholds and require improvement on critical slices with no intolerable regression. Preserve the prior model and baseline route for rollback when online error or latency exceeds guardrails.

workedExamples.title: Near-zero percentage explosion
workedExamples.body: Actual demand is 0.1 and a forecast is 0.3. The absolute error is only 0.2 units, but absolute percentage error is 200 percent. A second item with actual 100 and forecast 90 has a much larger ten-unit miss but only ten percent error. Whether that ordering is useful depends on the decision, not on the word percentage.

workedExamples.title: Aggregation reverses a ranking
workedExamples.body: Model A beats B by one unit on 900 small series, while B beats A by 100 units on ten revenue-critical series. Equal-series MAE favors A; volume-weighted cost can favor B. Reporting both reveals the stakeholder choice instead of pretending there is one neutral winner.

exercises.prompt: Which point forecast minimizes expected squared error?
exercises.solution: The conditional mean, assuming the expectation exists.

exercises.prompt: Why must a MASE denominator come from training data?
exercises.solution: Using evaluation outcomes leaks future scale and makes the score depend on information unavailable at the forecast origin.

exercises.prompt: A 90 percent interval has 99 percent coverage and doubles in width. Is it necessarily better?
exercises.solution: No. It may be over-dispersed; inspect sharpness and a proper interval or distributional score alongside calibration.

lessons.title: Prophet & Decomposable Forecasting
lessons.interviewAnswer: Prophet models a series as trend plus seasonality plus holiday/event effects. I use it when those components match the problem and fast, interpretable forecasting matters, but I still compare it with simpler and stronger baselines rather than treating it as universally best.

seasonality

lessons.description: Prophet & Decomposable Forecasting is a core topic in Time Series & Forecasting. Prophet is common in business forecasting and interviews because it demonstrates how domain events can be encoded explicitly. This chapter turns the interview-level summary into a complete engineering and analytical treatment. The starting mental model is: Think of the forecast as several interpretable curves added together: long-term movement, recurring calendars and known events. The formal and implementation discussion builds from trend, seasonality, holidays/events, diagnostics, while keeping the unit of data, objective, assumptions, and failure boundaries explicit. The original technical core is preserved: Prophet uses a piecewise trend with changepoints plus Fourier-style seasonal components and optional regressors/holiday effects. It handles missing observations and irregularities reasonably well, but does not replace careful backtesting. Rather than treating those statements as isolated facts, the chapter connects them to data preparation, evaluation design, numerical or systems behavior, and choices that change under scale or distribution shift. You will work through two concrete scenarios, a runnable Python lab with assertions, and two original conceptual visuals. The lab is intentionally small enough to run locally while still exposing an invariant that should remain true in a larger implementation. The production section translates the concept into monitoring, versioning, rollback, and failure-handling requirements. It is convenient for scheduled batch forecasts and interpretable component plots, but production still needs data-quality checks and retraining/monitoring. The broader module context is temporal structure, classical and modern forecasting, uncertainty and operational forecasting. The goal is not memorization: by the end, you should be able to define the contract, explain the mechanism, choose a defensible evaluation, diagnose common errors, and describe what has to be true before shipping the idea in a real Data, ML, or AI system.

deepSections.title: Define the problem contract before the technique
deepSections.body: A rigorous explanation of Prophet & Decomposable Forecasting starts with the contract, not the library call. In Time Series & Forecasting, the relevant artifact is a timestamped series and its information set, and the intended output is future values or predictive distributions. State the unit of observation or request, what information is available at decision time, which variables are controlled versus observed, and what success means. Prophet is common in business forecasting and interviews because it demonstrates how domain events can be encoded explicitly. The key ideas — trend, seasonality, holidays/events, diagnostics — only become meaningful when tied to a concrete input and output. For example, the same mechanism can be valid for an offline batch but invalid for an online request if it depends on unavailable future information, expensive global state, or a representation that is not versioned at serving time. Write down assumptions about independence, stationarity, label quality, ordering, capacity, or trust boundaries when they matter. Separate the statistical estimand or computational result from the estimator or implementation used to obtain it. Also separate correctness from convenience: a popular API can faithfully execute the wrong problem definition. A useful interview answer therefore names the goal, the information boundary, the dominant trade-off, and one failure mode before adding details. In production, this same contract becomes the basis for schemas, tests, SLOs, monitoring, and rollback.

deepSections.title: Mechanism and representation
deepSections.body: The working intuition for Prophet & Decomposable Forecasting is: Think of the forecast as several interpretable curves added together: long-term movement, recurring calendars and known events. The technical core is: Prophet uses a piecewise trend with changepoints plus Fourier-style seasonal components and optional regressors/holiday effects. It handles missing observations and irregularities reasonably well, but does not replace careful backtesting. Treat that description as a sequence of transformations and invariants. First identify what representation enters each step, what state or parameters are read, what transformation occurs, and what representation leaves. Then ask which quantities are learned, estimated, cached, partitioned, or fixed by design. The chapter's key points give a compact checklist: trend, seasonality, holidays/events, diagnostics. Each point should be explainable both conceptually and operationally. A concept is understood only when you can predict what changes after perturbing an input, removing a component, changing scale, or violating an assumption. Shape, units, ordering, normalization, and data type are part of the mechanism because many real failures are interface failures rather than failures of the underlying theory. For learned systems, distinguish forward computation from parameter updates; for data systems, distinguish event-time truth from processing-time state; for distributed or cloud systems, distinguish logical semantics from physical placement. This decomposition is also the basis for debugging: inspect intermediate values, compare against a tiny reference implementation, and verify local invariants before blaming the most sophisticated component.

deepSections.title: Formal view, objective, and invariants
deepSections.body: A compact formal statement prevents hand-waving. For Prophet & Decomposable Forecasting, the existing mathematical or logical anchor is: define the transformation as a function from valid inputs and state to outputs, then state the invariant that must hold for every valid execution. Do not memorize symbols without semantics. Name the domain of every quantity, whether it is observed or latent, and what is optimized or conserved. If an objective is minimized, ask what population quantity its empirical version estimates and whether weighting changes that target. If there is no optimization objective, identify the safety or correctness invariant instead: ordering, idempotence, conservation, normalization, boundedness, monotonicity, consistency, or resource limits. Numerical details matter whenever repeated operations amplify rounding or conditioning problems. Systems details matter whenever retries, parallelism, caching, or partial failure can produce a different logical result. Statistical details matter whenever data reuse or selection changes the sampling distribution. A strong implementation test usually expresses at least one invariant as an assertion on a toy case, plus a second test that fails when a key assumption is deliberately violated. The runnable lab follows that pattern so the chapter has an executable claim rather than code that merely prints a plausible number.

deepSections.title: Design choices and trade-offs
deepSections.body: There is rarely one universally best configuration of Prophet & Decomposable Forecasting. The useful question is which trade-off matters for the declared workload. Start with the key points trend, seasonality, holidays/events, diagnostics and ask how each affects accuracy or correctness, compute, memory, latency, sample efficiency, interpretability, and operational complexity. Prefer a simple baseline when it is easier to validate and already meets the decision threshold. Add complexity only when a measured failure mode justifies it. Hyperparameters and architecture choices should therefore map to observable consequences rather than folklore. At small scale, an exact method may be clearer; at large scale, approximation, batching, partitioning, caching, streaming, quantization, or asynchronous work may be necessary. Those changes create new error surfaces, so every optimization needs a quality or correctness comparison against the reference behavior. Also distinguish offline economics from online economics. A method that saves training time may increase serving cost; a denser representation may improve quality but violate memory limits; a stronger consistency guarantee may reduce throughput; a more aggressive safety rule may increase false positives. Document the chosen operating point, alternatives considered, and the condition that would trigger revisiting the choice. This turns a technical preference into an auditable engineering decision.

deepSections.title: Evaluation and diagnostics
deepSections.body: Evaluation for Prophet & Decomposable Forecasting must test the claim the system will make in operation. Appropriate evidence in this module includes rolling-origin backtests, naive baselines, horizon slices, and calibration. Do not collapse everything into one average. Slice by the dimensions that change difficulty: time, horizon, class, scale, entity, language, device, traffic regime, subgroup, or workload shape as appropriate. Always compare against a meaningful baseline on the same examples or requests. Keep comparisons paired when possible so improvement is not confused with a change in evaluation population. If labels or outcomes arrive late, define maturity before scoring. If the system is stochastic, use repeated seeds or confidence intervals; if observations are dependent, use a dependence-aware uncertainty procedure rather than row-level iid assumptions. Diagnostics should include input validity, intermediate-state checks, output distribution checks, and resource behavior. For probabilistic outputs, evaluate calibration as well as discrimination or sharpness. For ranking or generation, combine task metrics with qualitative failure review. For infrastructure, test both steady state and recovery behavior. A release gate should specify what must improve, what must not regress, and which failures are blocking even if the global average looks good.

deepSections.title: Failure modes and debugging strategy
deepSections.body: The dominant risks around Prophet & Decomposable Forecasting include temporal leakage, regime change, horizon decay, and delayed labels. Existing chapter cautions are also important: Saying Prophet is an LLM or neural network. Using automatic seasonality/changepoints without validating whether they match the business. A debugging process should make these risks observable. Start from the smallest reproducible case and verify the data contract. Check shapes, units, ordering, timestamps, identifiers, missingness, labels, masks, seeds, and configuration before changing the algorithm. Next verify a baseline and an invariant. Then inspect intermediate representations or state transitions to locate the first point where expected behavior diverges. Separate data bugs, objective mismatch, optimization or numerical issues, capacity limits, and deployment integration problems because they require different remedies. Introduce controlled perturbations: duplicate an event, reorder input, remove a feature, change batch size, delay a dependency, corrupt one field, or reduce precision. A robust implementation should either preserve its invariant or fail loudly according to a documented policy. Finally, test recovery. Retries should not duplicate side effects, model rollback should restore a compatible preprocessing path, and cached or checkpointed state should have a version. A system that works only on the happy path is not a complete implementation of the concept.

deepSections.title: Production operation, monitoring, and communication
deepSections.body: Shipping Prophet & Decomposable Forecasting means operating a versioned contract over time. It is convenient for scheduled batch forecasts and interpretable component plots, but production still needs data-quality checks and retraining/monitoring. Persist the model, code, data or schema version, configuration, dependencies, and any state needed to reproduce behavior. Monitor the inputs that drive the mechanism, the outputs users experience, and the internal resource or quality signals that predict failure. Use separate alerts for correctness, quality, latency, saturation, data freshness, and safety so one aggregate health score does not hide the cause. Canary or shadow changes when the blast radius is meaningful. Define rollback artifacts in advance and verify that rollback restores compatible schemas, feature logic, tokenizer or preprocessing state, and dependent services. Record enough request or batch metadata to reproduce failures without retaining data that violates privacy or retention requirements. When explaining the system to another engineer or interviewer, use a stable narrative: problem contract, mechanism, formal invariant, trade-off, evaluation evidence, failure mode, and production control. That sequence demonstrates understanding more reliably than listing tool names. The final question is always operational: what signal would tell you this implementation is no longer trustworthy, and what safe action follows?

lab.buildIt:
import numpy as np
y=np.array([10.,12.,11.,14.,15.,13.,16.,18.,17.,19.])
train=y[:7]; test=y[7:]
last=np.repeat(train[-1],len(test))
rolling=np.repeat(train[-3:].mean(),len(test))

last_mae=mae(test,last); rolling_mae=mae(test,rolling)

lessons.title: Causal Inference vs Prediction
lessons.interviewAnswer: Prediction estimates outcomes or labels under the observed data-generating process; causal inference estimates contrasts between well-defined interventions. A model can predict treatment recipients have worse outcomes because sicker people receive treatment even when treatment helps. I begin with a target trial or causal question: population, treatment strategies, assignment, time zero, follow-up, outcome, estimand and analysis. Potential outcomes define effects such as E[Y(1)-Y(0)], while a DAG makes assumptions about confounding, mediation, selection and timing explicit. Identification asks whether the estimand is expressible from observed data under consistency, exchangeability, positivity and interference assumptions; estimation then fits that observed-data functional. Flexible ML improves nuisance prediction but cannot repair an unidentified effect. I report assumptions, overlap, sensitivity, uncertainty, diagnostics and the population to which the result transports, never causal language from predictive accuracy alone.
keyPoints: Prediction concerns observed conditional distributions; causal inference concerns outcomes under interventions.
Define population, treatment versions, time zero, outcome horizon and estimand before choosing an estimator.
Identification assumptions connect unobserved counterfactual contrasts to observed-data quantities.
High predictive accuracy does not establish exchangeability, positivity, consistency or absence of interference.
Causal estimates require design diagnostics, sensitivity analysis and a stated target population, not only model metrics.
lessons.why: Many product and policy questions use verbs such as increase, prevent or cause, yet ordinary supervised learning only captures associations in historical behavior. A churn model may identify users who receive retention offers as high risk because the policy targets them; changing the offer cannot be evaluated by reading its coefficient. Confounding, reverse causation, selection, treatment timing and feedback all make observed comparisons differ from intervention effects. Conversely, causal estimation can sacrifice individual predictive accuracy while correctly estimating an average contrast. Separating question, identification and estimation prevents a powerful learner from hiding an impossible design. It also clarifies when randomized experiments, natural experiments, adjustment or partial identification are needed.
lessons.intuition: Prediction asks what usually happens to people who look like this under the current world. Causal inference asks what would change for the same target population if a decision rule were replaced. The first can be checked against observed labels. The second compares worlds that cannot both be observed for one unit, so it needs a design and assumptions to construct a credible counterfactual.
lessons.deepDive: Causal work is organized as question, estimand, identification, estimation and stress testing. Potential outcomes state intervention contrasts, DAGs encode structural assumptions and target-trial emulation aligns time and eligibility. Randomization supplies exchangeability by design; observational studies require defensible adjustment or quasi-experimental variation. Machine learning belongs inside nuisance estimation and heterogeneity analysis only after the causal functional is identified.
lessons.workedExample: High-risk patients are more likely to receive a beneficial treatment. Treated patients can have higher observed mortality because their baseline risk was much greater. Comparing treated with untreated answers an association question; a randomized or validly adjusted contrast targets the treatment effect.

commonMistakes.misconception: A highly accurate outcome model yields a causal treatment effect.
commonMistakes.correction: Prediction quality does not establish exchangeability, positivity, consistency or a valid intervention.

commonMistakes.misconception: Adding every available variable removes confounding.
commonMistakes.correction: Adjusting mediators or colliders can bias effects; choose covariates from temporal and causal structure.

commonMistakes.misconception: A nonsignificant estimate proves no effect.
commonMistakes.correction: It may reflect imprecision, weak support or design failure; report interval, estimand and assumptions.

commonMistakes.misconception: Machine learning replaces causal assumptions.
commonMistakes.correction: It can estimate nuisance functions flexibly after identification but cannot create missing counterfactual information.

followUps.question: What is the difference between an estimand and estimator?
followUps.answer: The estimand is the target causal quantity; the estimator is the data-based procedure used to approximate it under identification assumptions.

followUps.question: When is prediction sufficient?
followUps.answer: When the decision only requires forecasting under a stable observed policy and no intervention claim is made, while feedback and distribution shift are still monitored.

followUps.question: Can observational data identify causal effects?
followUps.answer: Yes under defensible adjustment or quasi-experimental assumptions and adequate support, with sensitivity analysis; the assumptions are not certified by fit alone.

lessons.production: Version the target trial, treatment versions, time zero, outcome horizon, estimand, DAG, adjustment set, population and estimator. Assert temporal availability and cohort eligibility, inspect overlap, balance, weights, adherence, interference and label maturity, and compute cluster-aware uncertainty. Report robustness and sensitivity rather than one model specification. Monitor treatment-policy and population drift, preserve randomized or exploratory evidence when possible, and require causal review before converting predictive signals into interventions. Retain the prior safe policy for rollback when overlap, outcome collection or assumed mechanisms change.
lessons.math: For binary treatment A, unit i has potential outcomes Y_i(1) and Y_i(0), but observes Y_i=A_iY_i(1)+(1-A_i)Y_i(0) under consistency. The ATE is E[Y(1)-Y(0)]; ATT is E[Y(1)-Y(0)|A=1]. The observed association E[Y|A=1]-E[Y|A=0] generally differs from ATE. Under conditional exchangeability Y(a) independent of A given X, positivity 0<P(A=a|X)<1 and consistency, E[Y(a)]=E_X E[Y|A=a,X], the g-formula. Standard errors quantify sampling variation conditional on the design, not uncertainty that assumptions are true.

lab.goal: Simulate confounding by indication, show a predictive association with the wrong sign, and recover the average effect under observed-confounder adjustment.
lab.buildIt:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression,LogisticRegression
rng=np.random.default_rng(7); n=12000; risk=rng.normal(size=n); propensity=1/(1+np.exp(-1.7*risk)); treatment=rng.binomial(1,propensity); true_effect=-2.; outcome=4*risk+true_effect*treatment+rng.normal(scale=1,size=n)
naive=outcome[treatment==1].mean()-outcome[treatment==0].mean()
adjusted=LinearRegression().fit(np.c_[treatment,risk],outcome).coef_[0]
lab.verifyIt:
assert naive>0
assert abs(adjusted-true_effect)<.08
assert abs(ipw-true_effect)<.12
assert np.all((ps>0)&(ps<1))
assert abs(treatment.mean()-propensity.mean())<.02
lab.shipIt: Persist the causal question, cohort, propensity and outcome models, overlap diagnostics and sensitivity analyses; monitor assignment policy and keep counterfactual evidence alive.

lessons.code:
ps=LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000).fit(risk[:,None],treatment).predict_proba(risk[:,None])[:,1]
weights=treatment/ps+(1-treatment)/(1-ps)
weighted_treated=np.sum(weights*treatment*outcome)/np.sum(weights*treatment); weighted_control=np.sum(weights*(1-treatment)*outcome)/np.sum(weights*(1-treatment)); ipw=weighted_treated-weighted_control
lessons.description: Causal inference and prediction solve different statistical problems. This chapter contrasts forecasts under the observed policy with outcomes under explicit interventions and builds a workflow from target question to estimand, identification, estimation and sensitivity analysis. It introduces potential outcomes, average treatment effects, consistency, exchangeability, positivity, interference and causal DAGs; distinguishes total, direct, mediated, intention-to-treat and per-protocol questions; and uses target-trial emulation to align eligibility, assignment, time zero and follow-up. It explains why predictive importance, coefficients and high accuracy do not identify effects, while randomized and quasi-experimental designs can identify effects without maximizing prediction. Worked examples expose confounding by indication and treatment-policy feedback. The lab simulates a beneficial treatment preferentially assigned to high-risk units, shows the naive association has the wrong sign, and recovers the effect with covariate adjustment under the simulated assumptions. Production guidance versions causal questions and cohorts, monitors overlap and treatment policy, reports sensitivity and uncertainty, and prevents decision systems from retraining on their own interventions without evaluation design.
learningObjectives: Translate a product or policy question into a target population, intervention, outcome horizon and estimand.
Separate identification assumptions from the statistical estimator used after identification.
Diagnose confounding, selection, timing, interference and policy-feedback failures in predictive analyses.
Design evidence and monitoring that support bounded causal claims and responsible decisions.

deepSections.title: Start with the intervention and estimand
deepSections.body: Write the decision before the regression. Specify eligible units, treatment versions, comparator, assignment time, follow-up, outcome, censoring and summary contrast. The treatment must be actionable enough that Y(a) has a coherent meaning: 'lower blood pressure' is not one intervention if drugs, exercise and surgery have different pathways. ATE averages individual contrasts over a target population; ATT targets those actually treated; risk ratios, quantiles and policy value answer other questions. Intention-to-treat compares assigned strategies, while per-protocol effects require handling adherence. Total effects include mediated paths; controlled direct effects intervene on a mediator and need stronger assumptions. Changing the population or treatment version changes the estimand even if the same estimator code runs. A target-trial protocol exposes ambiguities before data analysis and prevents immortal-time and eligibility misalignment.

deepSections.title: Observed prediction can conflict with intervention effects
deepSections.body: A predictor estimates patterns such as E[Y|X,A] under the historical policy. If high-risk units are preferentially treated, treatment status predicts poor outcome even when treatment reduces risk. This confounding by indication is not fixed by higher accuracy or a more flexible learner. Conditioning on downstream variables can block part of the effect or open collider paths. Policy feedback creates another trap: a deployed score changes who receives action, so future labels reflect both risk and intervention. Feature importance describes model reliance, not how changing a feature changes outcomes. Predictive validation remains useful for nuisance functions and operational forecasts, but a causal question needs a counterfactual design. Ask whether the intended action changes the distribution, whether treatment is manipulable, and what current policy determines exposure.

deepSections.title: Identification is the bridge from counterfactuals to data
deepSections.body: Only one potential outcome is observed for each unit, the fundamental missing-data problem of causal inference. Random assignment makes treatment exchangeable in expectation, while observational adjustment assumes measured covariates block confounding. Consistency requires observed outcome under received treatment to equal the corresponding potential outcome and treatment versions to be well defined. Positivity requires each relevant covariate stratum to have a chance of each strategy; extreme propensities make estimates unstable and nonpositivity makes target contrasts unsupported. SUTVA-style assumptions address interference and treatment versions; network spillovers require exposure mappings and different estimands. DAGs help decide adjustment sets from causal assumptions, not correlations. Identification can also come from instruments, discontinuities, parallel trends or synthetic comparisons, each with a distinct local population and assumptions.

deepSections.title: Estimate the identified functional and diagnose its support
deepSections.body: Once the g-formula or another functional is identified, estimate outcome regressions, propensity scores or both. Standardization predicts outcomes under each treatment for every target unit and averages contrasts. Weighting creates a pseudo-population according to a target estimand. Doubly robust estimators combine nuisance models, and cross-fitting lets flexible ML estimate them with reduced overfitting bias under conditions. None of these methods measures unobserved confounding. Inspect covariate balance, propensity overlap, influential weights, missing data, time alignment and negative controls where defensible. Report estimates across plausible specifications and sensitivity parameters. Cluster and repeated-unit structure determine uncertainty. Pre-specify the primary estimand and avoid searching subgroups until an attractive causal story appears.

deepSections.title: Causal evidence has a deployment lifecycle
deepSections.body: Translate an estimated effect into a policy only after considering transport to the deployment population, heterogeneous benefit, cost, capacity and harm. A historical ATE need not equal the effect under a new targeting rule or treatment saturation. Monitor eligibility, treatment propensity, overlap, adherence, interference, outcome maturity and effect-relevant covariates. Preserve exploration or randomized holdouts when policy feedback would eliminate counterfactual evidence. Version target-trial definitions, DAGs, assumptions, estimators and analysis populations. Triangulate experiments, quasi-experiments and observational results when possible. A failed overlap or policy-change alarm may require restricting the target population, redesigning data collection or reverting to a safe policy rather than automatically refitting a predictor.

workedExamples.title: Confounding by indication
workedExamples.body: High-risk patients are more likely to receive a beneficial treatment. Treated patients can have higher observed mortality because their baseline risk was much greater. Comparing treated with untreated answers an association question; a randomized or validly adjusted contrast targets the treatment effect.

workedExamples.title: Time zero misalignment
workedExamples.body: Users are classified as treated only after completing 30 days of a program, but untreated follow-up starts at signup. Treated users must survive 30 days to enter that group, creating immortal-time bias. Eligibility, assignment and follow-up must share time zero.

exercises.prompt: Why can treatment be positively associated with harm when it helps?
exercises.solution: Higher-risk units may receive treatment, so baseline risk confounds the observed treated-versus-untreated comparison.

exercises.prompt: What assumptions identify the g-formula from measured covariates?
exercises.solution: Consistency, conditional exchangeability given the adjustment set, positivity in the target population and an appropriate interference assumption.

exercises.prompt: Why is target-trial time zero important?
exercises.solution: Eligibility, treatment assignment and follow-up must align so future survival or information does not determine treatment groups.

lessons.title: DAGs, Confounders & Colliders
lessons.interviewAnswer: A causal DAG is a directed acyclic graph whose arrows encode direct causal relationships under a chosen level of abstraction. It is not learned from correlations alone; it records domain assumptions and lets us reason about open paths. A confounder is a common cause of treatment and outcome, creating a backdoor path that must be blocked. A mediator lies on the causal path and adjusting for it changes a total-effect question. A collider is a common effect; conditioning on it or its descendants can open a previously blocked path and create association. I define treatment, outcome, time order and target effect, draw all plausible common causes including unmeasured ones, apply d-separation or the backdoor criterion, and avoid descendants of treatment for total effects. I compare defensible adjustment sets, use negative controls or sensitivity analysis, and never treat an algorithmically discovered graph as identified truth without interventions or strong assumptions.
keyPoints: DAG arrows express causal assumptions, not regression coefficients or mere temporal correlation.
Confounders open noncausal backdoor paths; mediators carry effects; colliders block paths until conditioned on.
d-separation is a graphical rule for conditional independence implied by the assumed graph.
An adjustment set is effect- and graph-specific; adding variables can create rather than remove bias.
Unmeasured nodes belong in the graph because they determine identification even when absent from the dataset.
lessons.why: Regression tables encourage a harmful habit: call every pretreatment correlate a confounder and include every available field. Conditioning can block causal pathways, induce selection through colliders or encode post-treatment information. A DAG makes those consequences visible before modeling. It also separates what data can test from what subject-matter knowledge must assert. Multiple graphs can fit the same observed distribution yet imply different intervention effects, so graphical reasoning does not eliminate uncertainty; it organizes it. The practical value is a reviewable causal contract that connects temporal lineage, adjustment, missing variables, selection and the estimand.
lessons.intuition: Paths behave like pipes for association. A fork C→A and C→Y is open unless C is conditioned on, so treated and untreated groups differ through C. A chain A→M→Y carries the effect and closes when M is conditioned on. A collider A→K←Y is naturally closed because K requires two arrows to meet; selecting or conditioning on K opens a competition between its causes.
lessons.deepDive: DAG analysis distinguishes causal paths from noncausal associations using d-separation, graph surgery and effect-specific adjustment criteria. Correct use requires temporal and substantive assumptions, inclusion of latent causes, careful treatment of selection and measurement, and explicit recognition of Markov equivalence and causal-discovery limits.
lessons.workedExample: Baseline severity causes treatment and outcome, so it should be adjusted for the total treatment effect. Post-treatment biomarker lies on treatment→biomarker→outcome; adjusting for it changes the question and can introduce bias through unmeasured biomarker-outcome causes.

commonMistakes.misconception: Every variable associated with treatment and outcome is a confounder.
commonMistakes.correction: Mediators, colliders and proxies can share associations; role follows the causal graph and timing.

commonMistakes.misconception: More adjustment is always safer.
commonMistakes.correction: Conditioning on colliders or post-treatment variables can create bias and positivity problems.

commonMistakes.misconception: A DAG learned from data proves causal direction.
commonMistakes.correction: Discovery relies on strong assumptions and often identifies only an equivalence class; interventions and domain knowledge remain necessary.

commonMistakes.misconception: Unmeasured variables can be omitted from the graph because they cannot enter regression.
commonMistakes.correction: They determine whether observed adjustment identifies the effect and must remain visible in the assumptions.

followUps.question: What happens when you condition on a collider?
followUps.answer: It can open a previously blocked path between the collider's causes, inducing a noncausal association.

followUps.question: Can a variable be a confounder and mediator?
followUps.answer: Its role is query- and time-specific; a time-varying variable may mediate earlier treatment while confounding later treatment.

followUps.question: How do you choose among multiple valid adjustment sets?
followUps.answer: Prefer sets with reliable measurement, good positivity and precision, then test robustness; all rely on the same causal assumptions.

lessons.production: Version the DAG, node and treatment definitions, time order, latent causes, edge rationale, estimand and selected adjustment set. Assert that adjustment features precede treatment for total-effect analyses and flag filters or missingness rules that condition on selection. Compare plausible graph variants, run overlap and sensitivity diagnostics and maintain negative controls where justified. Review the graph whenever data collection or policy changes create new arrows. Keep the prior design and decision policy available when the updated system invalidates the original identification argument.

visual.title: Confounder vs collider
visual.caption: A confounder creates a backdoor path that often needs adjustment. Conditioning on a collider can create bias.
visual.adaptationNote: Atlas redraw: the structure and claims are grounded in the cited source material; the artwork is newly drawn for teaching rather than copied verbatim from a paper or website.

lessons.math: A path is blocked by conditioning set Z if it contains a noncollider in Z or a collider with neither it nor any descendant in Z. X and Y are d-separated by Z when every path is blocked. A backdoor path from A to Y begins with an arrow into A. A set Z satisfies the backdoor criterion if it contains no descendant of A and blocks every backdoor path. Then P(Y|do(A=a))=sum_z P(Y|A=a,Z=z)P(Z=z) for discrete Z. This equality follows from causal assumptions; ordinary probability alone does not license replacing do(A) with conditioning on A.
lessons.code:
confounder_bias=naive-2; adjusted_bias=adjusted-2; collider_bias=conditioned-open_path
results={'naive':naive,'adjusted':adjusted,'unconditioned_collider_graph':open_path,'conditioned_collider_graph':conditioned}

lab.goal: Simulate a confounder and a collider, then verify that conditioning removes bias in the first graph and creates bias in the second.
lab.buildIt:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
rng=np.random.default_rng(9); n=20000
c=rng.normal(size=n); a=.9*c+rng.normal(size=n); y=2*a+2*c+rng.normal(size=n)
naive=LinearRegression().fit(a[:,None],y).coef_[0]; adjusted=LinearRegression().fit(np.c_[a,c],y).coef_[0]
a2=rng.normal(size=n); y2=rng.normal(size=n); collider=a2+y2+rng.normal(scale=.3,size=n)
open_path=LinearRegression().fit(a2[:,None],y2).coef_[0]; conditioned=LinearRegression().fit(np.c_[a2,collider],y2).coef_[0]
lab.verifyIt:
assert abs(adjusted-2)<.03
assert abs(naive-2)>.5
assert abs(open_path)<.03
assert conditioned<-.8 and abs(collider_bias)>.8
assert all(np.isfinite(v) for v in results.values())
lab.shipIt: Persist the reviewed DAG and adjustment set, assert temporal feature lineage, and rerun collider, overlap and sensitivity audits when policy or data collection changes.

lessons.description: Directed acyclic graphs turn causal assumptions into a precise map for identification and bias analysis. This chapter defines nodes, arrows, paths, ancestors, descendants, forks, chains and colliders; derives d-separation; and explains why confounding, mediation and selection depend on graph position rather than variable names. It applies the backdoor criterion, distinguishes total from direct effects, analyzes M-bias, proxy adjustment, measurement error and selection on descendants, and explains why unmeasured causes must appear even when they cannot enter a model. It also covers Markov equivalence and the assumptions behind causal discovery. Worked examples show confounder adjustment removing bias and collider adjustment creating it. The lab simulates both structures and verifies their opposite regression consequences. Production guidance versions graphs, node semantics, time availability and adjustment sets, reviews new features for post-treatment status, maintains negative-control and sensitivity evidence, and treats every graph revision as a change to the causal claim rather than a cosmetic diagram update.
learningObjectives: Classify causal paths, forks, chains and colliders and apply d-separation correctly.
Choose adjustment sets for a declared total or direct effect using the backdoor criterion.
Diagnose collider, mediator, descendant and selection bias introduced by inappropriate conditioning.
Document latent causes, temporal assumptions, graph alternatives and sensitivity in a reviewable workflow.

deepSections.title: A DAG is a structural claim at a chosen abstraction
deepSections.body: Nodes represent variables or states and arrows represent direct causal relationships relative to the included variables and time scale. Absence of an arrow is also an assumption: no direct effect after accounting for the graph. Acyclicity excludes feedback within the represented time slice; real feedback can be unfolded over time with indexed nodes. Arrows do not encode effect sign, size, linearity or determinism. Draw treatment, outcome, baseline causes, mediators, selection and measurement processes before opening the data. Include latent common causes as unobserved nodes so missing identification is visible. The same real system can have different valid graphs for different granularities, but the nodes and intervention must remain coherent. Temporal order rules out some arrows but does not prove the remaining orientation. Review the graph with domain, data and causal experts and attach evidence or rationale to each contested edge.

deepSections.title: d-separation tracks which paths transmit association
deepSections.body: A chain X→M→Y and a fork X←C→Y are open until their middle noncollider is conditioned on. Conditioning blocks them. A collider X→K←Y is blocked by default and opens when K or one of its descendants is conditioned on. To test d-separation, enumerate paths without following arrow direction, classify each interior node on that path and apply the blocking rules. The causal Markov property implies d-separated variables are conditionally independent, subject to distributional faithfulness for using observed independences to recover structure. Failure to observe an expected independence can falsify a graph or reveal measurement and sampling issues, but observed independence cannot select a unique causal direction among Markov-equivalent DAGs. d-separation is qualitative identification logic, not a measure of how large residual bias is.

deepSections.title: Variable roles depend on the treatment-outcome query
deepSections.body: A baseline common cause of A and Y is a confounder and opens a backdoor path. A mediator lies on a directed path from A to Y; conditioning on it removes part of the total effect and may introduce mediator-outcome confounding affected by treatment. A collider is a common effect on a path and conditioning opens it. A variable can play multiple roles on different paths, and a confounder for one exposure may be a mediator for another. Prognostic causes of Y that do not cause A can improve precision without being required for identification. Instruments cause A and affect Y only through A under exclusion; adjusting for them is not necessary for confounding control and can amplify residual bias in some settings. Do not assign roles from correlation or a reusable feature label. State the exact A, Y, intervention time and estimand first.

deepSections.title: Backdoor adjustment blocks noncausal paths without blocking the effect
deepSections.body: For a total effect, remove arrows leaving A conceptually and identify paths entering A. A valid set contains no descendants of A and blocks all such paths. Minimal sets are often preferable to an indiscriminate superset because extra variables can open colliders, increase variance or worsen positivity. Selection is conditioning, whether implemented by a regression covariate, a filter, complete-case analysis or dataset membership. Restricting to hospitalized patients can open a path if hospitalization is caused by treatment-related and outcome-related factors. Adjusting for a proxy may reduce but not eliminate confounding, depending on measurement structure. When no measured set blocks every path, the effect is not backdoor-identified; use sensitivity, bounds, an alternative design or a narrower claim rather than letting regularization choose a convenient set.

deepSections.title: Graphs are versioned assumptions and diagnostic tools
deepSections.body: Store node definitions, timing, edge rationale, latent variables, target effect and candidate adjustment sets with the analysis. Map every model feature back to a node and flag descendants of treatment or outcome-window fields. Compare plausible alternative graphs and record whether the estimand remains identified. Use negative-control exposures or outcomes where their assumptions are credible to detect residual structure, not as automatic proof. Conduct quantitative sensitivity analyses for unmeasured confounding and selection. Causal discovery can generate hypotheses under Markov, faithfulness, causal sufficiency or other assumptions, but equivalence classes and hidden variables limit orientation. Production policy changes can alter edges—for example, a risk score begins causing treatment—so the graph and evaluation design must be reviewed whenever the system intervenes.

workedExamples.title: Confounder versus mediator
workedExamples.body: Baseline severity causes treatment and outcome, so it should be adjusted for the total treatment effect. Post-treatment biomarker lies on treatment→biomarker→outcome; adjusting for it changes the question and can introduce bias through unmeasured biomarker-outcome causes.

workedExamples.title: Collider selection
workedExamples.body: Skill and family connections independently cause admission. Among admitted applicants, low connections imply unusually high skill and vice versa, creating a negative association even if the causes are independent in the applicant population.

exercises.prompt: In A←C→Y, what does conditioning on C do?
exercises.solution: It blocks the backdoor fork between A and Y, supporting adjustment if the remaining assumptions hold.

exercises.prompt: Why avoid adjusting for A→M→Y when estimating the total effect?
exercises.solution: M carries part of the effect; conditioning blocks that pathway and changes the estimand, possibly adding mediator-related bias.

exercises.prompt: Why can filtering rows create collider bias?
exercises.solution: Dataset inclusion is conditioning on a selection variable; if multiple causes feed selection, their path can become open within the selected sample.

lessons.title: Profiling & Benchmarking ML Systems
lessons.interviewAnswer: I optimize only after measuring. I separate data loading, preprocessing, host-to-device transfer, model execution and postprocessing; warm up GPU kernels, synchronize correctly, and report latency distributions plus throughput rather than one timing number.
keyPoints: profile first
warmup
GPU synchronization
p50/p95/p99 + throughput
lessons.why: “The model is slow” can actually mean disk I/O, tokenization, CPU transforms or queueing. Bad benchmarks lead to expensive optimizations that change nothing.
lessons.intuition: Treat latency like a budget with line items. Measure each stage before deciding whether to change the model or infrastructure.
lessons.deepDive: GPU work is asynchronous, so naive wall-clock measurements can be misleading. Benchmark representative batch sizes and input shapes after warmup. Throughput and latency often trade off; p95/p99 expose tail behavior that averages hide.
lessons.workedExample: If a 200 ms request spends 130 ms decoding an image, 50 ms in the model and 20 ms elsewhere, TensorRT on the model cannot deliver a 5× end-to-end speedup.
commonMistakes: Timing one GPU inference without warmup/synchronization.
Optimizing FLOPs while ignoring data loading and serialization.

followUps.question: How do throughput and latency conflict?

lessons.description: Profiling & Benchmarking ML Systems is a core topic in AI / ML Performance & Scaling. “The model is slow” can actually mean disk I/O, tokenization, CPU transforms or queueing. Bad benchmarks lead to expensive optimizations that change nothing. This chapter turns the interview-level summary into a complete engineering and analytical treatment. The starting mental model is: Treat latency like a budget with line items. Measure each stage before deciding whether to change the model or infrastructure. The formal and implementation discussion builds from profile first, warmup, GPU synchronization, p50/p95/p99 + throughput, while keeping the unit of data, objective, assumptions, and failure boundaries explicit. The original technical core is preserved: GPU work is asynchronous, so naive wall-clock measurements can be misleading. Benchmark representative batch sizes and input shapes after warmup. Throughput and latency often trade off; p95/p99 expose tail behavior that averages hide. Rather than treating those statements as isolated facts, the chapter connects them to data preparation, evaluation design, numerical or systems behavior, and choices that change under scale or distribution shift. You will work through two concrete scenarios, a runnable Python lab with assertions, and two original conceptual visuals. The lab is intentionally small enough to run locally while still exposing an invariant that should remain true in a larger implementation. The production section translates the concept into monitoring, versioning, rollback, and failure-handling requirements. Production performance tests should run in CI/load tests on representative hardware and track regressions by model/version. The broader module context is profiling, mixed precision, quantization, distributed training and inference optimization. The goal is not memorization: by the end, you should be able to define the contract, explain the mechanism.

deepSections.title: Define the problem contract before the technique
deepSections.body: A rigorous explanation of Profiling & Benchmarking ML Systems starts with the contract, not the library call. In AI / ML Performance & Scaling, the relevant artifact is models, kernels, tensor shapes, memory, hardware, and request workloads, and the intended output is lower latency/cost or higher throughput without unacceptable quality loss. State the unit of observation or request, what information is available at decision time, which variables are controlled versus observed, and what success means. “The model is slow” can actually mean disk I/O, tokenization, CPU transforms or queueing. Bad benchmarks lead to expensive optimizations that change nothing. The key ideas — profile first, warmup, GPU synchronization, p50/p95/p99 + throughput — only become meaningful when tied to a concrete input and output. For example, the same mechanism can be valid for an offline batch but invalid for an online request if it depends on unavailable future information, expensive global state, or a representation that is not versioned at serving time. Write down assumptions about independence, stationarity, label quality, ordering, capacity, or trust boundaries when they matter. Separate the statistical estimand or computational result from the estimator or implementation used to obtain it. Also separate correctness from convenience: a popular API can faithfully execute the wrong problem definition. A useful interview answer therefore names the goal, the information boundary, the dominant trade-off, and one failure mode before adding details. In production, this same contract becomes the basis for schemas, tests, SLOs, monitoring, and rollback.

deepSections.title: Mechanism and representation
deepSections.body: The working intuition for Profiling & Benchmarking ML Systems is: Treat latency like a budget with line items. Measure each stage before deciding whether to change the model or infrastructure. The technical core is: GPU work is asynchronous, so naive wall-clock measurements can be misleading. Benchmark representative batch sizes and input shapes after warmup. Throughput and latency often trade off; p95/p99 expose tail behavior that averages hide. Treat that description as a sequence of transformations and invariants. First identify what representation enters each step, what state or parameters are read, what transformation occurs, and what representation leaves. Then ask which quantities are learned, estimated, cached, partitioned, or fixed by design. The chapter's key points give a compact checklist: profile first, warmup, GPU synchronization, p50/p95/p99 + throughput. Each point should be explainable both conceptually and operationally. A concept is understood only when you can predict what changes after perturbing an input, removing a component, changing scale, or violating an assumption. Shape, units, ordering, normalization, and data type are part of the mechanism because many real failures are interface failures rather than failures of the underlying theory. For learned systems, distinguish forward computation from parameter updates; for data systems, distinguish event-time truth from processing-time state; for distributed or cloud systems, distinguish logical semantics from physical placement. This decomposition is also the basis for debugging: inspect intermediate values, compare against a tiny reference implementation, and verify local invariants before blaming the most sophisticated component.

deepSections.title: Formal view, objective, and invariants
deepSections.body: A compact formal statement prevents hand-waving. For Profiling & Benchmarking ML Systems, the existing mathematical or logical anchor is: define the transformation as a function from valid inputs and state to outputs, then state the invariant that must hold for every valid execution. Do not memorize symbols without semantics. Name the domain of every quantity, whether it is observed or latent, and what is optimized or conserved. If an objective is minimized, ask what population quantity its empirical version estimates and whether weighting changes that target. If there is no optimization objective, identify the safety or correctness invariant instead: ordering, idempotence, conservation, normalization, boundedness, monotonicity, consistency, or resource limits. Numerical details matter whenever repeated operations amplify rounding or conditioning problems. Systems details matter whenever retries, parallelism, caching, or partial failure can produce a different logical result. Statistical details matter whenever data reuse or selection changes the sampling distribution. A strong implementation test usually expresses at least one invariant as an assertion on a toy case, plus a second test that fails when a key assumption is deliberately violated. The runnable lab follows that pattern so the chapter has an executable claim rather than code that merely prints a plausible number.

deepSections.title: Design choices and trade-offs
deepSections.body: There is rarely one universally best configuration of Profiling & Benchmarking ML Systems. The useful question is which trade-off matters for the declared workload. Start with the key points profile first, warmup, GPU synchronization, p50/p95/p99 + throughput and ask how each affects accuracy or correctness, compute, memory, latency, sample efficiency, interpretability, and operational complexity. Prefer a simple baseline when it is easier to validate and already meets the decision threshold. Add complexity only when a measured failure mode justifies it. Hyperparameters and architecture choices should therefore map to observable consequences rather than folklore. At small scale, an exact method may be clearer; at large scale, approximation, batching, partitioning, caching, streaming, quantization, or asynchronous work may be necessary. Those changes create new error surfaces, so every optimization needs a quality or correctness comparison against the reference behavior. Also distinguish offline economics from online economics. A method that saves training time may increase serving cost; a denser representation may improve quality but violate memory limits; a stronger consistency guarantee may reduce throughput; a more aggressive safety rule may increase false positives. deepSections.title: Evaluation and diagnostics
deepSections.body: Evaluation for Profiling & Benchmarking ML Systems must test the claim the system will make in operation. Appropriate evidence in this module includes profiles, p50/p95/p99 latency, throughput, memory, quality deltas, and hardware utilization. Do not collapse everything into one average. Slice by the dimensions that change difficulty: time, horizon, class, scale, entity, language, device, traffic regime, subgroup, or workload shape as appropriate. Always compare against a meaningful baseline on the same examples or requests. Keep comparisons paired when possible so improvement is not confused with a change in evaluation population. If labels or outcomes arrive late, define maturity before scoring. If the system is stochastic, use repeated seeds or confidence intervals; if observations are dependent, use a dependence-aware uncertainty procedure rather than row-level iid assumptions. Diagnostics should include input validity, intermediate-state checks, output distribution checks, and resource behavior. For probabilistic outputs, evaluate calibration as well as discrimination or sharpness. For ranking or generation, combine task metrics with qualitative failure review. For infrastructure, test both steady state and recovery behavior. A release gate should specify what must improve, what must not regress, and which failures are blocking even if the global average looks good.

deepSections.title: Failure modes and debugging strategy
deepSections.body: The dominant risks around Profiling & Benchmarking ML Systems include memory bandwidth limits, synchronization, underutilization, numerical drift, and queueing. Existing chapter cautions are also important: Timing one GPU inference without warmup/synchronization. Optimizing FLOPs while ignoring data loading and serialization. A debugging process should make these risks observable. Start from the smallest reproducible case and verify the data contract. Check shapes, units, ordering, timestamps, identifiers, missingness, labels, masks, seeds, and configuration before changing the algorithm. Next verify a baseline and an invariant. Then inspect intermediate representations or state transitions to locate the first point where expected behavior diverges. Separate data bugs, objective mismatch, optimization or numerical issues, capacity limits, and deployment integration problems because they require different remedies. Introduce controlled perturbations: duplicate an event, reorder input, remove a feature, change batch size, delay a dependency, corrupt one field, or reduce precision. A robust implementation should either preserve its invariant or fail loudly according to a documented policy. Finally, test recovery. Retries should not duplicate side effects, model rollback should restore a compatible preprocessing path, and cached or checkpointed state should have a version. A system that works only on the happy path is not a complete implementation of the concept.

deepSections.title: Production operation, monitoring, and communication
deepSections.body: Shipping Profiling & Benchmarking ML Systems means operating a versioned contract over time. Production performance tests should run in CI/load tests on representative hardware and track regressions by model/version. Persist the model, code, data or schema version, configuration, dependencies, and any state needed to reproduce behavior. Monitor the inputs that drive the mechanism, the outputs users experience, and the internal resource or quality signals that predict failure. Use separate alerts for correctness, quality, latency, saturation, data freshness, and safety so one aggregate health score does not hide the cause. Canary or shadow changes when the blast radius is meaningful. Define rollback artifacts in advance and verify that rollback restores compatible schemas, feature logic, tokenizer or preprocessing state, and dependent services. Record enough request or batch metadata to reproduce failures without retaining data that violates privacy or retention requirements. That sequence demonstrates understanding more reliably than listing tool names. The final question is always operational: what signal would tell you this implementation is no longer trustworthy, and what safe action follows?

tensor cores

lab.goal: Use PyTorch autocast safely for inference and verify output shape/finite values.
lab.buildIt:
import torch
device=torch.device('cuda' if torch.cuda.is_available() else 'cpu')
device_type=device.type
amp_dtype=torch.float16 if device_type=='cuda' else torch.bfloat16
model=torch.nn.Sequential(torch.nn.Linear(128,256),torch.nn.ReLU(),torch.nn.Linear(256,10)).to(device).eval()
x=torch.randn(64,128,device=device)
with torch.inference_mode(), torch.autocast(device_type=device_type,dtype=amp_dtype):
    y=model(x)
lab.useIt:
# GradScaler is useful for CUDA FP16 training; it is disabled on CPU/BF16.
scaler=torch.amp.GradScaler('cuda',enabled=(device_type=='cuda'))
output_dtype=y.dtype
lab.verifyIt:
assert y.shape==(64,10)
assert torch.isfinite(y).all()
assert y.device.type==device_type
assert output_dtype in {torch.float16,torch.bfloat16,torch.float32}

lab.goal: Compare dynamic INT8 quantization with the FP32 module on CPU.
lab.buildIt:
import torch
m=torch.nn.Sequential(torch.nn.Linear(128,256),torch.nn.ReLU(),torch.nn.Linear(256,10)).eval()
x=torch.randn(32,128); y_fp=m(x)
q=torch.ao.quantization.quantize_dynamic(m,{torch.nn.Linear},dtype=torch.qint8)
y_q=q(x); print((y_fp-y_q).abs().mean().item())
lab.useIt:
import io
b1=io.BytesIO(); b2=io.BytesIO(); torch.save(m.state_dict(),b1); torch.save(q.state_dict(),b2)
print('bytes fp32/int8',len(b1.getvalue()),len(b2.getvalue()))
lab.verifyIt:
assert y_q.shape==y_fp.shape
assert torch.isfinite(y_q).all()

lessons.interviewAnswer: Pruning removes low-value parameters or structure; distillation trains a smaller student to mimic a larger teacher. Both can reduce serving cost, but structured pruning usually maps to hardware better than arbitrary sparsity, and distillation quality depends on the teacher targets and task.

lessons.description: Batching, Queueing & Throughput is a core topic in AI / ML Performance & Scaling. Production capacity is often limited more by poor batching than by raw model speed. This chapter turns the interview-level summary into a complete engineering and analytical treatment. The starting mental model is: One GPU prefers doing a useful chunk of work at once; users prefer not waiting for other requests. Serving design balances those goals. The formal and implementation discussion builds from batch size, latency-throughput trade-off, dynamic batching, queueing, while keeping the unit of data, objective, assumptions, and failure boundaries explicit. The original technical core is preserved: For LLMs, sequence lengths vary and continuous batching can admit new requests as others finish. Memory capacity, KV cache and tail latency often determine maximum useful batch size. Rather than treating those statements as isolated facts, the chapter connects them to data preparation, evaluation design, numerical or systems behavior, and choices that change under scale or distribution shift. You will work through two concrete scenarios, a runnable Python lab with assertions, and two original conceptual visuals. The lab is intentionally small enough to run locally while still exposing an invariant that should remain true in a larger implementation. The production section translates the concept into monitoring, versioning, rollback, and failure-handling requirements. Autoscaling should consider queue depth, GPU utilization and latency; overload protection is part of correctness. The broader module context is profiling, mixed precision, quantization, distributed training and inference optimization. The goal is not memorization: by the end, you should be able to define the contract, explain the mechanism, choose a defensible evaluation, diagnose common errors, and describe what has to be true before shipping the idea in a real Data, ML, or AI system.
