lessons.title: Missingness: MCAR, MAR & MNAR
lessons.interviewAnswer: Let R indicate whether a value is observed. MCAR means R is independent of observed and missing values; MAR means missingness may depend on observed data but not the missing value after conditioning; MNAR means it still depends on the unseen value or unobserved causes. These are assumptions about the data-generating process and MNAR versus MAR is generally not testable from observed data alone. I preserve missingness masks and reason codes, analyze patterns by time/source/covariates, choose design-consistent weighting or multiple imputation, prevent leakage, propagate uncertainty, and run MNAR sensitivity analyses.
keyPoints: Missingness is data with a mechanism and provenance
MAR is conditional, not 'random-looking'
Observed data cannot generally distinguish MAR from MNAR
Imputation model and analysis model must be congenial
Production missingness can shift and become informative
lessons.why: Nulls can mean not applicable, not measured, below detection, user refusal, device outage, late arrival, or join failure. Collapsing them into one `NaN` erases the mechanism needed for valid analysis. Complete cases may represent a healthier or more engaged population; mean imputation distorts variance and relationships; model-based imputation can leak outcomes or future data. Interviews ask MCAR/MAR/MNAR definitions, but robust work also tracks operational reason codes and uncertainty. In production, a missingness indicator can become a powerful proxy for workflow or access and then break when collection policy changes. The correct response begins with the generating process, not a preferred imputer.
lessons.intuition: Suppose blood pressure is missing. Under MCAR, a random label-printer failure decides which values vanish, unrelated to any patient information. Under MAR, older patients are more likely to miss the measurement, but after conditioning on observed age, missingness no longer depends on the unseen pressure. Under MNAR, people with very high unseen pressure avoid measurement even after known covariates are considered. The observed table can reveal age differences between observed and missing groups, contradicting MCAR, but it cannot reveal the unseen within-age pressure difference without assumptions or external data. Every method fills that information gap with an assumption, whether explicit or hidden.
lessons.deepDive: Missingness analysis augments the data model with indicators R and, when needed, a response model p(R|Y,X). The taxonomy is relative to which variables are observed and included, so richer auxiliary data can make a MAR assumption more plausible without proving it.
lessons.workedExample: A severity biomarker is observed only when clinicians order a test. Ordering depends on observed triage score and, within a triage level, on symptoms not recorded in the dataset. Conditioning on triage alone may leave MNAR selection. Mean imputation would flatten severity and bias relationships. Add available symptoms and clinician/site/time variables, use multiple imputation under a MAR model, then shift missing biomarker values upward in delta sensitivity analyses. Separately, a one-day device outage creates missing telemetry across all users; that pipeline mechanism is addressed by incident flags and time exclusion, not patient-level imputation. The report keeps these reasons distinct.
commonMistakes: Defining MAR as missingness that looks random or has no obvious pattern.
Assuming an imputer recovers truth without a missingness and outcome model.
Using mean/zero imputation and then treating filled values as observed with unchanged variance.
Fitting imputation on full data or using future/outcome information unavailable at prediction time.
Collapsing structural not-applicable values, censoring, refusal, and pipeline failure into the same null.

followUps.question: Can you test whether data are MNAR?
followUps.answer: Not generally from observed data alone, because the defining dependence involves unseen values. External follow-up, instruments, design information, or sensitivity assumptions are needed.

followUps.question: When is a missing indicator useful?
followUps.answer: It can represent an informative observation process and help prediction, but its meaning may be unstable or unfair. Keep reason provenance and monitor policy/source changes.

followUps.question: Why use multiple rather than single imputation?
followUps.answer: Multiple imputation propagates uncertainty about missing values through between-imputation variation; single imputation treats guesses as known and usually understates uncertainty.

lessons.production: Define a missingness taxonomy and store masks, reason codes, source stage, eligibility, detection/censoring limit, event/arrival times, and imputation version. Monitor rates and co-missingness by source, time, group, device, and model feature; alert on mechanism proxies and schema changes, not only overall percentage. Fit imputers within training boundaries and version features for serving parity. Validate support, constraints, calibration, downstream slice behavior, and uncertainty. Keep raw and imputed values separate and restrict sensitive reason codes. Provide fallback behavior when a required feature is missing, including abstention or alternate model. Refit or roll back imputer and dependent model together. Publish sensitivity ranges when MNAR could alter important decisions.
lessons.description: Missing data are generated by a process. MCAR, MAR, and MNAR describe conditional relationships between missingness indicators and data, not visual patterns a dataset can prove from observed cells alone. This chapter defines unit versus item nonresponse, structural versus censored missingness, Rubin's mechanisms, ignorability conditions, complete-case analysis, indicator methods, single and multiple imputation, inverse-probability weighting, likelihood-based estimation, and sensitivity analysis. You will learn why filling every null is not a solution, why outcome imputation must respect train/test and temporal boundaries, how missingness indicators can be predictive yet unstable, and why uncertainty from imputation must be propagated rather than treating guessed values as observed. The worked example contrasts lab tests ordered by severity with device-sensor outages. The lab simulates MCAR and outcome-related missingness, quantifies complete-case bias, applies a valid observed-covariate adjustment, and verifies assumptions. Production guidance covers reason codes, masks, imputation artifacts, monitoring, privacy, model serving, and rollback. The emphasis is defensible inference, not cosmetically complete tables.
learningObjectives: Define MCAR, MAR, and MNAR using missingness indicators and observed/unobserved data.
Distinguish structural absence, censoring, item nonresponse, unit nonresponse, and pipeline failures before choosing treatment.
Select complete-case, weighting, likelihood, or multiple-imputation methods with explicit assumptions and uncertainty propagation.
Design missingness diagnostics, sensitivity analyses, and production monitoring without leaking future or target information.

deepSections.title: Structural, censored, unit, item, and pipeline missingness
deepSections.body: Structural missingness is logically not applicable, such as pregnancy field for an ineligible unit, and should use an explicit category or mask rather than imputed biology. Censoring tells an inequality or interval, such as measurement below detection, and retains information. Unit nonresponse removes an entire sampled unit; item nonresponse removes fields. Attrition is longitudinal missingness whose hazard evolves. Pipeline missingness includes late data, parse failures, unmatched joins, and permission filters. Preserve reason, stage, timestamp, and eligibility denominator. Different mechanisms can coexist in one column, so a single imputation rule is rarely defensible.

deepSections.title: Rubin mechanisms in conditional form
deepSections.body: Write Y=(Y_obs,Y_mis) and R as observation indicators. MCAR asserts p(R|Y_obs,Y_mis)=p(R), a strong condition under which complete cases remain representative though precision falls. MAR asserts p(R|Y_obs,Y_mis)=p(R|Y_obs): after conditioning on observed variables included in the model, missingness does not depend on missing values. MNAR allows residual dependence on Y_mis. MAR does not mean missingness is unrelated to data, and it is model-relative. Observed patterns can reject simple MCAR explanations, but MAR versus MNAR generally needs untestable assumptions, follow-up, instruments, refreshment samples, or sensitivity parameters.

deepSections.title: Deletion, weighting, likelihood, and imputation
deepSections.body: Complete-case analysis can be valid for some parameters under MCAR or special outcome-dependent designs, but wastes information and often changes population. Pairwise deletion creates inconsistent covariance matrices and denominators. Inverse response weighting needs observed predictors of missingness, positivity, and a correct propensity model. Full-information likelihood integrates missing values under a joint model. Multiple imputation draws several plausible completed datasets, fits the analysis to each, and combines within- and between-imputation uncertainty. Single mean imputation understates variance and weakens correlations. Include outcomes and auxiliary variables appropriately during training analysis, but never leak future labels into production features.

deepSections.title: Compatible imputation, splits, and constraints
deepSections.body: Imputation models should respect variable support, nonlinearities, interactions, time ordering, clusters, survey design, and the substantive analysis. Predictive mean matching can preserve observed ranges but has donor assumptions. For time series, future values cannot impute past features in a forecasting evaluation. Fit preprocessing only on training folds and carry missing indicators consistently to validation/serving. Imputed categories must obey referential and logical constraints. Multiple imputation needs enough datasets for stable Monte Carlo error when missing information is high. Store imputation seeds and distinguish original from imputed values so audits and downstream models can treat them differently.

deepSections.title: Diagnostics and MNAR sensitivity
deepSections.body:
Plot missingness matrices, co-missingness, rates by time/source/group, and observed-variable distributions by R. Model R as an outcome to find operational predictors, not to prove MAR. Compare complete-case, weighted, imputed, and bounded analyses. Delta adjustment shifts imputed missing outcomes by plausible amounts; selection and pattern-mixture models parameterize MNAR differently. Report tipping points at which decisions reverse. Use targeted recontact or redundant sensors to learn about missing cases. Missingness fraction alone is not bias; association with outcomes and analysis structure determines harm. Monitor both rate and mechanism proxies after deployment.

Serving-time behavior must match training-time missingness semantics. Test absent fields, explicit nulls, stale values, and upstream timeouts separately because they may trigger different defaults. When a reason code changes, treat it as a schema change: reassess assumptions, recalibrate uncertainty, and compare decisions before and after deployment.

lessons.math: MCAR: R independent of (Y_obs,Y_mis). MAR: R independent of Y_mis conditional on Y_obs under the chosen model. MNAR violates that conditional independence. Under MAR and positivity, inverse-probability identity E[R Y/pi(X)]=E[Y] motivates weighting when pi(X)=P(R=1|X). Multiple-imputation total variance combines average within-imputation variance W and between-imputation variance B as T=W+(1+1/m)B for m imputations under Rubin's combining rules and their assumptions.

workedExamples.title: Clinician-ordered biomarker versus device outage
workedExamples.body: Separate clinical selection from operational loss, build a richer MAR analysis with uncertainty, perform MNAR delta sensitivity, and route the outage through incident-aware time handling rather than one universal imputer.

exercises.prompt: Missingness depends on observed age but not unseen income after age. Which mechanism relative to this model?
exercises.solution: MAR, because R may depend on observed age but is conditionally independent of missing income given included observed variables.

exercises.prompt: Why can complete-case analysis be biased under MAR?
exercises.solution: Complete cases have a different observed-covariate distribution. Unless the estimand/model has special invariance, dropping them changes the target; weighting or likelihood/imputation can adjust under assumptions.

exercises.prompt: What does a delta sensitivity analysis do?
exercises.solution: It shifts or otherwise relates the missing-value distribution to the MAR-imputed distribution by a plausible unobserved amount and measures when conclusions change.

lab.goal: Simulate MCAR and covariate-dependent missingness, quantify complete-case bias, and verify an observed-stratum adjustment under its assumptions.
lab.buildIt:
import random

def mean(xs): return sum(xs)/len(xs)
def simulate(seed=41,n=20000):
    rng=random.Random(seed); rows=[]
    for _ in range(n):
        group=int(rng.random()<0.4)
        y=10+5*group+rng.gauss(0,1)
        observed_mcar=rng.random()<0.6
        observed_mar=rng.random()<(0.8 if group==0 else 0.25)
        rows.append((group,y,observed_mcar,observed_mar))
    return rows
rows=simulate()
truth=mean([r[1] for r in rows])
mcar_mean=mean([r[1] for r in rows if r[2]])
mar_complete=mean([r[1] for r in rows if r[3]])
# Standardize observed group means to known population group shares.
shares={g:sum(r[0]==g for r in rows)/len(rows) for g in (0,1)}
observed_means={g:mean([r[1] for r in rows if r[0]==g and r[3]]) for g in (0,1)}
adjusted=sum(shares[g]*observed_means[g] for g in (0,1))
lab.useIt:
import numpy as np
a=np.asarray(rows,dtype=float)
numpy_truth=float(a[:,1].mean())
missing_rate_mar=float(1-a[:,3].mean())
lab.verifyIt:
assert abs(truth-numpy_truth) < 1e-12
assert abs(mcar_mean-truth) < 0.08
assert abs(mar_complete-truth) > 0.5
assert abs(adjusted-truth) < 0.08
assert 0 < missing_rate_mar < 1
assert simulate(seed=41,n=50)==simulate(seed=41,n=50)
lab.shipIt: Preserve masks and reason codes, fit adjustment/imputation only within valid train/time boundaries, version assumptions and seeds, monitor mechanism shifts, and publish MNAR sensitivity for decision-critical outcomes.

lessons.title: Choosing the Right Statistical Visualization
lessons.interviewAnswer: I start with the question: compare magnitude, see change over ordered time, inspect a distribution, relate variables, show composition, or locate geography. Then I map the most important quantitative comparison to aligned position or length; use lines only for ordered continuity, scatterplots for paired numeric observations, histograms/ECDFs for distributions, bars for category magnitudes, and small multiples for groups. I state aggregation and uncertainty, use honest scales and accessible redundant encodings, limit color, label units and denominators, and test the chart against raw data and audience decisions.
keyPoints: Task and data semantics determine the chart
Position and length support precise comparison
Aggregation and connection make statistical claims
Scales, baselines, and color carry meaning
Accessibility and uncertainty belong in the specification
lessons.why: A chart can be numerically correct yet make the wrong question easy. A pie chart forces angle comparisons when stakeholders need precise ranking; a line connects unordered categories and invents continuity; a mean bar hides a bimodal distribution; a heatmap makes a color legend carry differences that a table would show more accurately. Interviews ask chart choice because it reveals analytical reasoning. In production, charts are interfaces over semantic models, and their defaults—aggregation, sorting, filtering, scale, missingness—can change decisions. Treating encoding as a formal mapping makes visualization testable and maintainable rather than subjective decoration.
lessons.intuition: The eye is a measurement instrument with strengths and biases. It compares two marks along a common baseline quickly and accurately; it estimates angles, areas, and saturated colors less precisely. Put the decision's most important quantity on the strongest available channel. Every mark also implies a statistical object: one point can be an observation or a mean; a band can be spread or confidence; a line can be interpolation or mere connection. Labels and legends define those objects. Small multiples trade one overloaded view for repeated comparable panels, preserving a common scale so the eye can scan differences. Good design reduces the mental transformations required to answer the stated question.
lessons.deepDive: Visualization design can be described as data fields plus transformations plus marks plus encodings plus scales plus guides plus interaction. Each layer should be justified by the task and auditable against the underlying data.
lessons.workedExample: An executive chart uses clustered bars for monthly revenue, margin percentage, order count, and NPS on two axes across twelve regions, producing 576 marks and incomparable units. Redesign as a dashboard row: revenue trend with target and interval, margin small-multiple lines sharing a percent scale, ranked regional revenue dot plot, and NPS distribution with sample sizes. Use one highlight color for the selected region, direct labels, and a freshness timestamp. Each visual has one task, metric definition, unit, denominator, and uncertainty. The raw table is linked for lookup and accessibility.
commonMistakes: Choosing a chart type before defining the audience's comparison and the mark's statistical meaning.
Connecting unordered categories with lines or using area/angle when precise magnitude comparison matters.
Showing means without sample size, distribution, uncertainty, or aggregation definition.
Using truncated bar baselines, dual axes, rainbow scales, or 3D perspective to dramatize patterns.
Relying on color and hover alone, excluding color-vision, keyboard, mobile, print, or screen-reader users.

followUps.question: When should a bar chart start at zero?
followUps.answer: Because length from a baseline encodes magnitude, quantitative bars generally require zero. If a narrow range matters, use dots or lines with clearly labeled axes and context instead of truncated bars.

followUps.question: How do you show many overlapping points?
followUps.answer: Use transparency, small marks, jitter for discrete overlap, hexbin/density, stratified sampling with disclosure, or facets. Preserve totals and avoid a sample that distorts density.

followUps.question: What should an uncertainty band say?
followUps.answer: State whether it is SD, SE, confidence, credible, prediction, or another interval; name the level, independent unit, method, and what the center line estimates.

lessons.production: Store chart specifications beside metric contracts: field, grain, aggregation, filter, unit, scale, baseline, sort, palette, interval method, denominator, and empty/missing behavior. Validate spec/data type compatibility and snapshot outputs across light/dark, desktop/mobile, print, and localization. Run contrast and color-vision checks; provide keyboard navigation, alt summaries, and accessible tables. Track sampling and rendering thresholds for large data. Show freshness, source, filter state, and revision. Prevent sensitive small-cell disclosure in marks and tooltips. Monitor broken queries, stale data, clipped labels, and schema drift. Roll back metric and chart spec together; a visually unchanged chart over a redefined metric is a semantic incident.
lessons.description: Statistical visualization maps data fields and uncertainty to visual channels—position, length, angle, area, color, shape, texture, and facets—so a specific comparison becomes perceptually accessible. The best chart follows the analytical task, variable type, data grain, and audience; it is not chosen from a gallery by aesthetics. This chapter develops a task-first selection framework for distributions, trends, relationships, rankings, parts-to-whole, flows, geospatial patterns, and uncertainty. It explains perceptual accuracy, scales and transforms, overplotting, aggregation, small multiples, color semantics, accessibility, annotations, interactivity, and the distinction between raw observations, estimates, and model outputs. You will learn why bars need meaningful baselines, why line connections imply order, why area and angle comparisons are difficult, and how uncertainty must be encoded and labeled. The worked example redesigns a crowded multi-metric executive chart. The lab builds a declarative chart-spec validator and verifies task/type constraints alongside a matplotlib implementation. Production guidance covers semantic chart contracts, responsive design, accessible alternatives, testing, rendering, data freshness, privacy, and rollback.
learningObjectives: Choose a chart from the analytical task, field type, grain, ordering, and uncertainty rather than decoration.
Map high-priority comparisons to perceptually accurate channels and use facets or aggregation without hiding structure.
Select scales, baselines, color systems, labels, and accessibility features that preserve data meaning.
Design and test chart specifications as versioned semantic interfaces backed by data and metric contracts.

deepSections.title: Task and field semantics first
deepSections.body: Identify whether the user needs lookup, comparison, rank, trend, distribution, correlation, composition, deviation, flow, or spatial pattern. Classify fields as quantitative, ordinal, nominal, temporal, geographic, or identifiers; distinguish event time from processing time. State grain and whether marks represent rows, bins, aggregates, estimates, or predictions. A user ID is nominal even if stored as an integer. A Likert category is ordered but unequal spacing may not be defensible. Time supports order and duration but irregular gaps must remain visible. One chart should have a primary task; secondary questions can use linked detail or additional views.

deepSections.title: Perceptual channels and chart families
deepSections.body: Aligned position supports precise magnitude comparisons, followed by unaligned position and length; angle, area, volume, and color intensity are generally harder to compare exactly. Use bars for category magnitude with a meaningful zero baseline, dots for compact comparisons when zero is not essential, lines for ordered sequences, scatterplots for paired numeric values, ECDF/histogram for distributions, and matrices/heatmaps for dense two-dimensional patterns. Pie or donut charts may support a small simple part-to-whole message but perform poorly for close categories. 3D perspective and volume rarely improve quantitative judgment.

deepSections.title: Raw observations, summaries, and uncertainty
deepSections.body: Overplotting can hide density; use transparency, jitter for discrete overlap, hexbin/binning, sampling with disclosure, or density contours. A line plot that averages repeated units must label its estimator and uncertainty; otherwise readers may interpret one trajectory. Error bars need definitions—SD, SE, CI, credible, or prediction interval—and a visible reference. Show raw points or distribution when sample size permits. For unequal group sizes, bar height alone conceals precision and support. Aggregation can trigger Simpson's paradox, so offer meaningful facets or stratified views and keep denominators visible.

deepSections.title: Scales, baselines, color, and transforms
deepSections.body: Linear scales preserve additive differences; log scales preserve ratios and require positive support or a documented transform. Truncated bar baselines exaggerate length differences because bar length encodes magnitude; dot/line charts can use a focused range when clearly labeled. Dual axes invite arbitrary scaling and false correlation; prefer aligned panels. Sequential palettes encode ordered magnitude, diverging palettes require a meaningful midpoint, and qualitative palettes distinguish categories. Avoid rainbow palettes for ordered data. Use colorblind-safe contrast and redundant shape, text, or line style for critical categories. Missing values need an explicit visual state, not a misleading zero color.

deepSections.title: Faceting, annotation, and interaction
deepSections.body:
Small multiples reveal conditional patterns with repeated encodings; use shared scales for comparison or clearly flag free scales. Sort categories by task—value, natural order, or lookup order—not alphabetically by default. Direct labels reduce legend lookup. Annotations should state evidence and context without covering data. Interaction can reveal details, filters, and provenance, but default state must remain honest, URLs should preserve filters, and exports should include them. Tooltips are not an accessible substitute for visible labels or tables. Provide a text/table alternative and keyboard/focus support for essential information.

Test perception with representative tasks, devices, and audiences rather than judging only the authoring monitor. A chart that works at desktop width may collapse labels, hover-only context, or small color differences on mobile. Preserve a textual table or summary so the encoded evidence remains accessible and auditable without the graphic.

lessons.math: A visual encoding maps data value x through a scale s(x) to screen position, length, color, or size. For area encoding, radius must satisfy r proportional to sqrt(value) so area—not radius—represents magnitude. A log axis maps ratios to equal distances: s(x)=a log(x)+b. Aggregated mean at x is sum y_i/n_x, while uncertainty depends on independent units and design, not mark count. When sampling points for rendering, disclose the sampling scheme and retain aggregate invariants so visual density is not mistaken for population frequency.

workedExamples.title: Decompose an overloaded executive chart
workedExamples.body: Separate trend, ranking, and distribution tasks; give each metric its own honest scale and uncertainty; reuse selection state; and provide a table so the interface supports both perception and exact lookup.

exercises.prompt: You need to compare seven category values accurately. Which basic chart and why?
exercises.solution: A sorted bar or dot plot. Aligned position/length supports accurate comparison; direct labels can provide exact values.

exercises.prompt: Why is a line chart misleading for product categories A, B, C?
exercises.solution: A connecting line implies ordered continuity and meaningful interpolation between categories. Use bars/dots unless the x variable has a defensible order and distance.

exercises.prompt: A bubble should represent four times another value. What radius ratio is needed?
exercises.solution: Area must be four times, so radius ratio is sqrt(4)=2. Using four times radius would encode sixteen times area.

lessons.title: Misleading Charts & Visualization Pitfalls
lessons.interviewAnswer: I audit a chart at four layers: data and population; transformation, aggregation, denominator and filters; visual encoding, scale and baseline; and annotation/context. Common traps are truncated bar axes, 3D or area distortion, dual axes, cherry-picked windows, unequal time spacing, changing denominators, misleading bins/colors, overplotting, omitted uncertainty, and causal wording. I reconstruct the underlying table, compare alternate honest views, quantify how the claim changes, and add semantic tests so the correction is reproducible.
keyPoints: A chart inherits every upstream data and metric assumption
Visual geometry can amplify or suppress differences
Selection of windows, bins, groups, and annotations is analytical flexibility
Uncertainty and denominators are essential context
Semantic review complements pixel snapshots
lessons.why: Dashboards often become the final authority for decisions, so a subtle denominator change can matter more than a code bug. Visual distortion is not limited to deliberate propaganda: BI defaults may truncate axes, auto-sort, smooth, or aggregate; filters can persist invisibly; and a technically accurate percentage can compare different populations. Interviews ask classic misleading charts, but senior practice requires tracing the entire semantic pipeline and establishing preventive controls. Correcting a chart without correcting its metric, query, or historical annotations leaves the incident unresolved.
lessons.intuition: A visualization is an argument made with geometry. If the bar baseline begins at 95, a change from 96 to 98 occupies three times the visible height even though the actual ratio is 1.02. If bubble radius doubles, area quadruples. If two time series get independently chosen axes, almost any pair can look correlated. If only a favorable month is shown, the x-axis performs selection. Ask what physical screen distance the chart assigns to a numerical change, which observations are absent, and which alternative framing would reverse the impression. Then inspect whether the stated question actually needs that geometry.
lessons.deepDive: Chart integrity is a chain property. Correct rendering of a wrong denominator is still wrong; correct data on a perceptually deceptive scale can still mislead. Audit from source to sentence, not just pixels.
lessons.workedExample: A retention dashboard shows improvement from 96% to 98% using bars starting at 95%, so the new bar is three times the visible height. The old metric used all activated users; the new month excludes users whose events arrived after seven days, shrinking the denominator and preferentially dropping churners. Restoring a zero-baseline dot/bar alternative and a consistent matured cohort changes rates to 96.0% versus 96.4%, with interval spanning the business threshold. The correction notes the historical denominator bug, rebuilds all months, updates the metric contract, and invalidates decisions made from the old view.
commonMistakes: Auditing only axis labels while trusting filters, joins, denominators, and aggregation.
Treating every nonzero baseline as deceptive instead of distinguishing bars from positional charts and documenting task.
Using dual axes or 3D because defaults make unrelated trends look compelling.
Changing bins, windows, color limits, or smoothing until a desired pattern appears without disclosing selection.
Correcting the picture while leaving historical metrics, narrative text, exports, and downstream decisions unchanged.

followUps.question: Are truncated axes always wrong?
followUps.answer: Truncated bar axes are usually misleading because length encodes magnitude. Focused dot/line charts can use nonzero ranges when ticks, context, and task make the positional difference explicit.

followUps.question: Why are dual axes risky?
followUps.answer: Each series has an independent affine mapping to pixels, so origins/ranges can manufacture slope alignment. Use shared units, indexed change, or separate aligned panels.

followUps.question: How do you automate chart integrity?
followUps.answer: Validate metric/denominator contracts, field types, baselines, time order, scale transforms, missing-value states, color accessibility, filter state, and snapshot rendering; combine with human semantic review.

lessons.production: Require chart review to inspect query, semantic metric, population, numerator/denominator, filter defaults, data maturity, aggregation, scale, and annotation. Encode invariants in chart specs and metric tests: zero baseline for bars, monotonic time, stable denominator definition, explicit missing state, area proportionality, and uncertainty metadata. Snapshot across themes/devices but treat pixel tests as only layout evidence. Track dashboard versions, filter URLs, freshness, source lineage, and exports. Provide accessible tables and avoid sensitive small cells. When a misleading chart ships, assess affected decisions, rebuild history, publish correction and incident notes, and roll back metric/query/spec together. Monitor definition drift and stale annotations after schema changes.
lessons.description: Misleading visualization can arise from incorrect data, dishonest transformations, perceptual distortion, omitted context, or interaction defaults that selectively reveal a story. This chapter analyzes truncated baselines, distorted area and 3D perspective, dual axes, unequal time spacing, cumulative-versus-period confusion, cherry-picked windows, inappropriate smoothing, bin and color manipulation, denominator changes, map-area bias, missing uncertainty, overplotting, and deceptive annotation. You will learn to audit a chart by reconstructing its data transformation, scale, baseline, aggregation, filters, and encoding; distinguish intentional deception from harmful defaults; and design automated semantic checks alongside human review. The worked example deconstructs a dashboard where a truncated axis and changing denominator exaggerate a retention improvement. The lab implements chart-integrity checks for baselines, time order, denominator consistency, and proportional areas, then verifies them against deliberately bad specs. Production guidance covers metric lineage, query review, accessible exports, snapshot testing, issue severity, monitoring, and correction/rollback communication. Every published view should remain reconstructable from its data and specification.
learningObjectives: Trace a visual claim back through filters, aggregation, denominators, transformations, scales, and source data.
Recognize perceptual distortions from baselines, area/volume, dual axes, color, bins, smoothing, and map geometry.
Detect selection and context failures involving time windows, missing groups, uncertainty, and annotation.
Implement semantic visualization checks and correction workflows without assuming every misleading chart is malicious.

deepSections.title: Population, filters, denominators, and aggregation
deepSections.body: Verify source snapshot, eligibility, deduplication, joins, time zones, and exclusions. Recompute numerator and denominator for every rate; inspect whether the population changes across periods or groups. A total can rise while per-user rate falls. Cumulative curves should not be compared with period flows as if equivalent. Weighted averages require weights and component denominators. Aggregation can hide subgroup reversals. Show sample sizes and missing categories, including zeros that a groupby dropped. A chart can faithfully display a query that silently excludes failed records or late outcomes, so query review is part of visualization review.

deepSections.title: Baselines, area, volume, and perspective
deepSections.body: Bar length encodes distance from baseline and should normally start at zero. Focused dot or line plots may truncate with clear ticks because position, not length, carries the comparison. Pictograms, bubbles, and maps must scale area proportional to value; scaling radius or diameter by value squares area distortion. 3D bars add perspective and occlusion without a useful variable, making back marks smaller. Choropleth land area visually dominates population; normalize rates and consider cartograms or dot density when appropriate. Aspect ratio can make slopes look dramatic or flat, so choose and document it for the task.

deepSections.title: Dual axes, time spacing, and selected windows
deepSections.body: Dual y-axes have independently chosen origins and ranges, so visual correlation can be tuned. Prefer indexed values, standardized changes with caveats, or aligned panels. Time axes must preserve irregular gaps; categorical spacing can imply continuity where none exists. Starting after a decline or ending at a peak cherry-picks trend. Compare multiple defensible windows and annotate policy breaks. Seasonal data need year-over-year or seasonal context. Smoothing can lag turning points and conceal extremes; name the method/window and show raw data. Forecast lines need observed/predicted distinction and uncertainty.

deepSections.title: Bins, color, missing data, and overplotting
deepSections.body: Histogram bins can split or merge modes; report rule and inspect sensitivity. Heatmap bin boundaries and color limits can saturate important differences or exaggerate noise. Diverging palettes require a meaningful midpoint; rainbow order is perceptually irregular. Mapping missing values to the minimum color falsely turns unknown into zero. Opacity and sampling can hide density; disclose sampling and use count-preserving alternatives. Category colors should remain stable across panels, and inaccessible red/green distinctions need redundant labels or shapes. Legends must include units, transformations, and out-of-range handling.

deepSections.title: Uncertainty, annotation, and causal rhetoric
deepSections.body:
A point estimate without interval, sample size, or model uncertainty appears exact. Error bars must say what they represent. Selecting only significant or successful groups creates survivorship. Headlines and annotations can assert causation from observational association or call a tiny statistically precise change 'dramatic.' Decorative arrows and highlights steer attention; ensure they correspond to prespecified thresholds or complete context. Show benchmarks, practical thresholds, and adverse outcomes, not only headline wins. A narrative is unavoidable, so make selection criteria and limitations explicit rather than pretending a chart speaks for itself.

Maintain a correction path for published graphics. Store the exact query, transformation, chart specification, data cutoff, and rendered artifact together; then a denominator or scale error can be reproduced, fixed, and compared. Corrections should state what changed and which earlier decisions may have been affected, not silently replace history.

lessons.math: For a bar representing value v from baseline b, visible length is proportional to v-b, so ratios of visible lengths generally differ from ratios of values when b≠0. For bubble area A=pi r^2, encoding value v requires r=c sqrt(v); r proportional to v makes area proportional to v^2. A rate is numerator/denominator, and change in rates can be decomposed from numerator and population-composition changes. Dual-axis pixel mapping y_screen=a_j y+b_j for series j permits arbitrary apparent slope alignment.

workedExamples.title: Retention gain manufactured by baseline and denominator
workedExamples.body: Reconstruct the denominator, enforce outcome maturity, compare honest geometry, add uncertainty and business thresholds, and publish a correction whose lineage reaches both data and chart spec.

exercises.prompt: Values 100 and 110 are bars from baseline 90. What visible-length ratio appears?
exercises.solution: Lengths are 10 and 20, ratio 2, while value ratio is 1.1. The truncated baseline doubles the visual impression.

exercises.prompt: A bubble value is nine times another. What radius ratio encodes area correctly?
exercises.solution: sqrt(9)=3. A radius ratio of nine would create an area ratio of 81.

exercises.prompt: Why can a retention rate rise after excluding late-arriving outcomes?
exercises.solution: If late outcomes disproportionately belong to churners, the denominator/population changes selectively. The display then compares different matured cohorts rather than true improvement.

lessons.title: GroupBy, Pivot & Cohort Analysis
lessons.interviewAnswer: GroupBy is split–apply–combine: partition rows by keys, compute an operation per group, and return an output whose grain depends on aggregation, transformation, or filtering. I declare the output grain, null/category behavior, and additive components, then reconcile to source totals. Pivot reshapes a unique key combination; duplicates require an explicit aggregation, not accidental first value. For cohorts, assign each entity once, compute period age consistently, deduplicate entity-period activity, keep denominators tied to the original eligible cohort, and mark recent right-censored cells as unavailable rather than zero.
keyPoints: Every grouped result has a grain and key contract
Ratios should aggregate numerator and denominator
Pivot duplicates require an explicit rule
Cohort and calendar time are distinct axes
Censoring and late data define which retention cells are observable
lessons.why: A large share of analytics logic is grouping, yet many metric incidents come from grain errors rather than arithmetic. A mean of country conversion rates weights countries equally instead of users; a left join duplicates events before grouping; `dropna=True` removes unknown categories; a cohort dashboard labels unobserved future months as zero. Interviews test API fluency, but rigorous work predicts row counts and defines denominators. In production, grouped tables often become semantic models that feed dashboards and experiments, so reproducibility, incremental backfills, and reconciliation are essential.
lessons.intuition: Imagine sorting receipts into labeled bins, summarizing each bin, then arranging summaries in a grid. The bin label defines the output row. If you keep one result per receipt, that is a transformation, not an aggregation. A pivot only rotates labels into columns after deciding what one cell means. Cohorts add a clock that starts separately for every entity: month 0 is signup month, month 1 the next month. The diagonal edge of a cohort matrix is not poor retention; it is the future. Correct cohort analysis asks which original members were eligible to have reached each age and which were observed active, while preserving calendar date for outages and seasonality.
lessons.deepDive: Grouped analysis is relational algebra plus metric semantics. Associative additive components support distributed and incremental aggregation; ratios, distinct counts, medians, and cohort states require additional merge rules and state.
lessons.workedExample: A January cohort has 100 users and 60 active in month 1; February has 20 users and 18 active. The unweighted average of retention rates is (60%+90%)/2=75%, while user-weighted combined retention is 78/120=65%. Neither is universally correct, but a company-wide retained-user rate uses the latter and must keep counts. A March cohort dashboard displays month 2 as 0% even though the data cutoff is April 15; the cell is unobservable and should be NA. Duplicate event rows had also counted active users twice, producing values above 100%. Deduplicate entity-age and assert bounds.
commonMistakes: Averaging group percentages without preserving numerators, denominators, and intended weights.
Using pivot with duplicate index/column pairs and accepting an arbitrary value or aggregation.
Letting null group keys disappear or unobserved categorical combinations appear without an explicit policy.
Counting events rather than distinct entities in retention and allowing rates above one.
Filling not-yet-mature cohort cells with zero and comparing recent cohorts with complete older cohorts.

followUps.question: What is the difference between aggregate and transform?
followUps.answer: Aggregate reduces each group to summary rows at group grain; transform returns values aligned to the original rows, often broadcasting a group statistic.

followUps.question: Why is average of averages wrong?
followUps.answer: Group means have different denominators. An unweighted average targets an equal-group estimand; the combined individual mean requires weighting by valid counts or weights.

followUps.question: How do late events affect cohorts?
followUps.answer: They can add activity to past cells or reveal an earlier first event that moves an entity's cohort and all ages. Incremental logic must identify and rebuild affected history.

lessons.production: Publish group and cohort metrics from a semantic layer with explicit grain, keys, numerator, denominator, distinctness, null/category behavior, time zone, cutoff, and maturity rule. Preserve long-form components and pivot only for display. Incremental jobs must be idempotent, watermark-aware, and able to rebuild entities whose first event changes. Test source reconciliation, output-key uniqueness, no rates outside bounds, no duplicate entity-age, and full-versus-incremental equality. Monitor cohort sizes, late-event age, unknown groups, sparse/high-cardinality explosion, and freshness. Suppress or aggregate sensitive small cohorts. Version definitions and backfill history deliberately. Rollback model, generated matrices, and dashboard together.
lessons.description: GroupBy and pivot operations transform event-level rows into metrics at a declared output grain. Cohort analysis adds two time axes—when an entity entered and how long it has progressed—so lifecycle behavior is separated from calendar conditions. This chapter develops split–apply–combine semantics, aggregation versus transformation, multi-key grouping, observed versus unobserved categories, null-key handling, weighted rates, ratios of sums, pivot uniqueness, margins, cohort assignment, age calculation, right censoring, retention denominators, and reconciliation. You will learn why average of averages is usually wrong, why groupby can silently drop null keys, how duplicate entity-period rows inflate retention, and why incomplete recent cohorts must not be compared with mature cohorts. The worked example builds a monthly signup-retention matrix and diagnoses a denominator bug. The lab implements grouping and cohort retention from first principles, compares with pandas, and verifies totals, grain, and monotonic eligibility. Production guidance covers semantic models, incremental recomputation, late events, time zones, sparse output, privacy, monitoring, and rollback.
learningObjectives: Declare input and output grain for groupby, aggregation, transformation, and pivot operations.
Compute weighted rates and ratios from additive components without averaging subgroup averages incorrectly.
Construct cohort and age indices with stable entity assignment, mature denominators, and late-event handling.
Verify grouped outputs through reconciliation, uniqueness, category/null semantics, and incremental consistency.

deepSections.title: Input grain, grouping keys, and output shape
deepSections.body: State whether rows are events, entity-days, orders, or snapshots. Group keys define partitions, but aggregation defines one row per observed key combination, transformation returns input-aligned values, and filtering may retain arbitrary rows. In pandas, `as_index`, `group_keys`, `observed`, `sort`, and `dropna` affect shape and semantics; verify current documented defaults rather than rely on memory. Null keys may represent unknown groups and should not vanish silently. Categorical groupers can produce unobserved combinations. Assert uniqueness of output keys and expected row bounds.

deepSections.title: Additive components, weights, and average-of-averages
deepSections.body: Sums and counts combine across partitions. A rate should usually be sum(successes)/sum(eligible), not mean of group rates unless equal group weighting is the estimand. Weighted mean is sum(w x)/sum(w), with weight meaning and support documented. Distinct counts are nonadditive across overlapping groups; use exact set unions or validated sketches. Medians and quantiles need raw values or mergeable summaries with approximation error. Keep numerator and denominator columns in semantic models so downstream slices recompute correctly. Reconcile grouped sums with source totals over complete partitions.

deepSections.title: Pivot, pivot_table, and duplicate cells
deepSections.body: A strict pivot maps each unique index–column pair to one value and should fail when duplicates exist. `pivot_table` aggregates duplicates with an explicit function. First/last is meaningful only with a deterministic order and business rule. Missing cell can mean no activity, not applicable, or incomplete data; choose fill values accordingly. Margins and totals may reapply aggregation rather than sum displayed cells, especially for means and ratios. Wide output can explode with high-cardinality categories; keep long form for computation and pivot at presentation boundaries. Column order should follow time or domain order, not accidental lexical sorting.

deepSections.title: Cohort assignment, age, and retention
deepSections.body: Assign cohort once using first eligible event under a stable identity and time zone. Define period boundaries and age: calendar-month difference, exact-day windows, or billing cycles are not interchangeable. Deduplicate active entity within cohort-age so many events do not count multiple times. Denominator may be original cohort size for classic retention, at-risk population for survival, or eligible exposed population for product analysis; label it. Separate acquisition cohort from activity calendar date. Recent cohorts lack later ages, so cells are censored/NA, not zero. Reinstatement, deletion, identity merges, and backfilled first events require explicit policies.

deepSections.title: Late data, incremental state, and reconciliation
deepSections.body:
Incremental aggregates must be idempotent and update affected groups when late or corrected events arrive. A new earlier signup can move an entity's entire cohort history. Track source watermark and impacted entities/partitions; rebuild a bounded window or maintain change logs. Snapshot facts can double-count state if summed across dates. Time-zone changes shift period boundaries. Verify full-refresh and incremental results on fixtures, reconcile numerator/denominator totals, and monitor cohort-size drift, impossible retention above one, duplicate entity-age records, and mature-cell coverage. Version metric and cohort definitions so historical matrices are interpretable.

When aggregates are computed across partitions, verify associativity before merging partial results. Sums and counts combine cleanly; medians, distinct counts, ratios, and percentiles need sufficient intermediate state or explicit approximation. Reconcile partitioned output against a trusted batch calculation so execution strategy cannot silently redefine the metric.

lessons.math: For group g, weighted mean mu_g=sum_{i in g}w_i x_i/sum_{i in g}w_i. Overall rate=sum_g successes_g/sum_g eligible_g, not generally mean_g(successes_g/eligible_g). For entity u with cohort period c_u and activity period t, age a=t-c_u under the chosen period arithmetic. Classic retention R_{c,a}=|{u:c_u=c and active at age a}|/|{u:c_u=c}|, defined only when cohort c has matured through age a and observation is complete.

workedExamples.title: Weighted retention and censored cohort cells
workedExamples.body: Retain cohort-size and active-user components, distinguish equal-cohort from user-weighted estimands, deduplicate entity-age activity, and mask ages not yet observable at the data cutoff.

exercises.prompt: Groups have rates 10/20 and 90/180. What are unweighted and combined rates?
exercises.solution: Both group rates are 50%, so unweighted and combined are 50%. This equality is incidental; different group rates and sizes generally differ.

exercises.prompt: January cohort is 100 users and 40 active at age 2; data cutoff occurs before March activity is complete. What should the cell show?
exercises.solution: NA/incomplete rather than 40% or 0%, unless the maturity rule says age 2 is fully observed. Denominator and cutoff must be explicit.

exercises.prompt: Why can strict pivot failure be useful?
exercises.solution: Duplicate index/column pairs reveal grain ambiguity. Failing forces an explicit aggregation or deduplication rule instead of silently losing or combining values.

import pandas as pd
df=pd.DataFrame(events,columns=['user','cohort','period'])
df['age']=df['period']-df['cohort']
pd_active=df.drop_duplicates(['user','cohort','age']).groupby(['cohort','age'])['user'].nunique()
pd_sizes=df.drop_duplicates(['user','cohort']).groupby('cohort')['user'].nunique()

lessons.title: Sampling Distributions & Standard Error
lessons.interviewAnswer: A sampling distribution describes how a statistic would vary over repeated samples from the same data-generating process and design. Its standard deviation is the statistic's standard error. For an independent sample mean with finite variance, SE is sigma divided by square root n, estimated by s divided by square root n. That is different from the standard deviation of individual observations. The formula changes under clustering, time dependence, unequal weights, or finite-population sampling, and a small SE says nothing about selection bias.
keyPoints: Random data make estimators random before sampling
Standard error measures estimator variability, not raw spread
Independence and design determine effective information
Bias and variance are separate failure modes
Simulation can audit analytic uncertainty formulas
lessons.why: Every confidence interval, p-value, power calculation, and error bar assumes some sampling distribution. If that hidden layer is wrong, polished downstream inference is wrong. A common analytics mistake treats millions of events as millions of independent units even when only thousands of users generated them. The naive standard error then shrinks dramatically while the real information has barely changed. Another mistake reports a small standard error from a convenience sample and calls the estimate accurate, ignoring systematic coverage or nonresponse bias. Interviewers ask about standard error because the answer reveals whether a candidate understands repeated-sampling uncertainty, unit of analysis, and asymptotic approximation rather than memorizing a formula. In production, the sampling distribution is also the basis of alert thresholds and metric-change detection. It must reflect how data arrive, which units are randomized, and which sources of variation will recur.
lessons.intuition: Imagine repeatedly drawing 100 orders from the same population and computing the mean order value. The histogram of all order values may be broad and skewed. Each sample has its own empirical histogram. The histogram of the thousands of sample means is a third object: it is narrower because positive and negative deviations partly cancel. Increasing sample size usually narrows that distribution, but duplicating the same customers' orders does not add the same information as observing new independent customers. Standard error is the width of that estimator histogram. Bias is the displacement of its center from the target. An estimator may be centered correctly but too noisy, or tightly concentrated around the wrong value. The central limit theorem often makes the center of the sampling distribution approximately normal even when observations are not normal, provided the required independence or weak-dependence and finite-variance conditions are credible. That approximation is a claim to diagnose, not a license to ignore heavy tails, rare events, or dependence.
lessons.deepDive: Inference starts by declaring a target estimand, a sampling or assignment mechanism, and an estimator. Repetition means rerunning that mechanism, not arbitrarily reshuffling a fixed spreadsheet. The standard error is the standard deviation across those hypothetical repetitions. Analytic formulas, bootstrap resampling, and Monte Carlo simulation are different ways to approximate the same conceptual object under different assumptions.
lessons.workedExample: Suppose 4,000 orders have standard deviation 40 euros. Treating orders as iid gives SE=40/sqrt(4000)=0.63 euros. But the orders come from 1,000 customers with four orders each and intra-customer correlation rho=0.30. The equal-cluster design effect is 1+(4-1)(0.30)=1.9, so the adjusted SE is approximately 0.63*sqrt(1.9)=0.87 euros and the effective sample size is about 4000/1.9=2,105 independent orders. The point estimate is unchanged; its claimed precision changes. If high-value customers were undercovered, neither SE repairs the bias. A defensible report therefore states the customer clustering, uses customer-level resampling or cluster-robust variance, and separately evaluates coverage bias.
commonMistakes: Dividing the raw standard deviation by square root of the number of rows when rows are not independent units.
Calling the sample's empirical histogram a sampling distribution.
Equating a small standard error with low total error while ignoring selection, measurement, or model bias.
Invoking the CLT without checking tail behavior, dependence, sample size, or whether the statistic is regular.
Using event-level bootstrap resampling when assignment and dependence operate at user or cluster level.

followUps.question: Why is standard error usually smaller than standard deviation?
followUps.answer: Standard deviation describes heterogeneity of individual values, while the mean averages deviations. Under iid sampling, averaging n observations divides variance by n and standard deviation by square root n. Dependence can substantially weaken that reduction.

followUps.question: Can an estimator have zero standard error and still be wrong?
followUps.answer: Yes. A constant estimator has zero variance but may be badly biased. More realistically, a huge nonrepresentative sample can yield a tiny estimated SE around a biased target. Precision and validity are different dimensions.

followUps.question: How would you estimate SE when no closed form is available?
followUps.answer: Use a design-respecting bootstrap, jackknife, influence-function or Monte Carlo simulation. The resampling unit and mechanism must mimic the source of repeated-sample variation; otherwise computation only produces precise nonsense.

lessons.production: Define metric grain, estimand, independent unit, exposure window, and sampling design in the metric contract. Preserve cluster IDs and weights so uncertainty can be reproduced. Compare analytic and resampling SEs on stable reference datasets; large disagreement is a diagnostic. Monitor raw count, distinct independent units, weight concentration, cluster-size distribution, missingness, tail quantiles, and estimated design effect. Version variance code with the metric definition and log seeds for simulations. For streaming metrics, account for autocorrelation and delayed outcomes; do not emit iid error bars on every event. Apply privacy controls to small slices and avoid leaking individual records through debugging samples. When the design changes, invalidate historical uncertainty thresholds or recompute them. Rollback means restoring the estimator, variance method, and population definition together, not only reverting a dashboard query.
lessons.description: A sampling distribution is the probability distribution of a statistic over repeated samples generated by the same population and sampling design. It is the bridge from observed data to uncertainty about an estimator. This chapter separates the population distribution, the empirical distribution of one sample, and the sampling distribution of an estimator; derives the standard error of a mean; explains why standard deviation and standard error answer different questions; and shows how dependence, unequal weights, clustering, and finite populations change the calculation. You will learn when a central-limit approximation is credible, why an unbiased estimator can still be too noisy to use, and why a low standard error cannot repair selection bias. The worked example and lab simulate repeated samples so that sampling variability is visible rather than merely asserted. Production guidance covers unit-of-analysis mistakes, correlated observations, design-aware uncertainty, reproducible simulation, and monitoring effective sample size. The goal is to make every later interval, test, and power calculation rest on a clear data-generating and sampling model.
learningObjectives: Distinguish a population distribution, a sample distribution, and an estimator's sampling distribution.
Derive and interpret standard error for independent means and recognize when the square-root-n rule fails.
Diagnose how bias, dependence, weighting, clustering, and finite-population sampling affect uncertainty.
Estimate sampling uncertainty analytically or by simulation and verify the result against repeated samples.

deepSections.title: Three distributions that must not be confused
deepSections.body: The population distribution describes values for units in the target population or superpopulation. The empirical distribution gives probability 1/n to each observed value in one sample. A sampling distribution describes a statistic T(X1,...,Xn) across repeated samples. The first concerns units, the second summarizes observed units, and the third concerns an estimator. Their spreads have different meanings. Population standard deviation measures heterogeneity among units; standard error measures uncertainty in a statistic. A sample mean of 10,000 purchases can have a tiny SE while purchases themselves vary enormously. Conversely, a robust median may have a larger SE than the mean under a clean Gaussian model but behave better under contamination. Always name the random unit and the target statistic before writing a denominator.

deepSections.title: Deriving the square-root-n rule
deepSections.body: For independent identically distributed Xi with mean mu and variance sigma squared, Var(Xbar)=Var(sum Xi/n)=n sigma squared/n squared=sigma squared/n, so SE(Xbar)=sigma/sqrt(n). Replacing unknown sigma by sample s yields the estimated SE. The reduction is proportional to 1/sqrt(n): halving uncertainty requires roughly four times as many independent observations. The derivation depends on covariance terms being zero. With correlation, Var(Xbar) includes 2 times the sum of pairwise covariances divided by n squared. Positive within-user, household, device, school, or time correlation reduces effective sample size. Negative dependence can reduce variance. For sampling without replacement from a finite population, multiply by the finite-population correction sqrt((N-n)/(N-1)) when the design and target warrant it.

deepSections.title: Bias, variance, consistency, and efficiency
deepSections.body: The sampling distribution exposes estimator quality. Bias is E[T]-theta; variance is E[(T-E[T]) squared]; mean squared error equals variance plus squared bias. Unbiasedness alone is not optimal if a slightly biased estimator has much lower variance and lower MSE. Consistency asks whether the estimator converges to the target as information grows. Efficiency compares variances among estimators under a model. Robustness asks how sensitive the estimator is to contamination or model violations. These are properties of a procedure under specified conditions, not permanent labels. Sample variance with denominator n-1 is unbiased under iid sampling, but an unbiased formula does not fix an unrepresentative sample. Regularized estimators deliberately introduce bias to reduce variance. Report the target, loss, and operating conditions when comparing estimators.

deepSections.title: Design-aware and dependence-aware uncertainty
deepSections.body: Simple iid SE formulas fail for clustered samples, repeated measurements, time series, spatial data, survey weights, and adaptive collection. Cluster-robust or sandwich estimators aggregate score contributions at the independent cluster level. Block methods preserve local dependence in time or space. Survey estimators incorporate stratification, primary sampling units, unequal selection probabilities, and sometimes finite-population corrections. Unequal weights often lower effective sample size; one useful diagnostic is (sum w)^2/sum(w^2), though a complete design variance needs more than that scalar. When clusters are few, asymptotic cluster corrections can be unreliable. Validate analytic SEs against design-respecting simulation or resampling and avoid silently switching the unit from users to events.

lessons.math: Let T=T(X1,...,Xn) estimate theta. Bias(T)=E[T]-theta, Var(T)=E[(T-E[T])^2], and MSE(T)=Var(T)+Bias(T)^2. For iid Xi with variance sigma^2, Var(Xbar)=sigma^2/n. If every distinct pair has correlation rho, Var(Xbar)=sigma^2[1+(n-1)rho]/n, giving the design effect 1+(n-1)rho. The effective independent sample size is approximately n divided by that design effect. A standardized statistic (T-theta)/SE(T) may approach a reference distribution, but only under the theorem's regularity conditions.

workedExamples.title: Order value with repeated customers
workedExamples.body: Start with the iid SE, identify customer as the independent cluster, calculate a design effect, and compare against customer-level bootstrap results. The example shows why row count is not information count and why uncertainty and representativeness require separate checks.

exercises.prompt: A sample has raw SD 12 and n=144 iid observations. Estimate the mean's SE and explain the unit.
exercises.solution: SE=12/sqrt(144)=1. It is the repeated-sample standard deviation of the sample mean, expressed in the original measurement unit, not the spread of individual observations.

exercises.prompt: Ten observations are exact duplicates of each of 100 independent units. Should n be 1,000 in the iid formula?
exercises.solution: No. Duplicate rows add no independent information. Aggregate or cluster by the 100 independent units; otherwise the naive SE is understated by treating copies as new evidence.

exercises.prompt: An estimator has bias 2 and variance 9. Compute MSE.
exercises.solution: MSE=variance+bias squared=9+4=13. This demonstrates why variance alone is not total estimation error.

import numpy as np

lessons.title: Bootstrap & Resampling
lessons.interviewAnswer: The nonparametric bootstrap treats the empirical distribution as an estimate of the population: draw many size-n samples with replacement, recompute the entire estimator, and use the resulting distribution for standard errors or intervals. It works when the observed sample represents the repetition mechanism and the estimator is sufficiently regular. Resample the independent unit—pairs, users, clusters, or time blocks—not blindly rows. Bootstrap cannot repair selection bias, absent rare classes, or a fundamentally misspecified pipeline, and interval choice and Monte Carlo error must be reported.
keyPoints: Resampling approximates repeated sampling from an estimated population
Replacement preserves iid draws from the empirical distribution
The estimator must be recomputed end to end
Dependence determines the resampling unit
Coverage must be checked rather than assumed
lessons.why: Modern metrics are often ratios, quantiles, ranking scores, or outputs of fitted pipelines whose standard errors are messy. The bootstrap turns a difficult derivation into a simulation procedure that exposes estimator variability. That convenience also encourages misuse. Row bootstrap on repeated user events invents independence; bootstrapping only final predictions ignores model-training variation; independently resampling paired outcomes destroys the pairing; and resampling a biased dataset reproduces its bias. Interviews ask for the algorithm, but a strong answer states the target repetition mechanism and failure cases. In production, a stochastic interval must also be reproducible, computationally bounded, and stable enough for decisions. The bootstrap is best understood as a model—the empirical distribution plus a resampling design—not as a magical guarantee.
lessons.intuition: The observed sample is the only concrete glimpse of the population. Place equal probability mass on each observed independent unit, then pretend that discrete empirical distribution generated new studies. Sampling with replacement allows some units to appear multiple times and others not at all, producing the variation that sampling would create. Recompute the statistic for each pseudo-study. The spread of those values estimates standard error; their shape reveals skewness or instability. Without replacement, every size-n resample would merely reorder all observations and many statistics would not change. The approximation is strongest when the original sample captures the population features relevant to the statistic. If no failure event appears, the empirical distribution assigns it probability zero, so no bootstrap replicate can discover it. If dependence exists, the empirical units must be clusters or blocks rather than rows.
lessons.deepDive: The bootstrap substitutes the empirical distribution F_n for unknown F and estimates the distribution of T(F_n*)-T(F_n) conditional on data. Its validity depends on whether this conditional distribution approximates the true distribution of T(F_n)-T(F) at the relevant scale.
lessons.workedExample: Delivery method A has median time 28 minutes and B has 31, so the observed median difference A-B is -3 minutes. Resample orders with replacement separately within methods, preserving the original group sizes, and recompute both medians 20,000 times. Suppose the 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles are -5.4 and -0.8 minutes. Under this percentile procedure, the data support faster median delivery for A. Before acting, check whether repeated orders from the same courier or geography require cluster resampling, whether censored cancellations were excluded, and whether the sample period represents future traffic. The interval reflects the chosen design—not every source of uncertainty.
commonMistakes: Resampling rows when users, devices, schools, or time blocks are the independent units.
Bootstrapping only the final metric while holding learned preprocessing or model parameters fixed.
Believing more bootstrap replicates compensate for a tiny or unrepresentative original sample.
Using a percentile interval without checking bias, skewness, boundaries, or empirical coverage.
Forgetting that paired observations and treatment strata must remain paired or stratified.

followUps.question: Why sample with replacement?
followUps.answer: The empirical distribution generates independent draws with replacement. Without replacement, a size-n resample contains every observed unit exactly once, so permutation-invariant statistics such as the mean would not vary.

followUps.question: What does increasing B accomplish?
followUps.answer: It reduces Monte Carlo error in approximating the bootstrap distribution conditional on the observed data. It does not add information to the original sample or repair a statistically invalid bootstrap scheme.

followUps.question: When would you use a block bootstrap?
followUps.answer: When observations have local serial or spatial dependence and blocks can preserve the dependence relevant to the statistic. Block length is a modeling choice and should be checked by sensitivity analysis.

lessons.production: Specify bootstrap target, independent resampling unit, strata or blocks, replicate count, interval method, full pipeline steps, RNG algorithm, and seed derivation in configuration. Parallelize with independent random streams and make results deterministic for the same artifact version. Monitor failed fits, degenerate replicates, class loss, interval width, quantile Monte Carlo error, cluster coverage, and runtime. Cache only when data and code hashes match. Avoid storing raw replicate samples when estimates suffice, especially for sensitive records. Validate coverage with simulated and historical replay cases, including rare outcomes. Set failure behavior: widen, fall back to an analytic conservative interval, or suppress the estimate rather than silently dropping failed replicates. Version and roll back the resampler with preprocessing and estimator code.

lab.goal: Build a bootstrap confidence interval for a median, compare with SciPy BCa output, and verify reproducibility and narrowing with more data.
lab.buildIt:
import random
import statistics

def bootstrap_statistic(xs, statistic, repeats=5000, seed=17):
    rng = random.Random(seed); n=len(xs)
    return [statistic(rng.choices(xs,k=n)) for _ in range(repeats)]

def percentile_interval(values, level=0.95):
    ys=sorted(values); tail=(1-level)/2
    lo=ys[int(tail*(len(ys)-1))]; hi=ys[int((1-tail)*(len(ys)-1))]
    return lo,hi

x=[8,9,10,10,11,12,13,17,22,30,31,35]
replicates=bootstrap_statistic(x,statistics.median)
interval=percentile_interval(replicates)
lab.useIt:
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import bootstrap
rng=np.random.default_rng(17)
result=bootstrap((np.asarray(x),),np.median,confidence_level=0.95,n_resamples=5000,method='BCa',rng=rng)
scipy_interval=(float(result.confidence_interval.low),float(result.confidence_interval.high))
lab.verifyIt:
assert bootstrap_statistic(x,statistics.median,100,17)==bootstrap_statistic(x,statistics.median,100,17)
assert interval[0] <= statistics.median(x) <= interval[1]
assert scipy_interval[0] < scipy_interval[1]
wide=percentile_interval(bootstrap_statistic(x*8,statistics.median,3000,19))
assert wide[1]-wide[0] <= interval[1]-interval[0]
