lessons.description: The bootstrap estimates an estimator's sampling behavior by repeatedly sampling with replacement from the empirical distribution and recomputing the complete statistic. It is powerful because it can approximate standard errors, bias, and confidence intervals when analytic derivations are inconvenient, but it is not assumption-free. This chapter develops the plug-in principle, explains why replacement matters, distinguishes ordinary, paired, stratified, cluster, block, parametric, and residual bootstraps, and compares percentile, basic, normal, and bias-corrected accelerated intervals. You will learn when the empirical distribution is a reasonable stand-in for the population, why rare events and nonsmooth statistics cause instability, and why resampling rows breaks dependence. The worked example estimates a difference in medians while preserving treatment groups. The lab implements a bootstrap distribution from first principles, compares it with SciPy's current API, verifies reproducibility and interval behavior, and demonstrates the effect of sample size. Production guidance covers resampling grain, pipeline refitting, Monte Carlo error, seeds, compute budgets, privacy, and coverage audits.
learningObjectives: Explain the empirical plug-in principle and why bootstrap resamples have the original sample size with replacement.
Choose a resampling scheme that preserves pairing, groups, clusters, time dependence, weights, and model-fitting steps.
Compare common bootstrap interval constructions and diagnose skewness, bias, discreteness, and boundary failure.
Implement reproducible bootstrap uncertainty and verify it against simulation or an official library.

deepSections.title: The plug-in distribution and algorithm
deepSections.body: Given iid observations x1,...,xn, the empirical distribution F_n places mass 1/n on each xi. A bootstrap sample draws n times independently from F_n, which is equivalent to sampling observed rows with replacement. For each replicate b, compute theta_hat_b*=T(x_b*), including every preprocessing and fitting step that would vary in a new sample. The bootstrap standard error is the sample SD of replicate estimates. Estimated bias is mean(theta_hat*)-theta_hat. Thousands of replicates reduce Monte Carlo noise but do not fix statistical invalidity. Report the number of replicates, random generator, seed policy, and interval method.

deepSections.title: Resampling must mirror the data design
deepSections.body: Paired measurements are resampled as pairs. Two independently sampled groups are resampled within group when estimating a two-sample effect. Cluster bootstrap samples independent clusters and carries all their rows. Stratified bootstrap samples within design strata. Time-series block bootstrap samples contiguous blocks long enough to retain relevant dependence; moving, circular, and stationary variants differ. Parametric bootstrap simulates from a fitted model, trading empirical flexibility for model dependence. Regression residual bootstrap assumes a residual structure; case bootstrap resamples observations; wild bootstrap can handle heteroskedasticity. Survey replicate weights may be preferable to ad hoc row resampling. The unit and scheme follow from the estimand and design.

deepSections.title: Bootstrap standard errors and interval choices
deepSections.body: The normal interval uses theta_hat plus-or-minus a critical value times bootstrap SE and assumes approximate symmetry. The percentile interval takes quantiles of theta_hat*, which is intuitive but can inherit bias and transformation issues. The basic interval reflects percentile endpoints around theta_hat. Studentized intervals bootstrap a pivotal statistic and can improve accuracy at extra computational cost. BCa adjusts for median bias and acceleration related to estimator influence, and SciPy currently defaults to BCa. No method dominates every setting. Compare interval shape, replicate histogram, jackknife influence, and simulation coverage across plausible distributions. Transform bounded positive parameters when appropriate.

deepSections.title: Where ordinary bootstrap breaks
deepSections.body: Nonsmooth estimators, sample extremes, parameters on boundaries, very small samples, infinite-variance distributions, weak identification, and model selection can defeat ordinary bootstrap approximations. The sample maximum's empirical bootstrap cannot exceed the observed maximum. Rare classes absent from the sample remain absent. Some estimators require an m-out-of-n or subsampling approach. Cross-validation metrics need resampling that accounts for training and evaluation roles; leaking the same rows across stages biases uncertainty. A bootstrap distribution can look smooth and still target the wrong population. Audit against synthetic data with known truth, alternative resampling schemes, influence diagnostics, and domain shifts.

deepSections.title: Bootstrapping learned pipelines and evaluation metrics
deepSections.body: For a trained model's future performance, uncertainty can arise from training-sample variation, evaluation-sample variation, hyperparameter selection, and deployment population drift. Bootstrapping only a fixed test set conditions on the fitted model and estimates a narrower quantity. To capture training variation, each replicate must redo feature fitting, model training, tuning logic, threshold selection, and evaluation on an independent or appropriately out-of-bag sample. Naive reuse can leak observations and create optimistic metrics. Nested resampling is expensive, so state which randomness is included. For paired model comparisons, resample evaluation units jointly so both models face the same cases; the covariance substantially improves precision. Distribution shift remains outside an iid bootstrap unless explicitly simulated.

lessons.math: For B bootstrap replicates theta_hat_1*,...,theta_hat_B*, bootstrap SE is sqrt(sum_b(theta_hat_b*-mean*)^2/(B-1)). A percentile (1-alpha) interval uses empirical quantiles alpha/2 and 1-alpha/2. A basic interval is [2 theta_hat-q_(1-alpha/2)*, 2 theta_hat-q_(alpha/2)*]. Monte Carlo uncertainty of estimated quantiles decreases with B but depends on density near the quantile. Statistical validity concerns n tending large; increasing B only approximates the conditional bootstrap distribution more precisely.

workedExamples.title: Difference in group medians
workedExamples.body: Resample within each independent group, recompute both medians, inspect the replicate distribution, and interpret its interval only after validating the unit and censoring rules.

exercises.prompt: Why does a bootstrap sample of size n contain about 63% distinct observations on average for large n?
exercises.solution: Each observation is omitted with probability (1-1/n)^n, approaching e^-1. Thus the included fraction approaches 1-e^-1, about 0.632.

exercises.prompt: How should 500 users with repeated sessions be bootstrapped for a user-level treatment effect?
exercises.solution: Sample users with replacement and carry all relevant sessions/outcomes for each sampled user. Row resampling would destroy within-user dependence.

exercises.prompt: You increase B from 1,000 to 100,000 and the interval remains biased. Why?
exercises.solution: B controls simulation precision conditional on the sample. Bias from an invalid resampling model, estimator, or unrepresentative data is a statistical problem, not Monte Carlo noise.

lessons.title: Permutation & Randomization Tests
lessons.interviewAnswer: A permutation test compares an observed statistic with values obtained by shuffling in a way justified under the null. In a randomized experiment, reassign labels according to the actual assignment mechanism; in observational data, a label shuffle additionally requires exchangeability. Preserve pairs, blocks, clusters, and treatment counts. Exact enumeration is possible for small designs; otherwise sample permutations and use a correction such as (b+1)/(B+1). The p-value is valid for the specified statistic, null, design, and extremeness rule—not because permutation is automatically nonparametric.
keyPoints: Randomization mechanism can supply the null distribution
Exchangeability is a substantive assumption
Pairs, blocks, and clusters constrain valid transformations
The statistic determines sensitivity and two-sided ordering
Monte Carlo p-values have simulation uncertainty
lessons.why: Permutation tests make the source of calibration visible: if treatment truly had no effect, would relabeling assignments produce a statistic as large as observed? They are useful for custom metrics whose parametric null distribution is difficult. But shuffling can erase real structure. Permuting sessions across users, observations across time, or outcomes across unequal-variance groups can generate worlds the design never allowed. In randomized experiments, the assignment algorithm—not a generic shuffle—is authoritative. In observational comparisons, exchangeability is rarely guaranteed without conditioning or adjustment. Interviewers value these tests because the algorithm is simple but correct use requires deep design reasoning. In production, exactness also depends on reconstructing assignment and predefining the statistic, not merely calling a resampling API.
lessons.intuition: Freeze every observed outcome and ask which treatment-label arrangements could have occurred under the assignment process if treatment changed none of them. Compute the chosen effect statistic for each allowed arrangement. The observed assignment is one member of that reference set. If its statistic lies in an extreme tail, the no-effect assignment model has difficulty explaining it. In a matched-pair experiment, only swapping labels within pairs is allowed; a global shuffle breaks the match. In a cluster-randomized experiment, whole cluster labels move together. For observational groups, the same picture requires the stronger claim that units were exchangeable under the null. A nonparametric test does not mean assumption-free—it relocates assumptions from a distribution family to invariance and design.
lessons.deepDive: A permutation test is defined by a group of transformations G under which the joint data distribution is invariant under H0. The reference distribution is {T(gX): g in G}. Randomization tests obtain G from known assignment probabilities; permutation tests often posit exchangeability.
lessons.workedExample: In a completely randomized experiment, 6 of 12 stores receive a promotion. The observed difference in average weekly sales is 4.2 units. There are choose(12,6)=924 possible assignments with six treated stores, small enough to enumerate. Recompute the mean difference for every assignment while holding outcomes fixed. If 18 assignments have an absolute difference at least 4.2, the two-sided exact p-value is 18/924=0.0195. If stores were randomized in matched regional pairs, enumerating all six-of-twelve allocations would be wrong; only the 2^6 within-pair swaps belong to the design.
commonMistakes: Saying permutation tests make no assumptions.
Globally shuffling labels when randomization occurred within blocks, pairs, or clusters.
Using observational label permutation as if it proved a causal effect despite confounding.
Changing the statistic or one-sided direction after observing the result.
Reporting zero from finite random permutations instead of a corrected Monte Carlo estimate and its precision.

followUps.question: What is exchangeability?
followUps.answer: It is invariance of the joint distribution under the permitted permutations under H0. It is weaker or stronger depending on the transformation set and is a substantive design/model condition, not a property produced by shuffling.

followUps.question: When is a permutation test exact?
followUps.answer: When the null makes outcomes invariant to transformations, the transformation probabilities match the actual design or symmetry, and the statistic and tail rule were fixed. Exact enumeration removes Monte Carlo error, not design error.

followUps.question: Why studentize a permutation statistic?
followUps.answer: Dividing by an estimated standard error can make the statistic closer to pivotal and improve behavior when nuisance variance differs, especially for testing equal means rather than identical distributions. Validity still depends on conditions.

lessons.production: Persist the randomization configuration, eligibility set, blocks, clusters, assignment probabilities, exposure logs, statistic code, tail definition, number of permutations, and RNG seed. Reconstruct the exact design rather than inferring it from observed treatment counts. Batch vectorized computations but compare optimized code with exact small fixtures. Monitor assignment integrity, missing outcomes, interference indicators, failed metric calculations, Monte Carlo precision, and runtime. Store aggregate null statistics only when privacy permits; avoid retaining duplicated sensitive rows. Predefine how ties and NaNs are handled. Use more permutations or an exact method near action thresholds. Label exploratory metrics and confirm them on fresh data. Roll back both metric and transformation rules when experiment design changes.
lessons.description: Permutation and randomization tests build a reference distribution by applying transformations that are valid under a null hypothesis—often reallocating treatment labels or swapping paired signs—and comparing the observed statistic with that distribution. Their strength is transparent design-based calibration with few distributional assumptions; their danger is the casual belief that any labels may be shuffled. This chapter distinguishes Fisher randomization inference from observational permutation tests, defines exchangeability, shows exact and Monte Carlo tail calculations, handles paired and blocked designs, and explains studentization, ties, two-sided definitions, and the plus-one correction for sampled permutations. You will learn how interference, clustering, covariate-adaptive assignment, unequal variances, and data-dependent statistic selection invalidate naive shuffles. The worked example uses a randomized conversion experiment with a difference-in-means statistic. The lab enumerates a small exact test, compares it with SciPy, and verifies symmetry and p-value bounds. Production guidance covers assignment reconstruction, reproducible RNG, batch computation, audit logs, precision, and sequential use.
learningObjectives: Identify the exact transformation group justified by random assignment or exchangeability under the null.
Construct exact and Monte Carlo permutation distributions for independent, paired, blocked, and clustered designs.
Choose and predefine a statistic and two-sided extremeness rule appropriate to the alternative.
Diagnose invalid shuffles caused by dependence, unequal assignment, interference, or post-selection.

deepSections.title: Randomization inference and the null being tested
deepSections.body: Under Fisher's sharp null, every unit's outcome would be identical under every treatment, so all missing potential outcomes are known and outcomes can be held fixed while assignments vary. Recompute the statistic over assignments allowed by the experiment, respecting fixed treatment counts, blocks, unequal probabilities, or clusters. The resulting p-value is exact conditional on the observed outcomes and assignment design. A weak null such as zero average effect does not impute every missing potential outcome; an unstudentized randomization test may not be exact for it under heterogeneous effects. State whether the null is sharp, distributional equality, equal means, or conditional independence.

deepSections.title: Exchangeability and constrained permutations
deepSections.body: Exchangeability means the joint distribution is invariant to the permitted label permutations under H0. Independent identically distributed samples support broad permutations under a distribution-equality null. Paired data support within-pair swaps or sign flips. Blocked experiments permute within blocks. Repeated measures may require subject-level transformations. Time and spatial structures rarely permit arbitrary global shuffles; cyclic shifts or restricted permutations may be justified under specific stationarity claims. Covariate-adaptive randomization must be replayed faithfully. If the transformation destroys dependence or changes nuisance distributions, the reference distribution is wrong even if the code executes.

deepSections.title: Statistic choice, exact tails, and Monte Carlo estimates
deepSections.body: Choose a statistic before unblinding: mean difference for location, studentized difference for unequal variances, rank statistic for stochastic ordering, or a domain metric for practical sensitivity. Two-sided p-values can be based on absolute statistic, doubled smaller tail, or probability ordering; definitions differ for asymmetric discrete distributions. Exact p is the fraction of allowed transformations at least as extreme, typically including the observed arrangement. When B random permutations are sampled, (b+1)/(B+1) avoids zero and yields a valid conservative Monte Carlo estimate under standard sampling. Report B and simulation uncertainty; a p-value near a threshold may need more permutations.

deepSections.title: Confounding, interference, and post-selection
deepSections.body: Permutation does not create randomization in observational data. Confounding can make labels nonexchangeable even under no causal effect. Matching or conditioning can narrow the transformation set, but validity then depends on the adjustment and design. Interference means one unit's assignment changes another's outcome, violating usual potential-outcome structure. Missing outcomes and noncompliance complicate estimands. Selecting the largest statistic from many metrics and testing it with a single-metric permutation distribution is invalid; permute the whole selection procedure or adjust multiplicity. Sequentially rerunning permutation tests requires a sequential design. Computational expense is not the main risk—the wrong invariance claim is.

deepSections.title: Inverting randomization tests for effect intervals
deepSections.body: Randomization tests can produce more than a p-value. Under an additive constant-effect model, subtract a candidate effect from treated outcomes, test the resulting sharp null, and collect candidate effects not rejected; this inverts the test into a confidence set. The construction inherits the assignment-based calibration and may be asymmetric or discrete. It does not establish that treatment effects are truly constant, so interpret the interval for the model being inverted. Hodges–Lehmann-style estimates use the effect value that centers a rank or randomization statistic. In clustered or blocked experiments, inversion must replay the same restricted assignments at every candidate. This connection shows that design-based estimation and testing belong to one coherent procedure rather than isolated significance output.

lessons.math: For transformation set G and statistic T, an exact upper-tail p-value is |{g in G:T(gX)>=T(X)}|/|G| when transformations are equally likely. With unequal assignment probabilities, weight assignments accordingly. For B randomly sampled transformations and b exceedances, p_hat=(b+1)/(B+1). Conditional Monte Carlo standard error is approximately sqrt(p_hat(1-p_hat)/(B+1)), useful as a precision diagnostic but not a substitute for design validity.

workedExamples.title: Twelve-store randomized promotion
workedExamples.body: Enumerate only assignments allowed by the actual randomization, compute the statistic for each, count the appropriate two-sided tail, and contrast complete randomization with paired assignment.

exercises.prompt: A paired experiment has 8 pairs. How many exact within-pair label swaps exist?
exercises.solution: Each pair has two orientations, so 2^8=256 transformations, assuming every pair can be swapped independently.

exercises.prompt: In 999 random permutations, 4 are at least as extreme. Give the plus-one estimate.
exercises.solution: (4+1)/(999+1)=0.005. It avoids claiming an impossible zero tail probability from finite Monte Carlo sampling.

exercises.prompt: Why is a global shuffle invalid for cluster randomization?
exercises.solution: It assigns different treatments to rows within a cluster, creating assignments the experiment could never produce and breaking within-cluster dependence. Shuffle whole cluster labels according to the design.

lab.goal: Enumerate an exact two-sample permutation test, verify its tail calculation against SciPy, and preserve fixed group sizes.
lab.buildIt:
import itertools

def mean(xs): return sum(xs)/len(xs)
def exact_difference_test(a,b):
    pooled=list(a)+list(b); n_a=len(a)
    observed=abs(mean(a)-mean(b)); stats=[]
    for idx in itertools.combinations(range(len(pooled)),n_a):
        chosen=set(idx)
        left=[x for i,x in enumerate(pooled) if i in chosen]
        right=[x for i,x in enumerate(pooled) if i not in chosen]
        stats.append(abs(mean(left)-mean(right)))
    p=sum(t >= observed-1e-12 for t in stats)/len(stats)
    return observed,p,stats
a=[8,9,11,12]; b=[3,4,6,7]
observed,p_value,null_stats=exact_difference_test(a,b)
lab.useIt:
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import permutation_test
res=permutation_test((np.asarray(a),np.asarray(b)),lambda x,y: np.mean(x)-np.mean(y),permutation_type='independent',alternative='two-sided',n_resamples=np.inf)
lab.verifyIt:
import math
assert len(null_stats)==math.comb(len(a)+len(b),len(a))
assert 0 <= p_value <= 1
assert abs(p_value-res.pvalue) < 1e-12
assert exact_difference_test(a,a)[1] == 1.0

Documents exact and randomized permutation types, tail definitions, precision warnings, and current RNG interface.

lessons.title: Multiple Testing & False Discovery Rate
lessons.interviewAnswer: With m tests, individual alpha does not control the overall error. Bonferroni and Holm control the probability of at least one false rejection in a defined family; BH controls the expected false discovery proportion under its conditions and is usually more powerful when many discoveries are acceptable. For BH, sort p-values, find the largest k with p_(k)<=kq/m, and reject through k. Define the family before seeing results, account for dependence and selection, report adjusted values and effect sizes, and do not call FDR the probability each discovery is false.
keyPoints: Multiplicity begins with a declared family
FWER controls any false rejection; FDR controls expected false proportion
Holm dominates simple Bonferroni while retaining strong FWER control
BH is a step-up rule with dependence conditions
Adjustment does not repair biased tests or post-selection
lessons.why: A dashboard with 100 metrics, a genomics screen with 20,000 genes, and an ML evaluation sliced across dozens of groups all create multiple chances to see small p-values. At m independent true nulls tested at 0.05, the chance of at least one false rejection is 1-0.95^m, about 99.4% for 100. The appropriate response depends on consequences. A safety investigation may demand strong FWER control; discovery screening may tolerate some false leads for greater power and use FDR with later confirmation. Interviews often ask Bonferroni versus BH, but operational maturity means defining which hypotheses belong together, how exploratory and confirmatory stages interact, and how dependent metrics affect guarantees. Hiding failed tests is a data-governance bug, not merely a statistical detail.
lessons.intuition: Imagine fishing with many hooks. Even if no fish exist, enough hooks will snag debris that looks like a catch. FWER asks to keep the probability of any false catch in the basket below a limit. FDR allows a controlled expected fraction of false catches among everything declared, which is useful when a screening stage can tolerate follow-up work. Bonferroni gives each hook a tiny share alpha/m. Holm starts with the smallest p-value and relaxes thresholds as hypotheses are removed. BH draws an increasing line kq/m against sorted p-values and accepts the largest prefix beneath it. None of these methods knows whether a test was biased, chosen after inspection, or omitted from the count. The family and evidence pipeline must be honest.
lessons.deepDive: Let V be false rejections, R total rejections, and m0 true nulls. FWER=P(V>=1). False discovery proportion is V/max(R,1), and FDR is its expectation. Different criteria answer different risk questions and cannot be compared only by the number of rejections.
lessons.workedExample: Ten preregistered metrics yield sorted p-values [0.001,0.006,0.011,0.020,0.031,0.070,0.20,0.42,0.60,0.90]. At q=0.05, BH thresholds are [0.005,0.010,0.015,0.020,0.025,...]. Ranks 1–4 satisfy their thresholds, rank 5 does not, and no later rank satisfies, so reject the first four. This controls expected false discovery proportion under BH conditions, not the chance of any false claim. Effect estimates and intervals still determine usefulness. If the ten metrics were selected from 200 inspected metrics, m=10 is not an honest confirmatory family.
commonMistakes: Adjusting only the significant p-values while omitting all tests attempted.
Saying FDR q is the probability that each discovery is false.
Applying BH without considering dependence assumptions or how the family was selected.
Using multiplicity correction as a substitute for valid individual tests, effect sizes, or replication.
Treating repeated dashboard updates as one fixed batch family without an online or sequential method.

followUps.question: When prefer FWER over FDR?
followUps.answer: Prefer FWER when even one false claim is costly, such as a small confirmatory safety family. Prefer FDR for large screening settings where some false leads are acceptable and discoveries receive follow-up.

followUps.question: Why is Holm generally preferable to plain Bonferroni?
followUps.answer: Holm uses progressively less stringent denominators after ordering p-values, retains strong FWER control under broad dependence, and is never less powerful than the single-step Bonferroni rule.

followUps.question: Does BH work under correlated tests?
followUps.answer: It controls under independence and certain positive dependence conditions; arbitrary dependence needs additional justification or more conservative/structured methods. Correlation should be part of the method choice, not ignored.

lessons.production: Maintain a hypothesis registry with family ID, owner, estimand, metric version, population, planned direction, decision, and every attempted analysis. Freeze batch families before unblinding or use a formally designed online procedure for incoming tests. Compute adjusted values centrally to prevent teams from omitting tests. Monitor family size, rejection count, p-value histogram, dependence structure, exploratory-to-confirmatory conversion, and replication rate. Store raw and adjusted p-values plus effect intervals; never overwrite raw evidence. Access-control sensitive subgroup findings and apply minimum-cell rules. Version the correction algorithm and sort/tie behavior. Test implementations with known fixtures and invariants. If a family definition or metric changes, create a new analysis version rather than silently recomputing history. Rollback should restore both decisions and their full multiplicity context.
lessons.description: Testing many hypotheses creates many opportunities for false discoveries. Multiplicity is not solved by interpreting each p-value in isolation; the analyst must define a family, choose an error criterion, and apply a procedure whose dependence assumptions and selection process match the problem. This chapter derives why unadjusted family-wise error grows, contrasts family-wise error rate with false discovery rate, explains Bonferroni, Holm, Benjamini–Hochberg, and Benjamini–Yekutieli ideas, and distinguishes adjusted p-values from local false-discovery probabilities. You will learn how hierarchical testing, gatekeeping, preregistration, holdout confirmation, and selective inference control different risks; why correlated tests complicate guarantees; and why adding hypotheses after looking changes the family. The worked example applies BH to ten feature metrics and interprets the rejection threshold. The lab implements Holm and BH from scratch, verifies monotonic adjusted values against SciPy, and checks invariants. Production guidance covers metric-family governance, lineage, online testing, dashboards, reproducibility, and audit of all attempted analyses.
learningObjectives: Quantify how repeated testing inflates the chance and number of false positives.
Choose between FWER and FDR according to the cost and volume of false discoveries.
Implement Bonferroni/Holm and Benjamini–Hochberg procedures with valid ordering and monotonicity.
Define hypothesis families and diagnose dependence, selection, and reporting practices that invalidate nominal control.

deepSections.title: How multiplicity accumulates
deepSections.body: If m true-null tests are independent at per-test alpha, P(at least one false rejection)=1-(1-alpha)^m, bounded above by m alpha via the union bound. Dependence changes the exact value but not the need for a family-level procedure. Expected false rejections under valid marginal tests is m0 alpha. Multiple outcomes, time points, subgroups, transformations, models, and stopping looks all consume opportunities. A family is the collection over which a claim or decision is made. It may be all primary outcomes for one experiment, all model variants competing for launch, or all genes in a screen. Define it by scientific and decision context, not by which results look promising.

deepSections.title: Bonferroni and Holm family-wise control
deepSections.body: Bonferroni rejects p_i<=alpha/m and controls FWER under arbitrary dependence by the union bound, but can be conservative. Adjusted p-values are min(m p_i,1). Holm's step-down procedure sorts p_(1)<=...<=p_(m), compares p_(k) with alpha/(m-k+1), and stops at the first failure; it strongly controls FWER under broad conditions and is never less powerful than Bonferroni. Closed testing and gatekeeping can exploit logical structure. FWER suits high-cost false claims, final confirmatory analyses, and small families where any false launch is serious. It does not guarantee that every nonrejected hypothesis is true or control selection bias.

deepSections.title: Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery control
deepSections.body: For target q, BH sorts p-values and finds largest k with p_(k)<=kq/m, rejecting all p_(1)...p_(k). Under independent true-null p-values and certain positive dependence structures it controls FDR at or below q m0/m. The original paper introduced this less stringent criterion to gain power when controlling the proportion of false discoveries is appropriate. Benjamini–Yekutieli adds a harmonic-factor correction for arbitrary dependence and can be conservative. BH-adjusted p-values are monotone reverse cumulative minima of m p_(k)/k. FDR is an expectation over repeated studies; q=0.05 does not mean each reported discovery has 5% probability of being false.

deepSections.title: Hierarchies, dependence, and selective reporting
deepSections.body: Correlated outcomes can make standard assumptions uncertain; permutation-based max statistics, hierarchical FDR, knockoffs, or domain-specific methods may be appropriate. Testing parent hypotheses before children can conserve error and match scientific structure. Independent holdout confirmation separates exploration from validation when the selection process is complex. Online FDR methods address hypotheses arriving over time; rerunning batch BH on a growing dashboard does not automatically provide online guarantees. Data-dependent filtering is safe only under conditions such as independence from null p-values. Record every hypothesis, preprocessing variant, and stopping look. Adjustment applied after suppressing inconvenient tests is not control.

deepSections.title: Discovery, confirmation, and replicability
deepSections.body: Error control within one screen does not guarantee that discoveries replicate in a new population. Winner's curse makes selected effect estimates too large because selection favors positive noise. A two-stage design can use FDR for discovery, then independent confirmatory data with a stricter family-wise criterion. Split proportions should reflect discovery volume and follow-up cost. Shrinkage estimates can improve magnitude reporting but do not retroactively change the testing family. Track directional errors as well as false rejections when sign matters. For recurring products, measure empirical replication and calibration by p-value bins; systematic failure may reveal bias, dependence violations, or shifting populations. Publish the complete discovery and confirmation funnel so consumers do not equate an adjusted p-value with durable truth.

lessons.math: Under independence, FWER=1-(1-alpha)^m when all m nulls are true. Bonferroni uses alpha/m. Holm compares ordered p_(k) to alpha/(m-k+1). BH at target q finds k*=max{k:p_(k)<=kq/m}; reject ranks <=k*. Adjusted BH values in sorted order are qtilde_(i)=min_{j>=i}(m p_(j)/j,1), then mapped back to original hypotheses. The reverse cumulative minimum is essential so adjusted values are nondecreasing with rank.

workedExamples.title: BH on ten preregistered metrics
workedExamples.body: Sort p-values, compare each with its rank-dependent line, select the largest passing rank, reject the prefix, and interpret FDR as a repeated-procedure expectation rather than per-result probability.

exercises.prompt: Compute the chance of at least one false positive for 20 independent true nulls at alpha=0.05.
exercises.solution: 1-0.95^20, approximately 0.642. This illustrates why per-test alpha is not family-wise control.

exercises.prompt: For m=5 and q=0.10, what is the BH threshold at rank 3?
exercises.solution: kq/m=3*0.10/5=0.06. This rank passes if the third sorted p-value is at most 0.06.

exercises.prompt: Why must BH adjusted p-values use a reverse cumulative minimum?
exercises.solution: Without it, adjusted values could decrease at later, larger raw p-values, violating the ordered rejection structure. The cumulative minimum enforces monotonicity across ranks.

lab.goal: Implement Holm FWER and BH FDR adjusted p-values, verify monotonicity, and compare BH output with SciPy.
lab.buildIt:
def adjust_bh(pvalues):
    m=len(pvalues); order=sorted(range(m),key=pvalues.__getitem__)
    raw=[m*pvalues[i]/rank for rank,i in enumerate(order,1)]
    monotone=[0.0]*m; running=1.0
    for pos in range(m-1,-1,-1):
        running=min(running,raw[pos],1.0); monotone[pos]=running
    out=[0.0]*m
    for pos,i in enumerate(order): out[i]=monotone[pos]
    return out

def adjust_holm(pvalues):
    m=len(pvalues); order=sorted(range(m),key=pvalues.__getitem__)
    out=[0.0]*m; running=0.0
    for rank,i in enumerate(order):
        running=max(running,min(1.0,(m-rank)*pvalues[i])); out[i]=running
    return out

p=[0.001,0.006,0.011,0.020,0.031,0.070,0.20,0.42,0.60,0.90]
bh=adjust_bh(p); holm=adjust_holm(p)
lab.useIt:
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import false_discovery_control
scipy_bh=false_discovery_control(np.asarray(p),method='bh')
lab.verifyIt:
assert all(0 <= x <= 1 for x in bh+holm)
order=sorted(range(len(p)),key=p.__getitem__)
assert all(bh[order[i]] <= bh[order[i+1]] for i in range(len(p)-1))
assert all(holm[i] >= min(1.0,p[i]) for i in range(len(p)))
assert np.allclose(bh,scipy_bh)

lessons.title: Effect Size vs Statistical Significance
lessons.interviewAnswer: Effect size is the magnitude of the estimand—such as a 1.2 percentage-point lift, relative risk, mean difference, correlation, or standardized mean difference. A p-value combines magnitude with uncertainty and sample size, so a tiny effect can be significant in a huge sample and a useful effect nonsignificant in a small one. Report the effect in domain units first, its interval, baseline risk, and a predefined minimum worthwhile effect. Standardized measures aid comparison but depend on the chosen standard deviation and population.
keyPoints: Magnitude and evidence are separate
Domain units usually lead communication
Relative measures require baseline risk
Standardized effects depend on reference variability
Practical thresholds should be set before results
lessons.why: Decisions care about outcomes, costs, and harms—not whether a test statistic crossed 1.96. Significance-only reporting encourages shipping negligible wins in high-volume data and discarding potentially valuable but uncertain effects in small studies. Standardized effects can compare different scales, but a 'small' d may be important for cheap population-wide interventions and a 'large' d may be irrelevant if the outcome is a proxy. Relative lifts sound dramatic when baseline rates are tiny; absolute differences reveal impact. Interviews test this distinction because it connects statistics with product judgment. Production dashboards should expose both magnitude and uncertainty, with thresholds determined by economics, safety, reversibility, and opportunity cost.
lessons.intuition: Two archers can hit different distances from the bullseye. Effect size is the distance between their average hits. Statistical evidence also considers how scattered the arrows are and how many were fired. Ten thousand tightly grouped arrows can establish a one-millimeter difference; five scattered arrows cannot precisely establish a ten-centimeter difference. A standardized effect divides the distance by a spread measure, making it unitless, but that denominator belongs to a population and design. If one group becomes more heterogeneous, standardized effect changes even when the raw difference does not. For binary outcomes, moving from 1% to 2% is a one-point absolute increase and a 100% relative increase; both are true, but operational consequences depend on population volume and cost.
lessons.deepDive: An effect measure should be chosen from the estimand and action. Raw differences preserve units. Relative and odds measures describe multiplicative comparisons. Standardized measures compare signal with variability. No universal scale labels effects as meaningful independent of context.
lessons.workedExample: Experiment A estimates a +0.08 percentage-point conversion lift with 95% interval [0.03,0.13] and p=0.002. Experiment B estimates +0.80 points with interval [-0.20,1.80] and p=0.12. A has stronger evidence but may be below a +0.30-point minimum worthwhile effect; B is much less certain but includes valuable gains and possible harm. The correct decisions may be 'do not launch A on economics' and 'collect more information for B,' not 'A wins because significant.' Baseline conversion and cost translate these percentages into expected value.
commonMistakes: Calling a smaller p-value a larger effect.
Reporting only relative lift without baseline rate or absolute difference.
Using universal small/medium/large labels for standardized effects without domain context.
Comparing Cohen's d values computed with incompatible populations or variance denominators.
Ranking subgroup effects without uncertainty, multiplicity control, or shrinkage.

followUps.question: Why can a tiny effect have a tiny p-value?
followUps.answer: Standard error shrinks with independent information. A tiny estimate many SEs from zero can be statistically incompatible with the null while remaining practically negligible.

followUps.question: When prefer raw over standardized effect?
followUps.answer: Use raw units when stakeholders understand them and decisions have costs in those units. Add standardized measures for cross-scale comparison, but disclose the denominator and report raw effects too.

followUps.question: Why can odds ratio exaggerate intuition for common outcomes?
followUps.answer: Odds and probabilities diverge as baseline risk grows. An odds ratio is not a risk ratio; translate it to absolute risks for representative baselines before communicating impact.

lessons.production: Define estimand, unit, population, horizon, contrast, baseline, effect scale, variance method, and minimum worthwhile benefit/maximum acceptable harm in a metric registry. Show absolute and relative changes with intervals and sample design. Monitor baseline risk, outcome variance, denominator composition, attrition, effect heterogeneity, weight concentration, and decision sensitivity. Use shrinkage and minimum-cell rules for slices, and protect sensitive subgroup data. Validate effect calculations with synthetic fixtures and invariance tests. Keep statistical evidence separate from expected-value modeling but link them in decision records. Version thresholds so teams cannot move them after results. Roll back launches based on guardrail effects and uncertainty, not headline significance alone. Re-estimate when population variance or baseline rate drifts because standardized and relative effects may change meaning.
lessons.description: Effect size describes the magnitude of a difference or association; statistical significance describes how incompatible data are with a null model relative to sampling uncertainty. They answer different questions. This chapter covers raw effects, relative effects, standardized mean differences, correlations, odds and risk ratios, number needed to treat, and model-performance changes. It explains why standardization aids comparison but can hide domain meaning, how small-sample bias corrections such as Hedges' g work, and why odds ratios are often misread as risk ratios. You will learn to define a smallest effect of practical interest, pair estimates with uncertainty, distinguish clinical or business importance from detectability, and avoid interpreting noisy subgroup effect sizes without shrinkage. The worked example compares an accurately estimated tiny conversion lift with a larger uncertain one. The lab implements Cohen's d and Hedges' g, verifies scale/translation invariance, and checks against the raw mean difference. Production guidance covers estimand contracts, metric units, heterogeneous effects, decision curves, monitoring, and communication.
learningObjectives: Select raw, relative, standardized, or probability-scale effect measures that match the decision and outcome type.
Explain why p-values depend on effect magnitude, noise, sample size, and design while effect size is not significance.
Compute standardized mean differences with appropriate pooled variance and small-sample correction.
Interpret effects against predefined practical thresholds and report uncertainty, baseline risk, and heterogeneity.

deepSections.title: Raw, relative, and standardized measures
deepSections.body: For continuous outcomes, mean or median differences are directly interpretable. Standardized mean difference d divides a mean difference by a within-group SD, often pooled under homoscedastic assumptions. Glass's delta uses a control SD when treatment changes variability. Hedges' g corrects small-sample upward bias in d. Correlation r measures linear association and r squared describes variance explained only under a specified setting. For binary outcomes, risk difference gives absolute change, risk ratio gives multiplicative change, and odds ratio compares odds. Odds ratios increasingly exceed risk ratios as outcomes become common. Number needed to treat is reciprocal absolute risk difference under conditions and can be unstable near zero.

deepSections.title: How magnitude, noise, and n produce evidence
deepSections.body: A test statistic is often effect estimate divided by standard error. Holding variance and design fixed, larger effects or larger independent samples produce stronger evidence. Thus p-value is not a magnitude measure. Confidence intervals reveal the range of effects compatible with the procedure. A significant effect can lie entirely below the minimum worthwhile effect. A nonsignificant interval may contain both zero and large benefit, signaling insufficient information rather than no effect. Equivalence tests can support that effects are confined within prespecified negligible bounds. Power planning should use a meaningful alternative, not an effect reverse-engineered from a desired sample size.

deepSections.title: What standardization clarifies and hides
deepSections.body: Dividing by SD makes an effect unitless and facilitates meta-analysis or comparison across instruments, but the chosen SD is influenced by measurement reliability, population heterogeneity, range restriction, and treatment effects on variance. Standardized values can differ across populations for the same raw effect. Conventional labels such as 0.2, 0.5, and 0.8 are context-dependent heuristics, not laws. Report the raw effect alongside standardized effect, specify denominator and weighting, and avoid standardizing binary outcomes without a clear latent-scale model. Feature importance scores are not automatically causal effect sizes.

deepSections.title: Heterogeneous effects and decision consequences
deepSections.body: An average effect can hide benefit for some groups and harm for others. Subgroup estimates have larger uncertainty and multiplicity; use prespecified interactions, hierarchical shrinkage, and validation rather than ranking noisy slices. Decision value combines effect distribution with implementation cost, risk, capacity, fairness, and reversibility. A treatment policy may target units with positive expected net benefit, but observational heterogeneity can reflect confounding. Report distributional outcomes and guardrails when averages conceal tails. Sensitivity to missing data and estimand choices—intention-to-treat versus per-protocol, risk difference versus ratio—belongs in the decision record.

deepSections.title: Intervals and transformations for effect measures
deepSections.body: Effect estimators have sampling distributions that can be skewed, especially ratios and number-needed-to-treat near a zero risk difference. Construct intervals on a stable scale when appropriate: log risk ratio or log odds ratio, then exponentiate endpoints. A symmetric interval on the ratio scale can include impossible negative values. Standardized mean differences also have nontrivial small-sample uncertainty because the denominator is estimated. For paired or clustered designs, effect and standard error must use the matching covariance structure. When communicating transformed measures, show representative absolute consequences at realistic baselines. An interval for a relative effect does not imply a constant absolute effect across populations with different baseline risk. Sensitivity to scale is substantive, not merely formatting.

lessons.math: For two independent groups, raw effect Delta=Xbar1-Xbar0. With equal-variance convention, pooled s_p=sqrt(((n1-1)s1^2+(n0-1)s0^2)/(n1+n0-2)), and Cohen's d=Delta/s_p. Hedges' g=J d with approximate J=1-3/(4(n1+n0)-9). For binary outcomes, risk difference=p1-p0, risk ratio=p1/p0, and odds ratio=[p1/(1-p1)]/[p0/(1-p0)]. The standard error of an effect, not the effect alone, determines a test statistic.

workedExamples.title: Precise tiny lift versus uncertain large lift
workedExamples.body: Compare both intervals with zero and with a prespecified business threshold, then add baseline volume and cost. Statistical ranking and decision ranking need not agree.

exercises.prompt: Conversion rises from 2% to 2.5%. Give absolute and relative effects.
exercises.solution: Absolute risk difference is 0.5 percentage points. Relative risk is 2.5/2=1.25, a 25% relative increase.

exercises.prompt: Means differ by 4 and pooled SD is 8. What is Cohen's d?
exercises.solution: d=4/8=0.5. Its importance depends on outcome, population, costs, and uncertainty—not a universal label.

exercises.prompt: A 95% interval is [0.01,0.05] but minimum worthwhile effect is 0.10. What follows?
exercises.solution: The effect is statistically above zero under the procedure but the entire compatible range is below the predefined worthwhile threshold, arguing against action on benefit grounds.

lab.goal: Compute Cohen's d and Hedges' g, verify translation/scale invariance, and keep the raw effect beside the standardized result.
lab.buildIt:
import math

def mean(xs): return sum(xs)/len(xs)
def variance(xs):
    m=mean(xs); return sum((x-m)**2 for x in xs)/(len(xs)-1)
def standardized_effect(a,b):
    n1,n0=len(a),len(b); v1,v0=variance(a),variance(b)
    pooled=math.sqrt(((n1-1)*v1+(n0-1)*v0)/(n1+n0-2))
    d=(mean(a)-mean(b))/pooled
    correction=1-3/(4*(n1+n0)-9)
    return mean(a)-mean(b),d,correction*d
a=[14,15,13,17,16,18,15,16]; b=[10,12,11,13,9,14,12,11]
raw,d,g=standardized_effect(a,b)
lab.useIt:
import numpy as np
a_np=np.asarray(a,float); b_np=np.asarray(b,float)
pooled=np.sqrt(((a_np.size-1)*a_np.var(ddof=1)+(b_np.size-1)*b_np.var(ddof=1))/(a_np.size+b_np.size-2))
numpy_d=(a_np.mean()-b_np.mean())/pooled
lab.verifyIt:
assert abs(d-numpy_d) < 1e-12
assert abs(g) < abs(d)
_,shifted_d,_=standardized_effect([x+100 for x in a],[x+100 for x in b])
_,scaled_d,_=standardized_effect([x*3 for x in a],[x*3 for x in b])
assert abs(shifted_d-d) < 1e-12
assert abs(scaled_d-d) < 1e-12
assert raw == mean(a)-mean(b)

lessons.title: ANOVA & Comparing Multiple Groups
lessons.interviewAnswer: One-way ANOVA tests H0 that all group means are equal by comparing between-group mean square with within-group mean square. F=MS_between/MS_within, with k-1 and N-k degrees of freedom under the classical independent normal equal-variance model. A significant F says at least one mean differs; it does not identify which. Inspect residuals and design, use Welch ANOVA for unequal variances when appropriate, then apply prespecified contrasts or multiplicity-adjusted post-hoc tests and report effect sizes and intervals.
keyPoints: ANOVA partitions variability around the grand mean
The F statistic compares explained with residual variation
Omnibus rejection does not identify pairs
Residual independence and variance structure matter
Contrasts and post-hoc tests need multiplicity discipline
lessons.why: Teams often compare several models, campaigns, regions, or treatments. Repeating unadjusted pairwise tests inflates false-positive risk and fragments one scientific question. ANOVA provides a coherent omnibus comparison and a framework for richer designs. Yet the label is frequently misused: analysts infer that all groups differ, ignore an unbalanced heteroskedastic design, or stop at p<0.05 without estimating meaningful contrasts. Interviews ask for between versus within variance because it reveals whether the candidate understands the geometry. In production, the experimental unit, assignment design, and planned contrasts determine validity. ANOVA is a linear model with categorical predictors, which connects it directly to regression, covariate adjustment, interactions, and robust standard errors.
lessons.intuition: Place each observation around its group mean and each group mean around the grand mean. If group labels contain no mean signal, the movement of group means should be small relative to scatter within groups. ANOVA measures both on comparable per-degree-of-freedom scales. F near one means between-group variation resembles residual variation under the model; a large F is unusual when all means are equal. Large F could arise because one group differs while the rest match, because several move gradually, or because assumptions are broken. The omnibus statistic deliberately compresses these patterns, so follow-up contrasts recover the scientific question. A plot of group estimates and uncertainty often communicates more than the test table.
lessons.deepDive: One-way fixed-effects ANOVA is the regression y_ij=mu+alpha_j+epsilon_ij with a parameter constraint or reference coding. The omnibus F test compares a model with group indicators against an intercept-only model.
lessons.workedExample: Three campaigns have outcomes A=[8,9,10,11], B=[9,10,11,12], C=[15,16,17,18]. Their means are 9.5, 10.5, and 16.5; grand mean is 12.167. Within-group variation is small relative to group-mean separation, so F is large. The omnibus result establishes that not all means are equal. It does not require A versus B to differ. A planned contrast comparing C with the average of A and B directly tests the campaign question; a Tukey or Holm procedure can handle all pairs if they were planned. Report C's raw lift and interval, not only the F test.
commonMistakes: Concluding every pair differs after a significant omnibus F test.
Running all unadjusted pairwise t-tests instead of a planned family-level procedure.
Checking normality of pooled raw outcomes rather than residual structure and design.
Ignoring unequal variances, unbalanced groups, clustering, repeated measures, or outliers.
Reporting only p-values without group estimates, contrasts, intervals, or effect size.

followUps.question: Why not just run pairwise t-tests?
followUps.answer: Unadjusted pairwise tests inflate family-wise error and answer fragmented questions. An omnibus model plus planned or adjusted contrasts provides coherent error control and often better power.

followUps.question: What does significant ANOVA tell you?
followUps.answer: It rejects the hypothesis that all modeled group means are equal. It does not identify which groups differ, guarantee practical importance, or prove assumptions.

followUps.question: When use Welch ANOVA?
followUps.answer: When independent groups have meaningfully unequal variances, especially with unequal sample sizes. It adjusts the reference calculation; still inspect outliers, independence, and the estimand.

lessons.production: Register experimental unit, groups, allocation, factors, interactions, contrasts, primary outcomes, variance method, and multiplicity family before analysis. Validate group counts, randomization balance, missingness, residuals, influence, variance ratios, and cluster structure. Build reusable tests that verify SST=SSB+SSW and match reference libraries on fixtures. Monitor group composition and variance drift; historical thresholds may fail after population change. Report marginal/group means and contrast intervals in domain units with practical boundaries. Protect small-cell results and sensitive categories. Persist model matrix, coding, contrast weights, software versions, and excluded records. When assumptions fail, switch via a documented rule rather than shopping for significance. Rollback conclusions and downstream launch decisions if assignment or outcome instrumentation was faulty.
lessons.description: Analysis of variance tests whether group means exhibit more between-group variation than expected from within-group variation under a specified model. It avoids the uncontrolled multiplicity of running every pairwise t-test, but a significant omnibus F test says only that not all means are equal. This chapter derives the sums-of-squares decomposition and F ratio, explains degrees of freedom, effect sizes, diagnostics, planned contrasts, post-hoc comparisons, Welch ANOVA, nonparametric alternatives, and extensions to factorial and repeated-measures designs. You will learn why normality concerns residuals rather than raw outcomes, why independence is usually more important than mild normality, and why unequal variance with unbalanced groups can distort classical ANOVA. The worked example decomposes three campaign groups and follows the omnibus test with corrected comparisons. The lab computes one-way ANOVA from first principles, verifies decomposition and translation invariance, and compares with SciPy. Production guidance covers experimental units, contrast registries, assumptions, multiplicity, drift, and reporting estimates rather than only an F statistic.
learningObjectives: Derive between-, within-, and total sums of squares and explain the F ratio as signal relative to noise.
Interpret an omnibus rejection without claiming every group differs from every other group.
Choose classical, Welch, robust, permutation, or rank-based alternatives according to design and residual behavior.
Plan contrasts and adjust post-hoc comparisons while reporting group estimates, intervals, and effect sizes.

deepSections.title: Partitioning total variability
deepSections.body: Let ybar_j be group j mean, ybar the grand mean, and n_j group size. Total sum of squares SST=sum_ij(y_ij-ybar)^2. Between sum SSB=sum_j n_j(ybar_j-ybar)^2. Within sum SSW=sum_ij(y_ij-ybar_j)^2. The identity SST=SSB+SSW is geometric: fitted group deviations and residuals are orthogonal in least squares. Degrees of freedom are N-1 total, k-1 between, and N-k within. Mean squares divide each component by its df. F=MSB/MSW. Under H0 and classical assumptions, both estimate common variance but the numerator grows when group means differ.

deepSections.title: What the classical F reference needs
deepSections.body: Observations should be independent at the experimental-unit level. Residuals within groups are modeled normal with common variance for the exact small-sample F distribution. Moderate normal departures are often less damaging with adequate balanced samples than outliers, dependence, or severe variance imbalance. Diagnose residual versus fitted plots, group spreads, tails, leverage, missingness, and assignment integrity. Do not test normality mechanically and then choose a method solely from another p-value. In clustered or repeated data, use mixed models, generalized estimating equations, cluster-robust methods, or design-based randomization inference.

deepSections.title: Welch, robust, rank, and permutation approaches
deepSections.body: Welch ANOVA adjusts weighting and degrees of freedom when variances differ and can be preferable for heteroskedastic groups. Robust trimmed-mean methods reduce sensitivity to outliers. Kruskal–Wallis tests distributional/rank differences and is not simply 'ANOVA on medians'; interpretation depends on distribution shapes. Permutation ANOVA can calibrate a chosen statistic when assignment or exchangeability justifies shuffling, with restrictions for blocks and clusters. Transformations may stabilize variance but change the estimand. Choose the method from the data-generating and decision model, then report the effect scale it actually targets.

deepSections.title: Contrasts, post-hoc tests, and effect size
deepSections.body: An omnibus rejection licenses investigation under the planned error procedure; it does not show every pair differs. Planned orthogonal or scientifically motivated contrasts are more powerful and interpretable than all pairs. Tukey's method targets family-wise error for pairwise comparisons under its assumptions; Holm can adjust general contrast p-values. Games–Howell is useful for unequal variances. Report group means or marginal means, contrast estimates, intervals, and practical thresholds. Eta squared SSB/SST describes sample variance attributed to group but is biased upward; omega squared applies a correction. Interaction or trend contrasts may answer the real question better than pairwise lists.

deepSections.title: Factorial ANOVA, interactions, and estimable contrasts
deepSections.body: With two or more factors, main effects average over levels of other factors and can be misleading when interactions are present. An interaction asks whether one factor's effect changes across another factor. Inspect interaction plots and estimate simple effects or planned contrasts instead of interpreting a main-effect p-value in isolation. In unbalanced observational data, sums of squares labeled Type I, II, and III test different hypotheses and depend on coding; there is no universally correct type. Write the estimable contrast explicitly and use a model matrix that matches it. Random factors, repeated measures, and nested units require mixed or hierarchical models rather than treating every level as a fixed independent group. The design determines the error term and denominator degrees of freedom.

lessons.math: SSB=sum_j n_j(ybar_j-ybar)^2, SSW=sum_j sum_i(y_ij-ybar_j)^2, SST=SSB+SSW. MSB=SSB/(k-1), MSW=SSW/(N-k), and F=MSB/MSW. Under H0 with iid normal errors of common variance, F follows F_(k-1,N-k). Eta squared=SSB/SST. A common omega-squared estimate is (SSB-(k-1)MSW)/(SST+MSW), truncated or interpreted cautiously when negative in samples.

workedExamples.title: Three campaigns with one separated group
workedExamples.body: Decompose total variability, compute F, then use a planned C-versus-average(A,B) contrast to show why an omnibus result and pairwise claims are different.

exercises.prompt: ANOVA with k=4 groups and N=40 has what degrees of freedom?
exercises.solution: Between df=k-1=3, within df=N-k=36, and total df=N-1=39.

exercises.prompt: If F is significant, may you claim group 1 differs from group 2?
exercises.solution: Not without a corresponding planned or multiplicity-adjusted contrast. The omnibus result only says not all group means are equal.

exercises.prompt: Why can variance imbalance be especially harmful with unequal n?
exercises.solution: The pooled within variance weights groups in a way that may mismatch the sampling variance of mean differences, distorting the classical F reference; the direction depends on the pairing of variances and sizes.

lab.goal: Compute one-way ANOVA from first principles, verify the sums-of-squares identity and translation invariance, and compare F with SciPy.
lab.buildIt:
def mean(xs): return sum(xs)/len(xs)
def one_way_anova(groups):
    all_values=[x for g in groups for x in g]; grand=mean(all_values)
    ss_between=sum(len(g)*(mean(g)-grand)**2 for g in groups)
    ss_within=sum(sum((x-mean(g))**2 for x in g) for g in groups)
    ss_total=sum((x-grand)**2 for x in all_values)
    df_b=len(groups)-1; df_w=len(all_values)-len(groups)
    f=(ss_between/df_b)/(ss_within/df_w)
    return f,ss_between,ss_within,ss_total
groups=[[8,9,10,11],[9,10,11,12],[15,16,17,18]]
f,sb,sw,st=one_way_anova(groups)
lab.verifyIt:
assert abs(st-(sb+sw)) < 1e-12
assert abs(f-scipy_result.statistic) < 1e-12
shifted=[[x+100 for x in g] for g in groups]
assert abs(one_way_anova(shifted)[0]-f) < 1e-12
assert f > 1

lessons.title: Chi-square Tests for Categorical Data
lessons.interviewAnswer: Pearson's chi-square statistic sums (observed-expected)^2/expected across categorical cells. For an r-by-c independence table, expected count is row total times column total divided by grand total and df=(r-1)(c-1), assuming independent units and adequate asymptotic counts. A significant result says the variables are associated, not which cells differ or that one causes the other. Inspect standardized residuals, report an effect size such as Cramér's V, adjust post-hoc analyses, and use exact or Monte Carlo methods for sparse tables.
keyPoints: Expected counts come from the null and fixed margins
Each cell contributes a squared standardized discrepancy
Degrees of freedom reflect marginal constraints
Sparse or dependent data break the usual reference
Association magnitude and cell pattern follow the omnibus test
lessons.why: Categorical questions appear everywhere: device by failure type, region by churn state, model by error category, or treatment by outcome. A contingency table is easy to create, which makes it easy to misuse. Analysts test percentages instead of counts, treat thousands of repeated events as independent, combine categories after seeing significance, or conclude causation from association. A single chi-square p-value also hides whether one rare cell or a broad pattern drives the result. Interviews ask expected-count formulas and assumptions, but production work additionally needs category lineage, stable denominators, privacy safeguards, and effect interpretation. Chi-square is best seen as a model comparison for counts rather than a ritual attached to a crosstab.
lessons.intuition: Under independence, knowing the row should not change the column distribution. If 30% of all observations converted, each row is expected to have roughly 30% conversions, scaled to its row total. Compare every observed cell with that expected value. A discrepancy of 10 matters more when only 5 were expected than when 5,000 were expected, so Pearson divides squared discrepancy by expected count. The contributions add; cells with large contributions reveal where the table departs from the null. Because row and column totals constrain the table, only (r-1)(c-1) cell directions vary freely. As sample size grows, even tiny association can be highly significant, so pair the test with residuals and a magnitude measure.
lessons.deepDive: Categorical-count tests begin with a multinomial, product-multinomial, or randomization sampling model. Similar formulas can correspond to different conditioning schemes, and independent observational units remain essential. The chi-square reference is an asymptotic approximation to the statistic's null distribution.
lessons.workedExample: A channel-by-conversion table is [[90,10],[160,40],[150,50]] for Email, Search, and Social with columns no/yes. Row totals are 100, 200, 200; the conversion total is 100 of 500, so independence expects yes counts [20,40,40]. Email has 10 fewer conversions than expected and Social has 10 more; Search matches expectation. Compute all six cell contributions, not only the yes cells, and sum to X^2. If the omnibus test rejects, standardized residuals identify Email and Social as drivers. Report channel conversion rates 10%, 20%, and 25%, Cramér's V, and note that channel was not randomized, so this is association rather than channel causal effect.
commonMistakes: Applying the formula to percentages rather than original counts and sample sizes.
Treating repeated rows from the same unit as independent categorical observations.
Using an asymptotic chi-square reference with sparse expected counts or structural zeros without diagnosis.
Concluding causation or claiming every category differs after an omnibus rejection.
Inspecting many cell residuals without adjustment and reporting only the most surprising one.

followUps.question: How are expected counts computed for independence?
followUps.answer: Multiply the cell's row total by its column total and divide by grand total. This is the fitted count under the product of estimated marginal proportions.

followUps.question: What if expected counts are small?
followUps.answer: Inspect the whole table and design. Consider an exact or Monte Carlo test, substantively justified category pooling, or a sparse categorical model; do not rely mechanically on an asymptotic reference.

followUps.question: Does significant chi-square imply a strong relationship?
followUps.answer: No. Significance combines discrepancy with sample size. Report cell rates/residuals and an association measure such as Cramér's V, then judge practical importance.

lessons.production: Version category definitions, ordering, unknown handling, observation unit, population window, and table construction. Validate that counts reconcile with source totals and expected margins. Monitor rare-level frequency, structural/sampling zeros, expected-count distribution, residual hotspots, Cramér's V, sample size, and cluster duplication. Apply design-aware methods for surveys and repeated units. Prespecify category pooling and post-hoc residual families. Enforce minimum cell sizes and disclosure controls for sensitive groups; avoid dashboards that expose rare identities. Keep raw counts alongside percentages and test metadata. Test implementations with known tables, transpose invariance, marginal preservation, and contribution sums. When taxonomy changes, do not compare old and new chi-square statistics without a mapping. Roll back downstream alerts if category instrumentation or deduplication failed.
lessons.description: Chi-square methods compare observed categorical counts with counts expected under a null model. The goodness-of-fit test asks whether one categorical distribution matches specified probabilities; the independence or homogeneity test asks whether two categorical variables are associated or whether group distributions agree. This chapter derives Pearson's statistic from standardized cell residuals, explains degrees of freedom and expected-count calculation, connects the contingency-table test with likelihood-ratio and log-linear models, and distinguishes association from causation. You will learn why tests operate on counts rather than percentages, when asymptotic calibration is unreliable, how sparse tables and structural zeros require exact, Monte Carlo, or category-restructuring approaches, and why a significant table needs cell-level residuals and effect sizes such as Cramér's V. The worked example analyzes channel by conversion status and identifies which cells drive the result. The lab computes expected counts and Pearson's statistic from first principles, verifies marginal preservation and decomposition, and compares with SciPy. Production guidance covers category contracts, rare-level handling, weighting, multiplicity, privacy, and drift.
learningObjectives: Distinguish chi-square goodness-of-fit, independence, and homogeneity questions and formulate their null models.
Compute expected counts, Pearson cell contributions, the total statistic, and correct degrees of freedom.
Diagnose sparse counts, structural zeros, dependence, sampling weights, and post-hoc cell inspection.
Report residual patterns and association magnitude without interpreting association as causation.

deepSections.title: Goodness of fit, independence, and homogeneity
deepSections.body: Goodness of fit compares one observed count vector O_i with fully specified null probabilities p_i, so E_i=n p_i and typically df=k-1 minus parameters estimated from the same data. Independence uses one joint sample cross-classified by two variables and tests p_ij=p_i+ p_+j, estimating expected counts from both margins. Homogeneity compares category distributions across independently sampled populations; its table statistic can be identical but the design and verbal conclusion differ. A two-by-two treatment table may also be analyzed through risk difference, ratio, odds ratio, exact randomization, or regression. Choose based on estimand rather than defaulting to chi-square.

deepSections.title: Expected counts, residuals, and degrees of freedom
deepSections.body: For r-by-c independence, E_ij=(row_i total)(column_j total)/N. Pearson X^2=sum_ij (O_ij-E_ij)^2/E_ij. Raw Pearson residual is (O-E)/sqrt(E); adjusted standardized residuals account for estimated row and column proportions and are more comparable. The total decomposes into cell contributions, but examining many residuals after a significant omnibus test creates multiplicity and selection concerns. Degrees of freedom (r-1)(c-1) arise because fixed margins impose r+c-1 independent constraints on rc cells. For goodness of fit, estimating model parameters consumes additional df. Software conventions should be verified.

deepSections.title: Sparse tables, zeros, and alternative calibration
deepSections.body: The chi-square approximation can be poor when expected counts are small or the table is sparse. The familiar 'all expected at least five' is a conservative heuristic, not a universal theorem. Fisher's exact test conditions on margins for a two-by-two table and tests an odds-ratio null; larger exact tests can be expensive. Monte Carlo sampling from the correct null provides calibrated approximations. Combining rare categories is acceptable only when substantively defensible and preferably prespecified. A structural zero is impossible by design and should not be treated as a sampling zero. For ordered categories, a trend test can be more powerful than an unordered omnibus test. Penalized or hierarchical models help with many sparse levels.

deepSections.title: Dependence, weights, effect size, and causality
deepSections.body: Repeated observations from a user, clustered survey samples, and time dependence violate multinomial independence. Survey-weighted tables require design-based tests such as Rao–Scott adjustments, not simply feeding weighted noninteger counts to an ordinary test. A significant association may reflect confounding, selection, measurement, or reverse causality. Cramér's V=sqrt(X^2/(N min(r-1,c-1))) summarizes strength but remains sample/population dependent and does not convey direction; for two-by-two tables report risks and odds ratios with intervals. Visualize observed-minus-expected residuals and report absolute cell rates. Large N can make negligible associations significant.

deepSections.title: Log-linear and regression connections
deepSections.body: A contingency table can be modeled with Poisson log-linear terms. Independence corresponds to row and column main effects without their interaction; adding the interaction saturates a two-way table. Pearson X-squared and likelihood-ratio G-squared compare observed counts with the fitted independence model and become asymptotically equivalent. Logistic regression conditions on one margin and expresses a binary column outcome through row predictors, allowing covariate adjustment and interpretable odds ratios. These models extend beyond an omnibus table but add specification choices and sparse-cell risks. For multiway tables, marginal associations can reverse after stratification, echoing Simpson's paradox. Choose a model that preserves the sampling design and report adjusted and unadjusted patterns rather than treating one aggregated chi-square result as complete.

lessons.math: For independence, E_ij=R_i C_j/N and X^2=sum_ij (O_ij-E_ij)^2/E_ij, approximately chi-square with (r-1)(c-1) df under H0 and regularity. The likelihood-ratio statistic G^2=2 sum O_ij log(O_ij/E_ij), treating zero terms as zero, has the same asymptotic reference. Cramér's V=sqrt(X^2/[N min(r-1,c-1)]). Pearson cell contributions are nonnegative and sum exactly to X^2, providing an audit trail from table to statistic.

workedExamples.title: Acquisition channel and conversion
workedExamples.body: Construct expected counts from margins, decompose Pearson's statistic by cell, inspect residual direction, and translate the association back to channel-specific rates without making a causal claim.

exercises.prompt: A row total is 80, column total 50, and N=200. What is expected count under independence?
What are df for a 3-by-4 independence table?
exercises.solution: (3-1)(4-1)=6, assuming no structural zeros or additional fitted constraints.

exercises.prompt: Why can a huge chi-square test reject for an unimportant association?
exercises.solution: The statistic scales with N for a fixed discrepancy in proportions. With huge samples, tiny deviations become detectable; effect size and domain consequences must be reported.

lab.goal: Compute a Pearson independence test from scratch, verify expected margins and cell decomposition, and compare with SciPy.
lab.buildIt:
def chi_square_independence(table):
    rows=len(table); cols=len(table[0])
    row_totals=[sum(row) for row in table]
    col_totals=[sum(table[i][j] for i in range(rows)) for j in range(cols)]
    total=sum(row_totals)
    expected=[[row_totals[i]*col_totals[j]/total for j in range(cols)] for i in range(rows)]
    contributions=[[(table[i][j]-expected[i][j])**2/expected[i][j] for j in range(cols)] for i in range(rows)]
    statistic=sum(sum(row) for row in contributions)
    return statistic,expected,contributions,(rows-1)*(cols-1)
table=[[90,10],[160,40],[150,50]]
statistic,expected,contrib,df=chi_square_independence(table)
lab.useIt:
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import chi2_contingency
result=chi2_contingency(np.asarray(table),correction=False)
lab.verifyIt:
assert abs(statistic-result.statistic) < 1e-12
assert df == result.dof == 2
assert np.allclose(expected,result.expected_freq)
assert all(abs(sum(expected[i])-sum(table[i])) < 1e-12 for i in range(len(table)))
assert abs(sum(sum(row) for row in contrib)-statistic) < 1e-12
