sourceNotes.contribution: Provides official applied definitions of chi-square reference distributions, tests, and count-based diagnostics.
Connects categorical tables, expected counts, inference, and interpretable effect reporting.
Documents the current contingency-table implementation used for independent verification.
Explains why complex survey weights and clustering require design-aware variance and test procedures.

lessons.title: Power, Minimum Detectable Effect & Sample Size
lessons.interviewAnswer: Power is P(reject H0|a specified alternative is true), equal to 1-beta for a fixed design and test. Sample size grows with variance, stricter alpha, higher target power, and smaller effect—often approximately inverse-square in the detectable effect. Plan using the smallest effect worth acting on, realistic baseline/variance, independent unit, allocation, attrition, clustering, multiplicity, and stopping rule. MDE is what a design can reliably detect, not necessarily what matters. Do not use observed post-hoc power as new evidence; report the effect interval.
keyPoints: Power is a curve over alternatives, not one universal number
Effect threshold and variance drive sample size
Independent information matters more than row count
Design corrections must be included before launch
Simulation audits formulas for real metrics and pipelines
lessons.why: Underpowered studies waste traffic and produce ambiguous intervals; overpowered studies may waste time detecting effects too small to matter. Product teams often choose 80% power by convention, back-solve an MDE from available traffic, then mistake detectability for value. Planning forces the decision threshold, baseline variability, unit, and analysis into the open. Interviews test how n changes with effect size and variance. Production planning must also incorporate cluster assignment, unequal traffic costs, guardrails, attrition, repeated looks, and ramp schedules. Because power is conditional on assumptions, a precise sample-size number should be accompanied by sensitivity analysis. Bias and instrumentation errors are not cured by large n.
lessons.intuition: Picture null and alternative sampling distributions of an estimator. Alpha chooses a rejection boundary in the null tail. Power is the area of the alternative distribution beyond that boundary. Increasing independent sample size narrows both distributions, separating them in standard-error units. A larger true effect also separates their centers. Stricter alpha moves the boundary outward, reducing power unless n grows. More noise broadens distributions and requires more information. If users generate correlated events, adding events without users barely narrows the relevant estimator. An MDE is the alternative whose power reaches the target under the planned design. A minimum worthwhile effect comes from economics or safety. Good plans align them or explain the gap.
lessons.deepDive: A power calculation is a prospective property of a fully specified decision rule. It includes estimator, variance method, alpha and sidedness, alternative, sample-size allocation, design, and stopping. Different alternatives yield a power function rather than a single property of the dataset.
lessons.workedExample: Baseline conversion is 10%, and the smallest worthwhile absolute lift is 1 percentage point to 11%. With two-sided alpha 0.05 and 80% power, an approximate two-proportion normal calculation yields about 14,700 users per arm (exact output varies by formula). If users are assigned by household with average size 2 and rho=0.10, DE≈1.1, raising analyzable users to about 16,170 per arm. With 8% outcome attrition, enroll roughly 17,576 per arm. Then simulate the planned estimator at p0=0.10 and p1 in [0.10,0.115], verify null false-positive rate, and translate users into calendar duration using eligible daily traffic.
commonMistakes: Choosing MDE only from available traffic and presenting it as a minimum worthwhile effect.
Computing post-hoc observed power and treating it as evidence beyond the estimate and p-value.
Using row count instead of independent assignment units or ignoring cluster design effect.
Planning with optimistic variance, baseline, compliance, or attrition and no sensitivity analysis.
Using a fixed-horizon power calculation while continuously peeking or adjusting many primary metrics.

followUps.question: What happens to n if the target effect is halved?
followUps.answer: Under common normal approximations, n scales as 1/delta squared, so halving the effect requires about four times the independent sample size, all else equal.

followUps.question: Is 80% power always correct?
followUps.answer: No. It is a convention. Choose power from the cost of missing a worthwhile effect, test cost, decision reversibility, available traffic, and error trade-offs; safety contexts may demand more.

followUps.question: Why avoid observed post-hoc power?
followUps.answer: Plugging the observed effect into the same test formula makes observed power largely a re-expression of the p-value and encourages circular conclusions. The confidence interval more directly shows uncertainty and compatible effects.

lessons.production: Maintain a versioned design document with estimand, unit, baseline, variance source, worthwhile effect, alpha, power, sidedness, allocation, covariates, clusters, attrition, multiplicity, stopping rule, ramp, and outcome delay. Generate sensitivity tables over plausible inputs and simulation-check Type I error and power. Forecast eligible independent units—not events—and monitor enrollment, balance, attrition, cluster sizes, ICC, metric variance, and data latency without unblinding effect-driven changes. Predefine blinded nuisance re-estimation if needed. Secure treatment outcomes and subgroup plans. Store simulator code, RNG streams, software versions, and result summaries. If traffic or variance assumptions fail, extend or stop according to the protocol rather than moving targets. Roll back decisions if integrity checks invalidate the planned operating characteristics.
lessons.description: Statistical power is the probability that a prespecified procedure rejects its null under a particular alternative. Sample-size planning connects that operating characteristic to a meaningful effect, variance, alpha, allocation, design, attrition, and decision horizon. This chapter derives normal-mean scaling, distinguishes minimum detectable effect from minimum worthwhile effect, explains one- versus two-sided tests, unequal allocation, clustering, multiple testing, sequential designs, and simulation-based power for complex estimators. You will learn why post-hoc observed power adds little beyond the p-value, why plugging optimistic variance or conversion assumptions understates required sample size, and why increasing rows does not overcome correlation or bias. The worked example plans a two-arm conversion experiment in absolute percentage points and inflates for attrition and design effect. The lab implements an approximate two-sample proportion calculation, verifies monotonic relationships, and compares a t-test case with statsmodels. Production guidance covers preregistered assumptions, traffic forecasts, guardrails, simulation, re-estimation without unblinding effects, monitoring, and stopping behavior.
learningObjectives: Define power as a function of a specific alternative, procedure, design, and sample size.
Distinguish minimum detectable, minimum worthwhile, and observed effects in planning and interpretation.
Compute approximate sample sizes and adjust for allocation, clustering, attrition, multiplicity, and sequential monitoring.
Use simulation to validate analytic power for complex metrics and avoid post-hoc observed-power misuse.

deepSections.title: Alpha, beta, effect, and the power curve
deepSections.body: For a one-sided normal test with known SE, choose a critical boundary so null rejection probability is alpha. Under alternative delta, power is the probability the shifted estimator crosses that boundary. At delta=0, power equals alpha for a simple boundary. As delta grows in the targeted direction, power rises. Two-sided tests allocate error to both tails and require more separation for the same directional effect. Power should be shown across a range including harm, zero, minimum worthwhile effect, and optimistic effect. Type S (wrong sign) and Type M (magnitude exaggeration conditional on significance) risks can be substantial in low-power studies.

deepSections.title: Approximate scaling and planning inputs
deepSections.body: For equal-size normal groups with common SD sigma and target raw difference delta, a common approximation per arm is n≈2 sigma^2(z_(1-alpha/2)+z_power)^2/delta^2. Halving delta quadruples n; doubling sigma quadruples n. Proportions require variance tied to baseline and alternative, and rare events may need exact or simulation methods. Unequal allocation increases total n for fixed precision unless one arm is cheaper or constrained. Use variance from representative historical data without leaking future treatment outcomes. Include uncertainty in baseline and variance through scenarios rather than one optimistic input.

deepSections.title: Clustering, attrition, multiplicity, and sequential designs
deepSections.body: For equal cluster size m and intraclass correlation rho, design effect is approximately 1+(m-1)rho; multiply simple-random sample size, then account for the number of independent clusters and small-cluster inference. Inflate for expected attrition by dividing by retained fraction, while addressing whether attrition is differential and biasing. Multiple primary comparisons may use adjusted alpha, increasing n. Covariate adjustment can reduce residual variance if planned and measured pre-treatment. Sequential or group-sequential designs have their own boundaries and expected sample sizes; do not mix a fixed-horizon calculation with continuous peeking. Ramp-up and delayed outcomes determine calendar duration.

deepSections.title: Simulation-based power and what not to do
deepSections.body: For ratios, quantiles, clustered assignment, CUPED, missing outcomes, complex models, or adaptive rules, simulate the full data-generating and analysis pipeline under many alternatives. Include assignment, preprocessing, estimator, exclusions, variance, stopping, and multiplicity. Verify Type I error at the null before trusting power. Post-hoc observed power computed by plugging the observed effect into the prospective formula is a monotone transformation of the test statistic and adds no independent information; use the confidence interval and sensitivity analysis. Re-estimating nuisance variance during a blinded design may be possible, but changing effect targets after seeing treatment differences compromises interpretation.

deepSections.title: Planning for estimation precision instead of rejection
deepSections.body: Some decisions need an interval narrow enough for action rather than a chosen rejection probability. Precision planning selects n so the expected or high-probability confidence-interval half-width falls below a tolerance. For a mean with known sigma, half-width is approximately z sigma/sqrt(n); proportions are widest near one-half. Precision criteria avoid framing an exact-zero null when the real question is how accurately an effect must be known. Assurance methods integrate power over uncertainty in nuisance parameters or prior beliefs, producing a probability that a future study meets its goal. Whatever criterion is used, simulate interval width and decision success across plausible baselines, variances, attrition, and effects. State whether n guarantees expected, median, or worst-case precision.

lessons.math: For equal-size two-sample means with known common sigma and two-sided alpha, approximate per-arm n=2 sigma^2(z_(1-alpha/2)+z_(1-beta))^2/delta^2. Standardized effect d=delta/sigma gives n≈2(z_alpha+z_power)^2/d^2. Cluster design effect DE=1+(m-1)rho under equal cluster sizes. Attrition inflation is n_enroll=n_analyzable/(1-a). Exact formulas vary with test, finite df, baseline proportion, allocation, correction, and sequential boundary; official software conventions must be verified.

workedExamples.title: Conversion experiment with clustering and attrition

exercises.prompt: If SD doubles while effect, alpha, and power stay fixed, how does approximate n change?
exercises.solution: n is proportional to sigma squared, so it increases by a factor of four.

exercises.prompt: A cluster design has m=5 and rho=0.20. Compute equal-size design effect.
exercises.solution: DE=1+(5-1)*0.20=1.8. Multiply the simple-random information requirement by roughly 1.8, then ensure enough independent clusters.

exercises.prompt: You need 10,000 analyzable units and expect 20% attrition. How many enroll?
exercises.solution: 10,000/(1-0.20)=12,500. This inflation addresses quantity, not bias from differential attrition.

lab.goal: Compute approximate two-proportion sample size, verify monotonic design relationships, and compare an independent t-test case with statsmodels.
lab.buildIt:
import math
from statistics import NormalDist

def n_per_arm_proportions(p0,p1,alpha=0.05,power=0.8):
    if not (0<p0<1 and 0<p1<1 and p0!=p1): raise ValueError('valid distinct probabilities required')
    z_alpha=NormalDist().inv_cdf(1-alpha/2)
    z_power=NormalDist().inv_cdf(power)
    pbar=(p0+p1)/2
    numerator=(z_alpha*math.sqrt(2*pbar*(1-pbar))+z_power*math.sqrt(p0*(1-p0)+p1*(1-p1)))**2
    return math.ceil(numerator/(p1-p0)**2)
n=n_per_arm_proportions(0.10,0.11)
n_smaller_effect=n_per_arm_proportions(0.10,0.105)
lab.verifyIt:
assert n > 0
assert n_smaller_effect > n
assert n_per_arm_proportions(0.10,0.12) < n
assert abs(t_power-0.80) < 1e-6
design_effect=1+(5-1)*0.20
assert design_effect == 1.8
lab.shipIt: Version all design assumptions, calculate on independent units, include clustering/attrition/multiplicity/stopping, and simulation-check both null error and power before enrollment.

Provides formal Type I/II error and power theory for statistical procedures.
Connects effect size, power, sample size, experimental design, and accessible interpretation.

lessons.title: Bayesian Updating: Prior, Likelihood & Posterior
lessons.interviewAnswer: Bayesian updating is posterior proportional to likelihood times prior: p(theta|y)=p(y|theta)p(theta)/p(y). The prior encodes assumptions before the current data, the likelihood is the data model, the evidence normalizes, and the posterior represents uncertainty conditional on both. Prediction integrates p(y_new|theta) over the posterior. Independent data batches can be updated sequentially, but duplicated or dependent evidence cannot be multiplied as if independent. Always check prior predictive implications, posterior sensitivity, model fit, and decision loss.
keyPoints: Bayes reverses conditioning through a generative model
The evidence normalizes and supports model comparison
Posterior uncertainty is conditional on model and prior
Prediction integrates rather than plugs in one parameter
Sequential updating requires correct conditional independence
lessons.why: Bayesian language appears in experimentation, forecasting, risk, personalization, anomaly detection, and ML. A candidate may recite Bayes' formula yet double-count evidence, use a prior fitted on the same data, or interpret a likelihood as a posterior. In production, posterior probability is attractive because it can answer decision-oriented questions such as P(lift exceeds a threshold), but that number is only as credible as the likelihood, prior, and selection process. Large samples can overwhelm weak priors under regular models, but they can also concentrate around a misspecified pseudo-truth. Bayesian updating therefore does not eliminate diagnostics or causal design. It supplies a coherent conditional calculus that must be embedded in a broader workflow.
lessons.intuition: Start with a weighted set of plausible worlds. The prior assigns more weight to some parameter values than others. Ask how likely the observed data would be in each world; the likelihood reweights them. Normalize the new weights so they sum or integrate to one: that is the posterior. A diagnostic-test update works the same way in odds: prior odds multiplied by a likelihood ratio become posterior odds. Prediction then averages future outcomes over all surviving worlds, giving more weight to posterior-plausible parameters. A plug-in prediction at the posterior mean discards parameter uncertainty and can distort nonlinear risks. If the data were chosen because they looked extreme or reused from prior construction, the simple reweighting story omits the selection mechanism.
lessons.deepDive: Bayes' theorem is an identity within a joint probability model. Bayesian inference adds modeling choices: a prior p(theta), likelihood p(y|theta), and often a decision utility. The posterior is conditional, not an unconditional certificate of truth.
lessons.workedExample: A product team uses Beta(2,8) for a segment's conversion rate, encoding prior mean 0.20 with modest strength. It observes k=6 conversions in n=20 visits. The posterior is Beta(8,22), with mean 8/30=0.2667. The MLE is 0.30; shrinkage reflects prior information. The probability that p exceeds 0.25 is an integral of the posterior, not a p-value. Prediction for the next visit is 0.2667, while uncertainty for ten future conversions uses the Beta–Binomial and is wider than Binomial(10,0.2667) because parameter uncertainty is integrated. Sensitivity to Beta(1,1) and a skeptical prior should be shown before a launch decision.
commonMistakes: Reversing p(data|theta) into p(theta|data) without a prior and evidence.
Multiplying likelihoods for duplicated, selected, or dependent evidence as if observations were conditionally independent.
Treating posterior probability as model-free certainty or as proof of causal effect.
Using a plug-in parameter for prediction while ignoring posterior uncertainty.
Choosing or tuning priors after seeing the final data without disclosing the reuse.

followUps.question: Why is the evidence often ignored in MCMC?
followUps.answer: For a fixed model and observed data it is constant in theta, so algorithms targeting relative posterior density can work with an unnormalized density. It is still required for normalized probabilities and Bayesian model comparison.

followUps.question: Does the prior always vanish with enough data?
followUps.answer: Under regular identifiable models a fixed positive prior often has diminishing local influence, but not under misspecification, weak identification, boundaries, growing dimension, or priors that exclude relevant values.

followUps.question: What is the difference between posterior and posterior predictive?
followUps.answer: The posterior is uncertainty about parameters conditional on data. The posterior predictive averages the future-data model over that parameter posterior, adding outcome variability to parameter uncertainty.

lessons.production: Create a model card containing population, parameterization, likelihood, observation window, censoring and missingness rules, prior rationale, sensitivity alternatives, decision loss, and predictive target. Generate prior predictive samples in CI and reject obviously impossible scales. Compute in log space and test analytic fixtures. Persist data hash, code, package versions, RNG streams, posterior representation, and diagnostics. Monitor prior–posterior conflict, posterior drift, calibration, predictive residuals, effective sample size or approximation quality, and decision sensitivity. Protect small-segment posterior summaries and do not let priors leak sensitive historical rates. When new data overlap old batches, deduplicate before updating. Rollback must restore the previous posterior, prior version, likelihood, and evidence cutoff. If diagnostics fail, freeze or widen decisions rather than emitting overconfident probabilities.
lessons.description: Bayesian updating combines a prior distribution with a likelihood to produce a posterior distribution and then integrates that posterior to make predictions and decisions. The algebra is short, but responsible use requires clarity about what is conditioned on, how priors are chosen, which likelihood generated the data, and what uncertainty remains. This chapter develops Bayes' rule in odds and density form, separates prior predictive, posterior, posterior predictive, evidence, and likelihood, and explains sequential updating, exchangeability, sensitivity, and calibration. You will learn why the normalizing constant matters for model comparison but can be avoided by many samplers, why a posterior can be sharply wrong under misspecification, and how decision losses convert beliefs into actions. The worked example updates a Beta prior with conversion observations and computes the predictive chance of future successes. The lab implements a grid posterior from first principles, verifies it against the analytic Beta posterior, and checks normalization and sequential coherence. Production guidance covers prior governance, data lineage, numerical stability, monitoring, privacy, and rollback.
learningObjectives: Apply Bayes' rule in probability, odds, and density form while keeping conditioning directions correct.
Distinguish prior, likelihood, evidence, posterior, and posterior predictive distributions.
Perform coherent sequential updates and diagnose when order, dependence, or data reuse breaks the calculation.
Evaluate prior sensitivity, model misspecification, predictive calibration, and decision consequences before deployment.

deepSections.title: Prior, likelihood, evidence, and posterior
deepSections.body: The joint model factors as p(theta,y)=p(theta)p(y|theta). Conditioning on observed y gives p(theta|y)=p(y|theta)p(theta)/p(y), where p(y)=integral p(y|theta)p(theta)dtheta. The likelihood is a function of theta with y fixed and need not integrate to one over theta. The evidence is the prior predictive probability or density of the observed data and makes the posterior normalize. In continuous models, densities depend on units while probability over regions does not. Posterior odds between two hypotheses equal prior odds times their Bayes factor, which is a likelihood ratio after integrating nuisance parameters under each hypothesis.

deepSections.title: Sequential updating and sufficient state
deepSections.body: For conditionally independent batches y1 and y2 given theta, p(theta|y1,y2) is proportional to p(y2|theta)p(theta|y1); the posterior after batch one becomes the prior for batch two. The final result is order-invariant in exact arithmetic if the same joint model is used. Dependence, overlapping records, adaptive sampling, and changing populations require a joint likelihood that conditions on history. Saving only a posterior mean is insufficient for general updates because shape and covariance matter. Conjugate families can compress the posterior into hyperparameters; particle or posterior draws can approximate it otherwise. Version the data cutoff so evidence is never counted twice.

deepSections.title: Posterior prediction and decisions
deepSections.body: The posterior predictive distribution p(y_new|y)=integral p(y_new|theta)p(theta|y)dtheta includes outcome noise and parameter uncertainty. A posterior parameter interval is generally narrower than a predictive interval. Decisions require an action a and loss L(a,theta) or utility: choose the action minimizing posterior expected loss. Under squared loss, posterior mean is optimal for a scalar parameter; asymmetric business costs yield quantiles or custom rules. A launch rule may use expected net value plus a harm constraint such as P(effect<-delta|data)<epsilon. Utility parameters and thresholds should be decided before results rather than tuned to justify a preferred action.

deepSections.title: Prior sensitivity, identifiability, and misspecification
deepSections.body: Prior choice is part of the model, especially in sparse, weakly identified, hierarchical, and high-dimensional settings. Use prior predictive simulation to expose implausible outcomes, compare reasonable priors, and report how decisions change. An improper prior may yield an improper posterior or make evidence undefined. Posterior concentration does not prove the likelihood describes reality; omitted heterogeneity, selection, censoring, and dependence can create overconfidence. Check posterior predictive behavior, held-out calibration, residual structure, and alternative likelihoods. If prior and likelihood conflict strongly, investigate data quality and model assumptions rather than automatically trusting whichever is numerically sharper.

deepSections.title: Normalization and computational forms
deepSections.body: For small discrete or one-dimensional problems, enumerate a grid and normalize weights using log-sum-exp. Conjugacy gives analytic updates. Higher-dimensional models use quadrature, Laplace approximation, variational inference, sequential Monte Carlo, or MCMC. Algorithms that need only the posterior up to proportionality can omit p(y) during sampling, but model comparison and evidence calculations cannot. Numerical underflow occurs when multiplying many likelihood terms; sum log densities and subtract a maximum before exponentiating. Computation adds approximation error on top of statistical uncertainty, so diagnostics and reproducible seeds are part of inference.

lessons.math: Bayes' rule is p(theta|y)=p(y|theta)p(theta)/integral p(y|u)p(u)du. In odds form, posterior odds H1:H0 equal prior odds times p(y|H1)/p(y|H0). For Beta(a,b) prior and k Bernoulli successes in n trials, posterior is Beta(a+k,b+n-k). Its mean is (a+k)/(a+b+n), and the next-trial predictive success probability is the same posterior mean. For m future Bernoulli trials, the predictive count is Beta–Binomial rather than Binomial at a fixed plug-in p.

workedExamples.title: Sequential Beta–Bernoulli conversion update
workedExamples.body: Update prior hyperparameters with successes and failures, compute posterior summaries and future predictive probability, then compare reasonable prior choices and verify that splitting the data into batches gives the same posterior.

exercises.prompt: A prior probability is 0.10 and evidence has likelihood ratio 4. What are posterior odds and probability?
exercises.solution: Prior odds are 0.1/0.9=1/9. Posterior odds are 4/9, so posterior probability is (4/9)/(1+4/9)=4/13≈0.3077.

exercises.prompt: Beta(3,7) prior observes 5 successes and 5 failures. What is the posterior?
exercises.solution: Beta(3+5,7+5)=Beta(8,12), with posterior mean 8/20=0.4.

exercises.prompt: Why can splitting conditionally independent data into two updates be safe?
exercises.solution: Bayesian multiplication is associative: likelihood factors for both batches multiply the prior, so using the first posterior as the second prior yields the same normalized posterior when the joint model and evidence are unchanged.

lab.goal: Build a grid posterior for a Bernoulli rate, verify it against the analytic Beta posterior, and test normalization and sequential coherence.
lab.buildIt:
import math

def normalize_log_weights(log_weights):
    peak=max(log_weights); weights=[math.exp(x-peak) for x in log_weights]
    total=sum(weights); return [w/total for w in weights]

def grid_update(grid, prior_weights, successes, failures):
    logs=[]
    for p,w in zip(grid,prior_weights):
        logs.append(math.log(w)+successes*math.log(p)+failures*math.log(1-p))
    return normalize_log_weights(logs)

grid=[(i+0.5)/1000 for i in range(1000)]
prior=[p**(2-1)*(1-p)**(8-1) for p in grid]
prior=[w/sum(prior) for w in prior]
posterior=grid_update(grid,prior,6,14)
grid_mean=sum(p*w for p,w in zip(grid,posterior))
lab.useIt:
from scipy.stats import beta
analytic_mean=beta.mean(8,22)
prob_above_025=beta.sf(0.25,8,22)
lab.verifyIt:
assert abs(sum(posterior)-1.0) < 1e-12
assert abs(grid_mean-analytic_mean) < 2e-4
first=grid_update(grid,prior,2,8)
sequential=grid_update(grid,first,4,6)
assert max(abs(a-b) for a,b in zip(posterior,sequential)) < 1e-12
assert 0 < prob_above_025 < 1

sourceNotes.contribution: Provides computational intuition for Bayesian updating, conjugate models, grids, and prediction.
Documents probability-model specification, log-density computation, inference algorithms, and reproducibility.
Provides official prior and posterior predictive simulation guidance for validating Bayesian model implications.
Provides current probabilistic programming APIs and examples for posterior and predictive inference.

lessons.title: Conjugate Priors
lessons.interviewAnswer: A prior is conjugate when the posterior stays in the same family after multiplying by a likelihood. Beta with Bernoulli/Binomial updates successes and failures; Gamma with Poisson updates shape by total counts and rate by exposure; Normal with known-variance Normal likelihood combines means by precision. Conjugacy gives exact, fast, sequential updates and useful test fixtures, but the likelihood and prior still need to fit the domain. Check rate-versus-scale conventions, predictive calibration, and whether drift or hierarchy requires a richer model.
keyPoints: Conjugacy is algebraic closure under updating
Sufficient statistics compress the evidence
Hyperparameters depend on parameterization conventions
Predictive distributions integrate parameter uncertainty
Computational convenience never replaces model criticism
lessons.why: Conjugate models reveal the mechanics hidden inside general inference engines. A conversion posterior updates two counts; a Poisson-rate posterior updates count and exposure; a Gaussian posterior averages prior and sample information by precision. These formulas support real-time risk estimates and serve as golden tests for MCMC or variational systems. Misuse appears when teams call a prior 'ten observations' despite a mismatched population, confuse Gamma rate and scale, or force a single-rate Poisson model onto overdispersed counts solely to keep conjugacy. Interviewers test the updates, but engineers must also know what happens when traffic drifts, exposures differ, or groups share information. Exact inference in the wrong model is exactly wrong.
lessons.intuition: Conjugate priors are containers designed to hold exactly the summaries that the likelihood adds. For coin flips, the likelihood contributes a power of p for each success and a power of 1-p for each failure; the Beta prior already has those powers, so exponents add. For Poisson counts, the likelihood contributes total count to the power of the rate and exposure to exponential decay; the Gamma prior has the same form. For a Gaussian mean, information is precision, inverse variance, so prior and data centers combine in proportion to their precision. The posterior distribution retains uncertainty; using only its mean would discard the remaining spread.
lessons.deepDive: Conjugacy follows from multiplying kernels. Constants independent of the parameter can be discarded to identify the posterior family, then the family's normalizing constant restores a probability distribution. The update state is usually a set of sufficient statistics.
lessons.workedExample: A service observes 12 incidents over 30 machine-days. Prior lambda~Gamma(shape=2,rate=10), mean 0.2 incidents/day. The posterior is Gamma(14,40), mean 0.35. The MLE 12/30=0.4 is shrunk toward prior information. For ten future machine-days, prediction integrates lambda; its variance exceeds a Poisson with fixed rate 0.35 because rate uncertainty contributes. If machines have different baseline risks or incidents cluster, use a hierarchical or overdispersed model. Before implementation, verify that the library's Gamma second parameter is rate 40 or scale 1/40.
commonMistakes: Treating conjugacy as evidence that the likelihood or prior is appropriate.
Confusing Gamma rate and scale or Normal variance and standard-deviation arguments.
Reading prior hyperparameters as literal sample counts without exchangeability or source justification.
Using a fixed-rate plug-in predictive distribution instead of integrating posterior uncertainty.
Discarding raw time, group, or covariate information needed to detect drift and heterogeneity.

followUps.question: Why are conjugate updates easy to stream?
followUps.answer: The posterior is summarized by fixed-size hyperparameters updated by additive sufficient statistics. Disjoint batches can merge their counts/exposures, provided the likelihood assumptions and data lineage remain valid.

followUps.question: What is the predictive distribution for Beta–Bernoulli?
followUps.answer: The next Bernoulli success probability is the posterior mean. A batch future count follows Beta–Binomial, which includes extra variance from uncertainty in p.

followUps.question: When should you leave conjugacy?
followUps.answer: When relevant heterogeneity, covariates, dependence, censoring, mixture structure, drift, or a scientifically appropriate likelihood cannot be represented by the conjugate model.

lessons.production: Define distribution parameterization explicitly in code and tests: shape/rate versus shape/scale, variance versus SD, exposure units, and support. Maintain sufficient-statistic lineage with unique event IDs and batch cutoffs so updates are idempotent. Reconcile distributed aggregates with source totals. Monitor posterior mean and spread, predictive calibration, dispersion, zero frequency, exposure mix, group heterogeneity, prior influence, and drift. Keep a richer holdout or residual view because sufficient statistics cannot reveal every model violation. Version priors and reset/discount rules; stationary conjugate accumulation can become dangerously overconfident under changing regimes. Protect small-group rates. Provide a validated analytic fallback when a heavier inference service fails, but label its assumptions. Rollback restores hyperparameters and the exact evidence watermark, not only a displayed mean.
lessons.description: A conjugate prior produces a posterior in the same distribution family as the prior for a chosen likelihood. Conjugacy turns Bayesian updating into hyperparameter arithmetic, making it valuable for intuition, streaming updates, exact benchmarks, and low-latency systems. It does not make a prior objectively correct or every model realistic. This chapter derives Beta–Binomial/Bernoulli, Gamma–Poisson, and Normal–Normal updates, interprets pseudo-counts and precision weighting carefully, and explains posterior predictive distributions, exponential-family structure, improper limits, and when conjugacy becomes a modeling trap. You will learn how parameterization conventions change formulas, why sufficient statistics enable constant-memory updates, how prior strength differs from sample size under heterogeneous data, and when mixtures or hierarchical priors preserve flexibility. The worked examples cover conversion and event-rate estimation. The lab implements Beta–Binomial and Gamma–Poisson updates, checks batch-order invariance, and verifies moments against SciPy. Production guidance covers parameterization tests, numerical bounds, nonstationarity, prior versioning, predictive calibration, and analytic fallbacks.
learningObjectives: Derive posterior hyperparameter updates for common conjugate likelihood–prior pairs.
Interpret hyperparameters through sufficient statistics without overclaiming literal prior sample size.
Compute posterior predictive distributions and distinguish them from plug-in likelihood predictions.
Recognize parameterization, support, misspecification, and nonstationarity cases where conjugacy should not drive model choice.

deepSections.title: Beta–Bernoulli and Beta–Binomial
deepSections.body: With p~Beta(a,b) and k successes in n Bernoulli trials, the likelihood kernel p^k(1-p)^(n-k) multiplies the prior p^(a-1)(1-p)^(b-1), yielding Beta(a+k,b+n-k). Posterior mean is (a+k)/(a+b+n), and interior mode is (a+k-1)/(a+b+n-2). Hyperparameters can be read as prior success/failure contributions, but this pseudo-count interpretation assumes exchangeability and compatible evidence. Jeffreys Beta(1/2,1/2), uniform Beta(1,1), and domain-informed priors behave differently near boundaries. A Beta–Binomial predictive distribution for future counts is overdispersed relative to a plug-in Binomial because it integrates uncertainty in p.

deepSections.title: Gamma–Poisson for rates with exposure
deepSections.body: Let counts y_i~Poisson(lambda t_i), where t_i is exposure, and lambda~Gamma(shape=a, rate=b). The likelihood kernel is lambda^(sum y_i) exp(-lambda sum t_i), so the posterior is Gamma(a+sum y_i,b+sum t_i) in shape–rate form. Shape–scale libraries instead use scale=1/rate; confusing them changes means and simulations. Posterior mean is (a+Y)/(b+T). The predictive count over future exposure t has a negative-binomial form after integrating lambda. If counts are more dispersed, zero-inflated, seasonally varying, or dependent, a single Poisson rate may be inadequate even though the update is exact.

deepSections.title: Normal mean with known observation variance
deepSections.body: For prior mu~N(m0,s0^2) and iid y_i~N(mu,sigma^2) with sigma known, posterior precision is 1/s0^2+n/sigma^2. Posterior mean is the precision-weighted average of m0 and ybar; posterior variance is the reciprocal precision. High-variance data contribute less information. Unknown variance leads to Normal–Inverse-Gamma or related conjugate families and Student-t predictives, with parameterization details. In multivariate Gaussian models, precision matrices add, but conditioning and positive-definiteness require care. Standardization changes the prior scale, so priors must be transformed with features.

deepSections.title: Exponential families and sufficient statistics
deepSections.body: Many likelihoods can be written h(y)exp(eta(theta)^T T(y)-A(theta)). Natural conjugate priors have a matching form whose hyperparameters accumulate T(y) and observation weight. This explains constant-memory sequential updates: retain sufficient totals instead of every row. It also clarifies limits—sufficiency is model-relative. Totals that preserve all information under an iid Bernoulli model lose ordering, covariates, drift, and dependence information. Keep raw or auditable aggregates when those assumptions may be revised. Distributed systems can merge additive sufficient statistics deterministically if data partitions are disjoint.

deepSections.title: When convenience becomes a constraint
deepSections.body: Real systems may need logistic regression, hierarchical varying rates, mixture components, censoring, measurement error, or nonstationary state models without simple closed forms. Approximate conjugate tricks can hide important dependence. Mixtures of conjugate priors retain analytic component updates and provide more flexible shapes, but component weights must update too. Empirical Bayes estimates hyperparameters from data and should not be described as a fixed external prior. Conjugate posteriors make excellent unit-test or fallback models; compare their predictions with richer models rather than forcing every question into them. Prior and posterior predictive checks remain mandatory.

lessons.math: Beta–Binomial: p|y~Beta(a+k,b+n-k). Gamma–Poisson in shape–rate form: lambda|y~Gamma(a+sum y_i,b+sum t_i). Normal–Normal: s_n^2=1/(1/s0^2+n/sigma^2) and m_n=s_n^2(m0/s0^2+n ybar/sigma^2). These updates are associative through sufficient statistics. Predictive distributions integrate parameters: Beta–Binomial, negative binomial for Gamma–Poisson, and Normal with variance sigma^2+s_n^2 for a future Gaussian observation with known sigma.

workedExamples.body: Aggregate total incidents and machine-time, update Gamma shape and rate, compute the posterior mean and predictive distribution, and test the result against the library's documented parameter convention.

exercises.prompt: Beta(4,6) prior sees 9 successes and 11 failures. Give posterior.
exercises.solution: Beta(13,17), with posterior mean 13/30.

exercises.prompt: Gamma(shape=3,rate=5) prior sees 7 events over exposure 20. Give posterior mean.
exercises.solution: Posterior Gamma(10,25), mean shape/rate=10/25=0.4 events per exposure unit.

exercises.prompt: Why is future Gaussian predictive variance sigma squared plus posterior variance of mu?
exercises.solution: A future observation equals uncertain mean plus independent observation noise; total variance adds E[noise variance]=sigma^2 and Var(posterior mean parameter)=s_n^2.

lab.goal: Implement Beta–Bernoulli and Gamma–Poisson conjugate updates, verify batch-order invariance, and compare posterior moments with SciPy.
lab.buildIt:
def beta_update(a,b,successes,failures):
    return a+successes,b+failures
def gamma_poisson_update(shape,rate,total_count,total_exposure):
    return shape+total_count,rate+total_exposure

a_post,b_post=beta_update(4,6,9,11)
shape_post,rate_post=gamma_poisson_update(3,5,7,20)
beta_mean=a_post/(a_post+b_post)
rate_mean=shape_post/rate_post
lab.verifyIt:
assert (a_post,b_post)==(13,17)
assert abs(beta_mean-scipy_beta_mean) < 1e-12
assert abs(rate_mean-0.4) < 1e-12
assert abs(rate_mean-scipy_rate_mean) < 1e-12
first=beta_update(4,6,4,6)
second=beta_update(*first,5,5)
assert second==(a_post,b_post)

lessons.title: Credible Intervals vs Confidence Intervals
lessons.interviewAnswer: A 95% credible interval has 95% posterior probability for the parameter conditional on the model, prior, and observed data. A 95% confidence interval comes from a procedure that covers the fixed true parameter in 95% of repeated samples under its assumptions. The observed frequentist interval does not assign 95% probability to the parameter. Credible intervals may be equal-tailed or highest-density and depend on priors; confidence constructions differ too. Report the framework, estimand, method, assumptions, and practical thresholds, and evaluate both posterior sensitivity and repeated-sample calibration when useful.
keyPoints: Credible probability is conditional on model, prior, and data
Confidence is a property of a repeated-sampling procedure
Equal-tailed and highest-density sets answer different geometric summaries
Prediction includes observation noise beyond parameter uncertainty
Numerical similarity does not erase interpretive differences
lessons.why: Teams increasingly mix Bayesian experiments with frequentist dashboards. If every interval is labeled '95%' without a framework, readers may treat coverage as posterior probability or interpret a credible interval as model-free calibration. Both errors create false certainty. Bayesian intervals answer natural questions such as P(effect>threshold|data), while confidence procedures offer operating guarantees under repetitions. Each depends on assumptions: priors and likelihoods for the former, sampling design and construction for the latter. Interviews emphasize the semantic difference; production systems also need consistent stopping, multiplicity, and calibration. The most useful practice is not framework tribalism but exact language, decision-aligned quantities, and diagnostics appropriate to the procedure.
lessons.intuition: For one observed dataset, a Bayesian posterior is a probability distribution over possible parameter values. Mark off a region containing 95% of its mass: that is a credible set. For a frequentist procedure, imagine generating many datasets from one fixed parameter and drawing an interval each time; about 95% of those random intervals should cover the fixed value. One picture holds data fixed and varies the parameter under a posterior; the other varies data while the parameter stays fixed. Their endpoints may converge in regular large samples because the likelihood becomes approximately normal and a weak prior contributes little locally. Near boundaries, with sparse data or informative priors, they can differ substantially.
lessons.deepDive: An interval is a compressed summary of a distribution or procedure. It cannot communicate multimodality, tail risk, decision asymmetry, or model uncertainty by itself. The construction and target must accompany the endpoints.
lessons.workedExample: Observe 3 conversions in 10 trials. With Beta(1,1) prior, posterior is Beta(4,8), and its 95% equal-tailed credible interval is given by Beta quantiles. The statement is that, under this prior and binomial model, posterior probability within those endpoints is 0.95. A Wilson 95% confidence interval uses the same data but is interpreted through repeated binomial samples at each fixed p. With only ten trials, endpoints can differ. Repeating the Bayesian analysis under Beta(2,8) reveals prior sensitivity; simulating fixed p values reveals coverage. Neither analysis corrects nonrandom traffic or dependence among trials.
commonMistakes: Saying an observed frequentist interval contains the fixed parameter with 95% probability.
Presenting a credible interval without the prior, likelihood, and conditioning data.
Treating any interval excluding zero as evidence of practical importance.
Confusing a parameter interval with a future-outcome prediction interval.
Using a highest-density interval as if it were invariant to nonlinear reparameterization.

followUps.question: Can a credible interval have 95% frequentist coverage?
followUps.answer: It can under particular priors, models, and parameter values or asymptotically, but posterior probability does not automatically guarantee repeated-sample coverage. Measure or derive coverage for the intended regime.

followUps.question: Why might equal-tailed and highest-density intervals differ?
followUps.answer: Skewed or multimodal posteriors distribute density unevenly. Equal-tailed intervals balance tail probabilities; highest-density sets prioritize local density and may be shorter or disconnected.

followUps.question: Which interval should a dashboard show?
followUps.answer: Use the framework actually implemented and decision question. Label it clearly, include method and assumptions, show practical thresholds, and avoid mixing posterior probability language with confidence coverage.

lessons.production: Require interval metadata: framework, estimand, population, unit, construction, confidence/credible level, sidedness, prior version, likelihood, variance method, stopping rule, multiplicity family, and data window. Render posterior probability statements only from an actual posterior. Run prior sensitivity and predictive checks for Bayesian intervals; run coverage simulations across fixed parameter and design scenarios for decision-critical procedures. Monitor interval width, boundary behavior, posterior drift, calibration, cluster structure, and small-cell instability. Preserve posterior draws or sufficient summaries needed to transform decisions correctly. Apply privacy thresholds. If a sequential policy changes, create a new interval version. Roll back displayed endpoints, labels, and decision status together when data or model integrity fails. Never let UI copy rewrite a confidence statement into a probability claim.
lessons.description: Bayesian credible intervals and frequentist confidence intervals can have similar numerical endpoints while making different probability statements. A credible interval contains a specified posterior probability under a prior and likelihood. A confidence interval is generated by a procedure with stated repeated-sample coverage under a sampling model. This chapter builds both from the same binomial example, compares equal-tailed and highest-density credible sets, explains parameter transformations, nuisance parameters, posterior predictive intervals, and the circumstances in which Bayesian and frequentist intervals approximately agree. You will learn why neither framework is assumption-free, why optional stopping and selection require framework-specific care, how prior sensitivity affects sparse-data credible intervals, and why a 95% posterior interval is not automatically calibrated across repeated real datasets. The worked example contrasts a Beta posterior interval with Wilson confidence coverage. The lab computes equal-tailed posterior intervals, simulates frequentist coverage, and verifies transformation behavior. Production guidance covers naming, metadata, calibration, priors, sequential policies, decision thresholds, privacy, and communication.
learningObjectives: State the probability interpretation of credible and confidence intervals without mixing frameworks.
Construct equal-tailed and highest-density credible sets and contrast them with score or likelihood-based confidence intervals.
Distinguish parameter uncertainty from posterior predictive uncertainty and transform intervals coherently.
Evaluate prior sensitivity, frequentist coverage, calibration, selection, and stopping for deployed interval procedures.

deepSections.title: Two probability spaces
deepSections.body: For posterior distribution p(theta|y), a credible set C(y) satisfies integral over C p(theta|y)dtheta=0.95. Probability conditions on observed y and the entire Bayesian model. A confidence procedure C(Y) satisfies P_theta(theta in C(Y))≈0.95 under repetitions Y~p_theta, ideally across relevant theta. Once y is observed, frequentist C(y) either contains theta or not. A confidence distribution is not automatically a Bayesian posterior. Likewise, a credible interval need not have nominal frequentist coverage, though some priors and regular asymptotic settings produce matching behavior. State what is random in the claim.

deepSections.title: Equal-tailed, highest-density, and one-sided credible sets
deepSections.body: An equal-tailed 95% interval cuts 2.5% posterior probability from each tail and transforms naturally under monotone transformations by transforming endpoints. A highest posterior density set contains points with density above a threshold and often minimizes length in one dimension, but it depends on parameterization and can be disconnected for multimodal posteriors. A single interval spanning a low-density valley can mislead; show the full posterior or disjoint regions. One-sided credible bounds may match risk questions better. The posterior probability above a business threshold is often more actionable than whether zero lies in a central interval, provided the decision model was prespecified.

deepSections.title: Confidence constructions and coverage
deepSections.body: Wald intervals use estimate plus-or-minus critical SE and can fail near boundaries or under skewness. Score/Wilson, likelihood-ratio/profile, exact, bootstrap, and randomization intervals have different finite-sample coverage and length. Exact discrete intervals may overcover. Coverage can be marginal rather than conditional in relevant subgroups. Repeated peeking, selecting a winner, or choosing the method after inspection changes operating characteristics unless accounted for. A confidence interval that excludes zero corresponds to a matching two-sided test, but equivalence needs an interval entirely inside prespecified negligible-effect bounds.

deepSections.title: Prediction, transformations, and nuisance uncertainty
deepSections.body: A parameter interval for a mean is not a prediction interval for a future outcome. Bayesian prediction integrates the likelihood over the joint posterior, including correlations among nuisance parameters. Frequentist prediction combines parameter-estimation and future-noise uncertainty through a procedure. For a monotone transform such as odds to probability, transform posterior draws or equal-tailed endpoints; highest-density regions may not transform into highest-density regions. For nonlinear functions or ratios, propagate joint uncertainty rather than transforming marginal intervals separately. Report the original and decision scale when stakeholders reason in absolute risk but modeling occurs in log odds.

deepSections.title: Bayesian calibration and frequentist sensitivity
deepSections.body: Bayesian simulation-based calibration can test whether an inference algorithm recovers prior-generated parameter ranks when data are generated from the model. Posterior predictive checks test data fit, not coverage directly. Repeated-sampling simulations can measure a Bayesian interval's coverage across fixed parameter values and a confidence interval's coverage under design variations. Prior sensitivity should examine posterior decisions under plausible alternatives; confidence sensitivity should examine nuisance, design, and robust-variance choices. Neither one diagnostic proves real-world validity when the data-generating process is outside all simulated models. Use external validation and decision loss as additional evidence.

deepSections.title: Intervals, thresholds, and posterior decisions
deepSections.body: A central interval is not always the best decision summary. If harm below h and benefit above b have different consequences, report posterior probabilities for both regions and expected utility, not only mass around the median. Frequentist decisions can similarly use one-sided bounds, equivalence intervals, or confidence sets inverted from decision-relevant tests. Predefine thresholds independently of observed endpoints. When several actions compete, a joint posterior or simultaneous confidence construction may be required; marginal intervals can understate the chance that at least one decision is wrong. Preserve the full draw-level or covariance information needed to evaluate new thresholds, but treat post hoc threshold search as exploratory. Interval presentation should support, not replace, a documented loss model.

lessons.math: For posterior CDF F(theta|y), an equal-tailed 1-alpha credible interval is [F^{-1}(alpha/2),F^{-1}(1-alpha/2)]. A highest-density set has {theta:p(theta|y)>=c} with c chosen to contain 1-alpha mass. A confidence procedure satisfies P_theta(theta in C(Y))>= or approximately 1-alpha. For Beta(a+k,b+n-k), posterior quantiles give a credible interval. A Wilson binomial interval instead inverts a score test and targets repeated-sample coverage without a prior.

workedExamples.title: Three conversions in ten trials
workedExamples.body: Compute a Beta posterior interval and a Wilson confidence interval, say each interpretation precisely, vary the prior, and use simulation to inspect repeated-sample coverage without declaring one endpoint universally correct.

exercises.prompt: State a 95% credible interval interpretation.
exercises.solution: Conditional on the specified prior, likelihood, and observed data, the posterior probability that the parameter lies in the reported set is 0.95.

exercises.prompt: State a 95% confidence interval interpretation.
exercises.solution: Across repetitions of the specified sampling and interval procedure, about 95% of intervals contain the fixed true parameter under the assumptions.

lab.goal: Compute a Beta credible interval, simulate its fixed-parameter coverage, and compare with a Wilson confidence interval.
lab.buildIt:
import math

def wilson_interval(k,n,z=1.959963984540054):
    p=k/n; denom=1+z*z/n
    center=(p+z*z/(2*n))/denom
    half=z*math.sqrt(p*(1-p)/n+z*z/(4*n*n))/denom
    return center-half,center+half

k,n=3,10
wilson=wilson_interval(k,n)
lab.useIt:
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import beta
credible=tuple(beta.ppf([0.025,0.975],4,8))
rng=np.random.default_rng(23)
true_p=0.30
counts=rng.binomial(n,true_p,size=20000)
credible_intervals=np.asarray([beta.ppf([0.025,0.975],1+c,1+n-c) for c in counts])
coverage=np.mean((credible_intervals[:,0] <= true_p) & (true_p <= credible_intervals[:,1]))
lab.verifyIt:
assert 0 < credible[0] < credible[1] < 1
assert 0 < wilson[0] < wilson[1] < 1
assert 0.90 < coverage < 0.99
logit_bounds=[math.log(x/(1-x)) for x in credible]
assert logit_bounds[0] < logit_bounds[1]

lessons.title: MCMC & Posterior Sampling
lessons.interviewAnswer: MCMC constructs a Markov chain with the posterior as its stationary distribution, then estimates posterior expectations from retained dependent draws. Metropolis–Hastings accepts a proposal with the target-density and proposal-ratio correction; HMC uses gradients to propose distant moves and NUTS adapts trajectory length. Run multiple dispersed chains, separate warmup, and check rank-normalized split R-hat, bulk and tail ESS, Monte Carlo SE, trace plots, divergences, treedepth, and model-specific calibration. A high acceptance rate or long chain alone does not prove convergence, and thinning rarely fixes autocorrelation.
keyPoints: Stationarity does not guarantee finite-chain exploration
Dependent draws reduce effective information
Multiple diagnostics target different failures
Geometry and parameterization dominate sampler performance
Computation must be validated against known and simulated truth
lessons.why: Most realistic Bayesian models lack closed-form posteriors. MCMC makes full posterior inference possible, but it also creates a second layer of uncertainty: the chain may not represent the target well. A model can produce plausible-looking histograms while one chain remains trapped in a mode, tail ESS is tiny, or HMC divergences avoid an important region. Interviews ask Metropolis acceptance and burn-in; advanced practice requires diagnostics and geometry. Production systems must turn those diagnostics into hard quality gates rather than warnings lost in logs. More iterations can reduce Monte Carlo error after mixing, but they do not repair a nonidentified model, disconnected modes, or systematically missed curvature.
lessons.intuition: Imagine exploring a landscape whose height is posterior density. Random-walk Metropolis proposes a nearby step and always accepts uphill moves, while sometimes accepting downhill moves so it does not freeze at a local peak. Tiny steps accept often but crawl; huge steps reject often and repeat the same state. HMC adds momentum and follows gradients, traveling across smooth valleys with fewer random walks. Warmup tunes step size, mass matrix, and sometimes proposal scales; those adaptive draws are not ordinary samples. Even after warmup, neighboring states remain correlated. Effective sample size asks how many independent draws would provide comparable precision. Multiple chains started apart reveal whether explorers agree on the same terrain.
lessons.deepDive: MCMC targets integrals E[f(theta)|y]. If a chain is ergodic with invariant posterior pi, averages of f(theta_t) converge under conditions. Finite-chain validity depends on initialization, adaptation, transition geometry, numerical correctness, and whether every important region is reachable.
lessons.workedExample: For Beta(8,22), run four random-walk Metropolis chains on logit p with dispersed starting values. A proposal SD of 0.02 in p-space accepts almost everything but moves slowly; SD 0.8 rejects most proposals; an intermediate logit proposal explores efficiently. Compare sample mean with analytic 8/30, quantiles with SciPy, chain means with one another, and autocorrelation/ESS. This successful one-dimensional benchmark verifies the kernel but not a later hierarchical model. A funnel can show acceptable marginal means while divergences avoid the narrow neck, requiring noncentering or stronger prior geometry.
commonMistakes: Treating high acceptance, one smooth trace, or many iterations as proof of convergence.
Dropping rejected states or adapting proposals forever without a valid adaptive scheme.
Using thinning as a cure for poor mixing instead of improving geometry or running longer valid chains.
Ignoring divergences, tail ESS, treedepth, or diagnostic failures in derived decision quantities.
Running all chains from nearly identical starts and declaring agreement despite missed modes.

followUps.question: Why retain repeated states after rejection?
followUps.answer: The self-transition is part of the Markov kernel that preserves the target. Removing rejections changes empirical weights and biases the sample toward accepted moves.

followUps.question: What is the difference between posterior SD and MCSE?
followUps.answer: Posterior SD is substantive uncertainty about the parameter under the model. MCSE is numerical uncertainty in an estimated posterior summary caused by a finite correlated simulation.

followUps.question: Why does noncentering help hierarchical models?
followUps.answer: With weak group data it separates standard latent effects from population scale, reducing funnel curvature and posterior dependence. With strongly informed groups, centered forms can sometimes be more efficient.

lessons.production: Run at least multiple independent chains with deterministic, independent RNG streams and versioned initializations. Separate adaptation from retained draws. Define quality gates for R-hat, bulk/tail ESS relative to required summary precision, MCSE, divergences, treedepth saturation, energy diagnostics, failed transitions, and model-specific invariants. Store compact posterior draws or reproducible summaries with data/code hashes, sampler configuration, package/compiler/hardware versions, and diagnostics. Limit raw posterior access when draws reveal sensitive small-group values. Benchmark runtime and cap resources, but never silently return partial chains as valid. Retry only with a documented diagnostic hypothesis; otherwise fall back to a simpler validated model or withhold the decision. Rollback restores model, parameterization, sampler, prior, and posterior artifact together. Monitor predictive calibration after deployment because perfect MCMC cannot rescue a wrong model.
lessons.description: Markov chain Monte Carlo approximates posterior expectations by constructing dependent draws whose stationary distribution is the target posterior. The central promise is asymptotic, while every real analysis uses finite chains that can fail to explore relevant modes or geometry. This chapter develops Metropolis–Hastings, Gibbs sampling, Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, and the No-U-Turn Sampler; distinguishes warmup from retained sampling; and explains detailed balance, autocorrelation, effective sample size, Monte Carlo standard error, rank-normalized split R-hat, divergences, treedepth, energy diagnostics, and multimodality. You will learn why acceptance rate alone is not convergence, why thinning usually discards information, how centered versus noncentered parameterizations change hierarchical geometry, and how to validate an implementation against conjugate truth and simulation-based calibration. The worked example samples a one-dimensional Beta posterior, then contrasts its easy geometry with a funnel. The lab builds random-walk Metropolis, compares posterior moments with SciPy, and checks multiple-chain mixing. Production guidance covers deterministic seeds, chain parallelism, diagnostics gates, compute budgets, artifact storage, privacy, and safe failure behavior.
learningObjectives: Explain how a Markov transition kernel can leave a posterior invariant and why retained draws are dependent.
Implement Metropolis–Hastings and relate proposal scale to exploration, acceptance, and autocorrelation.
Interpret R-hat, bulk/tail ESS, Monte Carlo SE, divergences, treedepth, and trace diagnostics jointly.
Diagnose multimodality, funnels, constraints, initialization, and parameterization failures before using posterior summaries.

deepSections.title: Metropolis–Hastings and invariance
deepSections.body: From current theta, propose theta'~q(theta'|theta). Accept with probability min(1, pi(theta')q(theta|theta')/[pi(theta)q(theta'|theta)]); otherwise retain theta. This correction establishes detailed balance for many kernels, implying pi is invariant. Symmetric random-walk proposals cancel q. Work in log density to prevent underflow. Rejections are valid repeated draws and must remain in the chain. Proposal tuning changes efficiency, not target, if adaptation stops or follows valid adaptive rules. Irreducibility and aperiodicity matter: a proposal that cannot cross a support gap never discovers the other mode regardless of iterations.

deepSections.title: Gibbs, HMC, and NUTS
deepSections.body: Gibbs sampling draws each block from its full conditional and accepts automatically; strong posterior correlations can still make coordinate updates slow. Hamiltonian Monte Carlo augments parameters with momentum, simulates approximate Hamiltonian dynamics using leapfrog integration, and corrects integration error with Metropolis acceptance. A mass matrix rescales geometry. NUTS expands trajectories until a no-U-turn condition and adapts step size during warmup. Gradients enable distant proposals, but discontinuities, boundaries, heavy tails, and funnels challenge HMC. Divergences flag trajectories where numerical integration cannot follow curvature and often indicate biased exploration, not harmless noise to suppress blindly.

deepSections.title: R-hat, ESS, MCSE, and visual diagnostics
deepSections.body: Rank-normalized split R-hat compares between- and within-chain behavior after splitting chains and transforming ranks; values near one are necessary but not sufficient. Bulk ESS assesses central-location estimation and tail ESS assesses quantiles/tails. ESS incorporates autocorrelation and can differ by parameter and function. Monte Carlo SE estimates numerical uncertainty in a posterior summary, distinct from posterior SD. Trace plots should look stationary and overlapping; rank plots expose chain-specific distribution differences; autocorrelation plots show persistence. For HMC, inspect divergence count/location, maximum treedepth, energy behavior, and acceptance adaptation. Check transformed quantities and decisions, not only raw parameters.

deepSections.title: Funnels, correlations, modes, and reparameterization
deepSections.body: Hierarchical scale parameters create funnel geometry: when group-scale is small, latent effects occupy a narrow neck; when large, they spread widely. Centered parameterization can be efficient with strongly informed groups but poor with weak data. Noncentering writes effects as population mean plus scale times standard-normal latent variables, often easing weak-data geometry. Highly correlated parameters need mass-matrix adaptation or reparameterization. Label switching in mixtures yields symmetric modes; identifiability constraints or permutation-invariant summaries may be needed. Disconnected modes cannot be diagnosed solely by local HMC statistics if every chain initializes in one mode. Use prior predictive insight, dispersed starts, alternative algorithms, and tempered methods when relevant.

deepSections.title: Warmup, initialization, and validation
deepSections.body: Warmup removes initialization influence and adapts sampler settings; discarding an arbitrary fraction without checking mixing is not a proof. Initialize multiple chains over plausible dispersed regions, but avoid pathological invalid values. Validate code on prior-only simulation, conjugate models, and simulated datasets where parameters are known. Simulation-based calibration tests rank uniformity across repeated prior-generated datasets and can detect inference implementation bias. Compare independent software or analytic results on small cases. Thinning usually increases Monte Carlo error for a fixed computation and is justified mainly for storage or expensive downstream calculations. If diagnostics fail, revise model or computation before interpreting posterior output.

lessons.math: For stationary scalar chain f_t with autocorrelations rho_k, asymptotic variance of the sample mean is Var_pi(f)/N times tau, where tau=1+2 sum_{k>=1}rho_k is integrated autocorrelation time; ESS=N/tau. MCSE(mean) is approximately posterior SD/sqrt(ESS). Metropolis–Hastings acceptance is alpha=min(1, exp(log pi(theta')-log pi(theta)+log q(theta|theta')-log q(theta'|theta))). Detailed balance pi(theta)K(theta,theta')=pi(theta')K(theta',theta) is sufficient, not necessary, for invariance.

workedExamples.body: Use a conjugate target as a golden test, vary proposal scale, retain rejected states, compare all chains with analytic moments, and distinguish acceptance rate from effective exploration.

exercises.prompt: A chain has N=10,000 and integrated autocorrelation time 20. Approximate ESS.
exercises.solution: ESS=N/tau=10,000/20=500 independent-equivalent draws.

exercises.prompt: Posterior SD is 2 and ESS is 400. Approximate MCSE of the mean.
exercises.solution: 2/sqrt(400)=0.1. This is simulation error in the posterior mean estimate, not posterior uncertainty of 2.

exercises.prompt: Why can four chains with R-hat near one still miss a mode?
exercises.solution: If all initialize in and remain within the same mode, they can agree locally. Use dispersed starts, model knowledge, alternative methods, and predictive/sensitivity checks to search for disconnected regions.
