lessons.title: Metric Design: North Star, Driver & Guardrail Metrics
lessons.interviewAnswer: I start from the decision and long-term user/business objective, then create an OEC or primary metric whose direction is credibly aligned with that objective. I add driver metrics for the causal mechanism and guardrails for reliability, safety, fairness, cost, and ecosystem harm. Every metric has a contract: population, unit, numerator, denominator, time window, attribution, aggregation, missingness, direction, and version. I validate sensitivity on historical experiments and directionality against long-term outcomes and known bad changes. I avoid arbitrary composites and average-of-averages, report uncertainty, and treat metric changes like schema migrations because they alter historical and experimental meaning.
keyPoints: Metrics operationalize values and assumptions
OEC, drivers, diagnostics, and guardrails serve different roles
Directionality and sensitivity must both be validated
Population, unit, denominator, and window define the estimand
Metric versions and lineage are part of scientific reproducibility
lessons.why: Teams optimize what dashboards reward. A click metric can encourage clickbait, time spent can reward confusion, short-term revenue can damage retention, and an average can improve by losing low-performing users. Even perfect randomization estimates the causal effect on the metric that was defined, not the value stakeholders intended. Research on online experimentation emphasizes directionality and sensitivity and documents recurring interpretation pitfalls. Interviews test whether a candidate can turn a vague goal into measurable components without laundering value judgments. In production, metrics are shared software artifacts whose bugs propagate to experiments, alerts, forecasts, and executive decisions.
lessons.intuition: Think of a metric system as an instrument panel. The primary gauge answers whether the product is moving toward durable value. Driver gauges reveal how the change worked. Guardrails light up when the route creates unacceptable damage. A single speedometer cannot show overheating, fuel, or collision risk; a wall of gauges without a decision hierarchy is equally useless. Each gauge needs calibration: it should move when the underlying property changes, stay stable when nothing changes, and not reward a shortcut that violates the real objective. Its denominator decides who counts and can change the story as much as its numerator.
lessons.deepDive: Metric design is measurement theory plus causal and operational reasoning. A metric is a versioned estimand computed from event data, not merely a SQL expression or a label on a chart.
lessons.workedExample: A recommender team proposes watch time as its North Star. A new ranker increases watch time 4% but also increases autoplay, complaint rate, and creator concentration while seven-day satisfied return falls. The metric tree is revised: satisfied sessions per assigned user is primary; successful content discovery and completion are drivers; complaints, latency, diversity, creator supply, and compute cost are guardrails. Raw watch time remains diagnostic. Each metric uses assignment-unit denominators and fixed windows. Long-term holdouts validate that satisfied return predicts retention better than minutes alone. The scorecard blocks the ranker despite its attractive engagement number.

commonMistakes.mistake: Choosing the easiest metric to move
commonMistakes.correction: Sensitivity without directionality rewards proxy gaming; validate relationship to durable user and business value.

commonMistakes.mistake: Averaging pre-aggregated rates
commonMistakes.correction: Preserve numerators and denominators or define the intended unit weights; average-of-averages usually changes the estimand.

commonMistakes.mistake: Making every metric a success criterion
commonMistakes.correction: Use a hierarchy: primary/OEC, drivers, diagnostics, and guardrails with prespecified decision roles.

commonMistakes.mistake: Silently changing a denominator
commonMistakes.correction: Definition changes are versioned migrations and invalidate direct historical or experimental comparison unless dual-run and reconciled.

followUps.question: What makes a good OEC?
followUps.answer: It is directionally aligned with long-term value, sensitive within experiment duration, computable and reliable, difficult to game, and paired with explicit guardrails.

followUps.question: Why can per-active-user metrics mislead?
followUps.answer: Treatment can change who becomes active, so conditioning on activity is post-treatment selection and denominator composition can drive the result.

followUps.question: Should guardrails be included in a composite?
followUps.answer: Usually severe noncompensable harms are clearer as constraints or decision gates; a composite can let primary gains conceal unacceptable damage.

lessons.production: Store metrics in a governed semantic layer with source lineage, SQL or transformation version, population, unit, windows, numerator/denominator, attribution, missingness, direction, owner, tests, and access policy. Materialize additive components so totals reconcile across slices. Validate schema, uniqueness, coverage, lateness, denominator positivity, range, and invariant relationships. Dual-run definition changes and compare experiment decisions before migration. Monitor drift, sensitivity, correlation with long-term outcomes, guardrail breach rate, and metric gaming signals. Restrict sensitive user and fairness slices. On a bug, freeze affected decisions, identify every dashboard and experiment version, backfill under a new label, publish corrections, and roll back the semantic model without erasing historical definitions.
lessons.description: Metric design translates a product objective into a measurable, sensitive, directionally trustworthy decision system. A North Star or Overall Evaluation Criterion (OEC) should predict long-term value closely enough to guide short experiments, driver metrics explain mechanisms, and guardrails prevent unacceptable harm. This chapter develops metric contracts, populations, units, numerators, denominators, windows, attribution, directionality, sensitivity, validity, reliability, gaming, ratio estimands, heavy tails, missingness, delayed outcomes, composite scores, proxy risk, and metric lifecycle governance. You will learn why more activity is not always better, why per-user and per-event averages answer different questions, how denominator changes can reverse a result, and how to validate short-term proxies against long-term outcomes and known interventions. A worked recommendation-system scorecard separates engagement from satisfaction and ecosystem health. The lab builds a semantic metric contract and ratio-of-sums calculator, rejects grain and denominator errors, and verifies invariants against pandas. Production guidance covers lineage, versioning, backfills, dashboards, experiment inference, access control, alerts, deprecation, correction, and rollback. The goal is not one magical number; it is an auditable map from user and business value to decisions under uncertainty.
learningObjectives: Define a metric through population, unit, event, numerator, denominator, window, attribution, direction, and missingness semantics.
Construct primary, driver, diagnostic, and guardrail metrics that map to a causal product theory rather than a dashboard inventory.
Evaluate directionality, sensitivity, validity, reliability, robustness, gaming risk, and long-term proxy quality.
Implement and test ratio metrics with grain, denominator, reconciliation, and versioning invariants.

deepSections.title: From objective to OEC, drivers, and guardrails
deepSections.body: Write the long-term objective and stakeholder before choosing observables. The OEC combines or selects near-term measures believed to causally predict that objective and must have a clear preferred direction. Driver metrics correspond to mechanisms in a product theory: discoverability, activation, task success, or repeat value. Diagnostic metrics explain implementation and segments but do not automatically become claims. Guardrails encode noncompensable or constrained outcomes such as crashes, latency, complaints, fairness gaps, creator supply, privacy incidents, and cost. Draw edges between intervention, drivers, primary outcome, guardrails, and long-term value; mark assumptions and expected time lags. Avoid adding metrics simply because data exist.

deepSections.title: The semantic metric contract
deepSections.body: Specify metric name and version; target population and eligibility; analysis unit; observation and attribution windows; event sources and accepted versions; numerator and denominator; aggregation order; deduplication and identity; timezone; late-data policy; missingness; outlier treatment; direction; owner; and quality tests. A conversion rate among exposed users differs from ITT conversion among assigned eligible users. Sessions per active user conditions on activity and can improve if low-activity users disappear. Per-user mean, ratio of totals, mean of user ratios, and average of group averages are different estimands. Include sample rows and reconciliation identities so reviewers can test meaning without reading every query.

deepSections.title: Directionality, sensitivity, validity, and reliability
deepSections.body: Directionality asks whether an increase consistently represents improvement in the target objective. Validate with domain theory, known harmful and beneficial launches, long-term holdouts, and downstream outcomes. Sensitivity asks whether the metric detects decision-relevant changes with acceptable variance; estimate standard error, MDE, and experiment hit rate without favoring noisy false positives. Construct validity asks whether it measures the intended concept; criterion validity compares trusted outcomes. Reliability asks whether repeated equivalent measurement is stable. Robustness covers heavy tails, bots, missing data, seasonality, and implementation changes. An easy-to-move but weak proxy is dangerous; a perfect long-term outcome arriving too late may be unusable for iteration.

deepSections.title: Ratios, transforms, and composite scores
deepSections.body: For a ratio metric, state whether the estimand is total numerator divided by total denominator or average of unit-level ratios; they weight units differently. Denominator treatment effects can make relative movements hard to interpret. Use influence-function, delta-method, bootstrap, or unit-level analysis consistent with randomization. Winsorization and log transforms change the estimand and must be prespecified. Composite scores require direction alignment, scaling, weights, and missing-component rules; weights express value trade-offs, not statistical truth. A composite can hide a severe loss behind compensation, so preserve component reporting and keep true guardrails outside the compensating score.

deepSections.title: Gaming, drift, and metric lifecycle
deepSections.body: Goodhart's law warns that an optimized proxy can decouple from its target. Perform threat modeling: how could a feature increase the metric without helping users, exclude difficult cases, shift cost, or delay harm? Monitor component and population drift, metric correlation with long-term outcomes, missingness, event coverage, and conflicting movements. Use immutable versions for definition changes and dual-run old/new metrics through backfills and live experiments. Recompute historical series only under explicit version labels. Document known limitations and deprecation reasons. When a metric bug is found, identify affected experiments and decisions, publish corrections, and prevent silent dashboard rewrites.

lessons.math: A ratio-of-sums estimand is R=sum_i A_i/sum_i B_i, while a mean-of-ratios is n^{-1}sum_i A_i/B_i; they are equal only in special cases. For experiment arms, Delta=R_T-R_C and uncertainty can use the influence value psi_i=(A_i-R B_i)/E[B] at the randomization unit. A composite S=sum_j w_j s_j requires defined scaling s_j and weights w_j. Sensitivity can be summarized by standard error or MDE, while directionality is a substantive claim requiring external or longitudinal validation.

workedExamples.title: Replacing raw engagement with a value-and-health scorecard
workedExamples.body: Trace the proxy's gaming path, define a directionally stronger primary outcome, separate drivers from diagnostics, and make ecosystem and reliability harms noncompensable guardrails.

exercises.prompt: Why does average session duration sometimes rise after a bad change?
exercises.solution: If the change causes short-session users to leave, the remaining-session denominator selects longer sessions; the average can rise while total user value falls.

exercises.prompt: Give a ratio-of-sums example.
exercises.solution: Click-through rate as total clicks divided by total eligible impressions; preserve both components and define deduplication and attribution.

exercises.prompt: How do you validate directionality?
exercises.solution: Use product theory, known interventions, long-term holdouts or downstream outcomes, component analysis, and attempts to find changes that game the proxy.

lessons.title: Funnels & Conversion Analysis
lessons.interviewAnswer: A funnel is a versioned sequence estimand, not just counts by event name. I define the eligible entity and entry cohort, strict or loose order, conversion window, repeat and re-entry rules, identity resolution, and whether conversion is unique entities or event completions. I deduplicate at the chosen unit, require complete follow-up or handle censoring, and reconcile cumulative counts so they cannot increase. I segment only with pre-step attributes for causal interpretation, inspect time-to-transition and alternative paths, and use experiments to test proposed causes. Drop-off shows where progression stops under the definition; it does not prove why.
keyPoints: Funnel definitions construct the population and path
Entity counts and event counts answer different questions
Conversion windows and maturity prevent unequal opportunity
Step drop-off is descriptive, not a causal explanation
Identity and event-contract quality dominate trustworthy funnel analysis
lessons.why: Onboarding, checkout, application, and activation flows are operationally sequential, so aggregate conversion can hide where a change occurred. But a user may skip steps, repeat them, switch devices, complete offline, or enter through another path. A dashboard can show a dramatic drop simply because one event was renamed or a recent cohort lacks time to convert. Funnel analysis is valuable when it turns a product theory into explicit state transitions and testable hypotheses. Interviews probe whether analysts define denominators and time correctly. In production, funnel metrics share instrumentation with experiments and can bias launch decisions if event loss differs by variant.
lessons.intuition: Imagine following each eligible person with a timestamped event ledger. A strict funnel asks whether the ledger contains step A, then a later B, then a later C, all within a clock that starts at A. Count each person once at the furthest qualified step. The narrowing bars are just an aggregation of these state-machine traces. If the last cohort entered yesterday and conversion allows seven days, its apparent failure is administrative censoring. If B is missing because an app version stopped logging, that is measurement loss, not user abandonment. Examine both the accepted path and what users did instead.
lessons.deepDive: A funnel is a temporal query over entity histories. Its scientific quality depends on state semantics, observation opportunity, identity, and the difference between descriptive transition rates and causal mechanisms.
lessons.workedExample: A checkout funnel shows 100,000 cart users, 70,000 payment-page users, and 45,000 purchases. After an app release, payment-to-purchase appears to improve, but entry-to-purchase falls. Investigation finds the new app creates a fresh anonymous ID after payment failure; the payment event is under the old ID and repeat purchase under a logged-in ID. A loose cross-device join matches only successful users, inflating the middle transition. The team repairs identity linkage, starts from assigned cart entrants, applies a seven-day maturity cutoff, and adds payment-error events. The corrected analysis shows increased failures, leading to rollback and a randomized fix.

commonMistakes.mistake: Counting events as users
commonMistakes.correction: Repeated events can inflate downstream steps; deduplicate the defined entity or use explicit journey IDs.

commonMistakes.mistake: Comparing immature recent cohorts
commonMistakes.correction: Require the full conversion window or use censoring-aware time-to-event analysis.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating drop-off as a cause
commonMistakes.correction: It locates an observed transition; errors, alternatives, selection, and experiments are needed to identify mechanisms.

commonMistakes.mistake: Joining only users with every step
commonMistakes.correction: That removes nonconverters from the denominator; begin with entry and left join later states.

followUps.question: What is a strict funnel?
followUps.answer: An entity must complete defined steps in order, typically within a conversion window; intervening events may or may not be allowed according to the contract.

followUps.question: Why can cumulative counts increase?
followUps.answer: They should not for a unique-entity strict funnel. An increase signals inconsistent populations, repeated-event counting, re-entry, identity, or query errors.

followUps.question: How do you compare funnel conversion in an A/B test?
followUps.answer: Use assigned eligible units or an assignment-invariant trigger as denominator, prespecify the end metric, and treat intermediate steps as drivers without post-treatment filtering.

lessons.production: Govern every step event with owner, schema, version, entity key, event-time semantics, and property tests. Build funnels from immutable entry cohorts and left-joined histories, using a versioned identity graph and late-data cutoff. Persist step counts, cumulative and transition rates, time distributions, window maturity, missingness, and alternate-path counts. Monitor monotonicity, event coverage, ordering violations, identity-link rates, transition shifts, and platform/version slices. Protect journey data and suppress small cohorts. Dual-log renamed events and reconcile before cutover. On instrumentation failure, freeze funnel-based decisions, publish the affected interval, backfill only under explicit versions, and roll back the metric or product change without rewriting prior definitions.

lab.goal: Build an ordered unique-user funnel from event histories, compare counts with pandas, and verify monotonicity, deduplication, and conversion-window semantics.
lab.verifyIt:
assert counts==[4,3,1]
assert counts==sorted(counts,reverse=True)
assert pandas_entry==counts[0]
assert reached['u1']==3 and reached['u2']==1
assert unique_event_users['purchase']==3 and counts[2]==1
assert ordered_funnel(events,steps,20)[0]==[4,3,2]
assert counts[2]/counts[0]==0.25
lab.shipIt: Version entity, step, order, window and identity semantics; build from entry with complete opportunity; persist additive counts and transition times; monitor event parity and monotonicity; and freeze decisions when instrumentation breaks.

lessons.description: Funnel analysis measures how eligible entities progress through a defined sequence of product states or events and where they fail, branch, repeat, or take too long. A funnel is not an objective map of user behavior: step definitions, order rules, identity, attribution, conversion window, denominator, and re-entry policy construct the result. This chapter develops strict and loose funnels, unique-user versus event conversion, closed versus open cohorts, step and cumulative rates, time-to-convert, competing paths, censoring, segmentation, instrumentation, causal limits, and experimental use. You will learn how repeated events and inner joins inflate conversion, why recent entrants have incomplete opportunity, how to distinguish a product obstacle from selection, and when a state machine or journey analysis is better than a linear funnel. A worked checkout example exposes an identity and window bug. The lab implements a deterministic ordered unique-user funnel from raw events, compares it with pandas, and verifies monotonic counts, window rules, deduplication, and denominator reconciliation. Production guidance covers event contracts, late data, sessionization, privacy, monitoring, metric versions, and rollback. The goal is a reproducible behavioral estimand that guides hypotheses, not a decorative narrowing chart that implies causality.
learningObjectives: Define funnel population, entity, step events, ordering, window, attribution, repetition, and denominator semantics precisely.
Compute cumulative and step conversion without double counting entities or granting unequal observation opportunity.
Diagnose instrumentation, identity, time, competing-path, and selection explanations for apparent drop-off.
Implement and verify an ordered funnel while preserving raw counts, transition times, and alternative paths.

deepSections.title: Entity, entry, steps, order, and window
deepSections.body: Name the entity: user, account, order, application, device, or session. Define eligibility and entry event with source and version. A strict funnel requires step order; a loose funnel may allow intervening events while preserving order; any-order completion answers a different question. Define whether timestamps may tie, whether one event can satisfy multiple steps, and whether all steps must share an order or item property. The conversion window begins at a stated event and uses event time with a timezone and late-data policy. Closed cohorts fix entry membership; open funnels can mix changing populations. Version every semantic choice.

deepSections.title: Unique entities, repeats, and denominators
deepSections.body: Unique-entity conversion counts each entity once, usually using the earliest eligible entry and earliest qualifying next step. Event-total funnels can count repeated completions and may exceed entry entities; label them explicitly. Step conversion N_k/N_{k-1} differs from cumulative conversion N_k/N_1, and their product reconciles when definitions align. Decide whether users can re-enter after failure or complete multiple journeys; then use a journey identifier rather than accidental event pairs. Preserve numerator and denominator for every transition. An inner join of completed steps drops nonconverters and can make conversion appear 100%; start from the entry population and left join forward.

deepSections.title: Time to convert and observation maturity
deepSections.body: Report transition-time distributions, not only means, because latency is often skewed and long tails determine the window. A fixed window classifies no completion by its end, but entities entering near the data cutoff have not had equal opportunity. Restrict to matured entrants, use cohort-age tables, or apply survival methods when time-to-event is the target and right censoring assumptions are defensible. Calendar shocks and app releases affect cohorts differently. Sessionization adds an inactivity threshold that can split or merge journeys; document it and test sensitivity. Late events can revise earlier funnels, so publish a data-completeness cutoff.

deepSections.title: Drop-off, segmentation, and competing paths
deepSections.body: A large drop identifies a transition worth investigation, not its cause. Inspect errors, latency, validation messages, alternate events, support contacts, and qualitative evidence. Segment by pre-entry attributes such as platform or acquisition channel, while recognizing composition and multiplicity. Segmenting on a later step selects converters and can reverse interpretation. Users may reach the same value through a different sequence, so path or state-transition analysis can reveal false drop-off. Compare step rates on common cohorts and complete windows; decompose an aggregate change into entry mix, within-segment transition changes, and logging coverage.

deepSections.title: Causal tests and data-quality controls
deepSections.body: Funnel patterns generate hypotheses such as a form field causing abandonment. Randomize the proposed change and estimate ITT effects on prespecified end conversion plus transition drivers and guardrails. Do not declare causal impact from users who happened to complete a step. In experiment funnels, denominator should normally begin with assigned eligible units or an assignment-invariant trigger; treatment-dependent exposure filters bias comparison. Test event schema, uniqueness, ordering, property consistency, assignment coverage, and arm-specific missingness. Maintain synthetic journeys and expected counts. When a step event changes, dual-log and reconcile before migrating the metric.

lessons.math: Let E be entry entities and S_k the subset that satisfies ordered steps 1..k within window W. Cumulative conversion C_k=|S_k|/|E| and step conversion c_k=|S_k|/|S_{k-1}|, with C_k=product_{j=2..k}c_j when sets and denominators align. Drop-off at k is |S_{k-1}|-|S_k|. Time-to-step T_k=t_k-t_entry is censored at the data cutoff or window for incomplete entities. Compare arms at the randomization-unit level and retain additive counts for reconciliation.

workedExamples.title: An identity reset that turns failures into apparent success
workedExamples.body: Trace raw entity histories, detect cross-step identity loss, rebuild from entry with complete windows, and separate instrumentation repair from the randomized product fix.

exercises.prompt: Counts are 1000, 800, 600. What are step and cumulative final conversion?
exercises.solution: Step conversions are 80% then 75%; final cumulative conversion is 600/1000=60%, equal to 0.8*0.75.

exercises.prompt: Why can a 30-day window bias the newest cohort?
exercises.solution: Members have not all had 30 days of follow-up; restrict to mature entries or use censoring-aware methods.

exercises.prompt: A user completes B before A. Do they convert?
exercises.solution: Only under an any-order definition. A strict ordered funnel excludes that sequence; the contract must decide.

lessons.title: Cohort Retention Analysis
lessons.interviewAnswer: Retention starts with a fixed cohort, usually entities sharing a first value event or acquisition period, and asks what fraction performs a defined return behavior at each age. I specify exact-period versus rolling retention, interval boundaries, identity, denominator, resurrection, and observation cutoff. Recent cohorts do not have mature later ages, so I leave those cells unavailable rather than zero. I compare cohorts at the same age, inspect calendar effects and acquisition mix, and use survival or hazard methods when time-to-churn and censoring matter. A better curve is descriptive until an experiment or causal design supports attribution.
keyPoints: Cohort time and calendar time are separate axes
Retention depends on the value event and denominator contract
Recent cohort cells are censored, not zero
Exact, rolling, and survival retention answer different questions
Composition and identity changes can mimic product retention gains
lessons.why: Aggregate active-user rates mix new, mature, resurrected, and seasonal users. Growth can make activity look healthy while every cohort decays, and acquisition quality can make a product change appear to improve retention. Cohorts align users by lifecycle age so teams can see activation and durable return patterns. Yet a signup cohort may include people who never experienced value, while an activated cohort conditions on a behavior treatment can change. Interviews test whether analysts handle denominator and censoring. In production, retention drives lifetime-value models and experiment decisions, so semantic drift creates large downstream errors.
lessons.intuition: Imagine giving every user two clocks. The calendar clock says March or April; the lifecycle clock says week zero, one, or two since first value. A cohort matrix places acquisition time on rows and lifecycle age on columns. Comparing down a column asks whether newer cohorts retain better at the same age. Reading across a row shows decay for one cohort. The lower-right cells do not exist yet because those users have not aged enough. Exact retention asks for activity in one interval; rolling retention asks whether activity occurs on or after that age; survival retention asks whether a defined churn event has not yet occurred.
lessons.deepDive: Retention is a longitudinal estimand over a cohort and behavior process. The matrix is a compact view of event histories, observation opportunity, and population composition.
lessons.workedExample: A subscription product's month-one retention rises from 52% to 60% after a new onboarding launch. Cohort decomposition shows the launch coincided with ending a low-intent paid channel; within organic and partner channels, retention is unchanged. A diagonal dip across every cohort at calendar April reflects an outage, not lifecycle decay. The newest cohort's month-three cell was mistakenly recorded as zero despite only six weeks of follow-up. After correcting maturity and standardizing acquisition mix, the apparent improvement largely disappears. The team runs a randomized onboarding test with all assigned new users as denominator and a mature retention window.

commonMistakes.mistake: Filling unavailable future cells with zero
commonMistakes.correction: They are right-censored because follow-up has not occurred; mark them unavailable and compare only mature ages.

commonMistakes.mistake: Calling any return event retention
commonMistakes.correction: Choose a behavior that represents product value and specify exact or rolling semantics.

commonMistakes.mistake: Comparing aggregate active rates
commonMistakes.correction: They mix cohort ages and acquisition volumes; align entities by lifecycle age.

commonMistakes.mistake: Attributing activated-user retention to onboarding
commonMistakes.correction: Activation is selected and may be treatment-affected; use ITT in a randomized design to estimate causal impact.

followUps.question: What is rolling retention?
followUps.answer: The fraction of the original cohort active at or after a given age; it differs from activity within exactly that interval and can revise as future data arrive.

followUps.question: Why is the cohort table triangular?
followUps.answer: New cohorts have not existed long enough to reach later ages, so those cells lack observation opportunity.

followUps.question: When should you use survival analysis?
followUps.answer: When the target is time to a defined event and right-censored entities should contribute their observed at-risk time under defensible censoring assumptions.

lessons.production: Materialize an immutable cohort-membership table and a deduplicated entity-period activity table with source and identity versions. Compute additive cohort sizes and retained counts before percentages. Enforce one cohort per entity, nonnegative age, unique entity-period rows, mature-cell cutoff, late-event policy, and raw-event reconciliation. Monitor cohort volume, event coverage, identity merges, acquisition mix, calendar anomalies, and unexpected revisions. Attach minimum-support and privacy suppression. Version exact/rolling, start and return events, intervals, grace periods, and resurrection rules. On a definition or instrumentation bug, freeze downstream LTV and experiment decisions, publish affected dates, recompute under a new version, and retain the old series for audit and rollback.
lessons.description: Cohort retention analysis follows entities from a common starting event and measures whether they return to a value-defining behavior at comparable ages. It separates lifecycle decay from calendar-time shocks, but only when cohort assignment, activity, interval boundaries, identity, denominator, and observation maturity are defined consistently. This chapter develops acquisition and behavioral cohorts, exact-period, rolling, and bracket retention, survival-style retention, resurrection, churn, cohort-age matrices, censoring, composition, seasonality, segmentation, uncertainty, and experimental interpretation. You will learn why recent cohorts form an incomplete triangle, why retention can rise when low-value users never enter the denominator, how identity and late events reshape curves, and when Kaplan-Meier or hazard analysis is more appropriate. A worked subscription example separates acquisition-mix change from product improvement. The lab builds a monthly exact-period retention matrix from first activity and later events, compares with pandas, and verifies cohort size, maturity, identity uniqueness, and denominator invariants. Production guidance covers semantic models, incremental updates, backfills, privacy, monitoring, causal tests, and rollback. The goal is a lifecycle measurement system that reveals durable value, not a color grid interpreted without population or time context.
learningObjectives: Define cohort membership, start event, retained behavior, age interval, denominator, and resurrection semantics.
Compute exact, rolling, and survival-style retention while handling right censoring and incomplete recent cohorts.
Decompose retention changes into cohort composition, lifecycle, calendar time, instrumentation, and product mechanisms.
Implement and validate a cohort matrix with maturity and reconciliation checks.

deepSections.title: Cohort and retained-behavior contract
deepSections.body: Choose the entity and immutable cohort anchor: signup, first purchase, activation, contract start, or first exposure answer different questions. Define timezone and interval boundaries, and assign one first qualifying cohort unless repeat journeys are intentionally modeled. Define retained behavior as a value event, not any telemetry heartbeat. The denominator can be all acquired users, activated users, payers, or eligible accounts; each changes the estimand. State treatment of internal users, bots, merged identities, deleted accounts, pauses, and resurrected users. Store cohort membership separately from mutable user profiles so later property changes do not rewrite history.

deepSections.title: Exact, rolling, bracket, and survival retention
deepSections.body: Exact-period retention at age k counts cohort entities active during that interval divided by original cohort size. Rolling retention at k counts those active at k or any later observed interval and can be monotone by construction, but future activity means values revise as data mature. Bracket retention groups multiple periods to reduce noise. Unbounded return within a window answers yet another question. Churn may mean contract cancellation, no activity for a grace period, or absorbing death; noncontractual inactivity is not directly observed churn. Kaplan-Meier estimates survival under censoring assumptions when a well-defined event time exists. Label the definition in every chart.

deepSections.title: Right censoring and the incomplete triangle
deepSections.body: A cohort entering near the data cutoff cannot contribute an observed month-six outcome. Mark cells beyond maximum observable age as unavailable. Even an age-k cell needs complete event ingestion through the interval end, including late-arrival allowance. Treating unavailable as not retained systematically makes recent cohorts look worse. Restrict comparisons to mature cells, use survival estimators for time-to-event, or model censoring under explicit assumptions. Administrative censoring at a common cutoff differs from loss to follow-up that may depend on outcome. Preserve cohort sizes and at-risk counts because percentages without support invite unstable rankings.

deepSections.title: Lifecycle, calendar, composition, and causality
deepSections.body: A diagonal disturbance across cohorts often indicates a calendar outage or holiday; a horizontal row pattern can indicate a particular acquisition campaign; a vertical age effect suggests lifecycle behavior. Decompose changes by acquisition channel, country, platform, plan, and eligibility using pre-cohort attributes while protecting small cells and multiplicity. Simpson reversals arise when channel mix changes. Instrumentation releases can create false activity or loss. Correlation between an activation behavior and later retention reflects selection as well as mechanism. Use randomized interventions to test whether causing activation or onboarding changes retention, and measure ITT from assigned cohorts rather than only users who activated.

deepSections.title: Uncertainty, forecasting, and metric operation
deepSections.body: Attach binomial or cluster-aware uncertainty to cohort-age rates and avoid overreacting to tiny cohorts. For forecasting, evaluate on chronological cohort cutoffs so future activity never leaks into features or labels. Retention curves feed LTV only after revenue, margin, churn, and discount assumptions are stated; a flat early curve does not prove a permanent plateau. Incremental pipelines must update mature cells for late events without changing cohort anchors. Reconcile active sets to raw events, monitor cohort-size and identity-link shifts, and dual-run definition migrations. Preserve old versions when return-event or grace-period semantics change.

lessons.math: For cohort c with fixed member set C_c and exact retained set A_{c,k} active in age interval k, R_{c,k}=|C_c intersection A_{c,k}|/|C_c|. Rolling retention R^roll_{c,k}=|C_c intersection union_{j>=k}A_{c,j}|/|C_c| and may revise until follow-up closes. An available cell requires cohort_end(c)+end(k)<=data_cutoff-lateness. Approximate independent-binomial SE is sqrt(R(1-R)/n_c), but repeated users, clusters, and weighted populations need design-aware uncertainty.

workedExamples.title: A retention improvement created by acquisition mix
workedExamples.body: Separate cohort age from calendar time, mark immature cells unavailable, stratify by pre-acquisition channel, standardize composition, and confirm onboarding causally with randomized assignment.

exercises.prompt: A cohort has 100 users; 40 are active in month two. Exact retention?
exercises.solution: 40%, provided all 100 had complete month-two observation and activity semantics are fixed.

exercises.prompt: Why can rolling month-two retention exceed exact month-two retention?
exercises.solution: It also counts cohort members who return after month two even if inactive during month two itself.

exercises.prompt: How does a calendar outage appear in a cohort matrix?
exercises.solution: Often as a diagonal pattern because different cohorts encounter the same calendar period at different lifecycle ages.

lessons.title: Churn, Lifetime Value & Unit Economics
lessons.interviewAnswer: LTV is expected discounted future contribution margin over a stated horizon, conditional on current information and policy. In subscriptions, churn may be an observed cancellation or nonrenewal; in noncontractual products, inactivity is latent and needs a repeat-purchase/dropout model or an operational lapse rule. I handle right censoring, customer heterogeneity, refunds and variable costs, validate on mature chronological cohorts, and report cohort calibration and uncertainty rather than only individual rank. CAC comparison uses incremental fully loaded acquisition cost. A high predicted LTV does not imply targeting will cause value; intervention decisions need treatment effects and costs.
keyPoints: LTV is a horizon- and policy-dependent expectation
Contribution margin differs from revenue
Churn is observed only in some business settings
Censoring and heterogeneity are central, not edge cases
Predictive value and incremental intervention value are different estimands
lessons.why: Acquisition bidding, onboarding, account management, and financial planning depend on future economics rather than today's purchase. Simple LTV formulas can be useful sanity checks but often assume constant retention, constant margin, homogeneous customers, and infinite horizons. They overstate value when high-risk customers disappear early, costs scale with usage, or the model ignores refunds and support. Customer-base research emphasizes different probability models for contractual and noncontractual settings. Interviews test whether candidates connect retention, survival, uncertainty, and unit economics. Production models also influence who receives offers, changing future data and creating feedback loops.
lessons.intuition: Picture each future period as a possible cash-flow box. The chance a customer is still active shrinks with time, and a discount factor makes distant margin worth less today. Expected LTV adds survival probability times expected contribution margin in each box. In a subscription, cancellation may reveal the event time. In retail, silence does not prove permanent death; a customer may buy again, so frequency and dropout are latent processes. Customers differ, and mixing them into one retention rate can produce a curve that represents nobody. A prediction describes expected value under current policy, not the causal gain from contacting that customer.
lessons.deepDive: LTV combines a behavioral event process, an economic cash-flow model, and a decision horizon. Every output inherits definitions and uncertainty from all three layers.
lessons.workedExample: A subscription charges $20 monthly, but contribution margin after payment, support, and serving cost is $12. A naive formula uses 95% monthly retention forever and reports a large value. Cohort hazards show new customers have much higher first-three-month churn and long-tenure customers are heterogeneous; refunds also cluster early. A twelve-month survival-weighted contribution forecast gives $93 with an uncertainty interval, versus $150 gross-revenue arithmetic. Channel CAC is $70 but rises at the margin. The team uses payback and downside scenarios, then randomizes a retention offer because predicted churn risk alone cannot show who is persuadable.

commonMistakes.mistake: Calling last activity the churn date
commonMistakes.correction: In noncontractual settings dropout is latent; use a lapse definition or probabilistic repeat-purchase/dropout model and allow resurrection.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using revenue as LTV
commonMistakes.correction: Economic decisions need contribution margin after relevant variable costs, refunds, incentives, and service costs.

commonMistakes.mistake: Dropping active customers from duration modeling
commonMistakes.correction: They are right-censored and contribute known survival time; deleting them biases lifetime downward.

commonMistakes.mistake: Targeting the highest predicted risk
commonMistakes.correction: Risk is not treatment responsiveness; optimize incremental effect minus cost under policy and fairness constraints.

followUps.question: What is right censoring?
followUps.answer: The event has not been observed by the cutoff, so lifetime is known only to exceed the observed follow-up; survival methods use that partial information.

followUps.question: How does LTV differ in contractual and noncontractual businesses?
followUps.answer: Contractual churn can often be observed, while noncontractual dropout is latent and repeat-purchase plus dropout processes must be modeled or operationally defined.

followUps.question: How do you validate LTV?
followUps.answer: Use chronological mature cohorts, aggregate and segment calibration, ranking and error, uncertainty coverage, financial baselines, and decision outcomes under the deployment policy.

lessons.production: Version churn and resurrection rules, cohort/start, cutoff, horizon, margin and cost tables, discount rate, feature timestamps, model, policy, and calibration. Maintain censored duration data and label-maturity checks. Reconcile predicted aggregate value with realized cohort revenue and contribution, tracking refunds and service costs. Monitor survival calibration, hazard drift, channel mix, prediction intervals, ranking, LTV/CAC, payback, and targeting treatment effects. Use randomized holdouts to measure incremental interventions and prevent policy feedback. Protect financial and behavioral data, audit slice outcomes, and cap bids or incentives. On model or cost-pipeline failure, revert to conservative cohort baselines and prior bid caps while retaining predictions and decisions for audit.
lessons.description: Customer lifetime value (LTV or CLV) is the discounted expected contribution margin generated by a customer or cohort over a declared future horizon, while churn describes a contractual cancellation or a modeled loss of future activity. Both are forecasts with behavioral, accounting, censoring, and policy assumptions; neither is a timeless label stored on a user. This chapter develops contractual versus noncontractual settings, retention and hazard, right censoring, revenue versus margin, discounting, acquisition cost, payback, cohort versus individual prediction, BG/NBD-style customer-base models, survival models, calibration, chronological validation, treatment effects, uncertainty, and decision use. You will learn why last activity is not observed churn, why a constant-retention formula can be dangerously optimistic, how heterogeneity changes aggregate value, and why marketing intervention can invalidate passive forecasts. A worked subscription example separates gross revenue from incremental contribution value. The lab implements Kaplan-Meier survival and discounted cohort LTV from first principles, compares grouped calculations with pandas, and verifies censoring and monotonicity invariants. Production guidance covers label maturity, leakage, policy feedback, monitoring, fairness, cost, rollback, and human review.
learningObjectives: Define churn, survival, margin, horizon, discounting, and acquisition cost for contractual and noncontractual businesses.
Estimate retention under right censoring and translate survival or repeat-purchase forecasts into discounted expected contribution value.
Validate LTV models chronologically with calibration, ranking, aggregate value, policy, and uncertainty metrics.
Distinguish predictive customer value from incremental value caused by a retention or acquisition action.

deepSections.title: Contractual, noncontractual, and operational churn
deepSections.body: In a contractual business, cancellation or failure to renew can define churn, though pauses, delinquency, upgrades, and reactivation need rules. In a noncontractual setting there is no observed termination; a 90-day lapse is an operational label, not proof the customer will never return. Buy-till-you-die models jointly represent purchasing while alive and latent dropout. Define entity, cohort, start, event, grace period, resurrection, horizon, and policy. Avoid deriving a churn label using future inactivity beyond the prediction cutoff without accounting for label maturity. Different products or regions may require distinct definitions rather than one global threshold.

deepSections.title: Retention, hazard, and censoring
deepSections.body: Survival S(t)=P(T>t) is the probability the event time exceeds t; hazard describes event risk among those still at risk. Kaplan-Meier multiplies conditional survival across observed event times and lets right-censored customers contribute until their last known follow-up. Its interpretation assumes censoring is independent of event time conditional on the analysis information; loss caused by treatment or data-source exit may violate this. Cohort retention at fixed periods is related but may define recurring activity rather than an absorbing event. Compare survival curves, hazards, and at-risk counts, and use Cox or parametric models only after checking proportionality or distributional assumptions.

deepSections.title: Revenue, contribution margin, discounting, and CAC
deepSections.body: Forecast incremental contribution, not gross revenue, when evaluating economics. Subtract variable fulfillment, payment, service, promotion, returns, fraud, and support costs according to ownership. For period t, expected value combines survival/activity probability, expected transactions or revenue while active, margin, and discount factor 1/(1+r)^t. Use a finite policy horizon unless a defensible terminal value is modeled. Customer acquisition cost (CAC) includes the incremental channel spend and allocated costs relevant to the decision; blended averages hide channel and marginal-cost differences. Payback time and downside risk often matter alongside mean LTV/CAC.

deepSections.title: Models and chronological validation
deepSections.body: Baselines include cohort curves, empirical Bayes shrinkage, and simple survival plus margin models. Contractual settings can use discrete-time hazard or survival regression; noncontractual repeat purchase may use Pareto/NBD or BG/NBD with a spend model under assumptions about frequency, dropout, and monetary value. Flexible ML can forecast horizon revenue but must respect censored labels and future leakage. Split by acquisition time, train only on information available at cutoff, and evaluate on mature future windows. Measure aggregate cohort calibration, MAE or deviance, quantile calibration, ranking, uncertainty coverage, and financial decision regret. Compare with simple recency-frequency-monetary baselines.

deepSections.title: Interventions, feedback, and responsible use
deepSections.body: High predicted value may identify customers who would remain anyway; high churn risk may identify users too late to help. Targeting should estimate incremental treatment effect or uplift, subtract contact and incentive cost, and honor eligibility and fairness constraints. Offers change observed retention and margin, so retraining on treated outcomes without policy features creates feedback. Maintain randomized holdouts or exploration to learn intervention effects. Avoid using value predictions to deny essential service or systematically exclude protected or low-income groups without governance. Report cohort-level economics and uncertainty, cap automated bids, and provide human review for material account actions.

lessons.math: For discrete periods t=1..H, LTV=sum_t S(t) E[M_t|active at t]/(1+r)^t minus future incremental costs, where S(t) or purchase probability and margin M_t are model outputs. Kaplan-Meier is S_hat(t)=product_{u<=t}(1-d_u/n_u), with d_u events and n_u at risk just before u. For constant retention q and margin m starting next period over an infinite horizon, LTV=m q/(1+r-q), but this strong homogeneous stationary approximation should be a sanity check, not a default truth.

workedExamples.title: From headline revenue to incremental contribution value
workedExamples.body: Estimate censored survival, apply period-specific margin and finite-horizon discounting, compare marginal CAC and payback, and test retention interventions rather than targeting on risk alone.

exercises.prompt: Why is a current active subscriber not missing data?
exercises.solution: Their event time is right-censored: you know they survived through follow-up, which contributes information to survival estimation.

exercises.prompt: Revenue is $100 and variable cost $40. Which enters contribution LTV?
exercises.solution: $60 before other relevant incremental costs and discounting, not the full $100 revenue.

exercises.prompt: Why can one constant retention rate mislead?
exercises.solution: Customer hazards vary with tenure and latent segment; averaging heterogeneity can distort both curve shape and long-horizon value.

lab.goal: Implement Kaplan-Meier survival and finite-horizon discounted contribution LTV, compare grouped risk calculations with pandas, and verify censoring and monotonicity.
lab.buildIt:
def kaplan_meier(durations,events):
    times=sorted(set(durations)); survival=1.0; curve=[]
    for t in times:
        at_risk=sum(d>=t for d in durations); failures=sum(d==t and e for d,e in zip(durations,events))
        if failures:survival*=1-failures/at_risk
        curve.append((t,survival,at_risk,failures))
    return curve
def discounted_ltv(curve,margin,discount,horizon):
    by_time=dict((t,s) for t,s,_,_ in curve); last=1.0; value=0.0
    for t in range(1,horizon+1):
        if t in by_time:last=by_time[t]
        value+=last*margin/(1+discount)**t
    return value
durations=[1,2,2,3,4,4]; events=[1,1,0,1,0,1]
curve=kaplan_meier(durations,events); ltv=discounted_ltv(curve,12,0.01,4)
lab.verifyIt:
survivals=[s for _,s,_,_ in curve]
assert all(b<=a for a,b in zip(survivals,survivals[1:]))
assert curve[0][2]==6 and curve[-1][2]==2
assert pandas_failures=={1:1,2:1,3:1,4:1}
assert 0<ltv<12*4
no_events=kaplan_meier([1,2,3],[0,0,0])
assert all(s==1 for _,s,_,_ in no_events)
assert discounted_ltv(curve,12,0.05,4)<ltv

lessons.title: Potential Outcomes & Average Treatment Effects
lessons.interviewAnswer: The potential-outcomes framework defines Y_i(a) as unit i's outcome under treatment strategy a. For a binary treatment, the individual effect Y_i(1)-Y_i(0) is fundamentally unobservable because only one potential outcome is revealed. We therefore target population quantities such as ATE E[Y(1)-Y(0)], ATT, risk ratio, quantile effect or policy value. Consistency connects observed Y to Y(A); positivity supplies support; exchangeability connects treatment groups to counterfactual outcomes; and SUTVA-style assumptions require well-defined versions and manageable interference. Randomization establishes exchangeability by design, while observational analyses need measured-confounding assumptions or another identification strategy. I specify time zero, treatment versions, population and outcome horizon, distinguish assignment from receipt, report intention-to-treat and adherence estimands clearly, and avoid claiming individual treatment effects are validated from factual outcomes alone.
keyPoints: Potential outcomes define causal effects by comparing intervention states for the same target units.
Only one potential outcome per unit is observed, so individual effects require untestable structure or remain unidentified.
ATE, ATT, CATE, risk ratio, quantile and policy effects are different estimands with different target populations.
Consistency, exchangeability, positivity and interference assumptions connect potential outcomes to observed data.
Assignment, treatment receipt, adherence and treatment versions must not be collapsed into one ambiguous variable.
lessons.why: Causal statements become vague when they do not say whose outcome, under which alternatives and over what horizon. 'The campaign worked' could mean assignment increased average conversion, exposure helped compliers, or a personalized policy improved total value. Potential outcomes force these distinctions. They also expose the central missing-data problem: the counterfactual is never observed for the same unit. Randomized groups solve an average comparison through design, not by revealing both individual outcomes. In observational settings, precise notation prevents an estimator from quietly changing the population, treatment version or effect scale. It also stops heterogeneous-effect models from being judged like ordinary label predictors when individual causal labels do not exist.
lessons.intuition: Imagine two sealed outcome cards for each person: one under treatment and one under control. Assignment reveals exactly one card. A causal effect compares the two cards, but the individual difference stays hidden. Randomization makes the revealed treated cards representative of all treatment cards and the revealed control cards representative of all control cards, allowing an average contrast.
lessons.deepDive: Potential outcomes provide a precise language for interventions, estimands and identification. Their usefulness depends on treatment consistency, assignment design, overlap, interference and time alignment. Average effects can be estimated without recovering individual effects; heterogeneous and policy claims require additional data, structure and honest evaluation.
lessons.workedExample: In a randomized trial, person A reveals Y(1) and person B reveals Y(0). Neither person's counterfactual is observed, but group averages consistently estimate E[Y(1)] and E[Y(0)] under the assignment design, so their difference estimates ATE.

commonMistakes.misconception: A causal model predicts each unit's treatment effect label.
commonMistakes.correction: Individual effects are never jointly observed; evaluation targets average contrasts, calibration or policy value under assumptions.

commonMistakes.misconception: Randomization reveals both potential outcomes.
commonMistakes.correction: It balances which one is revealed across groups, enabling average inference while individual counterfactuals remain missing.

commonMistakes.misconception: ATE and ATT differ only by estimator.
commonMistakes.correction: They average effects over different populations and can genuinely differ under heterogeneity.

commonMistakes.misconception: SUTVA means only no interference.
commonMistakes.correction: It also includes treatment-version consistency; both require domain-specific interpretation.

followUps.question: Why is the individual treatment effect unobservable?
followUps.answer: At a given time the unit follows one treatment path, revealing one potential outcome while the alternative remains counterfactual.

followUps.question: What identifies ATE in a randomized trial?
followUps.answer: The assignment mechanism makes treatment independent of potential outcomes, with consistency, outcome observation and the appropriate interference assumptions.

followUps.question: Can ATT equal ATE?
followUps.answer: Yes under constant effects or when effect heterogeneity has the same average in treated and target populations, but not by definition.

lessons.production: Version population eligibility, treatment strategies and versions, assignment and receipt, time zero, follow-up, outcome, estimand and interference mapping. Preserve assignment logs, adherence and implementation fidelity. Analyze at the randomization or independent unit, monitor positivity and subgroup support, and backfill outcomes by assignment cohort. Separate discovery from estimation for heterogeneity and validate policies prospectively. Report sampling uncertainty plus sensitivity to missing outcomes, versions and spillovers. Keep the prior assignment policy available when treatment delivery or population changes invalidate consistency or transport.

visual.title: Potential outcomes
visual.caption: The individual treatment effect Y(1)−Y(0) cannot be observed directly because only one potential outcome is realized.

lessons.math: For binary A, observed Y=A Y(1)+(1-A)Y(0) under consistency. Unit effect tau_i=Y_i(1)-Y_i(0); ATE=E[tau], ATT=E[tau|A=1], and CATE tau(x)=E[tau|X=x]. In a randomized trial, A is independent of (Y(1),Y(0)), so E[Y|A=1]-E[Y|A=0]=ATE for the randomized population. Conditional identification gives E[Y(a)]=E_X E[Y|A=a,X]. The variance of a difference in independent sample means is approximately s1^2/n1+s0^2/n0, with design-specific or cluster-aware inference replacing this formula when assignment is not individual independent randomization.
lessons.code:
from scipy.stats import norm
interval=(estimate-norm.ppf(.975)*se,estimate+norm.ppf(.975)*se); att_truth=np.mean(individual_effect[a==1]); observed_counterfactual=np.where(a==1,y0,y1)

lab.goal: Simulate complete potential outcomes, reveal one through random assignment, and verify unbiased average-effect recovery and uncertainty behavior.
lab.buildIt:
import numpy as np
rng=np.random.default_rng(12); n=20000; x=rng.normal(size=n); y0=1+2*x+rng.normal(size=n); individual_effect=1+.6*x; y1=y0+individual_effect; true_ate=np.mean(y1-y0); a=rng.binomial(1,.5,size=n); observed=np.where(a==1,y1,y0); estimate=observed[a==1].mean()-observed[a==0].mean()
se=np.sqrt(observed[a==1].var(ddof=1)/a.sum()+observed[a==0].var(ddof=1)/(n-a.sum()))
lab.verifyIt:
assert abs(true_ate-1)<.02
assert abs(estimate-true_ate)<.06
assert interval[0]<true_ate<interval[1]
assert abs(att_truth-true_ate)<.03
assert np.all(observed+observed_counterfactual==y0+y1)
assert not np.array_equal(observed,observed_counterfactual)
lab.shipIt: Persist assignment, treatment-version and outcome-horizon contracts, analyze at the assignment unit, and monitor adherence, interference, support and outcome maturity by cohort.

lessons.description: Potential outcomes make causal questions explicit by defining what each unit would experience under each treatment strategy. This chapter introduces factual and counterfactual outcomes, the fundamental problem of causal inference, consistency, treatment versions, positivity, exchangeability and interference. It distinguishes individual effects from ATE, ATT, ATC, CATE, risk ratios, quantile effects and policy value; separates treatment assignment, receipt and adherence; and contrasts intention-to-treat with per-protocol questions. It derives identification under randomization and measured-confounding adjustment, explains finite-population versus superpopulation targets, and discusses cluster assignment, censoring and repeated outcomes. Worked examples show why the same experiment supports an average effect but not observed individual effects and why vague treatment versions break consistency. The lab simulates complete potential outcomes, hides one per unit, verifies that randomized difference in means recovers the known ATE and quantifies sampling uncertainty. Production guidance versions estimands and treatment protocols, monitors compliance, spillovers, overlap and outcome maturity, and keeps personalized-effect claims separate from observable predictive validation.
learningObjectives: Define potential outcomes and translate decisions into population, treatment, horizon and effect estimands.
Distinguish individual, average, treated-population, conditional and policy effects.
Derive randomized and conditional-exchangeability identification from explicit assumptions.
Design diagnostics for consistency, adherence, positivity, interference and outcome observation.

deepSections.title: Potential outcomes separate intervention worlds
deepSections.body: Y_i(a) is defined by a treatment strategy, not merely a recorded label. Binary notation is convenient, but doses, timing and dynamic regimes require many or longitudinal potential outcomes. The individual contrast tau_i cannot be observed because assignment reveals one branch. Population summaries can still be identified: ATE weights the target population, ATT weights the treated population, and CATE conditions on baseline covariates. Risk differences, ratios, odds ratios, means and quantiles describe different features and are not interchangeable. A policy effect compares two assignment rules and may be the operational estimand when capacity limits treatment. Define whether the population is finite enrolled units or draws from a superpopulation. Changes in eligibility or weighting change the estimand. Avoid choosing a convenient effect measure after seeing results, especially when noncollapsible measures such as odds ratios complicate marginal and conditional comparisons.

deepSections.title: Consistency requires a well-defined treatment mapping
deepSections.body: Consistency says that if unit i receives strategy a, its observed outcome equals Y_i(a). This seems tautological until treatment has multiple versions: an email can vary in content and send time, surgery varies by technique, and 'education' can mean different programs. If versions have different effects but are collapsed into A, the potential outcome is ambiguous unless the version mixture is part of the intervention. Treatment receipt and assignment also differ under noncompliance. Intention-to-treat compares assignment strategies and preserves randomization; per-protocol or treatment-on-treated questions need additional assumptions or instruments. Time zero aligns eligibility, assignment and follow-up. Outcomes must be defined with horizon and competing events. Measurement and censoring can break the observed connection even when treatment is well defined. Document implementation fidelity and deviations rather than interpreting one binary column as the intervention.

deepSections.title: Identification replaces missing counterfactual averages
deepSections.body: Random assignment makes treatment independent of potential outcomes according to the assignment mechanism, so treated factual outcomes estimate the population's treated potential outcomes and controls estimate control potential outcomes. Stratified or cluster randomization requires design-aware analysis. In observational data, conditional exchangeability assumes Y(a) is independent of A given measured X; this cannot be established from predictive fit and fails with unmeasured common causes. Positivity requires nonzero probability of every relevant treatment within every target covariate stratum. Structural violations mean some strategies never occur; practical violations create extreme variance. Consistency, exchangeability and positivity produce the g-formula. An interference assumption is also needed for unit-indexed Y_i(a); when one unit's treatment affects another, potential outcomes must depend on a treatment vector or exposure mapping and assignment design.

deepSections.title: Average effects are estimable without individual causal labels
deepSections.body: In a simple randomized trial, difference in means is unbiased for an appropriate average effect under the design. Regression adjustment can improve precision when prespecified and correctly analyzed, but randomization—not the regression—provides identification. Standard errors must follow the assignment unit, clustering, stratification and repeated measurements. Missing outcomes require assumptions and sensitivity; complete-case estimates can lose the randomized comparison if observation depends on treatment and outcome risk. Observational estimators include standardization, weighting, matching and doubly robust scores, each estimating a declared population contrast. Cross-fitting reduces overfit bias for flexible nuisance functions. Confidence intervals address repeated-sample or randomization variation under the design, not ambiguity about treatment versions, unmeasured confounding or interference. Report absolute effects and baseline risk, not only relative measures.

deepSections.title: Heterogeneity is a causal prediction problem without individual labels
deepSections.body: CATE models aim to predict conditional average contrasts, not each person's realized benefit. We never observe tau_i, so ordinary prediction error against individual treatment effects is unavailable. Randomized or unconfounded data permit transformed scores, orthogonal losses and honest sample splitting to evaluate average calibration and policy value. Subgroup discovery on the same outcomes used for estimation exaggerates differences; separate discovery and estimation or use honest methods. Positivity must hold within subgroups. A policy that treats estimated high-benefit units should be evaluated against a baseline policy with cost and capacity, preferably in a randomized experiment. Report uncertainty and population support, and avoid telling individuals an effect is known precisely when the evidence identifies only a noisy conditional mean.

workedExamples.title: Average effect without individual effects
workedExamples.body: In a randomized trial, person A reveals Y(1) and person B reveals Y(0). Neither person's counterfactual is observed, but group averages consistently estimate E[Y(1)] and E[Y(0)] under the assignment design, so their difference estimates ATE.

workedExamples.title: Ambiguous treatment version
workedExamples.body: A study codes all notifications as treated, but urgent alerts and promotional messages have opposite effects. Unless the intervention specifies their mixture or separates versions, Y(1) is not a stable potential outcome for future deployment.

exercises.prompt: What population does ATT average over?
exercises.solution: The units actually treated under the observed assignment mechanism, not automatically the full eligible population.

exercises.prompt: Why can two delivery versions violate consistency?
exercises.solution: If both map to A=1 but produce different outcomes, Y(1) is ambiguous unless the intervention defines or averages those versions coherently.

exercises.prompt: What changes under network interference?
exercises.solution: A unit's potential outcome depends on its own and others' assignments or an exposure mapping, so Y_i(a_i) alone is insufficient.
