lessons.title: Backdoor Adjustment & Confounding Control
lessons.interviewAnswer: Backdoor adjustment identifies a treatment effect by conditioning on pretreatment variables that block every path entering treatment, while avoiding treatment descendants. If Z is valid, consistency, conditional exchangeability and positivity imply the g-formula E[Y(a)]=E_Z E[Y|A=a,Z]. I choose Z from a reviewed causal DAG rather than p-values or feature importance, prefer a minimal well-measured set with adequate overlap, and define the target population. I can estimate by outcome-regression standardization, stratification, matching, inverse weighting or doubly robust methods; estimator flexibility addresses functional form, not unmeasured confounding. I inspect overlap, balance, model residuals, influential observations and sensitivity to alternative defensible sets. For total effects I do not adjust mediators or post-treatment colliders. When no measured set closes all backdoor paths, I state nonidentification or use another design instead of calling a predictive regression causal.
keyPoints: A valid adjustment set is determined by the causal graph and target effect, not association screening.
The adjustment formula averages treatment-specific conditional outcomes over one declared target covariate distribution.
Outcome regression, weighting and matching estimate the same identified contrast through different modeling choices.
Positivity and measurement quality can favor one valid set over another even when both block confounding.
No estimator or balance table detects confounding by variables absent from the identification set.
lessons.why: The phrase 'control for confounders' hides three distinct tasks: decide which causal paths must be blocked, identify the observed-data functional, and estimate it without excessive model bias or variance. Data-driven covariate selection can retain colliders, drop weakly predictive but important treatment causes, or include post-treatment variables. A correct set can still fail through near-nonoverlap or poor measurement. Conversely, a long regression may look robust while targeting an unclear conditional coefficient rather than a marginal effect. Backdoor adjustment becomes trustworthy when the graph, population averaging, treatment timing and diagnostics are explicit.
lessons.intuition: Within each value of baseline severity, compare treated and untreated units who are exchangeable under the assumed graph. Then average those within-stratum contrasts using the target population's severity distribution. The first step removes the common-cause imbalance; the second returns from stratum-specific comparisons to the population effect of interest.
lessons.deepDive: Backdoor adjustment combines graphical identification with standardization over a target population. It separates adjustment-set validity from estimator choice, emphasizes positivity and scale, and supports outcome, treatment and doubly robust estimators. Reliable applications use temporal feature lineage, overlap and balance diagnostics, cross-fitting for flexible nuisances, and explicit sensitivity to latent confounding.
lessons.workedExample: If baseline risk Z is low for 60% and high for 40%, with treated-minus-control risks -0.02 and -0.10 within those strata, the standardized ATE is 0.6(-0.02)+0.4(-0.10)=-0.052 for that target population.

commonMistakes.misconception: A variable must strongly predict outcome to be a confounder.
commonMistakes.correction: Confounding follows common-cause structure; weak marginal prediction does not make a required path disappear.

commonMistakes.misconception: Balanced measured covariates prove exchangeability.
commonMistakes.correction: Balance checks the implemented design for measured variables, not latent common causes or graph correctness.

commonMistakes.misconception: The treatment coefficient in an adjusted logistic regression is the marginal ATE.
commonMistakes.correction: It is a conditional log-odds parameter; standardize predictions to obtain marginal risk contrasts.

commonMistakes.misconception: Doubly robust means valid if both nuisance models are wrong.
commonMistakes.correction: It protects against one correctly specified nuisance under assumptions, not arbitrary joint misspecification or unmeasured confounding.

followUps.question: What makes an adjustment set minimal?
followUps.answer: It blocks all backdoor paths and no proper subset does, relative to the assumed graph and target effect.

followUps.question: Why can extreme propensity weights be a design warning?
followUps.answer: They show some target units have little probability of the observed comparison treatment, making inference extrapolative and unstable.

followUps.question: When do standardization and IPW target different effects?
followUps.answer: When they average over different populations or use trimming, stabilization or ATT/overlap weights; define weights and averaging explicitly.

lessons.production: Version the causal DAG, effect, pretreatment adjustment set, target population, treatment and outcome definitions, source snapshot, nuisance learners, folds and weighting rules. Assert feature availability before treatment. Monitor propensity overlap, balance, effective sample size, extreme weights, unsupported prediction regions and target-population drift. Compare standardization, weighting and augmented estimates, attach cluster-aware uncertainty and sensitivity to unmeasured confounding, and declare every trim or restriction as an estimand change. Preserve exploration or a safe prior policy when deployment destroys overlap.
lessons.math: If Z blocks all backdoor paths from A to Y and contains no descendants of A, then p(y|do(a))=sum_z p(y|a,z)p(z). Thus ATE=sum_z [E(Y|A=1,z)-E(Y|A=0,z)]p(z), or the corresponding integral. Standardization plugs in an outcome model m(a,z). IPW uses e(z)=P(A=1|Z): E[AY/e(Z)-(1-A)Y/(1-e(Z))]. An augmented score combines m and e and is consistent if either nuisance model is correct under regularity and identification assumptions; cross-fitting reduces own-observation overfit bias.
lessons.code:
ps=LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000).fit(z[:,None],a).predict_proba(z[:,None])[:,1]
ipw=np.mean(a*y/ps-(1-a)*y/(1-ps)); effective=(np.sum(a/ps+(1-a)/(1-ps))**2)/np.sum((a/ps+(1-a)/(1-ps))**2)

lab.goal: Estimate a known confounded treatment effect with g-computation and inverse weighting and verify the naive contrast remains biased.
lab.buildIt:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression,LogisticRegression
rng=np.random.default_rng(21); n=15000; z=rng.normal(size=n); e=1/(1+np.exp(-1.2*z)); a=rng.binomial(1,e); tau=1.5; y=2+2*z+tau*a+.5*a*z+rng.normal(size=n)
naive=y[a==1].mean()-y[a==0].mean(); outcome=LinearRegression().fit(np.c_[a,z,a*z],y); x1=np.c_[np.ones(n),z,z]; x0=np.c_[np.zeros(n),z,np.zeros(n)]; gcomp=np.mean(outcome.predict(x1)-outcome.predict(x0))
lab.verifyIt:
assert abs(gcomp-tau)<.05
assert abs(ipw-tau)<.1
assert abs(naive-tau)>.8
assert np.all((ps>0)&(ps<1))
assert effective>n*.3
assert abs(np.mean(.5*z))<.02
lab.shipIt: Persist the graph, target distribution and nuisance artifacts; gate on overlap, balance and weight stability; and publish sensitivity alongside the causal estimate.

lessons.description: Backdoor adjustment turns a causal DAG into an observed-data estimand. This chapter derives the adjustment formula from consistency, conditional exchangeability and positivity; distinguishes graphical validity from statistical estimation; and explains minimal versus sufficient sets, total versus direct effects, precision variables, instruments, proxies and M-bias. It develops stratification, regression standardization, inverse-probability weighting, matching and augmented doubly robust estimation as alternative implementations of the same target contrast. It covers nonlinearity, interactions, marginal versus conditional scales, target-population weighting, practical positivity, measurement error, flexible nuisance models and cross-fitting. Worked examples standardize stratum-specific risks and show why a post-treatment control changes the estimand. The lab simulates measured confounding, computes regression g-computation and inverse weighting, and verifies recovery of the known ATE while the naive difference is biased. Production guidance versions the DAG and adjustment set, asserts pretreatment availability, monitors overlap and weight tails, preserves target-population definitions and reports sensitivity to unmeasured confounding. Every restriction or trimming rule is reported as a population change rather than hidden as numerical cleanup.
learningObjectives: Derive the backdoor adjustment formula for a graph-validated covariate set.
Estimate marginal effects with standardization, weighting and doubly robust scores.
Diagnose adjustment-set, positivity, functional-form and target-population failures.
Separate robustness to nuisance estimation from sensitivity to unmeasured confounding.

deepSections.title: Choose adjustment variables from paths and timing
deepSections.body: Begin with the total or direct effect and a DAG containing measured and latent nodes. For total effects, find noncausal paths that enter treatment and select pretreatment nondescendants that block them. A minimal set avoids unnecessary conditioning; another sufficient set may improve measurement or overlap. Causes of outcome that do not affect treatment can improve precision. Pure instruments predict treatment but do not close confounding paths and can worsen variance or amplify residual confounding. Proxies may only partially control a latent cause. Mediators and treatment-induced confounders do not belong in ordinary total-effect backdoor adjustment. Selection filters behave like conditioning variables. Do not choose Z by stepwise significance, lasso outcome prediction or balance alone. Record why every included node blocks a named path and why every tempting post-treatment field is excluded.

deepSections.title: Standardize conditional outcomes to one population
deepSections.body: Under the assumptions, estimate m(a,z)=E[Y|A=a,Z=z], predict each target unit twice—once setting A=1 and once A=0 while keeping baseline Z—and average the paired predictions. Their average difference estimates a marginal ATE for the covariate distribution used in averaging. Averaging only treated units targets ATT; an external covariate distribution targets transport. Include nonlinearities and treatment-covariate interactions needed for the conditional response rather than interpreting one regression coefficient automatically as ATE. For binary outcomes, standardization yields marginal risks, risk differences or ratios even when the outcome model uses a nonlinear link. Restrict predictions to supported treatment-covariate combinations. Bootstrap or influence-function inference must repeat nuisance fitting and respect clusters or time.

deepSections.title: Treatment models reweight observed outcomes
deepSections.body: The propensity score e(Z) is a balancing score under conditional exchangeability. Inverse probability weights create a pseudo-population in which treatment is independent of measured Z for the targeted weighting scheme. ATE weights are A/e+(1-A)/(1-e); ATT, overlap and stabilized weights target different populations. Extreme scores produce unstable weights and reveal weak support, not merely a numerical nuisance. Trimming changes the target population and must be declared. Matching seeks comparable treated and controls, with replacement, calipers and distance choices affecting estimand and uncertainty. Balance after weighting or matching should be assessed on covariate distributions and important nonlinear terms, not by propensity prediction accuracy. Outcome information should not guide repeated design choices without accounting for selection.

deepSections.title: Orthogonal scores reduce nuisance-model fragility
deepSections.body: Augmented IPW combines outcome predictions with weighted residual corrections. If either the propensity or outcome nuisance model is consistently estimated, the ATE estimator can remain consistent under the causal assumptions; this is double robustness, not immunity to two bad models or unmeasured confounding. Flexible machine learning can estimate nuisances, but naive reuse of the same observations may overfit residuals and bias the target. Cross-fitting trains nuisances on other folds and evaluates scores on held-out rows. Neyman-orthogonal scores reduce first-order sensitivity to nuisance error under rate and regularity conditions. Report nuisance performance, overlap and score tails, but do not select the causal estimate solely because one method gives a desired result. Compare standardization, weighting and augmented estimates as diagnostics tied to the same estimand.

deepSections.title: Diagnostics test implementation, not the graph's truth
deepSections.body: Inspect propensity overlap by treatment, effective sample size, maximum and percentile weights, covariate balance, outcome residuals and influential rows. Evaluate missingness and measurement timing in Z; a covariate captured after treatment is invalid even if labeled baseline in a table. Negative controls and alternative valid sets can reveal inconsistencies under their own assumptions. Quantitative sensitivity analysis asks how strong unmeasured confounding must be to alter conclusions. E-values, bias formulas or Rosenbaum-style analyses answer different models and should be interpreted specifically. Version source snapshots, treatment mapping, adjustment set, nuisance learners, folds, target weights and estimand. When policy changes reduce overlap, restrict the population, restore exploration or redesign the study rather than extrapolating silently.

workedExamples.title: Discrete standardization
workedExamples.body: If baseline risk Z is low for 60% and high for 40%, with treated-minus-control risks -0.02 and -0.10 within those strata, the standardized ATE is 0.6(-0.02)+0.4(-0.10)=-0.052 for that target population.

workedExamples.title: A post-treatment control
workedExamples.body: Treatment changes adherence, which changes outcome. Adding adherence to a regression blocks part of the total effect and may open paths through unmeasured adherence-outcome causes. The coefficient no longer estimates the original total effect.

exercises.prompt: Why average standardized predictions over the same Z distribution for both treatments?
exercises.solution: It creates comparable intervention worlds for one target population rather than comparing differently composed groups.

exercises.prompt: What does trimming propensity scores change?
exercises.solution: It may improve stability but excludes units and therefore changes the target population and estimand.

exercises.prompt: Can outcome-model accuracy validate the backdoor set?
exercises.solution: No. It assesses conditional prediction, while adjustment validity depends on causal paths and unmeasured confounding assumptions.

lessons.title: Propensity Scores, Matching & Weighting
lessons.interviewAnswer: The propensity score e(X)=P(A=1|X) is the probability of treatment given a valid pretreatment adjustment set. Under conditional exchangeability, conditioning on the true score balances the distribution of X between treatment groups, reducing a multivariate design problem to a scalar balancing score. It does not balance unmeasured confounders and its purpose is causal design, not treatment prediction accuracy. I choose X from a DAG, estimate scores without post-treatment variables, inspect common support, then match, stratify or weight for an explicitly chosen estimand. ATE, ATT, overlap and stabilized weights are different. I check standardized mean differences and distributions after design, effective sample size and extreme weights; iterate the design without outcome-driven cherry-picking. Outcome analysis respects matching or weights and uncertainty. Poor overlap leads to population restriction or redesign, not silent clipping, and sensitivity analysis addresses residual unmeasured confounding.
keyPoints: The propensity score balances measured pretreatment covariates under its causal assumptions; it is not a causal effect.
Covariate choice follows confounding structure, while treatment-model flexibility follows balance and overlap diagnostics.
Matching, subclassification, ATE, ATT and overlap weighting target different populations and require matching inference.
Extreme scores expose weak support; trimming, calipers and clipping change either the population or the estimator.
Good balance on measured X cannot certify exchangeability with respect to unmeasured causes.
lessons.why: Observed treatment groups often differ across many baseline variables. Direct regression can hide extrapolation and functional-form dependence. Propensity designs make the treatment-assignment comparison visible: do treated and control units exist at similar covariate values, and what target population can their overlap support? But a high-AUC treatment model can worsen weights, and a perfectly balanced score can still omit the true common cause. Matching discards or reuses units according to a design, while weighting can concentrate the estimate on a few observations. The method is credible only when estimand, covariates, support, balance, uncertainty and sensitivity are declared together.
lessons.intuition: Two people with the same propensity score can have different covariates, but under the true score their treatment assignment has the same probability and the covariate distribution balances within score levels. Matching or weighting uses this property to construct treated and control groups that resemble the target population on measured baseline information. It is a design for comparability, not a guarantee of randomization.
lessons.deepDive: Propensity scores connect conditional exchangeability to balancing designs. Their use requires graph-based covariates, target-specific weights, overlap-aware estimation and post-design balance checks. Flexible estimation, cross-fitting and augmented outcomes can reduce nuisance error but do not replace measured-confounding or positivity assumptions.
lessons.workedExample: A treated unit with e=0.2 receives ATE weight 1/0.2=5 but ATT weight 1. A control with e=0.2 receives ATE weight 1/0.8=1.25 and ATT weight 0.2/0.8=0.25. The resulting pseudo-populations target different covariate distributions.

commonMistakes.misconception: A correctly predicted treatment assignment proves a good propensity model.
commonMistakes.correction: The design goal is measured covariate balance with overlap, not maximum classification accuracy.

commonMistakes.misconception: Matching on the score automatically balances all observed variables in the sample.
commonMistakes.correction: The theorem concerns the true score; finite-sample estimated designs require direct covariate balance checks.

commonMistakes.misconception: Clipping weights leaves the ATE unchanged.
commonMistakes.correction: It changes contributions and introduces an approximation; trimming explicitly changes the target population.

commonMistakes.misconception: Good propensity balance removes all confounding.
commonMistakes.correction: It addresses measured covariates only and depends on causal set, consistency and positivity assumptions.

followUps.question: Why not include post-treatment variables in the propensity model?
followUps.answer: They can mediate treatment or act as colliders, changing or biasing the total-effect estimand.

followUps.question: What does overlap weighting estimate?
followUps.answer: An effect in a population emphasizing units whose propensity is near one half, where treatment assignment has the most equipoise.

followUps.question: How do you evaluate propensity model quality?
followUps.answer: Primarily through support, weighted or matched balance, effective sample size and influence for the chosen estimand, not predictive AUC alone.

lessons.production: Version the reviewed pretreatment covariate set, treatment definition, score model, folds, matching or weight formula, calipers, replacement, trims and target estimand. Persist score distributions, balance tables, unmatched counts, effective sample size and weight quantiles. Assert temporal availability and group independence. Use outcome inference that respects design construction, attach augmented or sensitivity analyses and monitor assignment-policy drift. Any clipping, exclusion or overlap restriction creates a documented estimand change, and a loss of support triggers new data or policy design rather than silent extrapolation.
lessons.math: e(X)=P(A=1|X). If Y(a) is independent of A given X, then Y(a) is independent of A given e(X) under the propensity-score result. ATE weights are A/e+(1-A)/(1-e); ATT weights are A+(1-A)e/(1-e); overlap weights are A(1-e)+(1-A)e and target units with equipoise. Stabilized ATE weights multiply numerators by marginal treatment probabilities. Effective sample size is (sum w)^2/sum w^2. A standardized mean difference compares weighted covariate means divided by a declared pooled or reference standard deviation and should be checked beyond means for important variables.
lessons.code: weighted_effect=weighted_mean(y,w,a==1)-weighted_mean(y,w,a==0); naive=y[a==1].mean()-y[a==0].mean(); effective=w.sum()**2/np.sum(w**2); overlap=np.mean((ps>.05)&(ps<.95))

lab.goal: Estimate propensity scores, construct ATE weights, and verify improved measured balance and treatment-effect recovery.
lab.buildIt:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
rng=np.random.default_rng(31); n=14000; x=rng.normal(size=(n,2)); logits=1.1*x[:,0]-.8*x[:,1]; true_ps=1/(1+np.exp(-logits)); a=rng.binomial(1,true_ps); tau=2.; y=tau*a+2*x[:,0]-x[:,1]+rng.normal(size=n)
ps=LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000).fit(x,a).predict_proba(x)[:,1]; w=a/ps+(1-a)/(1-ps)
def weighted_mean(v,weight,mask): return np.sum(weight[mask]*v[mask])/np.sum(weight[mask])
def smd(v,weight):
    m1=weighted_mean(v,weight,a==1); m0=weighted_mean(v,weight,a==0); pooled=np.sqrt((np.var(v[a==1])+np.var(v[a==0]))/2); return (m1-m0)/pooled
before=np.array([smd(x[:,j],np.ones(n)) for j in range(2)]); after=np.array([smd(x[:,j],w) for j in range(2)])
lab.verifyIt:
assert np.max(np.abs(after))<.04
assert np.max(np.abs(before))>.5
assert abs(weighted_effect-tau)<.08
assert abs(naive-tau)>.8
assert effective>n*.35 and overlap>.9
assert np.all((ps>0)&(ps<1))

lessons.description: Propensity scores support observational-study design by balancing measured pretreatment covariates across treatment groups. This chapter derives the balancing-score result, separates causal covariate selection from statistical score estimation, and explains why treatment-prediction accuracy is not the objective. It compares nearest-neighbor, caliper, exact and full matching; subclassification; inverse-probability, stabilized, ATT and overlap weighting; and augmented doubly robust estimators. It covers common support, extreme weights, effective sample size, replacement, matching ratios, trimming, clipping, balance metrics, cross-fitting and variance estimation. Worked examples derive ATE and ATT weights and show a high treatment-model AUC signaling deterministic assignment rather than a successful design. The lab simulates measured confounding, estimates propensity scores, verifies inverse weighting reduces standardized imbalance and recovers the known effect. Production guidance versions treatment assignment, covariates, score model, target weights and exclusions, monitors overlap and weight tails, and pairs measured-balance evidence with sensitivity to unmeasured confounding. Design quality is judged on the covariates and population the effect actually requires.
learningObjectives: Derive the propensity score's balancing role under conditional exchangeability.
Choose matching, stratification or target-specific weights for a declared population estimand.
Evaluate common support, balance, weight influence and effective sample size after design.
Combine propensity designs with outcome estimation, uncertainty and unmeasured-confounding sensitivity.

deepSections.title: The score summarizes measured assignment probability
deepSections.body: The true propensity score is a balancing score: within its levels, measured X has the same distribution in treated and controls. If treatment is conditionally exchangeable given X, it remains so given the score. This result motivates design but does not make an estimated score magical. Include common causes and strong outcome predictors from a pretreatment causal set; exclude descendants of treatment and avoid adding instruments solely to improve treatment prediction. A variable weakly related to treatment can still matter for outcome precision. Treatment-model ROC AUC is not a success metric: perfect discrimination often means no overlap and no credible comparison. Fit flexible interactions or nonlinearities when balance requires them. Blinding outcome analysis during design reduces the temptation to choose a specification that yields a preferred effect.

deepSections.title: Matching constructs a supported comparison sample
deepSections.body: Nearest-neighbor matching pairs units close in propensity or covariate distance. A caliper rejects poor matches, improving comparability while changing which units are represented. Matching with replacement lets a strong control serve multiple treated units and requires reused-unit dependence in uncertainty; without replacement, order and scarcity matter. One-to-many matching trades bias and precision. Exact or coarsened matching preserves critical covariates before score distance. Full matching and subclassification retain more units with group weights. Always inspect raw covariates after matching, because close scores do not guarantee every important distribution is balanced in finite samples or under model misspecification. Report unmatched units, matching ratio, replacement, distance, caliper and target estimand. Analyze outcomes using the matched structure rather than treating the constructed sample as ordinary independent rows.

deepSections.title: Weight formulas define the target population
deepSections.body: ATE weighting expands treated and controls to the full covariate distribution, assigning large weights to treated units with low e and controls with high e. ATT keeps treated weight one and reweights controls toward treated covariates. ATC reverses the target. Overlap weights emphasize units with treatment equipoise and are bounded, yielding a different and often more supported population. Stabilization can reduce variance while preserving the estimand when defined correctly. Normalization affects finite-sample form. Truncating weights limits influence but introduces bias; trimming score regions removes target units. Neither is mere numerical hygiene. Report the weighted covariate distribution, effective sample size and maximum influence. If stakeholders want an effect for unsupported units, additional data or assumptions are required.

deepSections.title: Judge the design by balance and support, not fit
deepSections.body: Plot score distributions by treatment and identify regions with only one group. Compute standardized mean differences before and after design for covariates, nonlinear transforms and interactions that matter. Inspect variance ratios, quantiles and empirical distributions, not only means. Conventional thresholds such as absolute SMD below 0.1 are heuristics, not proof. Balance should use design weights and the chosen target standardization. Effective sample size reveals whether a large nominal sample collapses under variable weights. Check subgroup support and repeated entities. Iterate treatment-model specification when measured imbalance remains, while documenting the search. Do not test outcome differences during each iteration and then present nominal inference as if design were fixed. After balance, outcome regression can improve precision and augmented estimation can protect against one nuisance misspecification.

deepSections.title: Design diagnostics cannot see latent confounding
deepSections.body: Estimate outcomes with weighted means, weighted regression, matched-set analysis or augmented scores consistent with the design. Standard errors must reflect estimated weights, matching reuse, clusters and cross-fitting; naive weighted least-squares errors are often insufficient. Bootstrap the full design when appropriate, recognizing that some matching algorithms are nonsmooth. Negative controls can reveal residual bias under specific assumptions. Sensitivity methods quantify how an unmeasured factor's treatment and outcome associations could change the conclusion. Report estimates across reasonable calipers, trimming rules and valid covariate sets as design sensitivity, without selecting the favorite. Preserve propensity and balance reports with the causal result. When assignment policy changes, scores and target population must be re-estimated and the identification argument revisited.

workedExamples.title: ATE versus ATT weights
workedExamples.body: A treated unit with e=0.2 receives ATE weight 1/0.2=5 but ATT weight 1. A control with e=0.2 receives ATE weight 1/0.8=1.25 and ATT weight 0.2/0.8=0.25. The resulting pseudo-populations target different covariate distributions.

workedExamples.title: High AUC is a warning
workedExamples.body: If treatment is almost deterministic from eligibility score, the propensity model can achieve near-perfect AUC. That means treated and controls barely overlap, so causal comparison relies on extrapolation or enormous weights rather than a successful design.

exercises.prompt: What population do ATT weights represent?
exercises.solution: The observed treated population; controls are reweighted to resemble its baseline covariate distribution.

exercises.prompt: Why inspect effective sample size?
exercises.solution: Highly variable weights can make a large dataset behave like a much smaller comparison and yield unstable inference.

exercises.prompt: What should happen when a covariate stratum contains no controls?
exercises.solution: The ATE there is unsupported by observed comparison; restrict the estimand, collect data or adopt stronger transparent assumptions rather than rely on infinite weights.

lessons.title: Difference-in-Differences
lessons.interviewAnswer: Difference-in-differences estimates a treatment effect by comparing the treated group's before-after change with the control group's change. The key identifying assumption is parallel trends in untreated potential outcomes for the target groups, possibly conditional on covariates—not equality of outcome levels. In the canonical two-group, two-period design, DID is (Ybar_T,post-Ybar_T,pre)-(Ybar_C,post-Ybar_C,pre). I define treatment timing, anticipation, comparison group, outcome and estimand, plot raw trends and event time, and use inference clustered at the assignment unit. Pretrend tests can reveal contradictions but low power cannot prove parallel trends. With staggered adoption and heterogeneous dynamic effects, ordinary two-way fixed effects may combine inappropriate already-treated comparisons and nontransparent weights, so I estimate group-time effects using never- or not-yet-treated controls and aggregate explicitly. I also test composition, spillovers and concurrent shocks and report sensitivity to trend violations.
keyPoints: DID identifies change relative to a comparison trend, not a generic treatment coefficient.
Parallel trends concerns untreated potential outcomes and remains an assumption after passing pretrend tests.
Treatment timing, anticipation, composition and spillovers determine valid control observations.
Staggered adoption with heterogeneous effects requires group-time estimands rather than naive two-way fixed effects.
Inference must reflect serial correlation and the number and level of treatment-assignment clusters.
lessons.why: Policies and product launches are rarely randomized, but repeated outcomes can reveal whether treated units change differently from a credible control trend. The design removes permanent level differences and common time shocks, yet it fails when treated units were already on a different trajectory, anticipate treatment, experience another coincident shock or change composition. Modern staggered rollouts add a subtle problem: an already-treated cohort may serve as control for a later cohort even though its own effect evolves. DID is therefore a research design with a counterfactual trend assumption, not a fixed-effects formula. Clear cohort-time effects and diagnostics matter more than a single coefficient.
lessons.intuition: The treated group may start higher than control, so post-treatment levels are not comparable. Its own pre-period gives a baseline, while the control group's change estimates what common forces would have done. Subtracting changes removes both the stable group gap and the shared time shock. The remaining difference is causal only if untreated treated units would have followed the same trend.
lessons.deepDive: DID uses untreated outcome trends to identify counterfactual changes. Canonical identification extends to multiple periods through cohort-time effects, but requires explicit comparison sets and aggregation under heterogeneity. Credible studies diagnose anticipation, composition, spillovers, functional form and cluster-level uncertainty and stress-test deviations from parallel trends.
lessons.workedExample: Treated outcome rises from 10 to 16, while control rises from 8 to 11. The treated change is 6 and control change is 3, so DID is 3. The raw post-period gap of 5 would retain the original group difference.

commonMistakes.misconception: Parallel trends means treated and control outcomes must have equal levels.
commonMistakes.correction: Stable level differences cancel; the required counterfactual condition concerns changes without treatment.

commonMistakes.misconception: Nonsignificant pretrends prove parallel trends.
commonMistakes.correction: They may be underpowered and cannot exclude a treatment-time-specific differential shock.

commonMistakes.misconception: Unit and time fixed effects solve staggered DID automatically.
commonMistakes.correction: Already-treated comparisons and heterogeneous effects can make the coefficient an opaque mixture.

commonMistakes.misconception: Clustering by observation is enough with panel rows.
commonMistakes.correction: Uncertainty must respect serial correlation and the level of treatment assignment or common shocks.

followUps.question: What is the identifying assumption in canonical DID?
followUps.answer: In the absence of treatment, the treated and comparison groups would have experienced the same average outcome change over the studied periods.

followUps.question: Why can already-treated units be bad controls?
followUps.answer: Their outcome changes include evolving treatment effects, contaminating the untreated counterfactual for newly treated cohorts.

followUps.question: What should an event-study plot include?
followUps.answer: Lead and lag estimates, uncertainty, reference period, cohort and observation support, raw trends and the estimator's comparison-group definition.

lessons.production: Version treatment cohorts, adoption and anticipation windows, comparison groups, outcome definitions, sample composition, covariates, estimator and aggregation weights. Preserve raw group trends and cohort-time effects. Cluster at the assignment or shock level and use few-cluster methods when needed. Monitor migration, attrition, spillovers, concurrent interventions and outcome coding. Treat pretrend tests as diagnostics, report sensitivity to plausible trend violations and alternative controls, and never replace transparent group-time evidence with one unexplained fixed-effects coefficient.

lab.goal: Simulate a two-period panel, compute DID from group changes, and verify equivalence with a saturated interaction regression.
lab.buildIt:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
rng=np.random.default_rng(44); units=5000; group=rng.binomial(1,.5,size=units); base=3+2*group+rng.normal(size=units); effect=2.5
y_pre=base+rng.normal(scale=.5,size=units); y_post=base+1.2+effect*group+rng.normal(scale=.5,size=units)
did=(y_post[group==1].mean()-y_pre[group==1].mean())-(y_post[group==0].mean()-y_pre[group==0].mean())
y=np.r_[y_pre,y_post]; g=np.r_[group,group]; post=np.r_[np.zeros(units),np.ones(units)]; X=np.c_[g,post,g*post]; regression=LinearRegression().fit(X,y); interaction=regression.coef_[2]
lab.verifyIt:
assert abs(did-effect)<.04
assert abs(interaction-did)<1e-12 and abs(direct-did)<1e-12
assert abs((post_gap-placebo_pre_gap)-did)<1e-12
assert abs(placebo_pre_gap-2)<.05
assert len(changes)==units

lessons.math: For groups G in {T,C} and periods t in {0,1}, delta_DID=[E(Y|T,1)-E(Y|T,0)]-[E(Y|C,1)-E(Y|C,0)]. Parallel trends requires E[Y_1(0)-Y_0(0)|T]=E[Y_1(0)-Y_0(0)|C]. With staggered timing G=g, target ATT(g,t)=E[Y_t(1)-Y_t(0)|G=g] and compare with units untreated at t under suitable conditional assumptions. Aggregating ATT(g,t) requires declared weights by cohort size, calendar time or event time. Standard errors cluster where shocks and assignment correlate; few clusters need design-specific corrections or randomization inference.

lessons.description: Difference-in-differences identifies causal effects from changes in treated and comparison groups under a parallel-trends counterfactual. This chapter derives the canonical two-by-two estimator, regression representation and event-study contrasts; distinguishes equal levels from parallel untreated trends; and analyzes anticipation, treatment reversals, time-varying composition, spillovers and concurrent shocks. It explains why visual pretrends and placebo leads are diagnostics rather than proof, how covariate conditioning changes the assumption, and why scale choice matters. For staggered adoption, it develops cohort-time average treatment effects and explains how ordinary two-way fixed effects can use already-treated controls and combine heterogeneous effects with opaque weights. Worked examples compute a manual DID and expose a differential pretrend. The lab simulates panel outcomes, recovers the known effect by differencing and verifies equivalence with an interaction regression. Production guidance versions cohorts and event times, clusters inference at assignment level, monitors composition and spillovers, reports group-time estimates and aggregates only with decision-relevant weights.
learningObjectives: Derive the two-group, two-period DID estimator and its parallel-trends identification condition.
Diagnose anticipation, differential trends, composition, spillovers and concurrent-shock threats.
Estimate and aggregate staggered cohort-time effects without invalid already-treated controls.
Choose event-time displays, comparison groups and cluster-aware inference for the assignment design.

deepSections.title: The two-by-two contrast removes two nuisance components
deepSections.body: Suppose treated and control groups differ by a stable level and both face a common time shock. The treated before-after change contains the common shock plus treatment; the control change contains the common shock. Their difference removes both the group level and time shock. In a saturated regression with group, post and group-by-post indicators, the interaction equals the two-by-two DID. Identification requires that the treated group's untreated potential outcome would have changed like the control group's, not that their baseline levels match. Define treatment at the assignment unit, align time zero and ensure outcome measurement is comparable. Repeated cross sections can identify population changes only when group composition is stable or appropriately modeled; panels permit individual differencing but attrition can select the sample. Cluster treatment and inference at the actual assignment level.

deepSections.title: Parallel trends is a counterfactual assumption
deepSections.body: Multiple pretreatment periods allow raw and covariate-adjusted trend plots, event-study leads and placebo intervention dates. Clear differential pretrends undermine the design. A nonsignificant lead does not prove validity because tests can be underpowered, and conditioning selection on passing a pretest can distort inference. Even perfectly parallel history cannot rule out a treatment-time-specific shock. Use institutional knowledge to explain why controls share outcome determinants but are not exposed to treatment or spillovers. Consider alternative controls, outcome transformations, group-specific trends chosen before outcomes and sensitivity bounds for deviations. Conditional parallel trends permits trends to align within baseline covariates, requiring overlap and careful standardization. Avoid controlling for variables affected by treatment. Check whether units anticipate and change behavior before the official date; redefine event time or estimand where needed.

deepSections.title: Dynamic effects require explicit reference and support
deepSections.body: An event study indexes time relative to adoption and estimates leads and lags against an omitted pre-period. Plot estimates with uncertainty, number of contributing cohorts and calendar support. Far leads or lags may rely on few cohorts and changing composition. Leads diagnose anticipation or trend differences under their own assumptions; lags describe effect dynamics but can mix cohorts if estimated naively. The reference period choice changes coefficients but not underlying contrasts. Do not normalize away meaningful pre-treatment effects or interpret all pre-coefficients jointly from individual p-values. Smooth-looking dynamics can be artifacts of staggered weighting. Report raw group trends alongside regression estimates and separate calendar shocks from event-time exposure.

deepSections.title: Estimate cohort-time effects before aggregation
deepSections.body: With different adoption dates and heterogeneous effects, two-way fixed effects can compare newly treated units with already-treated units whose outcomes contain treatment effects. The coefficient becomes a weighted mixture of two-by-two comparisons and may not represent any policy-relevant average. Modern approaches estimate ATT(g,t) for cohort g at time t using never-treated or not-yet-treated controls, possibly conditional on covariates. Then aggregate by event time, calendar time or cohort with transparent nonnegative weights chosen for the question. Never-treated controls support long-run lags but may differ systematically; not-yet-treated controls require no anticipation and disappear as adoption saturates. Define whether treatment is absorbing, reversible or varying in dose. Report cohort support, control composition and sensitivity to comparison choice.

deepSections.title: Serial correlation and few assignments govern uncertainty
deepSections.body: Outcomes within a state, store or user are correlated over time, and treatment is commonly assigned to clusters. Row-level robust errors treat repeated observations as independent and can be severely anti-conservative. Cluster at the assignment or shock level, considering multiway dependence when relevant. With few treated clusters, conventional cluster asymptotics are fragile; use wild cluster bootstrap, randomization inference from a credible assignment mechanism or carefully justified small-sample methods. Placebo outcomes and unaffected groups test specific falsification implications. Check concurrent policies, migration, sample entry, outcome coding and differential attrition. Pre-specify primary windows and aggregations to limit event-study specification search. Publish the full cohort-time table and counts so one headline effect can be audited.

workedExamples.title: Manual DID
workedExamples.body: Treated outcome rises from 10 to 16, while control rises from 8 to 11. The treated change is 6 and control change is 3, so DID is 3. The raw post-period gap of 5 would retain the original group difference.

workedExamples.title: Differential trend threat
workedExamples.body: Treated stores were already growing three points faster per month before a promotion, and that difference would have continued. A post-launch DID attributes the continuing trend to promotion unless the counterfactual model addresses it credibly.

exercises.prompt: Treated changes by 7 and control by 4. What is DID?
exercises.solution: Three outcome units, under the parallel untreated-trends and other design assumptions.

exercises.prompt: Why is a pretrend test not a proof?
exercises.solution: It can miss meaningful violations and cannot test the unobserved post-treatment counterfactual trend.

exercises.prompt: How should staggered effects be summarized?
exercises.solution: Estimate valid cohort-time effects first, then aggregate with transparent weights matching event-time, cohort or calendar-time questions.

lessons.title: Instrumental Variables
lessons.interviewAnswer: An instrumental variable Z changes treatment A, is as-if independent of potential outcomes, and affects outcome Y only through A, with monotonicity or an appropriate structural model for interpretation. For a binary instrument and treatment, the Wald ratio [E(Y|Z=1)-E(Y|Z=0)]/[E(A|Z=1)-E(A|Z=0)] identifies the local average treatment effect for compliers under relevance, independence, exclusion and monotonicity. It is not automatically the population ATE. In linear settings, two-stage least squares projects treatment onto instruments and uses only that exogenous variation. I justify each assumption institutionally, report first-stage strength and reduced form, use weak-instrument-robust inference, cluster at assignment level, and inspect whether the instrument has direct pathways or changes sample composition. More instruments or strong treatment prediction do not repair invalid exclusion. I preserve assignment-to-instrument and treatment-receipt definitions and report intention-to-treat alongside LATE.
keyPoints: Relevance is empirically checkable; independence and exclusion are primarily design assumptions.
The Wald estimand is a ratio of reduced-form outcome and first-stage treatment effects.
Under monotonicity, binary IV identifies LATE for compliers, whose population depends on the instrument.
Weak instruments create biased, nonnormal estimates and require robust inference rather than a mechanical F threshold alone.
Two-stage prediction is not ordinary plug-in regression; uncertainty and controls must follow the IV design.
lessons.why: Unmeasured confounding can make backdoor adjustment impossible. A lottery, eligibility rule or randomized encouragement may shift treatment while remaining unrelated to latent outcome risk, providing a source of exogenous variation. The price is a narrower and assumption-heavy estimand. An instrument can be relevant yet invalid because it changes outcomes directly, alters another service or selects who is observed. A weak instrument can amplify noise dramatically. IV analysis is credible when the source of variation and compliance behavior are understood, the reduced form is visible, and the local population is described—not when an available column merely passes a first-stage significance test.
lessons.intuition: Use an encouragement that nudges some people into treatment but does not otherwise affect the outcome. Compare how encouragement changes average outcome and divide by how much it changes treatment uptake. The ratio scales the assignment effect to the treatment change among people whose treatment responds to the encouragement. It says nothing directly about always-takers or never-takers' treatment effects.
lessons.deepDive: IV identification uses exogenous treatment variation to bypass latent treatment-outcome confounding. Binary LATE logic clarifies compliance types and locality; 2SLS extends projection-based estimation. Robust work prioritizes institutional exclusion arguments, first-stage diagnostics, weak-IV inference, assignment-level clustering and transparent reduced forms.
lessons.workedExample: An encouragement raises treatment uptake from 30% to 50%, a 0.20 first stage, and lowers outcome risk from 12% to 10%, a -0.02 reduced form. Wald LATE is -0.02/0.20=-0.10, a ten-point risk reduction for compliers under the assumptions.

commonMistakes.misconception: Any strong predictor of treatment is a valid instrument.
commonMistakes.correction: It must also be as-if independent and affect outcome only through treatment under a defensible causal design.

commonMistakes.misconception: IV always estimates the population ATE.
commonMistakes.correction: Binary encouragement designs typically identify LATE for instrument-specific compliers under monotonicity.

commonMistakes.misconception: Run two OLS regressions and use the second OLS standard error.
commonMistakes.correction: The fitted treatment is estimated; use an IV procedure with design- and cluster-appropriate inference.

commonMistakes.misconception: A nonsignificant overidentification test proves exclusion.
commonMistakes.correction: It can have low power and tests joint consistency, not the validity of every instrument.

followUps.question: What does monotonicity exclude?
followUps.answer: Units whose treatment moves opposite the instrument's encouraging direction, known as defiers in the binary compliance framework.

followUps.question: Why report the reduced form?
followUps.answer: It is the direct assignment or encouragement effect on outcome and makes the numerator, scale and design evidence transparent.

followUps.question: What is a weak instrument?
followUps.answer: One that provides little conditional variation in treatment, making the causal ratio unstable and conventional inference unreliable.

lessons.production: Version instrument assignment, treatment receipt and versions, eligibility, time zero, covariates, exclusions and outcome horizon. Preserve assignment flow, uptake, first-stage strength, reduced form, missingness and cluster identifiers. Use IV-native weak-instrument-robust and cluster-aware inference. Audit direct pathways, co-interventions, manipulation, spillovers and attrition. Report the complier population and avoid transporting LATE to unsupported units. Keep intention-to-treat results and prior policy available when uptake or the instrument mechanism changes.
lessons.math: With binary Z and A, first stage pi=E[A|Z=1]-E[A|Z=0], reduced form rho=E[Y|Z=1]-E[Y|Z=0], and Wald LATE=rho/pi when pi is nonzero and assumptions hold. Compliance types are compliers A(1)>A(0), always-takers, never-takers and defiers; monotonicity excludes defiers. In linear 2SLS, first project A on Z and exogenous X, then estimate Y on projected A and X using an IV covariance formula and IV-appropriate standard errors. Weak first stages make ratio distributions unstable. Overidentification restrictions can reject a set of instruments but cannot prove all exclusions valid.

lab.goal: Simulate an endogenous treatment with a valid instrument, show OLS confounding, and recover the structural effect using two-stage least squares.
lab.buildIt:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
rng=np.random.default_rng(55); n=30000; z=rng.normal(size=n); u=rng.normal(size=n); a=1.4*z+1.5*u+rng.normal(size=n); beta=2.; y=beta*a+3*u+rng.normal(size=n)
ols=LinearRegression().fit(a[:,None],y).coef_[0]; first=LinearRegression().fit(z[:,None],a); ahat=first.predict(z[:,None]); stage2=LinearRegression().fit(ahat[:,None],y).coef_[0]
wald=np.cov(z,y,ddof=0)[0,1]/np.cov(z,a,ddof=0)[0,1]
lab.verifyIt:
assert abs(stage2-beta)<.03
assert abs(wald-beta)<.03 and abs(ratio-beta)<.03
assert abs(ols-beta)>.7
assert abs(stage2-ratio)<1e-12
assert first_coef>1.35 and first_r2>.25

lessons.description: Instrumental variables identify causal effects from treatment variation generated by an external assignment or encouragement. This chapter develops relevance, as-if independence, exclusion, monotonicity and stable treatment definitions; classifies compliance types; derives the binary Wald estimator and its local average treatment-effect interpretation; and separates first stage, reduced form, intention-to-treat and treatment-on-complier effects. It explains two-stage least squares, covariate adjustment, clustered designs, weak instruments, many instruments, overidentification tests and heterogeneous local effects. It also analyzes common failures such as direct instrument pathways, differential attrition, treatment versions and conditioning on post-instrument variables. Worked examples calculate a Wald effect and show why two instruments can target different complier populations. The lab simulates unmeasured confounding, verifies ordinary regression bias, and recovers the known structural effect with manual two-stage least squares. Production guidance versions assignment and receipt, reports first-stage and reduced-form evidence, uses weak-IV-robust uncertainty and keeps causal claims local to the instrument-induced population. Institutional evidence for exclusion remains central even when every numerical diagnostic looks strong.
learningObjectives: State and defend IV relevance, independence, exclusion and monotonicity assumptions.
Derive the Wald ratio, compliance-type LATE and linear 2SLS estimator.
Diagnose weak instruments, direct pathways, attrition, clustering and local-population limits.
Report first stage, reduced form, uncertainty and transport separately from the causal ratio.

deepSections.title: An instrument needs a causal design, not just correlation
deepSections.body: Relevance requires Z to shift A for some units. Independence says Z is as-if assigned independently of potential outcomes or latent causes, possibly conditional on baseline covariates. Exclusion says Z affects Y only through the treatment pathway represented by A. A physician preference instrument may change other care, violating exclusion; distance to a hospital may affect outcomes through access; eligibility thresholds may change multiple benefits. Monotonicity assumes changing Z in the encouraging direction does not make anyone move treatment oppositely. Treatment and instrument versions must be consistent, and interference may arise when encouragement changes capacity. Draw a DAG and institutional process, identify assignment timing and audit attrition. Balance of baseline variables supports but cannot prove independence, while exclusion has no universal statistical test.

deepSections.title: Binary IV identifies a local complier effect
deepSections.body: Potential treatments A(1) and A(0) define always-takers, never-takers, compliers and defiers. Under monotonicity there are no defiers. Independence makes Z comparable; exclusion makes outcome assignment operate through received treatment; relevance guarantees some compliers. The reduced-form outcome effect averages the treatment effect among compliers multiplied by their share, and the first stage estimates that share, so their ratio is LATE. Always- and never-takers contribute no instrument-induced treatment contrast. The complier group is latent and defined by the particular instrument; a different encouragement can move a different population and yield another valid LATE under heterogeneity. Describe observed characteristics whose first stages indicate where compliance occurs, but avoid claiming individual compliance type is observed.

deepSections.title: 2SLS isolates projected treatment variation
deepSections.body: In a linear constant-effect model, regress endogenous treatment on instruments and exogenous controls, then use the treatment component predicted by that projection in the outcome equation. The conceptual second stage is not ordinary prediction: standard errors from manually treating fitted A as fixed are wrong. Use an IV estimator that carries both stages and clustering. Include the same exogenous controls consistently in both stages; controls can improve precision or support conditional independence but post-instrument variables can bias. Report the first-stage coefficient and partial strength, reduced-form coefficient and 2SLS result. With heterogeneous effects and multiple instruments, 2SLS can be a weighted average of local effects with interpretation depending on the design. Nonlinear outcomes do not make nonlinear two-stage plug-in methods automatically causal.

deepSections.title: Weak identification changes the shape of inference
deepSections.body: When Z barely moves A, the Wald denominator approaches zero and small reduced-form noise creates enormous estimates. Conventional 2SLS confidence intervals and normal approximations can be badly misleading. First-stage F statistics are diagnostics whose appropriate threshold depends on instruments, heteroskedasticity and target distortion; report partial R-squared and robust strength measures. Use weak-instrument-robust tests and intervals such as Anderson-Rubin-style procedures when warranted. Many weak instruments overfit endogenous treatment and pull 2SLS toward confounded ordinary least squares. Selecting instruments by outcome performance or trying many definitions introduces further bias. Limited-information estimators can help under some settings but cannot repair invalid exclusion. Prefer one institutionally credible instrument to a large set of convenient proxies.

deepSections.title: The reduced form is often the most transparent result
deepSections.body: An encouragement's effect on outcome is an intention-to-treat contrast supported directly by assignment and may be decision-relevant even when treatment receipt is messy. Show treatment uptake by Z, outcome by Z, missingness and sample flow before the IV ratio. Evaluate baseline balance, manipulation, spillovers and whether Z changes other services. Cluster at the randomization, geography, provider or timing unit that generates Z. With multiple instruments, overidentification tests assess mutual restrictions under assumptions but low power or failure to reject is not validation. Sensitivity analysis can parameterize direct effects or monotonicity violations. Transporting LATE needs knowledge of compliers and effect heterogeneity; label it local and avoid extrapolating to mandated universal treatment without additional evidence.

workedExamples.title: Wald calculation
workedExamples.body: An encouragement raises treatment uptake from 30% to 50%, a 0.20 first stage, and lowers outcome risk from 12% to 10%, a -0.02 reduced form. Wald LATE is -0.02/0.20=-0.10, a ten-point risk reduction for compliers under the assumptions.

workedExamples.title: Different instruments, different effects
workedExamples.body: A reminder moves forgetful low-risk patients, while a transport voucher moves geographically isolated high-risk patients. Both can be valid yet identify different complier-average effects.

exercises.prompt: Reduced form is 0.06 and first stage is 0.30. What is Wald LATE?
exercises.solution: 0.06/0.30=0.20 outcome units per treatment among compliers, under the IV assumptions.

exercises.prompt: Why can geographic distance violate exclusion?
exercises.solution: Distance may affect outcome through travel burden, access to other services or environment, not only the target treatment.

exercises.prompt: What happens as the first stage approaches zero?
exercises.solution: The ratio becomes extremely unstable and conventional normal inference can fail; use weak-IV-robust methods or redesign.

lessons.title: Regression Discontinuity
lessons.interviewAnswer: Regression discontinuity uses a treatment rule that changes at a cutoff of a running variable. In a sharp design treatment jumps from zero to one; in a fuzzy design its probability jumps and the outcome discontinuity is divided by the treatment discontinuity for a local complier effect. Identification requires potential-outcome regression functions to be continuous at the cutoff absent treatment, no precise manipulation that sorts units around the threshold, and consistent treatment and outcome measurement. I estimate separate local linear regressions on each side with a justified bandwidth and kernel, use robust bias-corrected inference, and show a binned plot only as visualization rather than estimation. I report density and predetermined-covariate continuity checks, placebo cutoffs and bandwidth sensitivity. I avoid high-order global polynomials. The estimand is local to units near the cutoff and should not be extrapolated to distant scores without new assumptions.
keyPoints: RD identifies a local cutoff effect from a discontinuity, not from the overall running-variable slope.
Continuity of untreated and treated potential-outcome functions is the central identification condition.
Manipulation, sorting, other rules at the cutoff and discrete scores threaten the comparison.
Local polynomial order, bandwidth, kernel and robust bias correction determine estimation and inference.
Sharp RD targets assignment at the cutoff; fuzzy RD is a local IV for treatment compliers near the cutoff.
lessons.why: Eligibility cutoffs in scholarships, credit, medicine and policy can create comparisons that resemble local randomization: units just above and below are similar except for treatment access. The design is visually intuitive but easily overfit. Large bandwidths compare unlike units, tiny bandwidths are noisy, arbitrary bins can manufacture jumps, and high-degree polynomials oscillate at boundaries. People may manipulate a score, or another policy may share the cutoff. A credible RD makes the assignment mechanism and local population explicit, uses boundary-aware estimation and presents falsification and sensitivity evidence alongside the effect.
lessons.intuition: Imagine applicants with scores 69.99 and 70.01 when eligibility begins at 70. Far apart applicants differ substantially, but these two are nearly identical in score. If nobody can precisely sort and no other rule changes at 70, a sudden outcome jump at that point is evidence of the treatment effect for applicants at the margin.
lessons.deepDive: RD is a local identification design built from continuity and a discontinuous assignment rule. Modern analysis uses separate local polynomials, data-driven bandwidths and robust bias-aware inference, with density, covariate and placebo checks. Fuzzy designs inherit local-IV assumptions and all results remain tied to the cutoff population.
lessons.workedExample: The fitted outcome limit is 62 just below a scholarship cutoff and 67 just above. If assignment is sharp and continuity assumptions hold, the local scholarship effect is five outcome units at the cutoff.

commonMistakes.misconception: Include the entire running-variable range for more power.
commonMistakes.correction: Distant units increase functional-form bias; RD estimates local limits with a defensible bandwidth.

commonMistakes.misconception: A smooth density proves no manipulation.
commonMistakes.correction: It is one falsification check with limited power and does not rule out sorting or other cutoff changes.

commonMistakes.misconception: The RD effect applies to everyone above the cutoff.
commonMistakes.correction: It is local to units at the threshold unless additional transport or homogeneity assumptions are justified.

commonMistakes.misconception: Fuzzy RD estimates the effect of eligibility itself.
commonMistakes.correction: The reduced form estimates eligibility; dividing by receipt jump estimates a local treatment effect under IV assumptions.

followUps.question: Why prefer local linear over high-order global polynomial?
followUps.answer: It uses nearby support, behaves better at boundaries and avoids unstable oscillation driven by distant observations.

followUps.question: What does a donut RD do?
followUps.answer: It excludes a neighborhood around the cutoff to assess manipulation or heaping sensitivity, while changing the approximation and support.

followUps.question: What population does fuzzy RD identify?
followUps.answer: Units near the cutoff whose treatment receipt changes because the running variable crosses the threshold.

lessons.production: Version running-variable construction, cutoff, assignment and receipt, treatment versions, outcome horizon, bandwidth, kernel, polynomial order, clustering and exclusions. Preserve binned plots separately from estimation, density and covariate checks, placebo results, first-stage and reduced-form evidence. Monitor score heaping, manipulation, cutoff-rule changes, local sample counts and co-occurring policies. Report bias-robust uncertainty and bandwidth sensitivity, constrain claims to cutoff-supported units and retain prior policy when assignment mechanics change.

visual.title: Regression discontinuity
visual.caption: A discontinuity in treatment assignment at a cutoff can identify a local causal effect when units cannot precisely manipulate the running variable.

lessons.math: Let running variable R and cutoff c. Sharp treatment A=1(R>=c). The sharp RD estimand is tau_RD=lim_{r down to c}E[Y|R=r]-lim_{r up to c}E[Y|R=r], under continuity of E[Y(0)|R=r] and E[Y(1)|R=r] at c. Local linear estimation fits intercept and slope separately within bandwidth h, often with triangular weights K((R-c)/h). Fuzzy RD divides the outcome jump by lim E[A|R=r] right minus left, yielding a cutoff-local complier effect under IV assumptions. Robust bias-corrected intervals address smoothing bias not captured by conventional standard errors.
lessons.code: nearby={h:local_rd(h)[0] for h in (.35,.5,.7)}; left=y[(r<0)&(r>-.05)].mean(); right=y[(r>=0)&(r<.05)].mean(); raw_near_jump=right-left

lab.goal: Simulate a sharp threshold, estimate separate local slopes, and verify discontinuity recovery and bandwidth stability.
lab.buildIt:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
rng=np.random.default_rng(66); n=30000; r=rng.uniform(-2,2,size=n); treatment=(r>=0).astype(float); tau=3.; y=1+1.5*r+.5*r*r+tau*treatment+rng.normal(scale=.8,size=n)
def local_rd(h):
    keep=np.abs(r)<=h; rr=r[keep]; aa=treatment[keep]; yy=y[keep]; X=np.c_[aa,rr,aa*rr]; weights=np.maximum(1-np.abs(rr)/h,0); model=LinearRegression().fit(X,yy,sample_weight=weights); return model.coef_[0],keep.sum()
estimate,n_local=local_rd(.5)
lab.useIt: nearby={h:local_rd(h)[0] for h in (.35,.5,.7)}; left=y[(r<0)&(r>-.05)].mean(); right=y[(r>=0)&(r<.05)].mean(); raw_near_jump=right-left
lab.verifyIt:
assert abs(estimate-tau)<.08
assert all(abs(v-tau)<.12 for v in nearby.values())
assert abs(raw_near_jump-tau)<.15
assert n_local>7000
assert set(nearby)=={.35,.5,.7}
lab.shipIt: Persist score and cutoff lineage, local-support counts, bandwidth and bias-aware inference; alert on manipulation, heaping and coincident rule changes.

lessons.description: Regression discontinuity identifies a treatment effect at an assignment threshold by comparing limits of outcome functions on either side. This chapter distinguishes sharp, fuzzy, kink and local-randomization designs; derives the cutoff estimand and fuzzy Wald ratio; and states continuity, no-manipulation, exclusion and monotonicity assumptions. It develops boundary-specific local linear and quadratic regression, bandwidth and kernel choice, robust bias-corrected inference, clustered observations and discrete running variables. It explains why bins are for visualization, why global high-order polynomials are dangerous, and how density tests, predetermined covariates, placebo cutoffs, bandwidth sensitivity and donut analyses diagnose specific threats. Worked examples compute sharp and fuzzy effects and expose a second policy at the same threshold. The lab simulates a smooth running-variable response with a known discontinuity, fits separate local slopes through an interaction model and verifies effect recovery across neighboring bandwidths. Production guidance versions score construction and cutoff rules, monitors manipulation and heaping, preserves local support and prevents extrapolation beyond the margin.
learningObjectives: Derive sharp and fuzzy RD estimands from continuity and threshold assignment.
Fit and interpret local polynomial models with bandwidth, kernel and bias-aware inference choices.
Diagnose manipulation, heaping, co-occurring policies, covariate jumps and placebo discontinuities.
Communicate the cutoff-local population and prevent unsupported extrapolation.

deepSections.title: The assignment rule creates a local comparison
deepSections.body: Record the exact running variable, cutoff, whether treatment is deterministic, and whether eligibility or receipt is the intervention. Sharp RD uses a deterministic jump in assignment; fuzzy RD uses a discontinuity in treatment probability. Identification assumes potential-outcome conditional means evolve continuously through the cutoff absent the treatment. Then any outcome jump is attributed to the treatment rule. This is weaker than requiring units be identical but depends on no other discontinuous mechanism. The cutoff effect applies to units at R=c, not the average eligible population. If the running variable is a coarse integer, asymptotic continuity and local-randomization perspectives require special treatment. Multiple cutoffs can aid validation but may represent different populations. Define time zero at assignment and ensure outcome windows are not selected by post-cutoff survival.

deepSections.title: Estimate limits at a boundary, not one global curve
deepSections.body: Center R at c and fit separate intercepts and slopes on each side within bandwidth h. The treatment indicator coefficient in a saturated local linear model estimates the intercept jump. Triangular kernels emphasize observations nearest the cutoff and are efficient in common formulations; other kernels usually matter less than bandwidth. Smaller h reduces approximation bias but increases variance, while larger h increases support and functional-form risk. Data-driven bandwidth selectors optimize an estimation criterion, but report sensitivity around the chosen value. Local quadratic fits can estimate bias or check curvature, but high-order global polynomials use distant observations and can oscillate dramatically. Do not force the same slope unless justified. Predictions and confidence intervals must use RD-specific procedures that account for boundary smoothing and bandwidth selection.

deepSections.title: Fuzzy RD is an instrument at the cutoff
deepSections.body: When eligibility raises but does not determine receipt, the outcome jump is an intention-to-treat effect of crossing the cutoff. Divide it by the treatment-probability jump to estimate a local average treatment effect for units whose receipt responds to eligibility. Relevance is the first-stage discontinuity. Independence comes from local continuity or randomization assumptions; exclusion requires the cutoff to affect outcome only through the defined treatment; monotonicity excludes units who move treatment oppositely. A cutoff may change information, stigma or other benefits directly, violating exclusion. Report both jumps and weak-first-stage diagnostics. The complier population is near the cutoff and instrument-specific. If treatment intensity changes continuously rather than jumps, a regression-kink design relies on slope-change assumptions and requires separate methods.

deepSections.title: Falsification tests target particular design failures
deepSections.body: Plot the running-variable density and inspect whether units bunch just above the cutoff, considering institutional heaping and test power. A density discontinuity can indicate manipulation, but smooth density does not prove no sorting. Predetermined covariates should not jump if the local groups are comparable; test a prespecified set and account for multiplicity. Outcomes measured before treatment should remain continuous. Placebo cutoffs reveal broad functional-form artifacts, while placebo outcomes reveal coincident mechanisms. A donut RD excludes observations closest to a potentially manipulated cutoff but changes the local data and estimand approximation; report it as sensitivity, not a preferred result chosen after inspection. Audit other eligibility rules, administrative rounding and score revisions at the same threshold.

deepSections.title: Inference and communication stay local
deepSections.body: Use robust bias-corrected confidence intervals and standard errors suited to the selected local polynomial. Cluster when multiple observations share assignment units, schools, providers or time shocks. With few mass points or clusters, asymptotic methods can be unreliable; local randomization or randomization inference may be more appropriate if a credible window and assignment mechanism exist. Show the number of observations and unique running-variable values on each side. Report estimates across reasonable bandwidths and polynomial orders without selecting the most favorable. Never extrapolate the local effect to units far from the cutoff by extending the fitted lines. Policy expansion requires effect-homogeneity assumptions or new evidence at other margins.

workedExamples.title: Sharp cutoff jump
workedExamples.body: The fitted outcome limit is 62 just below a scholarship cutoff and 67 just above. If assignment is sharp and continuity assumptions hold, the local scholarship effect is five outcome units at the cutoff.

workedExamples.title: Fuzzy cutoff ratio
workedExamples.body: Eligibility raises participation by 0.25 and outcome by 1.5 units. The fuzzy RD estimate is 1.5/0.25=6 units for cutoff compliers under exclusion and monotonicity.

exercises.prompt: Outcome jump is 4 and treatment-probability jump is 0.5. What is fuzzy RD LATE?
exercises.solution: Eight outcome units for cutoff compliers, under the fuzzy-IV assumptions.

exercises.prompt: Why can another benefit beginning at the same cutoff invalidate RD?
exercises.solution: The outcome discontinuity can reflect both interventions, violating attribution or fuzzy exclusion for the target treatment.

exercises.prompt: What does bandwidth sensitivity reveal?
exercises.solution: Whether the estimated local jump depends strongly on including more distant observations and functional-form approximation.
