lessons.title: Synthetic Control
lessons.interviewAnswer: Synthetic control estimates the counterfactual trajectory of one or a few treated aggregate units as a weighted combination of untreated donor units. Weights are chosen using only pretreatment outcomes and predictors, commonly constrained to be nonnegative and sum to one, so the synthetic unit lies in the donor convex hull. The post-treatment gap is the estimated effect under assumptions that good pretreatment fit captures the relevant time-varying confounding, donors remain untreated and unaffected by spillovers, and no concurrent treated-unit shock creates the gap. I justify the donor pool and intervention date, show the full treated and synthetic paths, pretreatment RMSPE and weights, and conduct in-space and in-time placebo analyses, often scaling post gaps by pre-fit quality. Poor pre-fit means the counterfactual is unsupported. I do not read ordinary regression standard errors mechanically or generalize a single-unit effect without design evidence.
keyPoints: Synthetic control is a comparative case-study design, not merely a forecasting algorithm.
Donor eligibility, intervention timing, no spillovers and good pretreatment trajectory fit are core assumptions.
Nonnegative sum-to-one weights favor interpretable interpolation and expose convex-hull support.
Post-treatment gaps need placebo, permutation and fit-quality context rather than ordinary large-sample standard errors alone.
Researcher choices about donor pools, predictors and preperiods require transparent sensitivity and no post-outcome cherry-picking.
lessons.why: A statewide law, platform-wide launch or national event may affect one aggregate unit with no obvious single control. A weighted donor combination can reproduce its pre-intervention trajectory better than any donor and make the comparison explicit. Yet excellent post hoc fit can be manufactured by an enormous or contaminated donor pool, and a post-treatment gap may reflect spillovers, another policy or model extrapolation. Unlike ordinary panel regression, synthetic control foregrounds the treated path, donor weights and pre-fit. Credibility comes from comparative design, placebos and qualitative case knowledge—not from optimization alone.
lessons.intuition: Construct a fictional untreated version of the treated region by mixing unaffected regions until its pre-policy outcomes closely trace the treated history. Freeze the mixture at the intervention. The future difference between the real and synthetic paths estimates what changed, provided the preperiod captured relevant latent forces and nothing else uniquely changed the treated region.
lessons.deepDive: Synthetic control combines donor selection, constrained weights and longitudinal validation for comparative case studies. Good pre-fit supports interpolation but does not prove identification. Credible inference uses placebo assignments and transparent researcher-choice sensitivity, while extensions trade convex-hull interpretability for regularization, bias correction or multiple treated units.
lessons.workedExample: A synthetic region uses weights 0.6 on donor A and 0.4 on donor B. If their post outcomes are 20 and 30, the counterfactual is 24. A treated outcome of 19 gives an estimated gap of -5 for that period.

commonMistakes.misconception: Excellent pretreatment fit proves causal validity.
commonMistakes.correction: It supports trajectory comparability but cannot rule out postperiod shocks, anticipation, spillovers or overfit.

commonMistakes.misconception: Choose donors by whichever set yields the cleanest post gap.
commonMistakes.correction: Post-outcome donor selection is specification search; freeze eligibility from design knowledge and preperiod evidence.

commonMistakes.misconception: A synthetic control effect is an average policy effect.
commonMistakes.correction: Classical analysis targets the treated unit and event; broader transport requires additional evidence.

commonMistakes.misconception: Ordinary regression standard errors apply to one treated aggregate unit.
commonMistakes.correction: Use design-aware placebo or permutation evidence and transparent case-study uncertainty.

followUps.question: Why constrain weights to be nonnegative and sum to one?
followUps.answer: It makes the synthetic unit an interpretable interpolation within donor support and avoids unrestricted extrapolation.

followUps.question: What if pretreatment fit is poor?
followUps.answer: The classical donor pool does not support the counterfactual well; redesign, narrow the claim or use a justified extension rather than trust the post gap.

followUps.question: What does an in-space placebo do?
followUps.answer: It applies the full method to untreated donors as pseudo-treated units to contextualize how unusual the treated unit's post/pre divergence is.

lessons.production: Version treated unit, intervention and anticipation dates, donor eligibility, outcome and predictor sources, pretreatment window, optimization constraints and weights. Freeze all choices before postperiod monitoring. Publish treated and synthetic paths, RMSPE, weight concentration, placebo distributions, leave-one-out and credible specification sensitivity. Monitor source revisions, spillovers, donor interventions and concurrent treated-unit shocks. Keep conclusions local to the case, require human causal review for policy decisions and retain the pre-intervention design when updated donor data would rewrite history.

visual.title: Synthetic control
visual.caption: Before intervention the synthetic control should closely track the treated unit; the post-intervention gap estimates the effect.
visual.adaptationNote: Atlas redraw: the structure and claims are grounded in the cited source material; the artwork is newly drawn for teaching rather than copied verbatim from a paper or website.

lessons.math: For treated outcome Y_1t and J donors Y_jt, choose weights w_j>=0 and sum_j w_j=1 to minimize pretreatment discrepancy, often sum_{t<T0}(Y_1t-sum_j w_jY_jt)^2 or predictor-weighted distance. Counterfactual after T0 is Yhat_1t(0)=sum_j w_jY_jt and gap tauhat_t=Y_1t-Yhat_1t(0). Pretreatment RMSPE summarizes fit. In-space placebos assign treatment to each donor and repeat the full procedure; compare treated post/pre RMSPE ratio or gap with placebo distribution, excluding units whose pre-fit is not comparable under a prespecified rule.
lessons.code: pre_rmspe=np.sqrt(np.mean(gaps[:pre]**2)); post_effect=np.mean(gaps[pre:]); concentration=np.sum(weights**2); frozen_prediction=donors[pre:]@weights

lab.goal: Fit simplex-constrained donor weights on pretreatment outcomes and verify recovery of a known post-treatment counterfactual gap.
lab.buildIt:
import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import minimize
rng=np.random.default_rng(77); pre=35; post=12; time=np.arange(pre+post); factors=np.c_[np.ones(len(time)),np.sin(time/5),time/20]; load=rng.normal(size=(3,4)); donors=factors@load+rng.normal(scale=.03,size=(len(time),4)); true_w=np.array([.5,.3,.2,0.]); counterfactual=donors@true_w; effect=np.r_[np.zeros(pre),np.full(post,-4.)]; treated=counterfactual+effect+rng.normal(scale=.03,size=len(time))
def objective(w): return np.mean((treated[:pre]-donors[:pre]@w)**2)
fit=minimize(objective,np.full(4,.25),method='SLSQP',bounds=[(0,1)]*4,constraints={'type':'eq','fun':lambda w:w.sum()-1}); weights=fit.x; synthetic=donors@weights; gaps=treated-synthetic
lab.verifyIt:
assert fit.success
assert np.all(weights>=-1e-8) and abs(weights.sum()-1)<1e-8
assert np.max(np.abs(weights-true_w))<.06
assert pre_rmspe<.06
assert abs(post_effect+4)<.06
assert np.allclose(frozen_prediction,synthetic[pre:]) and concentration>.25
lab.shipIt: Freeze donor eligibility, preperiod and weights, persist paths and placebo diagnostics, and monitor donor contamination, source revisions and treated-unit concurrent shocks.

lessons.description: Synthetic control constructs a transparent counterfactual for an aggregate intervention from a weighted donor pool. This chapter derives constrained donor weights, predictor and pretreatment-outcome matching, convex-hull support and post-treatment gaps. It explains donor eligibility, spillovers, anticipation, time-varying latent confounding, intervention timing and why good pre-fit is necessary but not sufficient. It develops pretreatment RMSPE, leave-one-out donors, alternative windows, in-space and in-time placebos, post/pre fit ratios and researcher-choice sensitivity. It contrasts classical nonnegative simplex weights with regression, augmented and matrix-completion extensions while preserving the target case-study question. Worked examples compute a weighted counterfactual and diagnose an influential donor. The lab fits simplex-constrained weights to a simulated panel, verifies recovery of the donor mixture and known post-treatment effect, and checks that weights are frozen after intervention. Production guidance versions donor pools and source revisions, reports paths and weights, monitors spillovers and concurrent shocks, and avoids automatic causal claims from forecast accuracy.
learningObjectives: Construct and interpret simplex-constrained donor weights and a synthetic counterfactual trajectory.
Diagnose donor contamination, convex-hull failure, poor pre-fit, spillovers and concurrent shocks.
Perform placebo and specification sensitivity appropriate to a comparative case study.
Report weights, paths, fit and local case-study scope without unsupported generalization.

deepSections.title: The donor pool defines the untreated counterfactual space
deepSections.body: Select donors that were not exposed to the intervention, anticipation, spillovers or a similar contemporaneous shock. They should share outcome measurement and plausible latent outcome factors with the treated unit. Excluding a donor because its postperiod trajectory narrows the estimated gap is outcome-driven selection; freeze eligibility from pre-intervention and institutional evidence. Define intervention time and any anticipation window. Long pretreatment outcome histories often summarize latent factor loadings better than a few static predictors, but structural breaks can make distant history irrelevant. A donor pool that is too small may not span the treated path; a huge pool increases overfitting and researcher degrees of freedom. Record source revisions, geographic relationships and interference channels. Synthetic control usually targets the one treated unit under this event, not a superpopulation average.

deepSections.title: Constrained weights expose support and fit
deepSections.body: Classical weights are nonnegative and sum to one, making the synthetic trajectory an interpolation among donors. Predictor weights may prioritize variables by how well they reproduce pretreatment outcomes, creating a nested optimization that must use preperiod data only. Plot treated and synthetic outcomes throughout the preperiod and report RMSPE, not merely selected predictor balance. A low RMSPE supports but does not establish that future untreated paths would coincide. If no convex combination fits, the treated unit lies outside donor support; large extrapolative regression coefficients can improve fit while weakening design credibility. Inspect weight concentration and leave-one-out sensitivity. One dominant donor may be substantively reasonable or make the result hinge on a single comparison. Freeze weights before inspecting postperiod outcomes.

deepSections.title: The gap needs a comparative reference distribution
deepSections.body: The post-treatment effect path is the treated outcome minus its frozen synthetic counterfactual. Report pointwise gaps and cumulative or average summaries chosen in advance. Conventional standard errors based on many independent treated units are inappropriate when one case is treated. In-space placebo tests repeatedly treat each donor as if exposed and reconstruct it from remaining donors. If the actual post/pre RMSPE ratio or gap is extreme among comparably fitted placebos, that supports unusual postperiod divergence. Placebo timing before the event tests whether the procedure invents effects. Exclude terrible-fit placebos only by a declared threshold because their post gaps are not comparable. Permutation p-values are descriptive under the assignment interpretation, and a small donor pool yields coarse evidence. Qualitative evidence about alternative shocks remains essential.

deepSections.title: Researcher choices and extensions change the counterfactual
deepSections.body: Repeat analysis over credible pretreatment windows, predictor sets, anticipation dates and donor exclusions. Leave-one-out analysis reveals influential donors. Do not report only the configuration with the largest effect. Augmented synthetic control adds an outcome model to correct pre-fit bias; generalized synthetic control and matrix completion use factor structures across panels; ridge or elastic-net weights allow extrapolation and regularization. These methods can improve prediction but change assumptions and interpretability. Multiple treated units permit pooled or unit-specific effects with cluster-aware methods. Synthetic DID combines weighting ideas with DID-style adjustment. Choose an extension for the identified failure—poor convex-hull fit, multiple cases or noise—not because it produces narrower intervals. Preserve classical paths as a benchmark.

deepSections.title: Quantitative fit complements, not replaces, case knowledge
deepSections.body: Document the policy mechanism, treated unit history, donor institutions, concurrent events and outcome construction. A unique post-treatment recession, data-definition change or migration can mimic an effect. Spillovers into donor units shrink or reverse gaps. Anticipation can contaminate the preperiod used to fit weights. Monitor source revisions and rerun from versioned snapshots because aggregate historical series are frequently backfilled. Publish donor weights, pre-fit, placebo distribution and all prespecified sensitivities. Restrict conclusions to the treated case and observed postperiod. Transport to other regions requires effect-modifier evidence. For live policy monitoring, pre-register windows and freeze weights, but do not automatically trigger decisions from each noisy postperiod deviation.

workedExamples.title: Weighted counterfactual

workedExamples.title: Influential donor
workedExamples.body: One donor receives weight 0.85 and experiences an unrelated postperiod boom. The synthetic path rises and exaggerates a negative treatment gap. Leave-one-out and institutional review expose how dependent the conclusion is on that donor.

Why compare post/pre RMSPE ratios in placebos?

exercises.prompt: What does negative donor weight imply?
exercises.solution: The counterfactual extrapolates outside the donor convex hull; that may improve fit under an extension but changes classical interpretation and risk.

lessons.title: Heterogeneous Treatment Effects & Uplift Modeling
lessons.interviewAnswer: Heterogeneous treatment-effect modeling estimates CATE tau(x)=E[Y(1)-Y(0)|X=x] or learns a treatment policy, not an observable individual-effect label. Identification still needs randomized assignment or conditional exchangeability, positivity, consistency and an interference assumption. S-learners use one outcome model with treatment; T-learners fit separate outcome models; X-, R- and DR-learners use imputation or orthogonal residuals to improve robustness. Causal trees and forests split for effect differences and use honesty or cross-fitting so discovery does not reuse estimation outcomes. I evaluate global ATE recovery, calibration of predicted effects in held-out groups, rank-weighted treatment effects, policy value and overlap—not ordinary RMSE against factual outcomes. I predefine actionable baseline features, separate discovery from confirmation, report uncertainty and subgroup support, and validate any targeting policy prospectively. A high predicted uplift is not a known personal effect.
keyPoints: CATE is a conditional average causal estimand; individual treatment effects remain unobserved.
Meta-learners differ in how they estimate outcome and propensity nuisance functions and handle imbalance.
Honesty, sample splitting and cross-fitting reduce adaptive subgroup and nuisance overfitting.
Evaluate effect ranking, calibration and policy value on held-out causal evidence rather than factual prediction loss alone.
Targeting requires positivity, actionability, capacity, fairness, uncertainty and prospective policy validation.
lessons.why: An average effect can hide beneficiaries, unaffected units and harmed subgroups, motivating personalization. But heterogeneity search has far less observable supervision than ordinary ML: no row contains its true treatment contrast. Flexible models can discover dramatic subgroups from noise, especially when treatment groups are imbalanced or covariate overlap is weak. A model may predict outcomes accurately while estimating treatment differences poorly. Honest causal learning therefore combines identification, orthogonalization, separate discovery and estimation, causal evaluation metrics and policy experiments. The output should guide a bounded decision, not label people with certain counterfactual destinies.
lessons.intuition: Two outcome models estimate the response surface under treatment and control. Their difference at x is an estimated conditional benefit. We cannot check that difference for one person, but in a held-out group of people with similar predicted benefit, randomized treatment-control outcome differences should agree on average. Evaluation is groupwise and policy-level because individual counterfactual labels are missing.
lessons.deepDive: Heterogeneous-effect learning combines potential-outcome identification with flexible nuisance estimation and honest adaptive partitioning. Meta-learners expose different bias-variance trade-offs, while causal forests and orthogonal scores target treatment contrasts directly. Reliable deployment evaluates calibration and value, quantifies overlap and uncertainty, and confirms policies prospectively.
lessons.workedExample: A high-risk customer may churn regardless of offer and have near-zero uplift, while a medium-risk customer is persuadable. A churn-risk ranking wastes treatment capacity compared with a validated treatment-effect ranking.

commonMistakes.misconception: Train a regressor on observed outcome and call its prediction uplift.
commonMistakes.correction: Outcome risk is not a treatment contrast; the learner must model treatment-specific counterfactual response under causal identification.

commonMistakes.misconception: CATE RMSE can be computed from each row's factual outcome.
commonMistakes.correction: Individual treatment effects are unobserved; use causal losses, group calibration, ranking and policy value.

commonMistakes.misconception: A subgroup discovered by a causal tree has confirmatory inference automatically.
commonMistakes.correction: Adaptive search biases leaf effects unless discovery and estimation are separated or honest methods are used.

commonMistakes.misconception: Treat everyone with positive point-estimate CATE.
commonMistakes.correction: Consider uncertainty, cost, harm, capacity, overlap, fairness and prospective policy evidence.

followUps.question: When is a T-learner attractive?
followUps.answer: When both treatment groups have enough support and response surfaces differ substantially, with separate models offering useful flexibility.

followUps.question: What is honesty in a causal tree?
followUps.answer: Separate outcome information selects the partition and estimates effects within that fixed partition, reducing adaptive subgroup bias.

followUps.question: How do you validate CATE predictions?
followUps.answer: Use held-out causal calibration, ranked group effects, orthogonal scores and policy-value estimates rather than unavailable individual-effect labels.

lessons.production: Version the causal estimand, assignment mechanism, pretreatment features, nuisance and effect learners, cross-fitting folds, calibration protocol, policy objective, costs and capacity. Gate on local propensity support, honest held-out calibration, rank stability, value and adverse-effect guardrails. Preserve randomized exploration or periodic policy trials. Monitor predicted-effect mix, treatment rates, calibration groups, realized value and fairness by supported cohorts. Communicate conditional averages with uncertainty, canary new policies and retain the prior targeting rule and model for rollback.
lessons.math: CATE tau(x)=E[Y(1)-Y(0)|X=x]. An S-learner estimates m(a,x) jointly and subtracts m(1,x)-m(0,x); a T-learner estimates m1 and m0 separately. The R-learner residualizes outcome m(X)=E[Y|X] and treatment e(X)=E[A|X], then fits tau by minimizing sum[(Y-mhat(X))-(A-ehat(X))tau(X)]^2, commonly cross-fitted. A value policy pi has V(pi)=E[Y(pi(X))]; in randomized data it can be estimated by inverse propensity or doubly robust scores. Calibration bins compare average predicted tau with held-out causal effect estimates, not observed unit differences.
lessons.code: rmse=np.sqrt(np.mean((cate-truth)**2)); correlation=np.corrcoef(cate,truth)[0,1]; cuts=np.quantile(cate,[0,.25,.5,.75,1]); groups=np.clip(np.digitize(cate,cuts[1:-1]),0,3); calibration=[(cate[groups==g].mean(),truth[groups==g].mean()) for g in range(4)]

lab.goal: Fit a T-learner on randomized heterogeneous effects and verify held-out CATE accuracy, ranking and calibration against known simulation truth.
lab.buildIt:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.ensemble import ExtraTreesRegressor
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
rng=np.random.default_rng(88); n=14000; X=rng.normal(size=(n,3)); tau=1+1.2*X[:,0]; a=rng.binomial(1,.5,size=n); mu=2*X[:,0]+X[:,1]**2; y=mu+a*tau+rng.normal(scale=.5,size=n)
train,test=train_test_split(np.arange(n),test_size=.35,random_state=4); params=dict(n_estimators=240,min_samples_leaf=40,max_features=1.0,random_state=5,n_jobs=-1); m0=ExtraTreesRegressor(**params).fit(X[train][a[train]==0],y[train][a[train]==0]); m1=ExtraTreesRegressor(**params).fit(X[train][a[train]==1],y[train][a[train]==1]); cate=m1.predict(X[test])-m0.predict(X[test]); truth=tau[test]
lab.useIt: rmse=np.sqrt(np.mean((cate-truth)**2)); correlation=np.corrcoef(cate,truth)[0,1]; cuts=np.quantile(cate,[0,.25,.5,.75,1]); groups=np.clip(np.digitize(cate,cuts[1:-1]),0,3); calibration=[(cate[groups==g].mean(),truth[groups==g].mean()) for g in range(4)]
lab.verifyIt:
assert rmse<.35
assert correlation>.95
assert all(abs(pred-actual)<.2 for pred,actual in calibration)
assert calibration[-1][1]>calibration[0][1]+2
assert abs(cate.mean()-truth.mean())<.08
assert len(cate)==len(test)
lab.shipIt: Persist cross-fitted effect predictions and calibration groups, gate policy on overlap and held-out value, preserve exploration, and communicate CATE as a conditional average with uncertainty.

lessons.description: Heterogeneous treatment-effect and uplift modeling estimates how average causal effects vary with pretreatment features and turns those estimates into constrained policies. This chapter defines CATE, group effects, uplift and policy value while emphasizing that individual causal labels are never observed. It compares S-, T-, X-, R- and doubly robust learners; explains outcome and propensity nuisance estimation, treatment imbalance, cross-fitting and orthogonality; and develops honest causal trees and forests for adaptive subgroup discovery and inference. It covers uplift curves, Qini-style rankings, calibration by predicted-effect groups, best linear projection, RATE, policy-value estimation and prospective validation. Worked examples contrast predictive risk with treatment benefit and expose subgroup search bias. The lab simulates randomized heterogeneous effects, fits separate forest response surfaces and verifies held-out CATE ranking and calibration against known simulation truth. Production guidance restricts features to actionable pretreatment data, monitors overlap and policy capacity, quantifies uncertainty and fairness, preserves exploration and requires randomized confirmation before high-stakes personalized treatment.
learningObjectives: Define CATE, uplift and policy value without treating individual effects as observed labels.
Choose and implement S-, T-, X-, R-, DR- or forest learners for the design and sample regime.
Evaluate held-out heterogeneity through causal calibration, ranking, subgroup effects and policy value.
Deploy bounded targeting policies with overlap, uncertainty, fairness and prospective validation.

deepSections.title: Heterogeneity inherits every causal identification requirement
deepSections.body: Define the target population, treatment strategies, outcome horizon and baseline feature set before modeling. CATE conditions on X and can vary with effect modifiers, but including post-treatment variables changes or biases the estimand. Randomized experiments identify conditional effects where each treatment has support; observational studies additionally assume no unmeasured confounding given X and require nuisance adjustment. Sparse treatment within a region makes CATE extrapolative even if global overlap looks adequate. Distinguish predictive risk from benefit: high-risk people can have low treatment responsiveness, and low-risk people can benefit greatly. Decide whether the goal is scientific effect modification, a simple subgroup rule or a capacity-constrained policy. These targets require different summaries and tolerance for model complexity. Pre-specify important subgroups when confirmatory inference is needed.

deepSections.title: Meta-learners reorganize ordinary predictors around causal contrasts
deepSections.body: An S-learner fits one outcome model with A and X; shared structure helps when treatment effects are small but a highly regularized learner may ignore A interactions. A T-learner fits separate treated and control models; it is simple and flexible but can be noisy under imbalance and does not share information. The X-learner imputes treatment effects and can exploit imbalanced groups. R- and DR-learners residualize or augment with propensity and outcome nuisances, focusing the loss on treatment variation and gaining robustness under cross-fitting. Every learner still depends on overlap and causal assumptions. Use the same legal folds for nuisance predictions and effect fitting; hyperparameter search should target a causal or orthogonal loss rather than factual outcome accuracy alone. Compare simple linear interactions as a baseline.

deepSections.title: Honesty separates subgroup discovery from effect estimation
deepSections.body: A standard tree can search many splits and report extreme within-leaf differences created by the same noise used to choose them. Honest causal trees use one sample to select partitions and another to estimate effects inside fixed leaves, trading sample size for reduced adaptive bias and valid inference under conditions. Causal forests average many honest trees and use splits designed for treatment-effect heterogeneity rather than outcome prediction. They behave like adaptive local weighting estimators and can provide pointwise uncertainty under their theoretical assumptions. Minimum treated and control leaf sizes protect support. Feature importance from causal forests remains method-specific and can be unstable with correlated modifiers. Use held-out calibration and variable-priority diagnostics as hypothesis generation, not proof that a covariate causally modifies effect.

deepSections.title: Evaluate ranking and calibration without individual labels
deepSections.body: Check that the average predicted CATE matches a credible ATE. Divide held-out units into quantiles defined by predictions from models that did not use their outcomes, then estimate treatment-control effects within each group; plot observed group effects against average predictions with uncertainty. An uplift or gain curve orders units by predicted benefit and accumulates an inverse-propensity or doubly robust effect estimate; Qini conventions vary, so publish the formula and random-policy baseline. RATE summarizes rank-weighted heterogeneity. Policy value estimates outcomes if treatment follows a rule, accounting for assignment propensity and cost. Cross-validation must regenerate nuisance and effect predictions out of fold. Avoid selecting the best-looking subgroup and reporting its naive interval. Use randomization or cluster-aware inference according to the design.

deepSections.title: A treatment-effect model becomes a policy only with constraints
deepSections.body: Define treatment capacity, benefit and harm, abstention and eligibility. A rule might treat when estimated net benefit exceeds cost or select top K; uncertainty-aware rules can require a lower confidence bound. Preserve some randomized exploration or periodic trials, because a deterministic policy removes counterfactual support and makes future evaluation difficult. Monitor treatment propensity by feature region, predicted CATE distribution, calibration groups, realized value, adverse outcomes and subgroup access. Sensitive attributes may be necessary for audit while using them for differential treatment can raise legal and ethical constraints. Policy changes alter the observed data and nuisance models. Canary against an existing rule, use safety guardrails and keep rollback. Communicate conditional average evidence rather than telling an individual the model knows their personal outcome under both treatments.

workedExamples.title: Risk is not uplift
workedExamples.body: A high-risk customer may churn regardless of offer and have near-zero uplift, while a medium-risk customer is persuadable. A churn-risk ranking wastes treatment capacity compared with a validated treatment-effect ranking.

workedExamples.title: Adaptive subgroup bias
workedExamples.body: Searching hundreds of age and income splits in one experiment finds a leaf with a huge effect by chance. Estimating that same leaf on independent outcomes or using honest splitting reveals whether the effect persists.

exercises.prompt: Why can a high-risk model be a poor uplift model?
exercises.solution: Baseline outcome risk and treatment responsiveness are different functions; high risk does not imply the treatment changes the outcome.

exercises.prompt: What does cross-fitting accomplish in an R-learner?
exercises.solution: It produces out-of-fold nuisance predictions, reducing own-observation overfit bias in the residualized treatment-effect loss.

exercises.prompt: How should a top-K treatment policy be evaluated?
exercises.solution: Estimate held-out policy value and harm under the assignment design, include treatment cost and capacity, and confirm prospectively when consequential.

lessons.title: Trend, Seasonality, Cycles & Remainder
lessons.interviewAnswer: A time series is often described through level, trend, seasonal patterns, longer cycles, calendar effects, interventions and remainder. An additive representation Y_t=T_t+S_t+R_t fits seasonal amplitude that is roughly constant in target units; a multiplicative representation Y_t=T_t*S_t*R_t, often handled by logs, fits variation proportional to level. Components are modeling constructs, not uniquely observed truths: the decomposition depends on smoothing window, period, transform, endpoints and assumptions. I begin with frequency and timestamp quality, plot raw and transformed series, use domain calendars and spectral or ACF evidence for candidate seasons, and distinguish deterministic repeating seasonality from stochastic dependence. Multiple or evolving seasons need flexible bases or MSTL-like methods. I estimate components inside each training origin, inspect remainder structure and outliers, and never use a full-series decomposition as a leakage-free forecast feature.
keyPoints: Trend, seasonality, cycle and remainder are representation choices whose estimates depend on method and scale.
Additive seasonality has constant amplitude; multiplicative seasonality scales with level and is often modeled on logs.
Calendar effects such as trading days, holidays and moving festivals are not captured by a fixed numeric period alone.
A decomposition is useful only if the remainder and component stability are checked across time and forecast origins.
Full-series smoothing uses future observations and cannot be inserted directly into historical backtests or online features.
lessons.why: Forecasting methods encode different assumptions about what persists. A weekly seasonal pattern may be stable while trend changes; a retail holiday moves dates; a demand amplitude grows with business scale; an apparent cycle may be one structural break. Treating all structure as autoregression obscures operations, while assuming a clean decomposition can invent components at boundaries. Component analysis improves baseline choice, transformations, model architecture and diagnostics, but only when timestamp semantics, seasonal periods and point-in-time estimation are respected.
lessons.intuition: Think of the observed series as several transparent sheets stacked together: a slowly moving level, a repeating weekly pattern, occasional event shapes and noise. On an additive scale each sheet contributes a fixed number of units. On a multiplicative scale the seasonal sheet stretches when the level rises. The sheets are not handed to us; a decomposition algorithm chooses how to distribute the ink.
lessons.deepDive: Component representations separate predictable structures by timescale and mechanism. Additive and transformed multiplicative forms, calendar regressors, multiple seasons and robust smoothers support interpretation and model design. Identification is not unique, boundary estimates are fragile and all fitted components must remain origin-local in evaluation.
lessons.workedExample: A site's weekend traffic is about 80% of weekday level. When total traffic doubles, the weekend dip doubles in units, favoring a multiplicative or log-additive representation over a fixed additive dip.

commonMistakes.misconception: A decomposition reveals the true components.
commonMistakes.correction: Components depend on constraints, smoother settings, period, scale and sample; compare plausible representations.

commonMistakes.misconception: Use full-series STL components as ML features in backtests.
commonMistakes.correction: The smoother uses observations after historical origins; refit or update components within each training window.

commonMistakes.misconception: Every regular-looking oscillation is seasonality.
commonMistakes.correction: Seasonality repeats on a known calendar; cycles, trend and sampling artifacts can create apparent oscillation.

commonMistakes.misconception: Logging only changes the chart scale.
commonMistakes.correction: It changes the loss geometry, additive structure and back-transformation estimand and requires positive-domain handling.

followUps.question: How do you choose additive versus multiplicative seasonality?
followUps.answer: Assess whether seasonal amplitude is roughly constant in units or proportional to level, then validate transformed forecasts on the original decision scale.

followUps.question: Why is a centered moving average leaky?
followUps.answer: Its estimate at time t uses observations after t, which were unavailable at a forecast origin ending at t.

followUps.question: What should remain after decomposition?
followUps.answer: Ideally a stable remainder without actionable trend or seasonal structure, though this is a diagnostic goal rather than proof of model adequacy.

lessons.production: Version frequency, timezone, aggregation, periods, calendar and event definitions, transformation and inverse transform, smoother settings and seasonal normalization. Estimate every fitted component within forecast origins and persist component-level predictions. Test irregular timestamps, missing cycles, daylight-saving changes, zeros and endpoints. Monitor trend bias, seasonal phase errors, remainder variance and residual autocorrelation. Alert on calendar or operating-schedule changes, retain seasonal-naive and raw-scale fallbacks and rollback when component extrapolation or reconstruction becomes unstable.

visual.title: Time-series decomposition
visual.caption: Decomposition separates recurring structure from long-run movement and irregular variation.
visual.adaptationNote: Atlas redraw: the structure and claims are grounded in the cited source material; the artwork is newly drawn for teaching rather than copied verbatim from a paper or website.

lessons.math: Additive decomposition writes Y_t=T_t+S_t+R_t with seasonal constraints such as sum over one cycle S=0. Multiplicative form Y_t=T_t S_t R_t becomes log Y_t=log T_t+log S_t+log R_t for positive data. A centered moving average of length m estimates slow structure but uses future points and loses endpoints. Seasonal indices can average detrended values by phase. Fourier terms sin(2 pi kt/m), cos(2 pi kt/m) represent smooth deterministic seasonality; higher K increases flexibility. Components are not identifiable without constraints because a pattern can be shifted between trend and seasonality.
lessons.code: residual=y[interior]-reconstruction[interior]; component_rmse=float(np.sqrt(np.mean(residual**2))); seasonal_correlation=float(np.corrcoef(seasonal,pattern)[0,1])

lab.goal: Estimate additive trend and monthly seasonality from a synthetic series and verify normalization and interior reconstruction.
lab.buildIt:
import numpy as np
rng=np.random.default_rng(2); n=120; t=np.arange(n); true_trend=20+.08*t; pattern=np.array([-2,-1,0,1,2,3,2,1,0,-1,-2,-3.]); y=true_trend+pattern[t%12]+rng.normal(scale=.15,size=n)
window=12; kernel=np.ones(window)/window; raw=np.convolve(y,kernel,mode='valid'); trend=np.full(n,np.nan); trend[6:6+len(raw)]=raw
detrended=y-trend; seasonal=np.array([np.nanmean(detrended[(t%12)==k]) for k in range(12)]); seasonal-=seasonal.mean(); reconstruction=trend+seasonal[t%12]; interior=np.isfinite(trend)
lab.verifyIt:
assert abs(seasonal.sum())<1e-12
assert seasonal_correlation>.99
assert component_rmse<.25
assert interior.sum()==n-window+1
assert np.isnan(trend[:6]).all() and np.isnan(trend[6+len(raw):]).all()
assert np.allclose(reconstruction[interior]+residual,y[interior])
lab.shipIt: Persist periods, transforms and component states per origin, test calendar edges and endpoints, and monitor component-level drift with a seasonal-naive fallback.

lessons.description: Time-series components provide a vocabulary for level, trend, seasonality, cycles, calendar events, interventions and remainder. This chapter compares additive and multiplicative representations, explains log and Box-Cox-style transforms, and distinguishes fixed seasonal periods from holidays, trading-day effects and moving events. It derives moving-average trend and seasonal-index estimates, introduces Fourier bases and multiple seasonality, and discusses changing amplitude, damped trends, structural breaks, outliers and boundary uncertainty. It emphasizes that components are not uniquely observed and that decomposition choices allocate structure differently. Worked examples identify proportional seasonality and distinguish a one-time level shift from a recurring cycle. The lab simulates trend plus monthly seasonality, estimates a centered moving-average trend and phase means, and verifies reconstruction and zero-sum constraints on interior points. Production guidance validates frequency and timezone, versions calendar definitions and transforms, estimates components inside each backtest origin, monitors component drift and retains raw-series baselines when decomposition becomes unstable. The chapter keeps descriptive smoothing separate from the one-sided state available to a live forecaster.
learningObjectives: Identify plausible trend, seasonal, calendar, cycle and remainder structures from domain and diagnostics.
Choose additive, multiplicative or transformed representations from amplitude and support.
Estimate simple trend and seasonal components and understand identifiability and endpoint limitations.
Use component diagnostics without future leakage and monitor their stability in production.

deepSections.title: Components represent mechanisms and timescales
deepSections.body: Level is the local baseline around which observations vary. Trend is persistent direction over the forecast-relevant horizon, not necessarily a global straight line. Seasonality repeats at a known calendar or operational frequency such as hour of day or day of week. Cycles vary over longer durations without a fixed period and are difficult to distinguish from smooth trend in short samples. Calendar effects include month length, trading days, holidays and moving events; interventions include launches, outages and policy shifts. Remainder collects unmodeled structure, noise and anomalies. Start with timestamp audits, aggregation rules and domain mechanisms. A daily series from a global service can mix time zones and create artificial seasons. A short series cannot identify a multi-year cycle reliably. Name components by how they will be forecast or acted on, not by visual resemblance alone.

deepSections.title: Scale determines how seasonal amplitude behaves
deepSections.body: In an additive model, a December effect of plus 100 units remains plus 100 as the level changes. In a multiplicative model, December might be twenty percent above level, so its unit amplitude grows. Plot seasonal ranges against local level and inspect residual variance. Log transforms convert positive multiplicative structure to additive and stabilize some variance, but zeros and negatives need domain-aware transforms. Back-transforming a mean log forecast does not automatically yield the mean on the original scale; distributional correction may be needed. Percent effects can also become unstable near zero. Box-Cox transforms generalize the log under positivity and a fitted parameter that must be training-only. Evaluate all forecasts after the intended inverse transform and on the business scale. Do not choose multiplicative form solely because the series rises.

deepSections.title: Periods and calendars encode different kinds of repetition
deepSections.body: A period m means the statistical pattern repeats every m observations, which requires regular sampling. Weekly seasonality in hourly data has period 168, but daylight-saving transitions produce 23- or 25-hour days and need timezone-aware handling. Month seasonality is not exactly 30 days. Trading-day counts and moving holidays require explicit regressors or event windows. Fourier bases represent smooth seasonality compactly; categorical phase indicators represent arbitrary shapes but use more parameters. Multiple seasons such as intraday and weekly can overlap and change over time. Interactions may be required when weekend intraday shape differs from weekdays. Inspect enough complete cycles and validate at forecast horizons. An ACF peak suggests repetition but can also arise from trend; detrend or difference appropriately before interpreting it.

deepSections.title: Every decomposition imposes smoothing and identifiability choices
deepSections.body: Classical decomposition estimates trend with moving averages, then seasonal phase averages, and assigns the rest to remainder. Centered windows use future observations and are descriptive, not causal online filters. Endpoint trend values are missing or extrapolated. STL uses locally weighted regressions and can robustify against outliers, while MSTL iterates over multiple seasons. Smoother widths trade adaptation against noise and determine which variation is called trend. Enforce seasonal normalization so level and seasonal components are identifiable. Inspect remainder mean, variance, autocorrelation, seasonal residual patterns and outliers. Remaining structure means the decomposition is incomplete for forecasting; a white-looking remainder does not prove components will remain stable. Compare reconstruction and component stability across plausible settings rather than selecting the prettiest plot.

deepSections.title: Components become origin-local forecast states
deepSections.body: For historical origin o, estimate transformation, trend, seasonal indices and event effects using only data available by o. Forecast each component according to its mechanism: damp or extrapolate trend, repeat stable seasonality, populate known calendars and model residual dependence. Full-series decomposition leaks future trend into the past and exaggerates backtest quality. Store component forecasts and their sum so failures can be attributed. Monitor seasonal phase error, trend bias, remainder scale and event residuals by horizon. A changed operating schedule can invalidate seasonal indices instantly; a level shift can be mistaken for persistent trend. Use robust fallback seasonal-naive forecasts, cap implausible extrapolation and version calendars, periods, transforms and smoothing parameters with the model.

workedExamples.title: Proportional seasonality
workedExamples.body: A site's weekend traffic is about 80% of weekday level. When total traffic doubles, the weekend dip doubles in units, favoring a multiplicative or log-additive representation over a fixed additive dip.

workedExamples.title: Break is not a cycle
workedExamples.body: Demand jumps after a permanent store expansion and remains high. Calling the shift a long cycle encourages a forecast back toward the old level; an intervention or state-change model better represents the mechanism.

exercises.prompt: Seasonal amplitude doubles when level doubles. Which representation is natural?
exercises.solution: A multiplicative model, often expressed additively after a log or another positive-domain transform, subject to validation.

exercises.prompt: Why normalize additive seasonal indices to sum to zero?
exercises.solution: It prevents an arbitrary constant from being shifted between level or trend and the seasonal component.

exercises.prompt: How should moving holidays be modeled?
exercises.solution: With explicit calendar or event regressors and windows available for future dates, not a fixed observation period alone.

lessons.title: Lags, Rolling Windows & Leakage
lessons.interviewAnswer: Lag and rolling features summarize past information, but they must be constructed using only data available at prediction time. Centered windows or post-outcome aggregates silently leak the future.
keyPoints: Shift before rolling when necessary.

lessons.description: Lags, Rolling Windows & Leakage is a core topic in Time Series & Forecasting. Lags, Rolling Windows & Leakage appears frequently in data-science work because it connects mathematical assumptions to practical decisions, diagnostics and failure modes. This chapter turns the interview-level summary into a complete engineering and analytical treatment. The starting mental model is: Shift before rolling when necessary. The formal and implementation discussion builds from Shift before rolling when necessary., Feature availability timestamp matters., Use the same pipeline in backtests and production., while keeping the unit of data, objective, assumptions, and failure boundaries explicit. The original technical core is preserved: Lag and rolling features summarize past information, but they must be constructed using only data available at prediction time. Centered windows or post-outcome aggregates silently leak the future. Feature availability timestamp matters. Use the same pipeline in backtests and production. A strong practitioner separates the modeling assumption from the estimation procedure, checks diagnostics rather than trusting a single score, and explains what would make the method inappropriate. Rather than treating those statements as isolated facts, the chapter connects them to data preparation, evaluation design, numerical or systems behavior, and choices that change under scale or distribution shift. You will work through two concrete scenarios, a runnable Python lab with assertions, and two original conceptual visuals. The lab is intentionally small enough to run locally while still exposing an invariant that should remain true in a larger implementation. The production section translates the concept into monitoring, versioning, rollback, and failure-handling requirements. In production, validate assumptions on real data, monitor the quantities that can drift, and keep a simple baseline so added complexity has a measurable.

deepSections.title: Define the problem contract before the technique
deepSections.body: A rigorous explanation of Lags, Rolling Windows & Leakage starts with the contract, not the library call. In Time Series & Forecasting, the relevant artifact is a timestamped series and its information set, and the intended output is future values or predictive distributions. State the unit of observation or request, what information is available at decision time, which variables are controlled versus observed, and what success means. Lags, Rolling Windows & Leakage appears frequently in data-science work because it connects mathematical assumptions to practical decisions, diagnostics and failure modes. The key ideas — Shift before rolling when necessary., Feature availability timestamp matters., Use the same pipeline in backtests and production. — only become meaningful when tied to a concrete input and output. For example, the same mechanism can be valid for an offline batch but invalid for an online request if it depends on unavailable future information, expensive global state, or a representation that is not versioned at serving time. Write down assumptions about independence, stationarity, label quality, ordering, capacity, or trust boundaries when they matter. Separate the statistical estimand or computational result from the estimator or implementation used to obtain it. Also separate correctness from convenience: a popular API can faithfully execute the wrong problem definition. A useful interview answer therefore names the goal, the information boundary, the dominant trade-off, and one failure mode before adding details. In production, this same contract becomes the basis for schemas, tests, SLOs, monitoring, and rollback.

deepSections.title: Mechanism and representation
deepSections.body: The working intuition for Lags, Rolling Windows & Leakage is: Shift before rolling when necessary. The technical core is: Lag and rolling features summarize past information, but they must be constructed using only data available at prediction time. Centered windows or post-outcome aggregates silently leak the future. Feature availability timestamp matters. Use the same pipeline in backtests and production. A strong practitioner separates the modeling assumption from the estimation procedure, checks diagnostics rather than trusting a single score, and explains what would make the method inappropriate. Treat that description as a sequence of transformations and invariants. First identify what representation enters each step, what state or parameters are read, what transformation occurs, and what representation leaves. Then ask which quantities are learned, estimated, cached, partitioned, or fixed by design. The chapter's key points give a compact checklist: Shift before rolling when necessary., Feature availability timestamp matters., Use the same pipeline in backtests and production.. Each point should be explainable both conceptually and operationally. A concept is understood only when you can predict what changes after perturbing an input, removing a component, changing scale, or violating an assumption. Shape, units, ordering, normalization, and data type are part of the mechanism because many real failures are interface failures rather than failures of the underlying theory. For learned systems, distinguish forward computation from parameter updates; for data systems, distinguish event-time truth from processing-time state; for distributed or cloud systems, distinguish logical semantics from physical placement. This decomposition is also the basis for debugging: inspect intermediate values, compare against a tiny reference implementation, and verify local invariants before blaming the most sophisticated component.

deepSections.title: Formal view, objective, and invariants
deepSections.body: A compact formal statement prevents hand-waving. For Lags, Rolling Windows & Leakage, the existing mathematical or logical anchor is: define the transformation as a function from valid inputs and state to outputs, then state the invariant that must hold for every valid execution. Do not memorize symbols without semantics. Name the domain of every quantity, whether it is observed or latent, and what is optimized or conserved. If an objective is minimized, ask what population quantity its empirical version estimates and whether weighting changes that target. If there is no optimization objective, identify the safety or correctness invariant instead: ordering, idempotence, conservation, normalization, boundedness, monotonicity, consistency, or resource limits. Numerical details matter whenever repeated operations amplify rounding or conditioning problems. Systems details matter whenever retries, parallelism, caching, or partial failure can produce a different logical result. Statistical details matter whenever data reuse or selection changes the sampling distribution. A strong implementation test usually expresses at least one invariant as an assertion on a toy case, plus a second test that fails when a key assumption is deliberately violated. The runnable lab follows that pattern so the chapter has an executable claim rather than code that merely prints a plausible number.

deepSections.title: Design choices and trade-offs
deepSections.body: There is rarely one universally best configuration of Lags, Rolling Windows & Leakage. The useful question is which trade-off matters for the declared workload. Start with the key points Shift before rolling when necessary., Feature availability timestamp matters., Use the same pipeline in backtests and production. and ask how each affects accuracy or correctness, compute, memory, latency, sample efficiency, interpretability, and operational complexity. Prefer a simple baseline when it is easier to validate and already meets the decision threshold. Add complexity only when a measured failure mode justifies it. Hyperparameters and architecture choices should therefore map to observable consequences rather than folklore. At small scale, an exact method may be clearer; at large scale, approximation, batching, partitioning, caching, streaming, quantization, or asynchronous work may be necessary. Those changes create new error surfaces, so every optimization needs a quality or correctness comparison against the reference behavior. Also distinguish offline economics from online economics. A method that saves training time may increase serving cost; a denser representation may improve quality but violate memory limits; a stronger consistency guarantee may reduce throughput; a more aggressive safety rule may increase false positives. Document the chosen operating point, alternatives considered, and the condition that would trigger revisiting the choice. This turns a technical preference into an auditable engineering decision.

deepSections.title: Evaluation and diagnostics
deepSections.body: Evaluation for Lags, Rolling Windows & Leakage must test the claim the system will make in operation. Appropriate evidence in this module includes rolling-origin backtests, naive baselines, horizon slices, and calibration. Do not collapse everything into one average. Slice by the dimensions that change difficulty: time, horizon, class, scale, entity, language, device, traffic regime, subgroup, or workload shape as appropriate. Always compare against a meaningful baseline on the same examples or requests. Keep comparisons paired when possible so improvement is not confused with a change in evaluation population. If labels or outcomes arrive late, define maturity before scoring. If the system is stochastic, use repeated seeds or confidence intervals; if observations are dependent, use a dependence-aware uncertainty procedure rather than row-level iid assumptions. Diagnostics should include input validity, intermediate-state checks, output distribution checks, and resource behavior. For probabilistic outputs, evaluate calibration as well as discrimination or sharpness. For ranking or generation, combine task metrics with qualitative failure review. For infrastructure, test both steady state and recovery behavior. A release gate should specify what must improve, what must not regress, and which failures are blocking even if the global average looks good.

deepSections.title: Failure modes and debugging strategy
deepSections.body: The dominant risks around Lags, Rolling Windows & Leakage include temporal leakage, regime change, horizon decay, and delayed labels. Existing chapter cautions are also important: Applying the method without checking its assumptions or data-generating process. Choosing it because it is familiar rather than comparing against an appropriate baseline. A debugging process should make these risks observable. Start from the smallest reproducible case and verify the data contract. Check shapes, units, ordering, timestamps, identifiers, missingness, labels, masks, seeds, and configuration before changing the algorithm. Next verify a baseline and an invariant. Then inspect intermediate representations or state transitions to locate the first point where expected behavior diverges. Separate data bugs, objective mismatch, optimization or numerical issues, capacity limits, and deployment integration problems because they require different remedies. Introduce controlled perturbations: duplicate an event, reorder input, remove a feature, change batch size, delay a dependency, corrupt one field, or reduce precision. A robust implementation should either preserve its invariant or fail loudly according to a documented policy. Finally, test recovery. Retries should not duplicate side effects, model rollback should restore a compatible preprocessing path, and cached or checkpointed state should have a version. A system that works only on the happy path is not a complete implementation of the concept.

deepSections.title: Production operation, monitoring, and communication
deepSections.body: Shipping Lags, Rolling Windows & Leakage means operating a versioned contract over time. In production, validate assumptions on real data, monitor the quantities that can drift, and keep a simple baseline so added complexity has a measurable reason to exist. Persist the model, code, data or schema version, configuration, dependencies, and any state needed to reproduce behavior. Monitor the inputs that drive the mechanism, the outputs users experience, and the internal resource or quality signals that predict failure. Use separate alerts for correctness, quality, latency, saturation, data freshness, and safety so one aggregate health score does not hide the cause. Canary or shadow changes when the blast radius is meaningful. Define rollback artifacts in advance and verify that rollback restores compatible schemas, feature logic, tokenizer or preprocessing state, and dependent services. Record enough request or batch metadata to reproduce failures without retaining data that violates privacy or retention requirements. When explaining the system to another engineer or interviewer, use a stable narrative: problem contract, mechanism, formal invariant, trade-off, evaluation evidence, failure mode, and production control. That sequence demonstrates understanding more reliably than listing tool names. The final question is always operational: what signal would tell you this implementation is no longer trustworthy, and what safe action follows?

lessons.title: Naive, Seasonal-Naive & Drift Baselines
lessons.interviewAnswer: Forecast baselines are executable hypotheses about persistence. Mean forecasts assume reversion to a stable level; naive forecasts repeat the last observation and are optimal for a random walk under squared loss; drift extrapolates the average first-to-last slope; seasonal-naive repeats the last observed value from the same seasonal phase. I implement every baseline with exactly the data, update cadence and horizon available at each historical origin, and choose seasonal periods from the operational calendar rather than autocorrelation alone. I compare candidate models with paired errors by horizon and series, not only an aggregate. A complex model must beat relevant baselines such as seasonal-naive, current production and a known-future calendar rule after latency and cost. Baselines also serve as fallbacks and monitoring controls: if a model loses to them persistently, the issue may be drift, leakage in development or pipeline failure rather than insufficient architecture.
keyPoints: Each baseline encodes a concrete assumption about level, trend or seasonal persistence.
Naive and seasonal-naive forecasts must be generated recursively and point-in-time for every requested horizon.
A baseline is only fair when it receives the same information, origin schedule and target definition as the model.
Skill should be reported against multiple relevant baselines by horizon and series, with paired uncertainty.
Production baselines are low-dependency fallbacks and sentinels for data, model and regime failures.
lessons.why: Forecasting datasets contain strong persistence and seasonality, so sophisticated methods can appear accurate while adding no decision value. A seasonal-naive forecast may dominate a poorly backtested neural model, and a last-value rule may react faster to a level shift than a smooth trend model. Baselines expose leakage and metric errors, calibrate how hard a series is, and give operations a safe fallback when features or services fail. They are not intentionally weak straw men: the correct baseline matches the actual calendar, horizon, data latency and decision.
lessons.intuition: Before explaining tomorrow with a complex model, ask what happens if tomorrow looks like today, the same weekday last week or a continuation of the simplest observed drift. These rules are hard to beat because many series genuinely repeat. The complex model earns its place only by improving the decisions where these persistence assumptions fail.
lessons.deepDive: Naive, mean, drift and seasonal-naive methods are statistical models with clear data-generating assumptions. They anchor scaled metrics, backtest skill and fallback behavior. Robust use handles horizons, irregular calendars, transformations, panels and cold starts and preserves paired error ledgers for monitoring.
lessons.workedExample: A series moves from 10 at t=1 to 22 at t=7. Average drift is (22-10)/(7-1)=2 per step, so forecasts at h=1 and h=3 are 24 and 28. Endpoint noise makes this rule fragile.

commonMistakes.misconception: A baseline should be weak so the new model looks useful.
commonMistakes.correction: Use the strongest simple and production-relevant rules that share the same legal information.

commonMistakes.misconception: Rolling one-step seasonal-naive evaluates a fixed 28-day forecast.
commonMistakes.correction: It refreshes with future actuals; issue all 28 steps from each origin when that matches production.

commonMistakes.misconception: Seasonal period is always the number of rows per calendar cycle.
commonMistakes.correction: Irregular timestamps, daylight saving and moving holidays require calendar-aware semantics rather than fixed offsets alone.

commonMistakes.misconception: Positive average skill means the model is safe everywhere.
commonMistakes.correction: Inspect critical horizons, series, regimes and guardrails; aggregation can hide systematic losses.

followUps.question: When is naive forecasting hard to beat?
followUps.answer: For random-walk-like series, very short horizons or sudden level shifts where old history adds little stable information.

followUps.question: What if the MASE denominator is zero?
followUps.answer: The in-sample naive differences are all zero, so MASE is undefined; expose the case and use another declared metric or pooling rule.

followUps.question: Why keep current production as a baseline?
followUps.answer: It measures incremental release value and captures business rules or features absent from textbook persistence baselines.

lessons.production: Version baseline formulas, seasonal calendars, periods, origin and update cadence, transformation, cold-start fallback chain and aggregation. Generate baselines using the same data cutoff and known-future inputs as the candidate where appropriate. Persist paired forecast-level errors and report skill by horizon, series, lifecycle and regime with block-aware uncertainty. Package low-dependency baseline fallbacks, test calendar boundaries and monitor fallback frequency, negative skill and joint data failures. Roll back when the primary persistently loses on decision-critical evidence.

lessons.math: Mean forecast yhat_{T+h}=T^-1 sum_{t=1}^T y_t. Naive yhat_{T+h}=y_T for all h. Drift yhat_{T+h}=y_T+h(y_T-y_1)/(T-1). Seasonal-naive with period m is yhat_{T+h}=y_{T+h-m(k+1)} for the most recent observed same phase, equivalently repeating the final seasonal cycle for short horizons. Forecast skill can be 1-L_model/L_baseline for a declared aggregate loss; it is negative when the model loses. MASE divides absolute forecast error by the in-sample mean absolute seasonal-naive difference, connecting evaluation to the baseline scale.

lessons.description: Naive forecasting baselines turn simple persistence assumptions into rigorous benchmarks and fallbacks. This chapter derives historical-mean, last-value, drift and seasonal-naive forecasts and explains their links to stable-level, random-walk, linear-drift and repeating-season data-generating processes. It covers multi-step recursion, multiple seasonal periods, transformations, irregular calendars, intermittent demand, panels, cold starts and known-future event rules. It shows how baselines define MASE denominators and relative skill, why comparisons must share forecast origins and information, and how horizon and series aggregation can reverse rankings. Worked examples calculate drift and multi-step seasonal-naive forecasts. The lab implements all four methods over rolling origins, verifies formulas and demonstrates that seasonal-naive beats last-value on a seasonal synthetic series. Production guidance deploys baselines as low-dependency fallbacks, logs paired model-versus-baseline errors, monitors persistent negative skill and distinguishes model failure from data or regime change. Strong business rules and the current production system remain mandatory comparators when they use additional legal information.
learningObjectives: Derive and implement mean, naive, drift and seasonal-naive multi-step forecasts.
Match baseline assumptions and seasonal periods to the operational series and calendar.
Measure paired forecast skill by horizon, series and regime without aggregation artifacts.
Use baselines as production fallbacks and monitoring sentinels with explicit trigger rules.

deepSections.title: A baseline is a small model, not a deliberately bad forecast
deepSections.body: The historical mean is appropriate when observations fluctuate around a stable level and old history remains representative. The naive last-value forecast follows a random-walk assumption and adapts immediately to level changes, though uncertainty grows with horizon. Drift adds a straight-line extrapolation based on first and last values; it is sensitive to endpoint noise and can become implausible far ahead. Seasonal-naive repeats the most recent seasonal phase and is the minimum serious benchmark for stable calendar repetition. Current production, analyst rules and known-future schedules may be stronger operational baselines. Document which data each receives. A model that uses planned promotions cannot fairly compare against a baseline denied the same known plan if the question is incremental modeling value rather than total system value.

deepSections.title: Generate each baseline for the actual horizon and calendar
deepSections.body: Naive repeats the last available observation across horizons; it does not peek at actual intermediate outcomes unless the system will update before each horizon. Drift advances h slope units from the origin. Seasonal-naive indexes the last available same phase and repeats cycles when h exceeds m. Irregular timestamps require calendar joins rather than array offsets: one week earlier may be missing, daylight saving changes hourly counts and monthly periods vary. Moving holidays need event baselines or explicit calendars. For multiple seasonality, compare daily and weekly seasonal-naive variants or combine simple patterns. If production issues forecasts once but backtesting rolls one step at a time and refreshes with actuals, the baseline gets unfair information. Align issuance cadence, latency and horizon exactly.

deepSections.title: Panel baselines need lifecycle and aggregation rules
deepSections.body: A global collection can include mature seasonal series, new products, intermittent items and discontinued entities. Seasonal-naive is unavailable before one complete cycle, so define a fallback chain such as last value, category-level seasonal factor or pooled mean. New-series baselines may borrow group information but then are no longer purely local and must be trained point-in-time. Zero demand is a valid value distinct from missing observation. Aggregate-level naive forecasts can differ from sums of bottom-level baselines; decide whether coherence is required. Series with different scales need macro metrics or scaled errors alongside volume-weighted loss. Report baseline availability and fallback use by lifecycle. Do not exclude hard cold starts from evaluation just because the preferred seasonal baseline cannot score them.

deepSections.title: Paired errors reveal where complexity earns value
deepSections.body: Store the model and every baseline forecast for the same series-origin-horizon target. Compute paired loss differences, win rates and skill by horizon and regime. Overall averages can hide that a model wins long horizons but loses the first day, or improves large series while harming the median item. MASE uses a training-only naive scale and needs a nonzero denominator; RMSSE emphasizes large errors. Relative skill can explode when baseline loss is nearly zero. Use block or series bootstrap for uncertainty, keeping pairs together. Avoid declaring success from in-sample fit or one terminal window. A baseline can be optimal under one loss and not another; compare on the operational scorecard including cost and bias.

deepSections.title: Baselines protect the forecasting service
deepSections.body: Package last-value and seasonal-naive logic with minimal dependencies and tested calendar behavior. If primary model inference times out, features are stale or prediction is nonfinite, route to the declared fallback and log the reason. Monitor rolling paired loss after target maturity, baseline win rate, signed bias and fallback frequency. Persistent negative skill can signal data drift, a broken feature, an overfit model or a changed seasonal period. A sudden simultaneous failure of model and baseline suggests target or source issues. Promotion gates should require improvement over relevant baselines across critical horizons and no unacceptable guardrail regressions. Keep baseline forecasts in the same ledger so rollback decisions use exact paired evidence.

lab.goal: Decompose a seasonal series with STL.
lab.buildIt:
import numpy as np
t=np.arange(120)
y=.05*t + 2*np.sin(2*np.pi*t/12) + np.random.default_rng(0).normal(0,.3,len(t))

from statsmodels.tsa.seasonal import STL
r=STL(y,period=12,robust=True).fit()
print(r.trend[:5],r.seasonal[:5])
