deepSections.title: Define the problem contract before the technique
deepSections.body: A rigorous explanation of Forecast Monitoring & Retraining starts with the contract, not the library call. In Time Series & Forecasting, the relevant artifact is a timestamped series and its information set, and the intended output is future values or predictive distributions. State the unit of observation or request, what information is available at decision time, which variables are controlled versus observed, and what success means. Forecast Monitoring & Retraining appears frequently in data-science work because it connects mathematical assumptions to practical decisions, diagnostics and failure modes. The key ideas — Track error by horizon/segment., Bias can matter more than symmetric error., Backfill/revisions complicate evaluation. — only become meaningful when tied to a concrete input and output. For example, the same mechanism can be valid for an offline batch but invalid for an online request if it depends on unavailable future information, expensive global state, or a representation that is not versioned at serving time. Write down assumptions about independence, stationarity, label quality, ordering, capacity, or trust boundaries when they matter. Separate the statistical estimand or computational result from the estimator or implementation used to obtain it. Also separate correctness from convenience: a popular API can faithfully execute the wrong problem definition. A useful interview answer therefore names the goal, the information boundary, the dominant trade-off, and one failure mode before adding details. In production, this same contract becomes the basis for schemas, tests, SLOs, monitoring, and rollback.

deepSections.title: Mechanism and representation
deepSections.body: The working intuition for Forecast Monitoring & Retraining is: Track error by horizon/segment. The technical core is: Forecast systems need monitoring for bias, scale changes, missing updates, driver drift and horizon-specific error. Retraining cadence should reflect how quickly relationships change and whether new labels arrive. Bias can matter more than symmetric error. Backfill/revisions complicate evaluation. A strong practitioner separates the modeling assumption from the estimation procedure, checks diagnostics rather than trusting a single score, and explains what would make the method inappropriate. Treat that description as a sequence of transformations and invariants. First identify what representation enters each step, what state or parameters are read, what transformation occurs, and what representation leaves. Then ask which quantities are learned, estimated, cached, partitioned, or fixed by design. The chapter's key points give a compact checklist: Track error by horizon/segment., Bias can matter more than symmetric error., Backfill/revisions complicate evaluation.. Each point should be explainable both conceptually and operationally. A concept is understood only when you can predict what changes after perturbing an input, removing a component, changing scale, or violating an assumption. Shape, units, ordering, normalization, and data type are part of the mechanism because many real failures are interface failures rather than failures of the underlying theory. For learned systems, distinguish forward computation from parameter updates; for data systems, distinguish event-time truth from processing-time state; for distributed or cloud systems, distinguish logical semantics from physical placement. This decomposition is also the basis for debugging: inspect intermediate values, compare against a tiny reference implementation, and verify local invariants before blaming the most sophisticated component.

deepSections.title: Formal view, objective, and invariants
deepSections.body: A compact formal statement prevents hand-waving. For Forecast Monitoring & Retraining, the existing mathematical or logical anchor is: define the transformation as a function from valid inputs and state to outputs, then state the invariant that must hold for every valid execution. Do not memorize symbols without semantics. Name the domain of every quantity, whether it is observed or latent, and what is optimized or conserved. If an objective is minimized, ask what population quantity its empirical version estimates and whether weighting changes that target. If there is no optimization objective, identify the safety or correctness invariant instead: ordering, idempotence, conservation, normalization, boundedness, monotonicity, consistency, or resource limits. Numerical details matter whenever repeated operations amplify rounding or conditioning problems. Systems details matter whenever retries, parallelism, caching, or partial failure can produce a different logical result. Statistical details matter whenever data reuse or selection changes the sampling distribution. A strong implementation test usually expresses at least one invariant as an assertion on a toy case, plus a second test that fails when a key assumption is deliberately violated. The runnable lab follows that pattern so the chapter has an executable claim rather than code that merely prints a plausible number.

deepSections.title: Design choices and trade-offs
deepSections.body: There is rarely one universally best configuration of Forecast Monitoring & Retraining. The useful question is which trade-off matters for the declared workload. Start with the key points Track error by horizon/segment., Bias can matter more than symmetric error., Backfill/revisions complicate evaluation. and ask how each affects accuracy or correctness, compute, memory, latency, sample efficiency, interpretability, and operational complexity. Prefer a simple baseline when it is easier to validate and already meets the decision threshold. Add complexity only when a measured failure mode justifies it. Hyperparameters and architecture choices should therefore map to observable consequences rather than folklore. At small scale, an exact method may be clearer; at large scale, approximation, batching, partitioning, caching, streaming, quantization, or asynchronous work may be necessary. Those changes create new error surfaces, so every optimization needs a quality or correctness comparison against the reference behavior. Also distinguish offline economics from online economics. A method that saves training time may increase serving cost; a denser representation may improve quality but violate memory limits; a stronger consistency guarantee may reduce throughput; a more aggressive safety rule may increase false positives. Document the chosen operating point, alternatives considered, and the condition that would trigger revisiting the choice. This turns a technical preference into an auditable engineering decision.

deepSections.title: Evaluation and diagnostics
deepSections.body: Evaluation for Forecast Monitoring & Retraining must test the claim the system will make in operation. Appropriate evidence in this module includes rolling-origin backtests, naive baselines, horizon slices, and calibration. Do not collapse everything into one average. Slice by the dimensions that change difficulty: time, horizon, class, scale, entity, language, device, traffic regime, subgroup, or workload shape as appropriate. Always compare against a meaningful baseline on the same examples or requests. Keep comparisons paired when possible so improvement is not confused with a change in evaluation population. If labels or outcomes arrive late, define maturity before scoring. If the system is stochastic, use repeated seeds or confidence intervals; if observations are dependent, use a dependence-aware uncertainty procedure rather than row-level iid assumptions. Diagnostics should include input validity, intermediate-state checks, output distribution checks, and resource behavior. For probabilistic outputs, evaluate calibration as well as discrimination or sharpness. For ranking or generation, combine task metrics with qualitative failure review. For infrastructure, test both steady state and recovery behavior. A release gate should specify what must improve, what must not regress, and which failures are blocking even if the global average looks good.

deepSections.title: Failure modes and debugging strategy
deepSections.body: The dominant risks around Forecast Monitoring & Retraining include temporal leakage, regime change, horizon decay, and delayed labels. Existing chapter cautions are also important: Applying the method without checking its assumptions or data-generating process. Choosing it because it is familiar rather than comparing against an appropriate baseline. A debugging process should make these risks observable. Start from the smallest reproducible case and verify the data contract. Check shapes, units, ordering, timestamps, identifiers, missingness, labels, masks, seeds, and configuration before changing the algorithm. Next verify a baseline and an invariant. Then inspect intermediate representations or state transitions to locate the first point where expected behavior diverges. Separate data bugs, objective mismatch, optimization or numerical issues, capacity limits, and deployment integration problems because they require different remedies. Introduce controlled perturbations: duplicate an event, reorder input, remove a feature, change batch size, delay a dependency, corrupt one field, or reduce precision. A robust implementation should either preserve its invariant or fail loudly according to a documented policy. Finally, test recovery. Retries should not duplicate side effects, model rollback should restore a compatible preprocessing path, and cached or checkpointed state should have a version. A system that works only on the happy path is not a complete implementation of the concept.

deepSections.title: Production operation, monitoring, and communication
deepSections.body: Shipping Forecast Monitoring & Retraining means operating a versioned contract over time. In production, validate assumptions on real data, monitor the quantities that can drift, and keep a simple baseline so added complexity has a measurable reason to exist. Persist the model, code, data or schema version, configuration, dependencies, and any state needed to reproduce behavior. Monitor the inputs that drive the mechanism, the outputs users experience, and the internal resource or quality signals that predict failure. Use separate alerts for correctness, quality, latency, saturation, data freshness, and safety so one aggregate health score does not hide the cause. Canary or shadow changes when the blast radius is meaningful. Define rollback artifacts in advance and verify that rollback restores compatible schemas, feature logic, tokenizer or preprocessing state, and dependent services. Record enough request or batch metadata to reproduce failures without retaining data that violates privacy or retention requirements. When explaining the system to another engineer or interviewer, use a stable narrative: problem contract, mechanism, formal invariant, trade-off, evaluation evidence, failure mode, and production control. That sequence demonstrates understanding more reliably than listing tool names. The final question is always operational: what signal would tell you this implementation is no longer trustworthy, and what safe action follows?

lessons.title: Point, Contextual & Collective Anomalies
lessons.interviewAnswer: A point anomaly is unusual by itself, a contextual anomaly is unusual only relative to conditions such as time or peer group, and a collective anomaly is a sequence or set whose joint pattern is unusual even when each element is ordinary. Before choosing a detector, I define the observation unit, normal reference population, available context, score, alert budget, investigation action, and label process. I fit transformations only on clean historical reference data and avoid future leakage. Detection scores rank cases; thresholds are operational policies chosen from capacity and cost. I monitor score and alert-rate drift, duplicate incidents, group coverage, delayed labels, and the share of alerts caused by data-pipeline failures.
keyPoints: Anomaly is relative to a reference distribution, context, and action.
Point, contextual, and collective anomalies require different features and units.
A continuous anomaly score is separate from the alert threshold.
Reference contamination, future leakage, and cold starts can dominate algorithm choice.
Investigation feedback and alert burden are part of the model system.
lessons.why: Teams often begin with an algorithm and only later discover that nobody agreed on what an anomaly meant. A detector then flags weekend traffic because the baseline ignored seasonality, large customers because the reference mixed segments, or duplicate telemetry because the ingestion pipeline broke. The taxonomy prevents those mistakes by asking whether unusualness is global, conditional, or joint. It also clarifies evaluation. If the action is to investigate accounts, scoring transactions independently can produce a hundred alerts for one incident. If the goal is early warning, labels that arrive after an investigation cannot be treated as immediate ground truth. A simple robust contextual score with a clear baseline and response path can outperform a sophisticated unsupervised model whose alerts are unactionable. The purpose is not to find rare numbers; it is to identify deviations whose timely review changes an outcome.
lessons.intuition: Imagine a transaction amount of 500. Globally it may be common. For a customer who normally spends between 10 and 30, it is a contextual anomaly; for a wholesale merchant it may be routine. Now imagine twenty transactions of 20 dollars in one minute. Each point looks normal, but their temporal cluster is collectively abnormal. A point detector looks at position in feature space. A contextual detector first conditions or residualizes against time, entity, cohort, or state, then scores the remaining surprise. A collective detector changes the unit to a window, run, graph neighborhood, or sequence representation. These choices define what information is compared. The threshold comes afterward: a score of six has no intrinsic operational meaning until calibrated against a reference distribution, capacity, or risk. An alert is a decision with downstream cost, not a mathematical property of a row.
lessons.deepDive: Anomaly detection begins with a reference contract, not a model name. Point, contextual, and collective anomalies differ in the unit and comparison that make deviation visible. The score only ranks surprise under that representation; an operational policy converts it to finite investigation work. Reference contamination, selective labels, incident duplication, and drift therefore belong to the core statistical problem rather than to post-deployment cleanup.
lessons.workedExample: A 500-dollar payment is ordinary for wholesale accounts but 20 robust deviations above a personal account's past median. A contextual score flags the latter. Separately, twenty 20-dollar payments within one minute are individually typical but the rolling count is far above the account's historical minute-level rate, so a collective detector opens one incident. The response queue deduplicates both signals by account and time window and records which rule drove review.

commonMistakes.misconception: An anomaly is simply a rare value.
commonMistakes.correction: Rarity is relative to a reference and may be legitimate. Important anomalies can be common-valued points in an abnormal context or sequence.

commonMistakes.misconception: The contamination parameter discovers the true anomaly rate.
commonMistakes.correction: It usually controls the score threshold or expected flag fraction. Treat it as a policy or modeling assumption and validate against operations.

commonMistakes.misconception: Unreviewed alerts and nonalerts are negatives.
commonMistakes.correction: Review is selective and labels are delayed. Use audit samples, exploration, and explicit unknown status to avoid feedback bias.

commonMistakes.misconception: Retraining on the newest window automatically adapts safely.
commonMistakes.correction: A persistent attack or outage can be absorbed into normal. Quarantine updates, use trusted windows, and require drift and incident review.

followUps.question: What is the difference between novelty and outlier detection?
followUps.answer: Novelty detection learns from a reference assumed normal and scores new data; outlier detection allows contamination in the fitted data and identifies unusual training cases. APIs and evaluation semantics can differ.

followUps.question: How do you evaluate an unsupervised detector with few labels?
followUps.answer: Use incident replay, synthetic mechanism tests, expert review with blinded sampling, random audits of nonalerts, stability checks, and eventual label or downstream outcomes. Avoid treating injected points as the only truth.

followUps.question: Why aggregate alerts into incidents?
followUps.answer: One underlying failure can create thousands of anomalous rows. Incident grouping aligns evaluation and workload with the action unit and prevents alert storms from dominating metrics.

lessons.production: Deploy the reference builder, feature transformations, detector, threshold, and incident grouper as one versioned system. Enforce event-time semantics and past-only windows. Track missing or unseen contexts, reference age and contamination quarantine, score distribution, alert and unique-incident volume, per-entity concentration, reviewer yield, audit-sample misses, label delay, and time to detection. Store enough explanation and provenance for triage while minimizing sensitive data exposure. Rate-limit alert storms, define cooldown and escalation, and provide deterministic invariants as fallback when the learned detector or context store fails. A new mode may be legitimate business growth or an attack; do not auto-normalize it without review. Canary threshold or representation changes on replayed traffic and shadow queues. Roll back the full reference-plus-score-plus-policy bundle when workload, missed-incident, latency, or subgroup criteria exceed declared bounds.
lessons.description: An anomaly is an observation or pattern that violates an explicitly defined expectation in a context that matters. Point anomalies are individually unusual, contextual anomalies are unusual only given time, segment, or state, and collective anomalies are ordinary-looking elements whose sequence or group is abnormal. This chapter turns that taxonomy into an engineering contract: define the unit, reference population, context, score direction, contamination assumptions, action, label horizon, and cost of review before choosing an algorithm. You will distinguish anomaly detection from novelty detection, supervised rare-event classification, data-quality validation, and change-point detection. Robust scaling, peer groups, seasonal residuals, sequence windows, and representation choices are connected to the kinds of deviation they expose. A worked payment example shows why the same amount can be normal for one merchant and anomalous for another, while a burst of small transactions can be collectively suspicious. The lab builds contextual median/MAD scores and a collective window score, compares with standardized residuals, and verifies invariance and context behavior. Production guidance prioritizes alert budgets, deduplication, investigation feedback, drift, cold starts, and safe fallback over arbitrary score cutoffs.
learningObjectives: Classify point, contextual, and collective anomalies and connect each type to a valid reference set and representation.
Write an anomaly-detection contract covering unit, context, score, threshold, action, feedback, and failure costs.
Distinguish outlier detection, novelty detection, supervised rare-event prediction, change-point detection, and data validation.
Build and verify robust contextual and collective scores without using future or cross-entity information.

deepSections.title: Choose the anomaly unit before the algorithm
deepSections.body: A point anomaly is a single observation far from an expected distribution, such as an impossible sensor value or a transaction with an unusual feature combination. A contextual anomaly is unusual conditional on context: temperature in winter, latency for a route, amount for an account, or activity for a time of day. A collective anomaly is a group whose relationship, frequency, order, or duration is abnormal: a burst, a coordinated graph pattern, a stalled sequence, or a waveform. The same raw event can belong to multiple units. Define whether one score corresponds to a row, entity-day, session, rolling window, graph substructure, or incident. This determines labels, independence, deduplication, and action. The reference population must match the unit and intended normal regime. Global peer mixing can turn minority but valid modes into false positives. Context features must be available at scoring time and must not encode outcomes or future observations. When context is high-cardinality, use shrinkage or hierarchical baselines so cold entities borrow information rather than receiving unstable estimates.

deepSections.title: Separate neighboring problem formulations
deepSections.body: Outlier detection assumes the training data may contain anomalies and seeks unusual cases in that set. Novelty detection assumes training data represent normal behavior and scores new observations against the learned support; using a novelty API on its own training rows can change neighborhood semantics. Supervised rare-event classification has labeled positives and estimates a conditional event score or probability; its label and sampling biases differ from unsupervised detection. Change-point detection locates persistent distributional regime boundaries rather than isolated cases. Data validation checks declared invariants such as nonnegative amounts or referential integrity; a deterministic rule is preferable when the failure is known. Forecast-residual monitoring predicts an expected value and scores deviation conditional on past information. These formulations can be combined, but their evidence differs. A support score is not a calibrated event probability. An outlier is not necessarily bad data. A change point may describe a legitimate launch. State the target, available labels, contamination, reference update policy, and whether the objective is discovery, triage, prevention, or system health.

deepSections.title: Make normal behavior representable
deepSections.body: Raw distance is meaningful only after units, skew, categories, and periodicity are handled. Fit robust or standard scaling on the reference period, not on a batch containing the cases being judged. Log transforms can prevent large legitimate values from dominating, but preserve zeros and units explicitly. Contextual detection may subtract a seasonal forecast, compare within peer group, or form features such as deviation from an entity's rolling median using past-only windows. Collective detection aggregates counts, transitions, run length, spectral energy, or embedding sequences. Representation can erase anomalies: daily aggregation hides a one-minute burst, while a rolling maximum may expose it. It can also manufacture them: one-hot unseen categories or missing context may create extreme vectors. Start with domain rules, robust univariate baselines, and simple multivariate distance or density scores. Use synthetic and replayed incidents to verify that the representation exposes the intended failure before adding a complex detector. Record which transformations depend on mutable reference data.

deepSections.title: Turn scores into bounded, learnable operations
deepSections.body: A detector should usually produce a continuous score. Select a threshold or top-k policy using investigation capacity, false-negative severity, alert grouping, and latency. A fixed contamination fraction asserts how many cases to flag; it does not estimate the true anomaly rate. Calibrate thresholds on a later reference window and stress them under seasonal and volume changes. Group duplicate alerts into incidents and apply cooldowns so one outage does not exhaust the queue. Log score, contributing context, threshold version, model version, and disposition. Labels are selectively observed because only alerts are reviewed; unreviewed cases are not confirmed negatives. Random audits or exploration samples can measure blind spots and correct feedback bias. Monitor score distribution, alerts per unit time and entity, unique incidents, investigation yield, time to detection, label delay, and downstream loss. If reference behavior drifts, update cautiously with quarantine so recent anomalies do not become normal automatically. Provide deterministic fallbacks and rate limits when context or model service is unavailable.

lessons.math: A contextual robust score can be z_i^robust=|x_i-m_c|/[1.4826 MAD_c+epsilon], where m_c and MAD_c are median and median absolute deviation estimated from past reference observations in context c. A collective window score might be S_t=sum_{j=t-w+1}^t I(z_j^robust>q) or a deviation of window count from its contextual expectation. These are scores, not probabilities. A threshold h defines alert A_i=I(S_i>=h); h should minimize or constrain an operational loss using representative data and an incident-level unit.

workedExamples.title: Global score versus peer score
workedExamples.body: Two merchants have medians 25 and 600. A transaction of 500 is a global middle value, about 32 robust scales above the first merchant's median, and close to the second merchant's normal range. A global detector misses the contextual anomaly and may overflag the legitimate high-value merchant. Estimate peer baselines from past data with minimum-support shrinkage.

workedExamples.title: Collective burst from ordinary points
workedExamples.body: Each login request has normal device and location features. One account emits 40 requests in 30 seconds after months below three per minute. Point scores remain low, but a past-only rolling-count feature is extreme. Alert once at the account-window level and preserve event detail for investigation.

exercises.prompt: Why might daily aggregation miss a fraud burst?

lessons.title: Isolation Forest
lessons.interviewAnswer: Isolation Forest creates many random partition trees. Each node chooses a feature and a split within that feature's observed range; points that are few and different tend to be isolated in fewer edges. The anomaly score is roughly 2 raised to minus average path length divided by the expected path length c(psi) for a random binary-search tree of subsample size psi. Subsampling makes training fast and can reduce masking by large normal clusters. Tree scores rank unusualness; contamination generally sets a threshold and does not discover prevalence. I validate feature representation, stability across seeds and reference windows, score direction, alert budget, and labeled or audited incident yield, and I watch for clustered anomalies, duplicates, high-dimensional noise, drift, and unsupported novelty use.
keyPoints: Shorter average isolation path means more anomalous under the fitted forest.
c(psi) normalizes paths across subsample size.
Subsampling is central to both efficiency and detection behavior.
Feature representation shapes the random partitions even without distance metrics.
A threshold and contamination setting are policy layers over a score.
lessons.why: Distance and density estimation become expensive or unreliable in many dimensions, while anomaly labels are often scarce. Isolation Forest uses random partitioning with expected O(t psi log psi) construction for t trees of small subsample size psi and supports fast scoring. It works well when anomalies occupy sparse, easily separated regions. It also provides a useful nonlinear baseline that requires less scaling sensitivity than Euclidean methods under affine feature rescaling. Its apparent plug-and-play simplicity is dangerous, however. A high score means easy isolation under the encoded training reference, not fraud or failure probability. Random cuts can miss a dense anomalous cluster, and hundreds of irrelevant features reduce the chance of choosing an informative split. A production implementation needs the same reference, feature schema, score sign, and threshold semantics in every environment.
lessons.intuition: Place a lone point far from a cloud on graph paper. A random vertical or horizontal cut often separates it immediately. A point near the cloud center needs many cuts before it occupies a leaf alone. Repeat random trees and average the number of edges. This is isolation depth. A small tree built from a random subsample gives anomalies more chances to stand alone rather than being masked by the full population. The score converts average depth to a common scale: depth near the random-tree expectation suggests ordinary behavior, much shorter depth suggests anomaly, and much longer depth suggests dense normal structure. The mechanism is relative to observed ranges. Duplicate points cannot be separated by numeric cuts, dense anomalous groups may protect one another, and a curved normal manifold can be fragmented by axis-aligned splits. More trees reduce Monte Carlo variability but cannot repair a wrong representation.
lessons.deepDive: Isolation Forest replaces density estimation with randomized search depth. The forest is a fixed ensemble of partition trees; normalized path length yields a ranking whose semantics depend on subsample, features, reference, and score direction. The method is fast because it builds small trees, not because it can ignore representation or validation. Threshold selection and incident operations remain separate from the unsupervised score.
lessons.workedExample: A tree samples eight two-dimensional telemetry rows. Seven form a cloud between 0 and 2; one row is near 8 on both axes. The root selects feature one and split 5.4, isolating the distant row after one edge. A central row remains with seven points and needs several more splits. Across 200 trees, the distant row's mean path is far below c(8), so its normalized score is high. The alert threshold still depends on incident budget and validation.

commonMistakes.misconception: Isolation Forest estimates the probability that a case is anomalous.
commonMistakes.correction: It produces a normalized isolation score or transformed decision value. Probability requires a labeled calibration model and stable sampling process.

commonMistakes.misconception: Contamination learns how many true anomalies exist.
commonMistakes.correction: It usually sets an offset or threshold fraction. Validate it as an operational policy rather than interpreting it as discovered prevalence.

commonMistakes.misconception: Feature scaling never matters for Isolation Forest.
commonMistakes.correction: Affine scaling has limited effect on uniform range cuts, but nonlinear transforms, clipping, categories, sparse encodings, and feature selection materially change partitions.

commonMistakes.misconception: More trees fix any missed anomaly pattern.
commonMistakes.correction: More trees reduce random variance. They cannot fix a contaminated reference, irrelevant representation, dense anomaly cluster, or missing collective context.

followUps.question: Why use small subsamples?
followUps.answer: They keep trees shallow and cheap and reduce masking or swamping effects by limiting how many points compete in one tree. Psi also determines the scale of detectable structure.

followUps.question: What happens to duplicate observations?
followUps.answer: Numeric splits may be unable to separate identical rows, so leaves retain multiple points and add expected continuation length. Duplicate-heavy data can suppress anomaly contrast and should be diagnosed.

followUps.question: Is Isolation Forest suitable for novelty detection?
followUps.answer: Yes when fitted on a trusted normal reference and scored on new data, with API semantics and drift handled correctly. Fitting on the current contaminated batch asks a different outlier-detection question.

lessons.production: Version the training window, sampling query, feature transformations, missing and category handling, subsample and feature sample sizes, tree count, random seed, score sign, contamination setting, and threshold. Golden rows should verify exact score direction and stable rank. Track missingness, unseen categories, duplicates, feature support, score and path-depth distributions, alerts and unique incidents, top-alert stability, latency, reviewer yield, and audit misses. Do not refresh from unreviewed recent traffic automatically; quarantine candidate references and shadow-score them. Apply per-entity and global rate limits so an outage cannot consume the queue. Protect anomalous records because they often contain sensitive incidents. Retain domain-rule fallback and the prior forest/reference/threshold bundle. Canary representation or psi changes on replay and later data, then roll back the whole bundle when capacity, yield, missed-incident, subgroup, or latency limits fail.

lessons.description: Isolation Forest scores anomalies by how quickly random recursive partitions isolate them. Instead of estimating a density or distance directly, each tree selects a feature and a split between observed minimum and maximum; unusual points tend to reach small leaves along shorter paths. This chapter derives path length, the unsuccessful binary-search-tree normalization c(psi), ensemble scoring, subsampling, feature subsampling, and the separate role of contamination or threshold policy. You will understand why the method is computationally attractive, where axis-aligned random cuts work, and why clustered anomalies, irrelevant high-dimensional features, one-hot representations, duplicates, missing values, and concept drift can defeat it. The chapter distinguishes outlier fitting from novelty scoring and explains score-direction differences in library APIs. A worked telemetry example traces a shallow isolation path. The lab builds a true reusable isolation-tree ensemble from scratch, compares it with scikit-learn, and verifies deterministic, translation, range, and injected-outlier invariants. Production guidance freezes sampling, seed, feature and score conventions; monitors path and alert distributions, support, duplicate rates, and incident yield; and uses a later reference window plus an explicit alert budget rather than presenting contamination as a learned prevalence.
learningObjectives: Build isolation trees and compute normalized ensemble anomaly scores from path lengths.
Explain how subsample size, tree count, feature representation, and contamination affect behavior.
Diagnose masking, clustered anomalies, irrelevant features, duplicates, and drift.
Deploy Isolation Forest with reproducible score direction, thresholds, references, and incident-level monitoring.

deepSections.title: Random isolation trees and path length
deepSections.body: For each tree, draw without replacement up to psi reference observations. At a node, select a feature with nonzero range and choose a split uniformly between its minimum and maximum; send rows left or right and recurse until one row remains, all rows are identical on splittable features, or a height limit is reached. The path length h(x) is the number of edges followed by query x. When recursion stops with n_leaf>1, add an expected continuation c(n_leaf) rather than pretending every duplicate was isolated. For n>2, c(n)=2H_{n-1}-2(n-1)/n, using the harmonic number approximation from unsuccessful binary-search-tree paths; c(2)=1 and c(0)=c(1)=0. A forest averages h_t(x). Build each tree once and reuse it for all queries: randomly choosing new splits while scoring each point would not define one model. Persist tree structure or a deterministic library artifact and test scoring parity. Missing values need an explicit preprocessing or routing rule because standard split comparison is undefined.

deepSections.title: Normalized score, subsampling, and threshold policy
deepSections.body: The original normalized score is s(x,psi)=2^{-E[h(x)]/c(psi)}. Scores near one correspond to very short paths; scores near one-half correspond roughly to expected random-tree depth; lower scores indicate long paths in dense regions. Libraries may expose a decision function where larger is more normal, a raw score with the opposite sign, or labels -1 and 1 after subtracting an offset. Write a score-direction unit test. Psi controls locality and masking: a modest sample creates shallow trees and can expose rare points; too small may fragment legitimate local modes and too large raises cost or lets anomaly groups form their own dense region. Tree count reduces random variance. Feature subsampling can help when many irrelevant dimensions exist, but it may omit the only diagnostic feature on some trees. Contamination is commonly used to choose an offset or quantile for labels. Treat it as an assumed alert fraction or calibration setting. Choose the operational threshold on a later window using review capacity, recall constraints, or cost, and group row alerts into incidents.

deepSections.title: Representation determines what random cuts can isolate
deepSections.body: Affine scaling of one continuous feature preserves the relative positions of uniform range splits, so Isolation Forest is less sensitive to ordinary standardization than Euclidean neighbors. It is not invariant to nonlinear transforms, clipping, or category encoding. A heavy-tailed feature can devote broad ranges to legitimate extremes; a log transform may express operational separation better. Ordinal encoding invents order for categories, while one-hot encoding creates many sparse binary axes. Rare categories may be isolated merely because they are rare, and high-cardinality features can dominate. Duplicates and quantization create unsplittable leaves. Clustered anomalies can have long paths and be missed; a rare legitimate cluster can be overflagged. With many irrelevant features, random feature selection wastes depth and score contrast collapses. Correlated oblique structure can require many axis cuts, motivating extended isolation variants or a better representation. Fit on a trusted, time-appropriate reference and compare performance across feature subsets, seeds, psi, and later periods. Do not fit preprocessing on the scored batch, since a surge can redefine its own normality.

deepSections.title: Evaluate rankings and alerts as separate artifacts
deepSections.body: With labels, evaluate score ranking using precision-recall and recall at the review budget, then evaluate the chosen threshold at incident level. ROC AUC can look strong while a tiny false-positive rate produces an overwhelming queue. Without labels, replay known incidents, inject mechanism-faithful anomalies, run blinded expert review, and audit samples below threshold. Synthetic points should test a hypothesis, not serve as the sole benchmark. Measure stability of top alerts across seeds and reference windows. In production, log average path or score, feature/reference version, threshold, and incident group. Monitor score quantiles, alert count, unique incidents, per-entity concentration, path-depth distribution, duplicate rate, unseen categories, missingness, review yield, and delayed outcomes. Separate normal regime growth from attacks through quarantine and human review before refreshing the reference. A fallback may use domain invariants and fixed rate limits. Canary new forests in shadow mode and roll back the reference, trees, and threshold together.

lessons.math: For subsample size psi, average path hbar(x)=t^{-1}sum_j h_j(x). Define c(n)=2H_{n-1}-2(n-1)/n for n>2, c(2)=1, and c(n)=0 for n<=1. The original anomaly score is s(x,psi)=2^{-hbar(x)/c(psi)}. Short hbar gives score nearer one. Expected construction is roughly O(t psi log psi) for balanced trees, with scoring O(t log psi), although degenerate splits, representation, and implementation affect constants.

workedExamples.title: Trace an isolated point
workedExamples.body: With psi=256, c(psi) is approximately 10.25. If an observation averages path length 3, s=2^{-3/10.25}, about 0.82. If another averages 11, its score is about 0.48. The exact action boundary is not universally 0.5; calibrate it under the deployment reference and API convention.

workedExamples.title: A clustered attack can be masked
workedExamples.body: Five hundred coordinated events share one unusual feature pattern. When the forest fits on a window containing all of them, they split among themselves and may obtain ordinary path lengths. Use a trusted earlier novelty reference, temporal/count collective features, or supervised signals and quarantine reference refreshes.

exercises.prompt: What does a shorter path mean in an isolation tree?
exercises.solution: The point was separated from the sampled reference with fewer random cuts, which is evidence of unusual sparse placement under that representation.

exercises.prompt: Why can a dense anomalous cluster receive ordinary scores?
exercises.solution: Its members protect one another and require multiple partitions to isolate, especially if included in the fitting reference. Use trusted novelty data or collective/context features.

exercises.prompt: A library returns lower values for more anomalous cases. What should you do?
exercises.solution: Document the API convention and normalize score direction at the boundary. Add a golden test asserting that a known extreme ranks above normal cases in the application's convention.

lessons.title: Local Outlier Factor & One-Class SVM
lessons.interviewAnswer: LOF finds points whose local reachability density is low relative to their k nearest neighbors, so a point can be normal inside a sparse cluster even if it is globally far away. A score near one is locally comparable; much above one suggests a local outlier. One-Class SVM instead estimates a regularized support boundary in feature space, often with an RBF kernel; nu controls a trade-off related to training errors and support vectors, while gamma controls boundary scale. I fit scaling on a trusted reference, tune k or gamma/nu on later data and alert capacity, and distinguish LOF's default training-set outlier mode from novelty=True scoring of new points. I monitor distance concentration, neighbor/support-vector stability, reference contamination, score direction, and incident yield.
keyPoints: LOF compares local density with neighbor density rather than using one global threshold.
Reachability distance reduces unstable density estimates around very close neighbors.
One-Class SVM learns a kernel support boundary, not an event probability.
Scaling, metric, k, gamma, nu, and reference purity define the detector.
LOF outlier and novelty modes have different scoring semantics.
lessons.why: A dataset can have a dense city-center cluster and a sparse rural cluster, or high-volume and low-volume customer segments. Global distance or density thresholds often call the sparse legitimate mode anomalous. LOF asks a more local question and can surface a point that is isolated relative to nearby peers. One-Class SVM is useful when trusted normal examples define a complicated boundary and new observations must be accepted or rejected. Both methods are powerful precisely where their assumptions are risky: neighborhoods depend on a metric, kernels depend on scale, and a contaminated or drifting reference changes the definition of support. They can be computationally expensive and difficult in high-dimensional sparse encodings. The correct choice comes from the anomaly geometry and scoring mode, not from which method draws the most attractive two-dimensional boundary.
lessons.intuition: LOF asks whether a point lives in a neighborhood as crowded as the neighborhoods of its nearest neighbors. For each point, look at k neighbors and estimate how far one must reach to connect to them, using the neighbor's own k-distance as a floor. The inverse average reach is local density. Divide the neighbors' average density by the point's density. If the ratio is near one, it belongs locally; if much larger, the point is in a local pocket of low density. One-Class SVM has a different picture: map reference points through a kernel and place a maximum-margin boundary separating most of them from the origin. New points outside receive negative decision values. A narrow RBF kernel can wrap each point and overfit; a broad kernel can collapse distinct modes into a crude region. Both scores need an operational threshold and later evidence.
lessons.deepDive: LOF and One-Class SVM encode two distinct notions of normality: density relative to local neighbors and membership in a regularized kernel support. Their scores are inseparable from metric, scale, neighborhood or bandwidth, reference, and scoring mode. Correct API semantics and operational validation matter as much as formulas, especially when new modes, dimensionality, or reference contamination change the learned support.
lessons.workedExample: A dense urban cluster has typical neighbor distance 0.1; a sparse rural cluster has distance 0.8. A rural point with neighbors also spaced near 0.8 gets LOF near one even though it is globally distant. Another point one unit beyond the rural cluster has reach distances much larger than its neighbors' local scale and LOF above two. An RBF One-Class SVM can represent both modes if gamma and nu are tuned on a reference containing both, but can exclude the sparse mode when the boundary is too tight.

commonMistakes.misconception: LOF is simply distance to the kth neighbor.
commonMistakes.correction: LOF compares the point's local reachability density with neighbor densities, enabling different legitimate density regions.

commonMistakes.misconception: nu is the known anomaly percentage.
commonMistakes.correction: Nu controls the optimization trade-off and relates to bounds under assumptions. It is a tuning parameter, not a prevalence estimate.

commonMistakes.misconception: LOF fit_predict and novelty prediction are interchangeable.
commonMistakes.correction: Training-set scoring excludes self and uses transductive semantics; novelty mode scores unseen cases against the stored reference. Follow the exact API contract.

commonMistakes.misconception: Standard scaling solves high-dimensional neighbor failure.
commonMistakes.correction: It aligns units but does not prevent distance concentration, irrelevant features, sparse-category artifacts, or unstable neighbor identities.

followUps.question: Why use reachability distance instead of raw distance in LOF?
followUps.answer: The neighbor's k-distance floors very small pair distances, stabilizing local density within clusters and reducing sensitivity to tightly packed duplicate-like points.

followUps.question: How do you choose k?
followUps.answer: Match expected anomaly and cluster scale, then examine performance and ranking stability over a defensible range using later data, incidents, audits, and workload.

followUps.question: What does gamma do in RBF One-Class SVM?
followUps.answer: It sets kernel locality. Large gamma produces narrow, potentially fragmented support around points; small gamma produces a broader smoother boundary.

lessons.production: Serialize the exact scaler and transforms, metric, feature weights, reference identifiers, k and tie convention or kernel/gamma/nu, support vectors or neighbor index, score direction, offset, and threshold. Golden tests should cover known inliers, local outliers, and API novelty behavior. Monitor feature and k-distance drift, neighbor overlap, support-vector fraction, score distribution, alert and incident volume, latency, memory, approximate-index recall, missing contexts, and subgroup concentration. Quarantine reference refreshes and audit both alerts and nonalerts. Rate-limit neighbor-query failures and retain hard domain rules if the index or model is unavailable. Canary parameter and reference changes in shadow mode, comparing top-alert overlap and later yield. Roll back transforms, reference/index, estimator, and threshold as one unit when workload, detection, fairness, or latency criteria fail.
lessons.description: Local Outlier Factor (LOF) and One-Class SVM answer two different versions of support-based anomaly detection. LOF compares a point's local reachability density with the densities of its neighbors, making it useful when normal data contain regions of different density. One-Class SVM learns a regularized boundary around reference data in a kernel feature space and is naturally framed as novelty detection. This chapter derives k-distance, reachability distance, local reachability density, LOF, the one-class support-estimation objective, kernel and nu behavior, and the practical difference between transductive training-set outlier detection and scoring unseen observations. You will learn why distance scaling, categorical representation, neighborhood size, curse of dimensionality, reference contamination, kernel bandwidth, and computational cost control results. A worked two-cluster example shows why a global distance score can overflag a sparse legitimate cluster while LOF compares locally. The lab implements LOF from first principles, compares exactly with scikit-learn, adds an RBF One-Class SVM novelty score, and verifies density-ratio, permutation, and injected-outlier behavior. Production guidance freezes reference, scaler, metric, k, kernel, nu, and score direction while monitoring neighbor distances, support vectors, alert burden, and cold-start coverage.
learningObjectives: Compute LOF from k-neighbor reachability distances and explain local density-ratio interpretation.
Explain One-Class SVM support estimation, kernel bandwidth, nu, and decision score semantics.
Distinguish training-set outlier detection from novelty scoring and avoid invalid LOF API use.
Diagnose scaling, high-dimensional distance concentration, reference contamination, and computational constraints.

deepSections.title: From k-distance to local outlier factor
deepSections.body: Choose a distance metric and neighborhood size k. The k-distance of object o is the distance to its kth nearest neighbor, with tie handling defining the exact neighborhood. For query p and neighbor o, reachability distance reach_k(p,o)=max{k-distance(o), d(p,o)}. The floor prevents extremely close pairs from creating arbitrarily high density and makes density relative to the neighbor's local scale. Local reachability density lrd_k(p) is the reciprocal of the average reachability distance from p to its k neighbors. Finally LOF_k(p) is the average lrd of p's neighbors divided by lrd(p). Values around one mean comparable local density; values substantially greater than one indicate lower density than neighbors. LOF is a ranking, not a calibrated probability, and values below one can indicate unusually dense points. k defines the scale of locality. Too small makes scores noisy and duplicate-sensitive; too large crosses cluster boundaries and approaches a global comparison. Examine a range of k values and tie behavior, and align the neighborhood with the action and expected anomaly size.

deepSections.title: One-Class SVM as regularized support estimation
deepSections.body: One-Class SVM maps x to feature space phi(x) and finds a hyperplane that separates most mapped reference points from the origin while maximizing margin. A common primal minimizes ||w||^2/2 +(1/(nu n))sum_i xi_i-rho subject to w^T phi(x_i)>=rho-xi_i and xi_i>=0. The decision f(x)=w^T phi(x)-rho is positive inside the learned region and negative outside under common APIs. Nu in (0,1] controls a trade-off and has theoretical relationships as an upper bound on training outlier fraction and lower bound on support-vector fraction under conditions; it is not a known anomaly prevalence. With an RBF kernel exp(-gamma||x-x'||^2), gamma controls locality. Scaling changes distances and therefore the entire boundary. Small gamma gives a broad smooth support; large gamma creates fragmented regions and can label much of new space abnormal. Kernel fitting scales poorly with n, motivating linear approximations or alternative detectors for large streaming data. Fit on trusted normal data for novelty detection and validate boundary stability under legitimate modes.

deepSections.title: Scoring mode, representation, and dimensionality
deepSections.body: scikit-learn's default LOF performs outlier detection on the fitted sample and exposes negative_outlier_factor_. With novelty=False, scoring arbitrary new rows is intentionally unavailable. Set novelty=True only when training data are treated as reference normals; then predict or decision_function should be used on unseen data, not interpreted as reproducing fit_predict on training rows because neighbor membership differs. Normalize score direction at the application boundary. Both LOF and RBF One-Class SVM rely on meaningful distances. Standardize numeric features inside the reference pipeline, use robust transforms for skew, and choose categorical or learned representations that preserve semantic similarity. In high dimensions, pairwise distances concentrate and nearest-neighbor identities become unstable; irrelevant columns can overwhelm signal. Assess neighbor overlap across resamples, intrinsic dimension, feature subsets, and domain metrics. One-hot rare categories and missingness patterns can dominate. Approximate neighbor indexes change results and need recall-versus-latency tests. Reference contamination can create local density pockets or expand a support boundary, so quarantine updates and retain audit samples.

deepSections.title: Select scale and threshold with operational evidence
deepSections.body: Tune k, metric, scaler, gamma, and nu using known incidents, realistic injection, expert review, and later normal regimes. Avoid choosing parameters solely from the fraction of flags on the fit data. Evaluate precision-recall or recall at top-k when labels exist, plus incident-level workload and time to detection. For novelty systems, create chronological reference and test windows and include legitimate new modes. Compare LOF and One-Class SVM with robust univariate, Isolation Forest, and supervised baselines. Measure top-alert stability across bootstrap references and small parameter changes. In serving, LOF requires storing or indexing reference points; One-Class SVM stores support vectors. Budget memory and latency, version index build and approximate search settings, and define behavior when the reference or feature store is stale. Monitor k-distance distributions, support-vector fraction, score quantiles, unseen contexts, alert and incident volume, review yield, and subgroup concentration. A fallback should preserve hard safety rules and rate limits rather than return every request as normal.

lessons.math: For neighbor set N_k(p), reach_k(p,o)=max{kdist(o),d(p,o)}. Then lrd_k(p)=[|N_k(p)|^{-1}sum_{o in N_k(p)}reach_k(p,o)]^{-1} and LOF_k(p)=|N_k(p)|^{-1}sum_{o in N_k(p)}lrd_k(o)/lrd_k(p). A One-Class SVM solves min_{w,xi,rho} ||w||^2/2 +(nu n)^{-1}sum xi_i-rho with w^T phi(x_i)>=rho-xi_i. Its signed decision is f(x)=sum_i alpha_i K(x_i,x)-rho under the dual representation.

workedExamples.title: Calculate a simple LOF ratio
workedExamples.body: Suppose p's average reachability distance is 4, so lrd(p)=0.25. Its three neighbors have lrd values 0.5, 0.6, and 0.4. Their mean is 0.5, giving LOF(p)=0.5/0.25=2. The point is about half as locally dense as its neighbors under this k and metric.

workedExamples.title: Novelty mode changes the question
workedExamples.body: A detector learns from a month of reviewed normal telemetry and scores next month's events. Use LOF novelty mode or One-Class SVM. Do not call a training-set outlier API and assume its neighbor exclusions and thresholds transfer unchanged to unseen rows; validate the exact deployed method.

lab.goal: Implement Local Outlier Factor exactly, compare it with scikit-learn, and verify local-density, permutation, and One-Class SVM novelty behavior.
lab.buildIt:
import numpy as np
def lof_scores(X,k=10):
    X=np.asarray(X,float); dist=np.sqrt(((X[:,None,:]-X[None,:,:])**2).sum(2))
    np.fill_diagonal(dist,np.inf)
    neighbors=np.argsort(dist,axis=1)[:,:k]
    kdist=np.take_along_axis(dist,neighbors[:,-1:],axis=1).ravel()
    reach=np.empty((len(X),k))
    for i in range(len(X)):
        js=neighbors[i]; reach[i]=np.maximum(kdist[js],dist[i,js])
    lrd=1/np.maximum(reach.mean(1),1e-12)
    lof=np.array([lrd[neighbors[i]].mean()/lrd[i] for i in range(len(X))])
    return lof
rng=np.random.default_rng(8)
dense=rng.normal([0,0],[.18,.18],size=(60,2))
sparse=rng.normal([4,4],[.55,.55],size=(35,2))
X=np.vstack([dense,sparse,[[4,7]]])
lof=lof_scores(X,k=12)
lab.useIt:
from sklearn.neighbors import LocalOutlierFactor
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.svm import OneClassSVM
sk_lof=LocalOutlierFactor(n_neighbors=12,contamination='auto').fit_predict(X)
sk_score=-LocalOutlierFactor(n_neighbors=12,contamination='auto').fit(X).negative_outlier_factor_
oc=make_pipeline(StandardScaler(),OneClassSVM(nu=.05,gamma='scale')).fit(X[:-1])
oc_score=-oc.decision_function(X)
lab.verifyIt:
assert np.allclose(lof,sk_score,atol=1e-10)
assert lof[-1]==lof.max() and lof[-1]>1.5
assert oc_score[-1]>np.median(oc_score[:-1])
perm=np.random.default_rng(4).permutation(len(X))
permuted=lof_scores(X[perm],k=12)
restored=np.empty_like(permuted); restored[perm]=permuted
assert np.allclose(restored,lof,atol=1e-10)
assert 0.8<np.median(lof[:-1])<1.2
assert np.isfinite(lof).all()

lessons.title: Rare-event Evaluation & Alert Thresholds
lessons.interviewAnswer: For rare events I separate ranking, probability, threshold, and operations. I report precision-recall curves or average precision, recall at the actual top-k review capacity, and threshold-specific counts and cost; accuracy is usually uninformative and ROC AUC can conceal false-positive burden. Precision and AP depend on prevalence, so the evaluation population and sampling weights must match deployment. If scores are probabilities I also test calibration and proper losses. I choose the threshold on validation data from costs, capacity, or a recall constraint, then evaluate once on a later untouched window at the incident level. Because labels are delayed and only alerts may be reviewed, I track unknowns, random-audit nonalerts, and report uncertainty.
keyPoints: Ranking, calibration, threshold performance, and queue operations are different layers.
Precision and the PR baseline change with event prevalence.
Recall at k directly represents a fixed review budget.
Thresholds must be chosen outside the final evaluation window.
Selective and delayed labels require audits and explicit unknown status.
lessons.why: A model can have ROC AUC 0.98 and still generate thousands of false alerts for each true event if deployment prevalence is one in a million. Conversely, a modest precision can be economically valuable when an event is catastrophic and review is cheap. Rare-event systems are constrained queues and decision policies, not leaderboard classifiers. Evaluation must therefore show denominators and absolute counts, connect score thresholds to capacity and cost, and respect how cases become labeled. Investigators often review only high scores, creating a feedback loop where nonalerts appear negative by default. One underlying incident can create many positive rows and inflate recall while exhausting the queue. A rigorous evaluation aligns the observation and action unit, uses later representative data, reports uncertainty driven by the small number of events, and makes clear which conclusions depend on assumed costs or prevalence.
lessons.intuition: Imagine sorting one million cases by score and reviewing the top one thousand. The most useful question is how many true incidents appear in that queue and how many reviews are wasted—not how many of the 999,000 unreviewed negatives were ranked below a random positive. Precision is the fraction of reviewed alerts that are true; recall is the fraction of all true events found. As the threshold falls, recall tends to rise while the queue expands and precision often falls. The precision-recall curve traces this trade-off. Its no-skill precision baseline is the event prevalence, so a score with 10 percent precision is extraordinary when prevalence is 0.01 percent but poor when prevalence is 20 percent. Threshold selection places a price or constraint on one operating point. Calibration adds a different claim: among cases assigned probability p, roughly p should occur.
lessons.deepDive: Rare-event evaluation is a measurement and queue-design problem. Ranking metrics describe score order, probability metrics describe beliefs, threshold counts describe one rule, and incident operations describe the actual action. Prevalence, sampling, label maturity, review selection, and grouping alter the evidence. A credible claim therefore includes raw counts, capacity, uncertainty, and a locked later-window policy.
lessons.workedExample: A fraud stream has 100,000 transactions and 100 confirmed fraud incidents. Investigators can review 500. The top 500 scores contain 60 incidents: precision@500=12 percent, recall@500=60 percent, and lift is 0.12/0.001=120. The remaining 40 incidents define missed-event loss. If alerts cluster into 300 accounts, report both transaction and account-incident counts and evaluate queue capacity after grouping.

commonMistakes.misconception: High accuracy means a rare-event model works.
commonMistakes.correction: An all-negative classifier can have near-perfect accuracy while recall is zero. Show positive support, counts, precision, recall, and capacity metrics.

commonMistakes.misconception: ROC AUC fully captures false-alert burden.
commonMistakes.correction: FPR divides by a huge negative population. Inspect PR, absolute FP, precision, and the actual operating point or top-k queue.

commonMistakes.misconception: Average precision is independent of prevalence.
commonMistakes.correction: Its precision terms and random baseline depend on the event rate. Evaluate under representative prevalence or correct known sampling.

commonMistakes.misconception: Cases without a positive label are negatives.
commonMistakes.correction: Labels may be delayed, selectively reviewed, or unknown. Track maturity and audit nonalerts instead of silently assigning zero.

followUps.question: What is the difference between PR AUC and average precision?
followUps.answer: Average precision weights precision by recall increments without linear interpolation; trapezoidal PR area interpolates between operating points and can differ, sometimes optimistically.

followUps.question: When is recall at k preferable?
followUps.answer: When the system reviews a fixed number of cases per period. It directly measures the event fraction captured within that capacity.

followUps.question: How do you compare precision across populations?
followUps.answer: Account for prevalence and sampling. Report each population's event rate, counts, and threshold; use reweighting only when selection probabilities and transport assumptions are credible.

lessons.production: Version the label definition and maturity, observation and incident grouping, model score, calibration, capacity, costs, threshold or top-k policy, cooldown, and reviewer workflow. Dashboards should show TP, FP, FN estimates, unknowns, precision, recall or audited recall, top-k yield, backlog, time to review, time to detect, prevalence, label maturity, and subgroup counts with uncertainty. Sample nonalerts for audit and exploration to break selective-label feedback. Reconcile alert rows to unique incidents and downstream outcomes. Secure sensitive alert explanations and investigator notes. Define degradation behavior when volume exceeds capacity, labels stop arriving, or score service fails. Shadow and replay new score-policy pairs on identical cohorts, freeze final later-window evaluation, and roll back calibration, grouping, and threshold with the model when cost, yield, backlog, or fairness limits fail.
lessons.description: Rare-event evaluation asks whether a score produces useful decisions when positives are scarce, labels are delayed or selective, and false alerts consume real capacity. Accuracy and even ROC AUC can hide failure: predicting every case negative gives high accuracy, while a small false-positive rate can still overwhelm investigators. This chapter derives precision, recall, specificity, false-positive rate, precision-recall curves, non-interpolated average precision, lift, recall at k, calibration, proper scores, expected cost, and threshold selection. It explains why precision and average precision depend on prevalence, why evaluation must use the deployment sampling unit and time window, and why alert deduplication changes the metric denominator. You will handle uncertain labels, review selection, delayed outcomes, incident grouping, confidence intervals, and threshold overfitting. A worked fraud queue example turns a review budget into recall-at-capacity and net value. The lab implements confusion metrics, average precision, top-k recall, and coherent cost selection, then verifies them against scikit-learn. Production guidance versions score and policy separately, monitors queue and incident yield, audits nonalerts, and recalibrates or reselects thresholds when prevalence, cost, capacity, or label processes change.
learningObjectives: Compute and interpret rare-event ranking, threshold, probability, and capacity metrics without conflating them.
Explain how prevalence, sampling, label delay, and incident grouping affect precision-recall evidence.
Select a threshold from coherent costs or operational constraints on data independent of final evaluation.
Design production audits and confidence estimates for selective, delayed, and incomplete labels.

deepSections.title: Start with counts, denominators, and units
deepSections.body: At threshold h, true positives TP are alerted events that are positive, false positives FP alerted negatives, false negatives FN missed positives, and true negatives TN unalerted negatives. Precision=TP/(TP+FP), recall=TP/(TP+FN), specificity=TN/(TN+FP), and false-positive rate=FP/(FP+TN). Always report the four counts and undefined cases, since a ratio can hide tiny support. Accuracy=(TP+TN)/N is dominated by TN under extreme imbalance. Balanced accuracy averages recall and specificity but still does not show queue burden. Decide whether a positive is a row, account-day, episode, or unique incident. If one outage creates 10,000 anomalous metrics, row recall can be perfect while incident detection is one and alert volume is disastrous. Apply grouping and cooldown before calculating operational precision. For time-to-detection tasks, include latency and whether the event was detected before an action deadline. Stratify by source and subgroup, but show confidence intervals because rare slices may contain only a handful of positives.

deepSections.title: Evaluate ranking under the deployment prevalence
deepSections.body: ROC curves plot recall against false-positive rate, and ROC AUC is the probability a random positive outranks a random negative under standard assumptions. It is prevalence-invariant as a ranking statistic, but an apparently tiny FPR multiplied by a huge negative population creates a large queue. Precision-recall curves plot precision against recall and expose that burden. Average precision in scikit-learn is sum_n (R_n-R_{n-1})P_n over score thresholds; it is not trapezoidal interpolation and can differ from PR AUC. A random ranking's expected precision is prevalence. Precision, PR curves, and AP change when prevalence changes even if class-conditional score distributions are stable. Evaluate on a representative prevalence or use known sampling weights. Case-control or deliberately balanced test sets cannot produce deployment precision without correction. Recall at k asks what fraction of positives are found in the top k scores; precision at k gives queue yield. Lift at k divides precision at k by prevalence. Report variation across time because event clusters can make one period look much better than another.

deepSections.title: Choose one operating policy without contaminating the test
deepSections.body: Select a threshold on validation data after defining costs or constraints. With calibrated probability p, false-positive cost C_FP and false-negative cost C_FN under zero cost for correct decisions, alert when p>=C_FP/(C_FP+C_FN), assuming costs are coherent and constant. Real systems add investigation cost, intervention side effects, event severity, customer friction, and capacity; solve expected value or a constrained policy instead of forcing a universal F1 score. F_beta encodes a precision-recall trade-off but not explicit economic units. A top-k policy naturally handles fixed capacity and score-distribution drift, though its threshold and risk change with volume. Calibration is separate from ranking. Reliability diagrams, log loss, and Brier score help when probabilities drive decisions, but rare bins need uncertainty and representative sampling. Fit a calibrator on predictions from data independent of base-model fitting. Once threshold, grouping, and cooldown are selected, lock them and evaluate on an untouched later window. Repeatedly tuning to the test queue overstates performance.

deepSections.title: Account for selective labels, delay, and uncertainty
deepSections.body: Many event labels arrive after chargeback, failure analysis, or investigation. Exclude immature outcomes from final denominators or use survival and censoring methods; treating them as negatives creates temporal bias. Review labels are selectively observed because the score decides what investigators see. An unreviewed case is unknown, not a confirmed negative. Randomly audit a statistically useful sample of nonalerts and explore some score ranges to estimate missed-event rate and support future learning. Adjudication can be noisy or policy-dependent; record label source, timestamp, confidence, and definition version. Deduplicate correlated rows and use cluster or block bootstrap intervals when events share incidents, entities, or time. With ten positives, recall can change ten percentage points from one case; report intervals and raw counts. Compare policies using paired replay on identical cases. In production, monitor alert backlog, disposition delay, audit yield, label maturity, prevalence estimates, score and threshold drift, and incident outcomes. A queue that exceeds capacity changes which alerts receive labels and invalidates naive trend comparisons.

lessons.math: Precision=TP/(TP+FP), recall=TP/(TP+FN), FPR=FP/(FP+TN). Average precision AP=sum_n(R_n-R_{n-1})P_n at successive score thresholds. Precision at top k=TP_k/k and recall at k=TP_k/P, where P is total positives. Lift@k=precision@k/prevalence. With calibrated p and constant costs, alert if C_FP(1-p)<=C_FN p, equivalently p>=C_FP/(C_FP+C_FN). Costs, capacities, and sampling weights must correspond to the deployment unit.

workedExamples.title: Low FPR can still overload a queue
workedExamples.body: At prevalence 0.01 percent in ten million daily cases, there are about 1,000 positives and 9,999,000 negatives. Recall 90 percent with FPR 0.1 percent yields 900 TP and about 9,999 FP: precision is only about 8.3 percent and the queue is nearly 10,900, despite an impressive-looking FPR.

workedExamples.title: Delayed labels distort last week's precision
workedExamples.body: Chargebacks mature over 60 days. Calculating precision after seven days labels most recent alerts negative and makes a new policy appear worse. Freeze evaluation cohorts until maturity or use an explicit censoring model, and compare policies at equal label age.

lab.goal: Implement rare-event counts, top-k metrics, average precision, and cost-sensitive threshold selection, then verify against scikit-learn and imbalance invariants.
lab.useIt:
from sklearn.metrics import average_precision_score,confusion_matrix
sk_ap=average_precision_score(y,score)
threshold=best[1]
sk_tn,sk_fp,sk_fn,sk_tp=confusion_matrix(y,score>=threshold,labels=[0,1]).ravel()
lab.verifyIt:
assert abs(ap-sk_ap)<1e-12
assert (p3,r3)==(2/3,2/3)
tp,fp,fn,tn=counts(y,score,threshold)
assert (tp,fp,fn,tn)==(sk_tp,sk_fp,sk_fn,sk_tn)
all_negative_accuracy=np.mean(y==0)
assert all_negative_accuracy==0.85
assert top_k(y,np.zeros_like(score),len(y))[1]==1.0
assert best[0]<=8*np.sum(y)
assert abs(np.mean(y)-0.15)<1e-12
lab.shipIt: Version label and incident definitions, maturity window, score, grouping, costs, capacity and threshold; report raw counts and uncertainty, audit nonalerts, monitor backlog and prevalence, and roll back score-plus-policy together.

exercises.prompt: An all-negative classifier is 99.9 percent accurate. What is its recall?
exercises.solution: Zero if any positives exist. Accuracy is dominated by negatives and is not sufficient for rare-event evaluation.

exercises.prompt: Why can AP fall after deployment even if ranking distributions within classes are unchanged?
exercises.solution: A lower deployment prevalence reduces precision at operating points and therefore AP. Compare representative populations and prevalence.

exercises.prompt: You tuned the threshold on the final test window. What must change?
exercises.solution: Treat that window as validation, lock the policy, and evaluate once on a new untouched later window. Otherwise the reported operating performance is optimistically selected.
