lessons.title: Censoring, Survival & Hazard Functions
lessons.interviewAnswer: For event time T, survival is S(t)=P(T>t), cumulative incidence without competing risks is F(t)=1-S(t), hazard is the instantaneous event rate among those still event-free, and cumulative hazard H(t)=integral h with S(t)=exp(-H(t)). Right censoring at C observes Y=min(T,C) and delta=I(T<=C), so a censored row contributes evidence of survival through Y, not an event at Y and not no information. Kaplan-Meier and standard likelihoods need censoring independent of event time, often conditional on modeled covariates. I define time origin, event, entry, competing events, and label maturity; use risk sets that respect delayed entry; and inspect censoring and follow-up by segment before modeling.
keyPoints: Censoring preserves partial ordering information and is not ordinary missingness.
Hazard is a conditional rate among survivors, not a probability by itself.
S(t)=exp[-H(t)] in continuous time and F(t)=1-S(t) without competing risks.
Truncation changes who enters the sample; censoring limits what is observed after entry.
Time origin, risk set, censoring, and label maturity define the estimand.
lessons.why: If half of customers have not churned by the data cutoff, their eventual churn times are unknown but their observed tenure is valuable evidence. Ordinary regression discards them or substitutes the cutoff as if it were churn, biasing time estimates downward and changing the target with every extraction date. Survival analysis uses likelihood or risk-set contributions consistent with partial observation. The same ideas apply to failure, conversion, recovery, default, and time to next purchase. Most serious mistakes occur before the model: inconsistent time origins, future-derived features, invisible delayed entry, outcome definitions that change over calendar time, or censoring tied to severity. A mathematically correct estimator cannot recover a target that the dataset never observed. A full survival contract therefore begins with the observation process and supported horizon.
lessons.intuition: Picture one subject moving along a time line from an origin. An event marker ends the event-free path. A censor marker says observation stopped while the subject was still event-free; the true event lies somewhere to the right. At time t, the risk set contains subjects who entered and remain event-free and observed just before t. The survival curve is the remaining fraction in a probabilistic population, not simply the raw fraction without recorded events. Hazard asks: among those who made it to t, how rapidly do events occur next? A high hazard over a short interval can still correspond to a moderate probability, and a population with high early hazard changes composition as vulnerable subjects leave. Cumulative hazard adds rate over time, while survival exponentiates its negative. If people with worsening condition leave observation sooner, censoring carries outcome information and naive risk sets become optimistic.
lessons.deepDive: Survival analysis is built around partial observation of an ordered event time. Survival, hazard, and cumulative hazard are linked but answer different questions; censoring and truncation specify which pieces of each subject's path are observed. Independent censoring and cohort entry are identification assumptions, so the time and observation contract must be as carefully versioned as the model itself.
lessons.workedExample: Three customers start at signup. A churns at month 2, B is active at the month-4 extraction and is right-censored at 4, and C churns at 5 after entering an observed program at month 1. B tells us T_B>4. C belongs to risk sets only after month 1 if cohort observation truly begins then. Replacing B's time with an event at 4 invents churn; deleting B overrepresents short lifetimes.

commonMistakes.misconception: A censored time is the event time with a special flag.
commonMistakes.correction: It is a lower bound for right censoring: the subject remained event-free through that time. Its likelihood and risk-set contribution differ from an event.

commonMistakes.misconception: Hazard 0.3 means a 30 percent chance of immediate event.
commonMistakes.correction: Continuous hazard is a rate with inverse-time units. Probability over an interval depends on integrated hazard, approximately h dt only for a short interval.

commonMistakes.misconception: Independent censoring can be checked conclusively from observed data.
commonMistakes.correction: It is an identification assumption about unobserved event times. Observed patterns, reasons, sensitivity analyses, and covariates can support but not prove it.

commonMistakes.misconception: Dropping censored observations avoids assumptions.
commonMistakes.correction: It discards long event-free follow-up and usually biases the sample toward early events, adding stronger selection problems.

followUps.question: What is the relationship between hazard and survival?
followUps.answer: Cumulative hazard integrates the instantaneous rate and survival is exp(-H) in continuous time. Hazard can vary even when survival is always nonincreasing.

followUps.question: How is left truncation different from left censoring?
followUps.answer: Left truncation means subjects with early events never enter the observed sample; left censoring means a subject is observed but event time is known only to be before a bound.

followUps.question: What is restricted mean survival time?
followUps.answer: It is integral_0^tau S(t)dt, the expected event-free time accumulated through a chosen supported horizon tau, avoiding unsupported tail extrapolation.

lessons.production: Treat the event-time table as a versioned measurement product. Persist entity, origin, delayed entry, event definition and priority, competing event, cutoff, time zone, duration unit, censor reason, feature landmark, label maturity, and supported horizon. Validate timestamp ordering, unique entity episodes, no post-origin leakage, event ascertainment, and follow-up completeness. Monitor censoring fraction and reasons, number at risk by horizon, entry and calendar cohort, event incidence, delayed labels, competing events, and support across important groups. Protect sensitive event and health-like timelines. Refuse or flag predictions beyond training support and define fallback horizons. When upstream observation or intervention changes, shadow and revalidate rather than automatically treating the new censoring process as benign. Roll back extraction, transformations, estimator, and horizon policy together.
lessons.description: Survival analysis models the time until an event while preserving partial information from subjects whose event time is not fully observed. Right censoring says only that the event occurs after the last observed time; left censoring, interval censoring, delayed entry, and truncation encode different observation mechanisms and require different risk sets or likelihoods. This chapter develops the event time T, survival S(t), distribution F(t), density f(t), hazard h(t), cumulative hazard H(t), and their relationships. You will distinguish a conditional instantaneous hazard from event probability over an interval, state independent or conditionally independent censoring assumptions, and see why dropping censored rows or treating censoring time as the event creates bias. A worked subscription example traces a cohort through events, censoring, and changing risk sets. The lab computes survival, hazard, and cumulative hazard for a discrete event-time distribution, compares an exponential model with SciPy, and verifies monotonicity and algebraic identities. Production guidance fixes time origin, event, horizon, time zones, censoring, delayed entry, competing events, and label maturity; monitors censoring by segment and calendar time; and blocks evaluation beyond supported follow-up. Survival methods use censored information—they do not make informative loss to follow-up harmless.
learningObjectives: Define survival, cumulative distribution, density, hazard, and cumulative hazard and move correctly between them.
Distinguish right, left, interval censoring, left truncation, and delayed entry in both words and risk-set logic.
State the censoring and observation assumptions required for common estimators and diagnose likely informative censoring.
Construct a leakage-safe event-time dataset with explicit origin, event, maturity, entry, and competing-event semantics.

deepSections.title: Survival, hazard, and cumulative hazard describe different views
deepSections.body: Let nonnegative random variable T be time from a declared origin to an event. The distribution function F(t)=P(T<=t) and survival S(t)=P(T>t)=1-F(t). For continuous T with density f, hazard h(t)=lim_{dt to 0}P(t<=T<t+dt | T>=t)/dt=f(t)/S(t). It has units of inverse time and can exceed one; h(t)dt approximates a short-interval conditional probability. Cumulative hazard H(t)=integral_0^t h(u)du and S(t)=exp[-H(t)]. Thus a constant hazard lambda yields exponential survival exp(-lambda t), while increasing or nonmonotone hazards create different shapes. Discrete-time hazard p_t=P(T=t|T>=t) is a probability and survival is a product of (1-p_u), not a continuous integral. Median survival solves S(t)<=0.5 when identified. Mean survival is integral S(t)dt and may be unidentifiable beyond the last observed event without tail assumptions; restricted mean survival time integrates only to a declared horizon tau. Always state the time scale and whether functions are conditional on covariates.

deepSections.title: Censoring and truncation encode different observation mechanisms
deepSections.body: Under right censoring, observe Y=min(T,C) and event indicator delta=I(T<=C). A censored subject contributes survival through C. Left censoring says T is below a bound, such as an event already present at first inspection. Interval censoring says T lies between two visits. Administrative censoring occurs at a planned study cutoff; loss to follow-up can be informative. Left truncation or delayed entry means subjects are observed only if T exceeds entry time E; those who failed earlier never appear. Risk sets must include a subject only after E. Length-biased sampling can overrepresent long survivors. Right truncation includes only events observed before a boundary and uses a different likelihood. Recurrent events and multi-state transitions are not one terminal time repeated in rows without dependence modeling. Time-varying covariates require start-stop intervals built from information available at each time. Define whether the event at the exact censor time counts as observed, how ties are resolved, and how time zones and batch cutoffs affect ordering.

deepSections.title: Independent censoring is an identification assumption
deepSections.body: Product-limit and standard survival likelihood methods commonly require event time and censoring to be independent, perhaps conditional on included covariates or history. This does not mean censoring times and event times must look marginally unrelated. Administrative cutoff can censor recent entrants earlier while remaining conditionally noninformative given entry calendar time. Informative dropout occurs when latent risk influences observation termination after conditioning. Compare censoring curves, reasons, and follow-up across covariates, sites, treatment, and calendar cohorts. Model censoring with inverse-probability weights when a credible conditional exchangeability and positivity story exists, and use sensitivity analyses for unmeasured dependence. Weights can explode where continued observation probability is near zero, so truncate transparently and report effective sample size. Treating a competing event as independent censoring estimates a hypothetical cause-specific process, not real-world probability of the event of interest. Selection into the cohort and event ascertainment can be more damaging than right censoring itself. State which assumptions identify each reported estimand.

deepSections.title: Build one consistent event-time contract
deepSections.body: Choose entity and time origin, such as signup, device installation, diagnosis, or model scoring. Define the event and whether recurrence, competing outcomes, or terminal events stop follow-up. Store entry time, last known event-free time, event time when observed, event type, observation cutoff, censor reason, and data provenance. Compute durations from immutable timestamps in one unit and reject negative or zero durations according to model requirements. Features must be measured at baseline or represented as time-varying intervals; lifetime totals leak future information. For prediction at landmark time l, include only subjects event-free and observable at l and redefine horizon from that landmark. Freeze a label-maturity window so recent cohorts are not compared with mature cohorts. Report number at risk and censoring support at every horizon. In production, predicted survival beyond the training follow-up tail is extrapolation. Limit decisions to supported horizons, monitor changes in enrollment, observation, event capture, and intervention, and version the extraction cutoff with the model.

lessons.math: For continuous T, S(t)=P(T>t), F(t)=1-S(t), f(t)=dF/dt, h(t)=f(t)/S(t), H(t)=integral_0^t h(u)du, and S(t)=exp[-H(t)]. Right-censored observation is (Y,delta)=(min(T,C),I[T<=C]). Under a parametric model with independent censoring, an event contributes f(Y)=h(Y)S(Y) and a censored observation contributes S(Y), yielding likelihood product_i h(Y_i)^{delta_i}S(Y_i). Delayed entry conditions risk membership on E_i<=t<Y_i.

workedExamples.title: Hazard is not interval probability
workedExamples.body: At time t, a constant hazard of 0.2 per month gives one-month event probability 1-exp(-0.2)=0.181, not exactly 0.2. Over three months conditional survival is exp(-0.6)=0.549 and event probability 0.451.

workedExamples.title: Restricted mean when the tail is unsupported
workedExamples.body: If follow-up supports survival through 12 months but the curve never falls below 0.5, median survival is not identified in that window. Report 12-month survival and restricted mean to 12 months rather than extrapolating a median from an unverified tail.

lab.goal: Compute discrete survival, hazard, and cumulative hazard and compare a continuous exponential model with SciPy while verifying algebraic and monotonicity invariants.
lab.buildIt:
import numpy as np
def discrete_survival(pmf):
    pmf=np.asarray(pmf,float); assert np.all(pmf>=0) and pmf.sum()<=1+1e-12
    survival_before=1-np.r_[0,np.cumsum(pmf[:-1])]
    hazard=np.divide(pmf,survival_before,out=np.zeros_like(pmf),where=survival_before>0)
    survival_after=np.cumprod(1-hazard)
    return survival_before,hazard,survival_after
pmf=np.array([.10,.18,.144,.1152,.09216])
s_before,h,s_after=discrete_survival(pmf)
t=np.array([0.,1.,2.,3.]); rate=.2
S=np.exp(-rate*t); H=rate*t
lab.useIt:
from scipy.stats import expon
scipy_S=expon(scale=1/rate).sf(t)
scipy_h=np.full_like(t,rate)
lab.verifyIt:
assert np.allclose(s_after,1-np.cumsum(pmf))
assert np.all((h>=0)&(h<=1))
assert np.all(np.diff(s_after)<=0)
assert np.allclose(S,scipy_S)
assert np.allclose(S,np.exp(-H))
assert np.allclose(scipy_h,rate)
assert abs(s_before[0]-1)<1e-12
assert abs((1-S[-1])-(1-np.exp(-rate*t[-1])))<1e-12
lab.shipIt: Version origin, entry, event, event type, cutoff, censor reason, duration units and supported horizon; test timestamp ordering, monitor censoring and follow-up by cohort, and block unsupported tail predictions or stale label comparisons.

exercises.prompt: A user is active at a 90-day data cutoff. What does their row tell you?
exercises.solution: Their event time exceeds observed follow-up through 90 days, assuming event capture is complete. Encode right censoring rather than churn at 90 or deletion.

exercises.prompt: If h(t)=0.1 constantly, compute S(5).
exercises.solution: H(5)=0.5 and S(5)=exp(-0.5), approximately 0.607.

exercises.prompt: A high-risk patient is more likely to leave follow-up. Why is this dangerous?
exercises.solution: Censoring depends on latent event risk, so observed survivors are selectively healthier. Standard independent-censoring estimators can overstate survival without adjustment or sensitivity analysis.

lessons.title: Kaplan–Meier Estimator & Log-rank Test
lessons.interviewAnswer: At each distinct event time t_j, Kaplan-Meier multiplies the previous survival by 1-d_j/n_j, where d_j events occur among n_j subjects at risk just before the time. Censoring does not drop the curve; it removes subjects from later risk sets. The estimate assumes event and censoring times are independent, possibly conditional on group, and tails with few at risk are uncertain. The log-rank test compares observed group events with expected events from pooled risk sets across times and is most sensitive to roughly proportional hazard differences. I show confidence bands and numbers at risk, inspect crossing curves and censoring by group, predeclare the horizon and multiplicity plan, and avoid causal interpretation without an identified treatment comparison.
keyPoints: KM is a product of conditional survival fractions at event times.
Censoring removes later risk membership but does not create a survival drop.
Tail precision depends on numbers at risk, not only the plotted line.
Log-rank tests equality of survival experience with risk-set weighting.
Group curves and p-values do not adjust confounding or establish causality.
lessons.why: A raw fraction event-free at each time treats recently enrolled or lost subjects incorrectly. Kaplan-Meier uses each subject for exactly the period they are known to be event-free, producing a transparent nonparametric baseline for reliability, retention, recovery, and clinical follow-up. It reveals time shape before regression assumptions are imposed and supports group comparison. Its familiar step plot can create false confidence: a long flat tail may represent one censored subject, confidence intervals can be wide, and different censoring processes can distort comparisons. The log-rank test compresses a whole-curve comparison to one statistic and can miss or obscure time-varying differences. The chapter therefore treats risk tables, horizon support, estimand, and censoring diagnostics as part of the visualization rather than optional footnotes.
lessons.intuition: Survival to day 30 can be decomposed into surviving each event time along the way. If 10 subjects are at risk and two events occur, estimated conditional survival through that time is 8/10. If later five remain at risk and one event occurs, multiply by 4/5. A censored subject was event-free until their censor time, so they belong in earlier denominators and disappear afterward. The step curve falls only at events. Log-rank repeats a related comparison across groups: at each pooled event time, if group A contains 60 percent of the risk set, it is expected to contain about 60 percent of events under equal hazards. Sum observed minus expected differences and scale by their variance. Early times with large risk sets often contribute more stable information than sparse late times.
lessons.deepDive: Kaplan-Meier is a sequence of conditional risk-set calculations, not a smoothed fraction of observed events. Its transparency makes assumptions visible through steps, censor marks, and numbers at risk. Log-rank aggregates group event imbalance across those same risk sets. Both are powerful baselines, but tail support, censoring, nonproportional differences, multiplicity, and group assignment determine what their curves and p-values can support.
lessons.workedExample: Six subjects have observed times [2 event, 3 censored, 4 event, 4 event, 5 censored, 7 event]. At time 2, n=6,d=1, so S=5/6. At time 4, the time-3 censor has left, n=4,d=2, so S=(5/6)(2/4)=5/12. At time 7, only one subject remains and events, so S reaches zero. The large last step has little support and should be shown with number at risk one.

commonMistakes.misconception: The KM curve drops at censoring marks.
commonMistakes.correction: Censoring removes a subject from later risk sets but is not an event, so survival does not drop at that time.

commonMistakes.misconception: A flat late tail proves durable survival.
commonMistakes.correction: The tail may have almost nobody at risk. Show risk counts and uncertainty and restrict interpretation to supported horizons.

commonMistakes.misconception: A significant log-rank test quantifies the treatment benefit.
commonMistakes.correction: It tests a group difference and gives no standalone magnitude. Report survival or RMST contrasts and justify causal interpretation separately.

commonMistakes.misconception: Crossing curves can be summarized safely by one hazard ratio or log-rank p-value.
commonMistakes.correction: Effects can change sign and cancel. Examine time-varying contrasts, prespecified RMST, and appropriate interaction models.

followUps.question: Why is KM a product instead of one minus cumulative observed event fraction?
followUps.answer: Each event probability is conditional on remaining at risk; multiplying conditional survival fractions correctly incorporates changing denominators from censoring and events.

followUps.question: What happens if the median is not reached?
followUps.answer: It is not estimable within observed follow-up. Report supported fixed-horizon survival or restricted mean rather than calling the median infinite.

followUps.question: When is log-rank less powerful?
followUps.answer: When differences are strongly nonproportional or cross, when few events occur, or when censoring and group composition reduce comparable risk-set information.

lessons.production: Generate curves only from versioned cohort, event, entry, cutoff, censoring and tie definitions. Publish event counts, censor marks, pointwise or simultaneous uncertainty as appropriate, and a number-at-risk table at meaningful times. Define minimum risk count and maximum supported horizon; visually truncate or warn beyond it. Monitor group and calendar-cohort censoring, follow-up maturity, event capture, late-arriving data, curve changes, and risk-set composition. Small groups can disclose sensitive outcomes, so enforce aggregation and access controls. Predeclare comparison groups, horizons, weights, and multiplicity. Rebuild all groups on the same cutoff. Shadow extraction changes and retain prior tables and curves. Roll back the source cohort and rendering together if risk sets, censoring, or event counts no longer reconcile.

lab.goal: Implement Kaplan-Meier and the two-sample log-rank statistic, use SciPy for the chi-square tail, and verify censoring, monotonicity, symmetry, and identical-group behavior.
lab.buildIt:
import numpy as np
def kaplan_meier(time,event):
    time=np.asarray(time,float); event=np.asarray(event,int)
    event_times=np.unique(time[event==1]); surv=[]; at_risk=[]; events=[]; s=1.0
    for t in event_times:
        n=int(np.sum(time>=t)); d=int(np.sum((time==t)&(event==1)))
        s*=1-d/n; at_risk.append(n); events.append(d); surv.append(s)
    return event_times,np.array(surv),np.array(at_risk),np.array(events)
def logrank(t1,e1,t0,e0):
    times=np.unique(np.r_[np.asarray(t1)[np.asarray(e1)==1],np.asarray(t0)[np.asarray(e0)==1]])
    oe=0.0; var=0.0
    for t in times:
        n1=np.sum(np.asarray(t1)>=t); n0=np.sum(np.asarray(t0)>=t); n=n1+n0
        d1=np.sum((np.asarray(t1)==t)&(np.asarray(e1)==1)); d0=np.sum((np.asarray(t0)==t)&(np.asarray(e0)==1)); d=d1+d0
        oe+=d1-d*n1/n
        if n>1: var+=n1*n0*d*(n-d)/(n*n*(n-1))
    return oe*oe/var if var>0 else 0.0
time=np.array([2,3,4,4,5,7],float); event=np.array([1,0,1,1,0,1])
km_t,km_s,nrisk,deaths=kaplan_meier(time,event)
t1=np.array([2,4,5,7,8],float); e1=np.array([1,1,0,1,0])
t0=np.array([3,6,7,9,10],float); e0=np.array([1,1,0,1,0])
stat=logrank(t1,e1,t0,e0)
lab.verifyIt:
assert np.allclose(km_t,[2,4,7])
assert np.allclose(km_s,[5/6,5/12,0])
assert np.array_equal(nrisk,[6,4,1])
assert np.all(np.diff(km_s)<=0)
assert abs(logrank(t1,e1,t0,e0)-logrank(t0,e0,t1,e1))<1e-12
assert logrank(t1,e1,t1,e1)==0
assert 0<=pvalue<=1
# Censoring without an event does not create a KM step.
assert 3 not in km_t and 5 not in km_t
lab.shipIt: Version cohort, origin, entry, event, cutoff, censoring and tie rules; publish confidence and risk tables, suppress unsupported tails, monitor group censoring, and roll back data extraction and presentation with the estimator.

lessons.description: The Kaplan-Meier estimator reconstructs a survival curve from right-censored observations by multiplying conditional survival proportions at distinct event times. Censored subjects contribute to risk sets until censoring and then leave without causing a drop. This chapter derives the product-limit estimator, risk-set and tie conventions, Greenwood-style uncertainty, median and restricted-mean interpretation, group curves, and the log-rank test as an observed-minus-expected event comparison over pooled risk sets. You will understand why late tails become unstable when few subjects remain, why visually crossing curves violate the simple proportional weighting intuition of log-rank, and why a significant group comparison is not automatically a causal treatment effect. A worked cohort calculates every product step and a log-rank contribution. The lab implements Kaplan-Meier and log-rank from first principles, uses SciPy for the chi-square tail, and verifies censoring, symmetry, monotonicity, and identical-group invariants. Production guidance publishes number-at-risk tables and supported horizons, versions entry and tie rules, monitors censoring imbalance and label maturity, and avoids displaying or acting on survival tails supported by only a handful of subjects. KM is a marginal nonparametric estimate under censoring assumptions, not a covariate-adjusted prediction model.
learningObjectives: Compute a Kaplan-Meier curve from event counts and changing risk sets, including tied events and censoring.
Interpret survival steps, confidence bands, median survival, number at risk, and restricted mean within supported follow-up.
Derive the log-rank observed-minus-expected statistic and state its null, weighting, and assumptions.
Diagnose crossing curves, small tails, differential censoring, delayed entry, multiplicity, and causal overinterpretation.

deepSections.title: Build the product-limit estimator from risk sets
deepSections.body: Order distinct observed event times t_1<...<t_J. Let n_j be subjects entered, uncensored, and event-free just before t_j, and d_j the number experiencing the event at t_j. The Kaplan-Meier estimate is Shat(t)=product_{t_j<=t}(1-d_j/n_j). Between event times it is constant and conventionally right-continuous. Censoring does not enter d_j but changes later n_j. When events and censoring share a recorded time, a convention is needed; common implementations count subjects as at risk for events at that time and remove censoring afterward. With delayed entry, subjects join n_j only after their entry time. Case weights and survey designs require appropriate methods rather than casual row duplication. The estimate is marginal over the sample population and contains no adjustment for covariate imbalance. Its consistency requires independent censoring in the population represented by the risk sets. If all remaining subjects are censored before another event, the curve stays flat but the tail is not evidence of indefinite survival.

deepSections.title: Uncertainty grows as risk sets shrink
deepSections.body: Greenwood's variance for log survival accumulates d_j/[n_j(n_j-d_j)] across event times, then transforms to the survival scale. Direct symmetric intervals can leave [0,1], so software often uses log-log transformations. Pointwise confidence intervals cover one chosen time under assumptions; a simultaneous band covers a curve and is wider. Always print numbers at risk beneath the plot and avoid interpreting regions below a declared minimum support. Median survival is the first time Shat(t)<=0.5; if the curve never crosses one-half, the median is not observed rather than infinite. A percentile may be nonunique on steps. Restricted mean survival time to tau is the area under Shat from zero to tau and compares expected event-free time within a supported horizon; its contrast can remain meaningful when hazards are nonproportional. Choosing tau after inspecting curves introduces selection. Quantiles, fixed-horizon survival, and restricted means should be accompanied by intervals and censoring support.

deepSections.title: Log-rank compares observed and expected events over time
deepSections.body: For two groups at each pooled event time j, let n_1j and n_0j be at risk, d_1j and d_0j events, n_j total risk, and d_j total events. Under equal instantaneous event rates, expected group-one events are e_1j=d_j n_1j/n_j. Sum O_1-E_1=sum_j(d_1j-e_1j). With hypergeometric variance sum_j n_1j n_0j d_j(n_j-d_j)/[n_j^2(n_j-1)], the squared standardized difference is asymptotically chi-square with one degree of freedom. The ordinary log-rank weighting emphasizes times with information and is powerful under proportional hazards-like alternatives. Weighted variants emphasize early or late differences but should be predeclared because searching weights inflates error. The null concerns group survival or hazard experience under censoring assumptions. A nonsignificant result is not equivalence, and a significant result gives no effect size by itself. Report curves, fixed-horizon or RMST contrasts, confidence intervals, and event counts.

deepSections.title: Crossing curves and group assignment require more than one p-value
deepSections.body: Crossing KM curves may indicate time-varying effects, heterogeneous mixtures, nonproportional hazards, informative censoring, or chance. A log-rank statistic can cancel early benefit and late harm. Plot complementary cumulative hazard or estimate time-specific and restricted-mean contrasts, then use regression with time interactions when justified. Multiple groups, endpoints, horizons, and subgroup searches require a multiplicity plan. Observational group curves confound treatment or exposure with baseline differences. Randomization supports causal comparison when adherence, censoring, intercurrent events, and estimand are handled; otherwise adjustment and causal assumptions are needed. Differential censoring by group can bias even randomized comparisons if loss depends on outcome risk. In product settings, cohort calendar time, eligibility, and intervention policies can create composition differences. Version cohort definitions and use a common data cutoff. A KM plot is an estimator of marginal survival under the observation process, not proof about why groups differ.

lessons.math: Shat(t)=product_{j:t_j<=t}(1-d_j/n_j). A Greenwood approximation is Var[log Shat(t)]=sum_{j:t_j<=t}d_j/[n_j(n_j-d_j)]. For two-group log-rank, E_1=sum_j d_j n_1j/n_j and V=sum_j n_1j n_0j d_j(n_j-d_j)/[n_j^2(n_j-1)]. Statistic (O_1-E_1)^2/V is asymptotically chi-square_1 when V>0. RMST(tau)=integral_0^tau Shat(t)dt uses only a declared finite horizon.

workedExamples.title: Product-limit steps with censoring
workedExamples.body: Ten start, two events occur at month one: multiply by 8/10. One subject is censored at month two, so survival stays 0.8. At month three seven are at risk and one event occurs: multiply by 6/7, giving 0.686. The censored subject contributed through month two but not to the month-three denominator.

workedExamples.title: One log-rank contribution
workedExamples.body: At an event time, group A has 30 of 50 at risk and there are five pooled events. Under the null A expects 5*30/50=3 events. If A observes four, O-E contribution is one. The test sums such contributions and risk-set variance over all event times.

exercises.prompt: At an event time, n=20 and d=3. What is the KM multiplier?
exercises.solution: 1-d/n=17/20=0.85. Multiply the previous survival estimate by 0.85.

exercises.prompt: Why does censoring before a later event widen uncertainty?
exercises.solution: It reduces the later risk set, so each remaining event carries more weight and less information supports the tail.

exercises.prompt: Two observational cohorts have different KM curves. Can you call the difference causal?
exercises.solution: Not without assumptions and design addressing confounding, selection, censoring, consistency, and positivity. KM is an unadjusted marginal comparison.

lessons.title: Cox Proportional Hazards Model
lessons.interviewAnswer: Cox regression models h(t|x)=h0(t)exp(x beta). At each event time, partial likelihood compares the event subject's exp(x beta) with the sum over everyone then at risk, so beta can be estimated without parameterizing h0. Exponentiating a coefficient gives a conditional hazard ratio for a one-unit covariate change if hazards are proportional. After fitting beta, a Breslow-type estimator recovers cumulative baseline hazard and S(t|x)=exp[-H0(t)exp(x beta)]. I check Schoenfeld-residual trends and time interactions, model nonlinear continuous effects, specify ties and delayed entry, use robust or clustered inference when needed, and evaluate discrimination plus calibrated survival at supported horizons. Hazard ratios are not risk ratios, and observational coefficients are not causal effects without an identification design.
keyPoints: Partial likelihood compares each event with its contemporaneous risk set.
The baseline hazard cancels for coefficient estimation but is required for absolute survival.
Hazard ratios are conditional instantaneous-rate ratios, not probability or median ratios.
Proportional hazards is a testable modeling restriction, not a property guaranteed by the algorithm.
Time origin, delayed entry, ties, feature timing, and censoring belong in the model contract.
lessons.why: Event-time prediction usually needs covariate adjustment: two customers may have the same follow-up length but very different histories, devices, treatments, or usage. Cox regression provides a semiparametric compromise. It estimates relative effects while leaving the common time pattern flexible, making it more robust to baseline-shape misspecification than a fully parametric hazard. The model also uses censored subjects while they remain at risk. Yet its apparent simplicity hides important choices. Risk sets can be wrong when entry is delayed, ties are frequent, or features include post-origin information. A constant hazard ratio can conceal early benefit and late harm. Absolute predictions require an estimated baseline and population-specific calibration. The useful workflow therefore begins with the estimand and data timeline, exposes partial-likelihood mechanics, checks assumptions graphically and quantitatively, and judges whether the model is intended for explanation, ranking, or calibrated decisions.
lessons.intuition: At a time when one event occurs, imagine a lottery among all subjects still at risk. Cox assigns each subject a ticket weight exp(x beta). Partial likelihood rewards coefficients that give the observed event subject a large share of that risk-set weight. Repeat across event times and multiply the shares. A censored person never supplies an event numerator, but appears in denominators until censoring, so their event-free follow-up is informative. The unspecified baseline hazard is common to every member of one risk set and cancels from the probability of who fails at that time. This cancellation estimates relative risk, not absolute event probability. To predict survival, accumulate observed events relative to fitted risk totals to estimate baseline cumulative hazard, then scale it by each subject's relative risk. Proportional hazards means the ratio between two fitted hazards stays constant even though both hazards may change arbitrarily with time.
lessons.deepDive: Cox regression factorizes event timing into a shared baseline and exponential relative risk. Conditioning within risk sets removes the nuisance baseline from coefficient estimation, while a second step reconstructs absolute survival. This elegant separation is only valid for correctly constructed risk sets and a defensible proportional-effect structure. Ties, entry, time-varying features, dependence, censoring, and supported horizons are therefore core model inputs, not implementation details. The result can serve inference, prediction, or decision support, but those purposes demand different diagnostics and interpretations.
lessons.workedExample: At an event time, three subjects remain with x values 0, 1, and 2. If beta=log(2), their relative-risk weights are 1, 2, and 4. If the x=2 subject experiences the event, that partial-likelihood factor is 4/(1+2+4)=4/7. If x=0 fails instead, the factor is 1/7. Across all event times, optimization chooses beta that makes observed event subjects plausible relative to the exact people who could have failed then.

commonMistakes.misconception: A hazard ratio of 2 means twice the event probability by every horizon.
commonMistakes.correction: It compares conditional instantaneous hazards. Cumulative risk depends on baseline hazard, horizon, and competing processes.

commonMistakes.misconception: Cox makes no assumptions because the baseline is unspecified.
commonMistakes.correction: It still assumes proportional covariate effects, correct functional form, risk-set construction, and appropriate censoring and dependence conditions.

commonMistakes.misconception: Censored subjects are discarded.
commonMistakes.correction: They contribute to every risk set until censoring and therefore affect the partial likelihood.

commonMistakes.misconception: A good concordance score proves calibrated survival probabilities.
commonMistakes.correction: Ranking and calibration are distinct; evaluate time-specific probabilities and Brier scores as well.

followUps.question: Why does the baseline hazard cancel from partial likelihood?
followUps.answer: Within one event time it multiplies every at-risk subject's hazard equally, so conditioning on one event leaves only relative-risk weights.

followUps.question: How do you handle a covariate that violates PH?
followUps.answer: Verify timing and form, then consider a prespecified interaction with time, stratification, piecewise effects, or an alternative estimand and model.

followUps.question: What is the distinction between time-varying covariate and coefficient?
followUps.answer: A time-varying covariate changes its observed value over follow-up; a time-varying coefficient changes how a covariate value relates to hazard over time.

lessons.production: Define a versioned counting-process table with subject ID, origin, interval start and stop, event, entry, and feature availability timestamps. Assert that intervals do not overlap, events occur once where appropriate, and features precede their risk interval. Persist encoders, spline bases, penalties, tie method, coefficients, baseline cumulative hazard, and prediction horizon. Validate on chronologically later and important subgroup cohorts with concordance, dynamic Brier or AUC, calibration, event counts, censoring support, and decision utility. Monitor feature drift, risk-set composition, event latency, censoring, baseline incidence, PH diagnostics, coefficient stability, horizon support, and calibration. Shadow changes to event extraction and interval expansion. Use bounded outputs and abstain outside covariate or follow-up support. Protect sensitive event labels and small risk sets. Roll back model, preprocessing, event definition, and baseline hazard as one compatible bundle.
lessons.description: The Cox proportional-hazards model connects covariates to event timing without requiring a parametric baseline hazard. It writes the hazard as h(t|x)=h0(t)exp(x^T beta), so exp(beta_j) is a multiplicative hazard ratio under the proportional-hazards assumption. This chapter derives the partial likelihood from risk-set comparisons, explains why censored observations still contribute information, and separates coefficient estimation from recovery of the baseline hazard and absolute survival. It covers Breslow and Efron tie handling, delayed entry, time-dependent covariates, penalization, clustered dependence, Schoenfeld residuals, nonproportional effects, and the difference between predictive and causal interpretations. A worked example computes one partial-likelihood term. The lab exposes the mechanism with a one-covariate Newton optimizer, compares it with SciPy's general optimizer, and verifies permutation invariance, gradient convergence, and survival monotonicity. Production guidance treats the risk-set construction, time origin, feature availability, baseline-hazard version, and supported horizon as model artifacts. Cox is often a strong interpretable baseline, but a hazard ratio is neither a probability ratio nor a universal summary when effects vary over time.
learningObjectives: Derive Cox partial likelihood from event-wise risk sets and interpret coefficients as conditional hazard ratios.
Recover a baseline cumulative hazard and individual survival curves after estimating regression coefficients.
Diagnose proportional-hazards violations, tie and entry conventions, nonlinear effects, and dependent observations.
Design leakage-safe validation and deployment contracts for event-time regression.

deepSections.title: Partial likelihood learns relative risk inside each risk set
deepSections.body: For subject i with covariates x_i, Cox specifies h_i(t)=h0(t)exp(x_i^T beta). At a distinct event time t_i, condition on exactly one event occurring among risk set R_i. The conditional probability that i is the event is exp(x_i beta)/sum_{k in R_i}exp(x_k beta). Multiplying these terms gives the partial likelihood. Its score sums observed covariates minus risk-weighted means; its negative Hessian sums weighted covariance matrices. Concavity makes Newton or quasi-Newton optimization reliable when the design is identified. Censored subjects enter denominators until their censor time. With left truncation, R_i includes only subjects whose entry precedes t_i. Rows for time-varying covariates must represent start-stop intervals and use values known immediately before each event. Exact, Breslow, and Efron methods handle tied event times differently; Efron is often a practical default when ties are moderate, while coarse timestamps deserve sensitivity checks. Separation, sparse categories, and collinearity can send estimates or standard errors upward, motivating penalization and design review.

deepSections.title: Absolute survival requires a fitted baseline hazard
deepSections.body: Partial likelihood estimates beta but not h0(t). After fitting, the Breslow cumulative-baseline increment at event time t_j is d_j divided by sum_{k in R_j}exp(x_k beta), with tie conventions aligned to the coefficient fit. Accumulating increments gives H0hat(t), and Shat(t|x)=exp[-H0hat(t)exp(x beta)]. Absolute predictions therefore depend on the training population's event and censoring process, baseline covariate coding, and data cutoff. Re-centering covariates changes the numerical baseline but not individual fitted hazards if done consistently. Confidence intervals must reflect coefficient and baseline uncertainty. Extrapolation beyond the last supported event is not licensed by the semiparametric model: the estimated cumulative hazard simply stops receiving information. Report fixed-horizon risk only where follow-up is adequate. If deployment prevalence, interventions, or observation practices shift, ranking may remain useful while absolute survival becomes miscalibrated. Recalibration or baseline updating requires a defined target population and fresh mature outcomes.

deepSections.title: Proportional hazards and functional form need active diagnostics
deepSections.body: For two fixed covariate vectors, Cox assumes their hazard ratio exp[(x_a-x_b)beta] is constant in time. Scaled Schoenfeld residuals compare an event subject's covariates with their risk-set expectation; systematic residual trends against transformed time suggest nonproportionality. Complementary log-log survival plots can reveal gross violations but are not a substitute for modeling. Remedies include prespecified covariate-by-time interactions, stratification when a variable needs its own baseline hazard, piecewise coefficients, or a different estimand such as restricted mean survival. Continuous covariates also need functional-form checks using splines, transformations, or residual plots; proportionality does not imply linear log hazard. Global tests can miss localized departures and become overly sensitive in huge samples, so combine effect plots, subject-matter timing, and predictive consequences. Time-varying exposure must be distinguished from time-varying effect. Updating an exposure after origin addresses the former; interacting a baseline exposure with time addresses the latter.

deepSections.title: Dependence, causality, and decisions define what coefficients mean
deepSections.body: Naive standard errors assume independent subjects and a correct working model. Repeated episodes, centers, households, or matched sets can require cluster-robust variance, frailty models, or explicit multilevel structure. Penalized Cox models stabilize high-dimensional prediction but alter inferential interpretation and require leakage-safe tuning. A hazard ratio conditions on remaining event-free, a population whose composition changes over time; it is noncollapsible and can be difficult to compare across covariate sets. An observational treatment coefficient does not identify a causal effect merely because many confounders are included. Treatment timing, immortal-time bias, time-dependent confounding, censoring, competing events, and target estimand need a causal design. For prediction, evaluate concordance, time-dependent Brier score, calibration, and utility on temporal or external data. For explanation, report effect scale, reference values, uncertainty, functional form, and assumption diagnostics. For decisions, translate survival curves into horizon-specific consequences and thresholds rather than ranking on a hazard ratio alone.

lessons.math: h(t|x)=h0(t)exp(x^T beta), H(t|x)=H0(t)exp(x^T beta), and S(t|x)=exp[-H0(t)exp(x^T beta)]. With one event i at time t_i, L_p(beta)=product_i exp(x_i^T beta)/sum_{k in R_i}exp(x_k^T beta). The score is sum_i[x_i-E_beta(X|R_i)] and Hessian is minus the sum of risk-weighted covariance matrices. Breslow increments are Delta H0hat(t_j)=d_j/sum_{k in R_j}exp(x_k^T betahat). exp(beta_j) is the conditional hazard ratio per one-unit change when the functional form and PH restriction hold.

workedExamples.title: From coefficient to conditional hazard ratio
workedExamples.body: A fitted coefficient 0.405 for a binary exposure gives exp(0.405)=1.50. At any time where PH holds, exposed subjects have 50 percent higher instantaneous hazard conditional on covariates and remaining event-free. It does not say their cumulative event probability is 50 percent higher.

workedExamples.title: Breslow survival prediction
workedExamples.body: Suppose H0hat(12)=0.20 and x beta=log(1.5). The subject cumulative hazard is 0.20*1.5=0.30 and predicted survival through month 12 is exp(-0.30)=0.741. A different baseline estimate changes this probability even when beta is unchanged.

lab.goal: Expose Cox partial-likelihood mechanics, fit one coefficient with Newton's method, compare SciPy optimization, and verify risk-set and survival invariants.
lab.buildIt:
import numpy as np
def cox_components(beta,x,time,event):
    x=np.asarray(x,float); time=np.asarray(time,float); event=np.asarray(event,int); b=float(np.asarray(beta).reshape(-1)[0])
    ll=grad=hess=0.0
    for i in np.flatnonzero(event==1):
        xr=x[time>=time[i]]; z=b*xr; m=z.max(); w=np.exp(z-m); sw=w.sum()
        mean=np.sum(w*xr)/sw; var=np.sum(w*(xr-mean)**2)/sw
        ll+=b*x[i]-(m+np.log(sw)); grad+=x[i]-mean; hess-=var
    return ll,grad,hess
def fit_newton(x,time,event,start=0.0):
    b=float(start)
    for _ in range(60):
        _,g,h=cox_components(b,x,time,event)
        step=g/h; b-=step
        if abs(step)<1e-10: break
    return b
def breslow(beta,x,time,event):
    x=np.asarray(x,float); time=np.asarray(time,float); event=np.asarray(event,int)
    ts=np.unique(time[event==1]); inc=np.array([np.sum((time==t)&(event==1))/np.exp(beta*x[time>=t]).sum() for t in ts])
    return ts,np.cumsum(inc)
x=np.array([-1.2,-0.8,-0.3,0.0,0.4,0.7,1.1,1.5]); time=np.array([10,8,7,9,5,6,2,4],float); event=np.array([1,1,0,1,1,0,1,1])
beta_hat=fit_newton(x,time,event)
event_t,H0=breslow(beta_hat,x,time,event)
lab.useIt:
from scipy.optimize import minimize
objective=lambda b:-cox_components(b,x,time,event)[0]
jacobian=lambda b:np.array([-cox_components(b,x,time,event)[1]])
fit=minimize(objective,x0=np.array([0.0]),jac=jacobian,method='BFGS')
beta_scipy=float(fit.x[0])
lab.verifyIt:
assert np.isfinite(beta_hat) and beta_hat>0
assert fit.success and abs(beta_hat-beta_scipy)<1e-6
assert abs(cox_components(beta_hat,x,time,event)[1])<1e-8
perm=np.array([5,2,7,0,3,1,6,4])
assert abs(fit_newton(x[perm],time[perm],event[perm])-beta_hat)<1e-10
assert np.all(np.diff(H0)>=0)
s_high=np.exp(-H0*np.exp(beta_hat*x.max())); s_low=np.exp(-H0*np.exp(beta_hat*x.min()))
assert np.all(s_high<=s_low) and np.all(np.diff(s_high)<=1e-12)

lessons.title: Survival Model Evaluation
lessons.interviewAnswer: I evaluate survival models along four axes. Concordance measures whether higher predicted risk precedes observed events among comparable subjects, but Harrell's C can be optimistic under heavy censoring, so I also use IPCW or Uno-style estimates. At prespecified horizons I report cumulative/dynamic AUC for discrimination, time-dependent Brier score for probability error, and calibration of predicted versus observed survival. IPCW estimates the censoring survival distribution on training data and weights observable cases and controls; people censored before a horizon are not treated as event-free. I integrate only over horizons with adequate follow-up, validate on later cohorts, bootstrap at the subject or cluster level, show subgroup event and censoring counts, and connect scores to threshold-specific decisions. One metric never proves ranking, calibration, and utility simultaneously.
keyPoints: Censoring determines which pairs and horizon labels are observable.
Concordance evaluates ordering, not probability calibration or clinical/product utility.
IPCW corrects observable contributions under a censoring model and a positivity condition.
Time-dependent AUC, Brier score, and calibration must be indexed by supported horizons.
Evaluation preprocessing, censoring estimation, horizons, and bootstrap units must avoid leakage.
lessons.why: A survival model outputs a risk score, survival curve, cumulative incidence, or some combination. These outputs answer different questions. A ranking model can send scarce outreach to the riskiest subjects without predicting accurate probabilities; a pricing or capacity model needs calibrated event counts; a treatment decision needs net benefit under explicit consequences. Censoring makes ordinary evaluation invalid because the eventual status of an early-censored subject is unknown. Excluding all censored subjects changes the population, and calling them negative biases results. Survival metrics recover identifiable comparisons by using observable pairs or inverse censoring weights. They still rely on assumptions and support: if nearly everyone is censored before month twelve, no formula creates reliable month-twelve evaluation. A rigorous scorecard therefore declares the estimand, horizon, prediction type, censoring strategy, split, uncertainty method, and action before computing a number.
lessons.intuition: For ranking, an event at day 20 can be compared with a subject known to remain event-free past day 20. It cannot necessarily be compared with someone censored at day 10. Concordance counts correctly ordered comparable pairs. At a fixed horizon, a subject with an event before the horizon is a case; a subject observed event-free beyond it is a control; an event-free subject censored earlier is indeterminate. IPCW gives more weight to observable subjects who resemble portions of follow-up that censoring made rare. For probability accuracy, compare the model's predicted event or survival probability with the observable binary outcome, using censoring weights. Calibration then asks whether subjects predicted to have 70 percent survival actually exhibit about 70 percent censoring-adjusted survival. Decision analysis adds the costs of missed events and unnecessary intervention. Each layer catches failures hidden by the previous one.
lessons.deepDive: Survival evaluation is a family of estimands indexed by time, comparability, and censoring assumptions. Pairwise concordance tests ranking; dynamic AUC tests horizon-specific discrimination; Brier score tests full probability error; calibration tests probability meaning; and decision analysis tests whether actions improve outcomes or operations. IPCW does not make missing outcomes disappear: it transports information from observable subjects under an estimated censoring mechanism and adequate positivity. Honest time splits, mature labels, supported horizons, uncertainty, and subgroup counts are as important as the formula.
lessons.workedExample: At month six, subject A failed at month four and is a case; subject B is observed event-free through month nine and is a control; subject C was censored event-free at month three and has unknown month-six status. Calling C a control biases the label. An IPCW score uses A and B with weights based on remaining uncensored to their event or the horizon. If only half the source population is expected to remain observable to month six, each representative observable contribution receives roughly twice the weight, subject to the exact estimator.

commonMistakes.misconception: Treat everyone censored before a horizon as event-free.
commonMistakes.correction: Their horizon outcome is unknown. Use an identifiable survival metric with censoring adjustment and adequate support.

commonMistakes.misconception: A C-index of 0.8 means predicted probabilities are accurate.
commonMistakes.correction: Concordance only measures ranking among comparable pairs and is unchanged by monotone score transformations.

commonMistakes.misconception: Estimate censoring weights on the complete dataset for stability.
commonMistakes.correction: That leaks validation follow-up. Fit censoring models within training data and apply them forward.

commonMistakes.misconception: Integrating farther in time always gives a more comprehensive score.
commonMistakes.correction: Late horizons with near-zero censoring survival create unstable weights and unsupported claims.

followUps.question: Why can Harrell's C be optimistic with heavy censoring?
followUps.answer: The observable comparable pairs become a selected subset, often removing difficult long-horizon orderings; IPCW targets a defined restricted concordance under assumptions.

followUps.question: What is the difference between Brier score and calibration?
followUps.answer: Brier score combines calibration and resolution in mean squared probability error, while calibration diagnostics directly compare predicted and observed probabilities.

followUps.question: How should uncertainty be estimated with repeated interval rows?
followUps.answer: Resample whole subjects or natural clusters and repeat the required fitting steps; row-level bootstrap falsely treats dependent records as independent.

lessons.production: Maintain an evaluation manifest containing cohort query, cutoff, origin, event and censoring rules, subject grouping, label-maturity delay, prediction time, horizons, prediction orientation, comparable-pair convention, censoring estimator, weight truncation, integration grid, baselines, subgroups, and bootstrap seed. Run preprocessing and censoring estimation inside each training fold. Require minimum events, controls, comparable pairs, censoring survival, and subgroup size before publishing a metric. Monitor evaluation coverage, weight distribution, follow-up maturity, event latency, baseline incidence, discrimination, calibration, and decision outcomes by calendar cohort. Prevent test-set reuse through immutable result ledgers. Protect sensitive labels and suppress small-cell reports. When metric or label semantics change, shadow the new scorecard, reconcile subject-level contributions, and version or roll back it with the compatible model artifact.
lessons.description: Survival-model evaluation must respect censoring, time, and the prediction target. Ordinary accuracy and ROC calculations mislabel subjects censored before a horizon, while a single concordance number can reward ranking without calibrated probabilities. This chapter builds an evaluation stack around comparable pairs, Harrell's concordance, inverse-probability-of-censoring weighting, Uno-style concordance, cumulative/dynamic AUC, time-dependent Brier score, integrated Brier score, survival calibration, and decision utility. It explains which subjects define cases and controls at a horizon, why the censoring distribution must be estimated without test leakage, and how heavy censoring or short follow-up limits the estimand. A worked example separates an event case, an event-free control, and an indeterminate early censor. The lab implements comparable-pair concordance and an IPCW Brier score, then uses scikit-learn only on correctly defined horizon labels. Production guidance freezes evaluation horizons, split logic, censoring models, metric orientation, subgroup support, and label-maturity windows. Good evaluation reports discrimination, probability accuracy, calibration, and operational value together rather than declaring a model successful from one censoring-sensitive leaderboard number.
learningObjectives: Construct comparable event-time pairs and explain what Harrell and IPCW concordance estimate.
Define horizon-specific cases, controls, Brier scores, and cumulative/dynamic AUC under censoring.
Assess survival calibration and decision utility at supported horizons instead of relying on ranking alone.
Build temporal, leakage-safe, subgroup-aware evaluation pipelines with explicit censoring assumptions.

deepSections.title: Concordance uses only event-time orderings that can be known
deepSections.body: Harrell's concordance index examines pairs in which one subject has an observed event before the other's observed time. The pair is concordant if the earlier-event subject has higher predicted risk, discordant if lower, and commonly receives half credit for tied predictions. Pairs whose ordering is hidden by censoring are omitted. This makes C interpretable as a conditional ranking probability for the sampled comparable pairs, not a universal probability over all subject pairs. Heavy censoring changes which pairs survive and can make Harrell's estimator optimistic. Uno's concordance uses inverse censoring weights to target a time-restricted concordance with better behavior under censoring, provided the censoring survival is estimated consistently and remains positive. Concordance is invariant to monotone score transformations, so it cannot detect whether a 0.8 risk is numerically meaningful. Report metric orientation, tie handling, restriction time, comparable-pair count, confidence interval, and whether repeated records require subject- or cluster-level resampling.

deepSections.title: Time-dependent AUC defines cases and controls at each horizon
deepSections.body: For cumulative/dynamic AUC at horizon t, cumulative cases have experienced the event by t and dynamic controls are known event-free beyond t. A subject censored before t has unknown status and cannot be naively labeled a control. Incident/dynamic definitions instead focus on events near t, answering a different question. IPCW versions weight cases by the probability of remaining uncensored to their event time and controls by the probability of remaining uncensored through t. Estimate the censoring distribution on the training sample or within each training fold, then apply it to validation observations; fitting it on the full dataset leaks follow-up information. Covariate-dependent censoring may require a modeled G(t|x), while misspecification can leave bias. Truncate evaluation before censoring probabilities approach zero because weights then explode. AUC(t) should be plotted with uncertainty and event/control counts. An integrated AUC must state its time weighting and interval; averages across unsupported late horizons are misleading.

deepSections.title: Brier scores and calibration test the full probability scale
deepSections.body: At horizon t, the survival Brier score is the mean squared error between predicted S_i(t) and the indicator I(T_i>t), with IPCW contributions for observed events before t and subjects known event-free beyond t. Early-censored indeterminate outcomes contribute through the weighting formulation rather than being mislabeled. A lower score is better, but its scale depends on event prevalence and horizon; compare with meaningful null models such as marginal Kaplan-Meier survival. Integrated Brier score averages the curve over a declared interval, often with numerical integration, and must not extend past reliable censoring support. Calibration-in-the-large compares average predicted and observed risk, a slope assesses spread, and grouped plots compare predicted probability bins with censoring-adjusted observed survival. Flexible calibration curves reveal nonlinearity but need adequate sample size. Recalibration can correct a shifted baseline while preserving ranking, yet repeated tuning on one test cohort destroys honest evaluation. Confidence bands should reflect the complete fitting and grouping process.

deepSections.title: Evaluation design must match deployment time and action
deepSections.body: Random row splits can leak subject history, duplicate episodes, future feature transformations, or calendar policies. Prefer subject-grouped and chronological splits that reproduce when training labels become mature and when predictions are issued. Fit imputers, encoders, feature selection, survival model, and censoring model inside the training fold. Evaluate all candidate tuning choices on validation data and reserve a final temporal or external test. Bootstrap subjects or natural clusters rather than individual interval rows. Predeclare horizons based on operational decisions and available follow-up. Report subgroup discrimination and calibration with event, censoring, and risk-set counts; a point estimate for a tiny group is not evidence of fairness. Finally translate predictions into policies: capacity-constrained recall among observable cases, expected event capture, calibration for resource planning, and net benefit across thresholds. Include abstention and fallback behavior when horizons, features, or censoring support fall outside the contract.

lessons.math: Harrell C=(concordant+0.5*tied)/comparable over pairs where subject i has an observed event before subject j's observed time. At horizon tau, an IPCW Brier estimator is n^{-1}sum_i[I(T_i<=tau,delta_i=1)(0-Shat_i(tau))^2/Ghat(T_i-)+I(T_i>tau)(1-Shat_i(tau))^2/Ghat(tau)]. G is censoring survival. Cumulative/dynamic AUC(t)=P(score_i>score_j | T_i<=t, delta_i=1, T_j>t), estimated with appropriate censoring weights. IBS averages BS(t) over a declared supported interval.

workedExamples.title: Perfect ranking but poor probabilities
workedExamples.body: Suppose every earlier event receives a higher risk score, so concordance is 1.0. If all predicted twelve-month risks are compressed between 0.01 and 0.02 while observed risk is 0.30, ranking is perfect but calibration and Brier performance are poor.

workedExamples.title: Metric reversal across horizons
workedExamples.body: A model using acute-warning features may discriminate well at seven days but poorly at one year, while a stable history model does the reverse. Reporting one integrated score hides which deployment decision each model supports.

exercises.solution: A subject known to remain event-free beyond day 30. Someone censored before day 30 has indeterminate status.

exercises.prompt: Can two models have identical concordance but different Brier scores?
exercises.solution: Yes. Any monotone transformation preserves ranking while changing predicted probability levels and therefore probability error.

exercises.prompt: Why restrict evaluation before Ghat(t) approaches zero?
exercises.solution: Few subjects remain observable, inverse weights become extreme, variance rises, and positivity for the desired horizon is effectively lost.

lessons.title: Lagrange Multipliers, Duality & KKT Conditions
lessons.interviewAnswer: For minimize f(x) subject to g_i(x)<=0 and h_j(x)=0, the Lagrangian is L=f+sum lambda_i g_i+sum nu_j h_j with lambda_i>=0. KKT requires primal feasibility, dual feasibility, stationarity of L, and complementary slackness lambda_i g_i=0. Under a constraint qualification KKT is necessary for a local optimum; for a convex problem it is sufficient, and with Slater's condition strong duality holds. Multipliers are shadow prices: locally they quantify how the optimal value changes when a constraint bound is tightened, but their interpretation depends on units, sign convention, degeneracy, and perturbation size.
keyPoints: The Lagrangian prices constraint violation
KKT combines four conditions, not stationarity alone
Constraint qualifications prevent pathological necessity failures
Convexity turns a KKT point into a global optimum
Dual variables are local sensitivities with units and validity ranges
lessons.why: Capacity, budgets, fairness limits, service levels, conservation laws, and risk constraints turn unconstrained models into decisions. Lagrange multipliers reveal which constraints actually determine the answer and what an extra unit of capacity is worth. Dual bounds also tell us how far a candidate may be from the best possible value. Yet careless sign conventions, inactive constraints, or nonconvexity can make a plausible multiplier story false. In interviews, KKT questions test calculus, geometry, and assumptions together. In deployed decision systems, residuals and dual gaps are among the most useful solver health signals, while shadow prices help prioritize investments and debug surprising regime changes.
lessons.intuition: At a smooth constrained optimum, moving downhill may be blocked by the feasible boundary. The objective gradient is then balanced by normals to active constraints; the multipliers are the strengths of those normal forces. An inactive inequality has slack, exerts no force, and therefore has zero multiplier under complementary slackness. The dual problem asks for the best lower bound obtained by penalizing constraints. Weak duality says such a lower bound cannot exceed the primal minimum. When the two meet, the gap vanishes and the bound certifies optimality. A shadow price measures the slope of optimal value as a resource limit moves slightly, not the value of arbitrarily large expansion.
lessons.deepDive: KKT conditions unify local geometry and primal-dual certificates. Their exact role depends on problem curvature and regularity: necessity needs constraint qualifications, sufficiency needs convex structure, and sensitivity needs a stable local solution.
lessons.workedExample: Minimize (x-1)^2+(y-2)^2 subject to x+y>=4. Write g=4-x-y<=0 and L=(x-1)^2+(y-2)^2+lambda(4-x-y). The unconstrained point (1,2) is infeasible, so the boundary is active. Stationarity gives 2(x-1)-lambda=0 and 2(y-2)-lambda=0; with x+y=4, x=1.5, y=2.5, lambda=1. Primal and dual feasibility hold, and lambda*g=0. The convex objective and affine constraint make this the global optimum. Tightening the requirement from 4 to 4+delta increases optimal cost initially by about lambda*delta, but that linear sensitivity should be checked by re-solving for material delta.

commonMistakes.mistake: Checking only stationarity
commonMistakes.correction: A stationary Lagrangian point may be infeasible or have invalid multiplier signs; verify all four KKT conditions.

commonMistakes.mistake: Claiming KKT always proves a minimum
commonMistakes.correction: Necessity needs regularity and sufficiency needs convexity or appropriate second-order evidence.

commonMistakes.mistake: Interpreting every active constraint as valuable
commonMistakes.correction: An active constraint can have zero or nonunique multiplier, especially under degeneracy or redundancy.

commonMistakes.mistake: Extrapolating a shadow price indefinitely
commonMistakes.correction: It is a local sensitivity; large changes can switch the active set or, with discrete variables, create jumps.

followUps.question: What does complementary slackness mean?
followUps.answer: For each inequality, multiplier times slack is zero. A strictly slack constraint has zero multiplier; a positive multiplier can occur only when the constraint binds.

followUps.question: When are KKT conditions sufficient?
followUps.answer: For a convex differentiable problem with convex inequality constraints and affine equalities, any primal-dual KKT point is globally optimal.

followUps.question: What is Slater's condition used for?
followUps.answer: A strictly feasible point is a common constraint qualification for convex problems; it supports strong duality and existence of useful multipliers under standard assumptions.

lessons.production: Preserve the original constraint orientation and units in model metadata. Scale rows and variables, supply trustworthy derivatives, and record primal and dual statuses, objectives, gap, active set, multipliers, and normalized KKT residuals. Test analytic toy problems, perturb right-hand sides, and compare predicted shadow-price changes with re-solves. Time limits must distinguish a feasible incumbent from a certified optimum. Monitor active-set churn, infeasibility rate, residuals, multiplier spikes, solve time, and fallback use. Redundant constraints can destabilize prices; discrete models often lack smooth sensitivity. Protect confidential costs and capacities. If residual or status gates fail, return a previously approved feasible decision or a conservative rule, alert the owner, retain diagnostics, and roll back model/data/solver versions together.
lessons.description: Lagrange multipliers, duality, and the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions connect constrained optimization to geometry, economic sensitivity, and verifiable optimality. This chapter derives the Lagrangian for equality and inequality constraints, explains feasible directions and active constraints, distinguishes primal and dual problems, and develops weak duality, strong duality, Slater's condition, complementary slackness, constraint qualifications, and dual sensitivity. You will learn when KKT conditions are necessary, when they are sufficient, why multiplier signs depend on convention, and why stationarity alone never proves feasibility or global optimality. A worked resource-allocation problem computes the primal solution and shadow price by hand. The lab builds KKT residual checks for a constrained quadratic, compares the result with SciPy's SLSQP interface, and verifies primal feasibility, dual feasibility, stationarity, and complementarity. Production guidance covers scaling, degeneracy, infeasibility, inaccurate multipliers, solver status, sensitivity ranges, observability, and safe fallbacks. The payoff is the ability to interpret a constrained solver result as a scientific decision and certificate rather than an unexplained vector.
learningObjectives: Construct a Lagrangian with consistent inequality signs and derive stationarity, feasibility, and complementary slackness conditions.
Explain weak versus strong duality and identify conditions under which KKT conditions are necessary or sufficient.
Interpret optimal multipliers as local value sensitivities while stating sign, units, and range limitations.
Diagnose candidate solutions through scaled KKT residuals and solver termination evidence.

deepSections.title: Building the Lagrangian consistently
deepSections.body: Write a minimization problem as f(x) with inequalities g_i(x)<=0 and equalities h_j(x)=0. Define L(x,lambda,nu)=f(x)+lambda^T g(x)+nu^T h(x), with lambda>=0 and unrestricted nu. If an original constraint is a(x)>=b, rewrite it as b-a(x)<=0 before assigning the multiplier. Equality multipliers have no sign restriction because either direction can be violated. Units are informative: if f is dollars and a constraint is hours, its lambda is dollars per hour. A different sign convention is valid only if the dual-feasibility and sensitivity interpretations change consistently.

deepSections.title: The four KKT conditions
deepSections.body: Primal feasibility requires g_i(x*)<=0 and h_j(x*)=0. Dual feasibility requires lambda_i*>=0. Stationarity requires grad_x L(x*,lambda*,nu*)=0 for differentiable problems. Complementary slackness requires lambda_i* g_i(x*)=0: each inequality is either slack with zero price or active and possibly priced. Active does not imply a positive multiplier; degeneracy can produce active zero-price constraints or nonunique multipliers. For bounds, stationarity includes their normal cone. Nonsmooth convex problems replace gradients with subdifferentials. Check every condition numerically, because a small objective change can coexist with large feasibility error.

deepSections.title: Dual functions, weak duality, and strong duality
deepSections.body: The dual function q(lambda,nu)=inf_x L(x,lambda,nu) is a lower bound on the primal optimum for every dual-feasible lambda. Maximizing q gives the tightest such bound, so d*<=p* is weak duality. The primal-dual gap p*-d* is nonnegative and becomes an optimality certificate when small. Equality of optimal values is strong duality. Convexity alone does not always guarantee it; Slater's condition - existence of a strictly feasible point for convex inequalities and affine equalities - is a common sufficient regularity condition. Infeasible or unbounded problems require careful status and ray interpretation rather than fabricated multipliers.

deepSections.title: Constraint qualifications and global guarantees
deepSections.body: At a local optimum of a differentiable nonlinear problem, KKT is generally necessary only under a constraint qualification such as linear independence of active constraint gradients or weaker regularity conditions. Without one, an optimum can exist with no multipliers satisfying stationarity. In convex problems with convex inequalities and affine equalities, any primal-dual point satisfying KKT is globally optimal; under Slater, optimal multipliers exist and KKT characterizes optimality. In nonconvex problems, a KKT point may be a local minimum, maximum, saddle, or neither. Second-order conditions examine curvature of the Lagrangian along feasible critical directions.

deepSections.title: Shadow prices, residuals, and diagnostics
deepSections.body: Suppose a constraint is a(x)<=b and v(b) is the optimal value. Under stable regularity, the multiplier relates to the local derivative of v with respect to b, with sign determined by formulation. A large magnitude identifies a binding, valuable resource, but only locally; basis changes, discrete decisions, and degeneracy create kinks. Report a sensitivity range or re-solve meaningful scenarios. Scale stationarity, feasibility, complementarity, and duality-gap residuals relative to coefficients and units. Compare analytic or automatic derivatives with finite differences. If multipliers jump while decisions barely change, inspect redundant constraints, scaling, and nonuniqueness before telling an economic story.

lessons.math: For min f(x) subject to g(x)<=0 and h(x)=0, L=f+lambda^Tg+nu^Th with lambda>=0. KKT is g(x*)<=0, h(x*)=0, lambda*>=0, grad_x L=0, and lambda_i*g_i(x*)=0. The dual function q(lambda,nu)=inf_x L is concave and q<=p* for dual-feasible multipliers. Under convexity and an appropriate regularity condition such as Slater, p*=d*. Scaled residuals should separately measure primal violation, negative multipliers, stationarity, complementarity, and primal-dual gap.

workedExamples.title: A binding minimum-output constraint
workedExamples.body: Write the sign-consistent Lagrangian, solve the active-boundary equations, verify every KKT condition, and interpret the multiplier as a local marginal cost.

exercises.prompt: For g(x)<0 at a KKT point, what is lambda?
exercises.solution: Complementary slackness and dual feasibility imply lambda=0.

exercises.prompt: Why can a nonconvex KKT point fail to be a minimum?
exercises.solution: First-order balance does not determine curvature; the point can be a maximum or saddle along feasible directions.

exercises.prompt: A capacity multiplier is 8 dollars per unit. What may you safely say?
exercises.solution: Under the stated sign convention and stable regularity, a small one-unit relaxation changes optimal value by about 8 dollars. Verify units, direction, and a useful perturbation range by re-solving.
