lessons.title: Change-point Detection
lessons.interviewAnswer: A change point is a boundary where a distributional parameter changes persistently; a point anomaly is an isolated deviation. Offline methods segment a complete series by minimizing within-segment cost plus a penalty per change. Exact dynamic programming is quadratic in a basic form, PELT prunes candidates and can be near linear under conditions, and binary segmentation is faster but greedy. Online detectors such as CUSUM trade false-alarm average run length against detection delay. I residualize known seasonality and trend using past information, choose cost, penalty, minimum segment and tolerance on historical incidents or simulation, and evaluate boundary precision/recall plus delay. In production I group duplicate alarms, connect releases and data-pipeline changes, and define confirm, reset, cooldown, and rollback actions.
keyPoints: A change point marks persistent regime structure, not merely a large residual.
Cost specifies what changes; penalty controls how many boundaries appear.
PELT is exact for its objective while pruning candidates under stated conditions.
Online detection balances false alarms and delay and needs reset semantics.
Seasonality, dependence, and logging changes must be modeled or contextualized.
lessons.why: Mean dashboards often hide when a system changed. A release can shift latency, a sensor recalibration can alter variance, and a policy can change conversion behavior. Detecting the boundary supports attribution, rollback, and model retraining. Point-anomaly rules may fire repeatedly after a persistent shift, flooding alerts without recognizing that the baseline is obsolete. Conversely, a segmentation method can overreact to seasonality or one bad batch and invent regimes. Change-point methods make the trade-off explicit through a segment cost and complexity penalty. They also provide an operational vocabulary: how long to confirm a shift, how much delay is acceptable, whether to reset after alarm, and which intervention owns a boundary. The best detector is the one whose change definition and delay-cost trade-off match the response process.
lessons.intuition: Draw a time series with one horizontal level, then a sudden step to a new level. If split at the correct time, each side has small variation around its own mean. If not split, one mean must compromise and within-segment squared error is large. Add a cost for every split so noise does not create a segment at every point. Dynamic programming considers every possible last boundary and reuses the best earlier segmentation. PELT removes earlier candidates that can never become optimal later. In an online setting there is no future right segment yet. CUSUM accumulates small signed deviations from a reference; random noise tends to cancel, while a persistent shift creates steady growth until a threshold is crossed. A lower threshold alarms sooner but more often by chance. Known cycles should be removed first or encoded in the cost, otherwise every daily peak can resemble a regime change.
lessons.deepDive: Change-point detection is a model of piecewise stability plus a search and penalty. Offline segmentation trades within-segment fit against boundary count; online detection trades false alarms against delay. Neither can distinguish harmful behavior from a legitimate release without context. Ordered evaluation, tolerance matching, reset logic, and action ownership are therefore part of the detector contract.
lessons.workedExample: API latency is stable near 120 ms, has one 500 ms spike, returns to baseline, then after a release shifts to 170 ms for the next hour. A point detector flags the spike and many post-release rows. Penalized segmentation ignores the one-point spike when minimum segment length is ten and places one boundary near release time. The alarm joins deployment metadata, confirms persistence for five minutes, and triggers a rollback review.

commonMistakes.misconception: Every point anomaly is a change point.
commonMistakes.correction: A point anomaly is transient; a change point marks a persistent regime boundary. Minimum segments and persistence evidence separate them.

commonMistakes.misconception: PELT is always linear time.
commonMistakes.correction: PELT is exact for its objective and can have linear expected cost under conditions. Worst-case behavior and constants depend on data, penalty, and cost.

commonMistakes.misconception: Removing seasonality with a full-series smoother is harmless.
commonMistakes.correction: Using future observations can leak and move boundaries. For online claims, estimate expected structure with past-only or frozen training methods.

commonMistakes.misconception: More detected boundaries mean higher sensitivity and therefore a better system.
commonMistakes.correction: Oversegmentation creates false and duplicate alarms. Evaluate precision, delay, localization, and action cost under a declared tolerance.

followUps.question: What does the penalty do in offline segmentation?
followUps.answer: It charges for each additional boundary, balancing within-segment fit against complexity. Its scale depends on the cost and data.

followUps.question: How is PELT different from binary segmentation?
followUps.answer: PELT prunes dynamic-program candidates while preserving the exact penalized optimum under its conditions; binary segmentation greedily chooses splits and recurses, which can miss interacting changes.

followUps.question: How do you evaluate a detection that is five minutes late?
followUps.answer: Use a predeclared tolerance and report detection delay separately. Whether five minutes is acceptable depends on the response deadline and harm accumulation.

lessons.production: Freeze event-time and late-data policy, aggregation, residual or seasonal baseline, target parameter, cost, penalty, minimum segment, online statistic, confirmation, reset, cooldown, tolerance, and ownership routing. Reconcile ordering and gaps before scoring. Monitor baseline age, residual distribution, alarm and unique-incident rate, duplicate boundaries, false-alarm average run length, detection and confirmation delay, post-change persistence, missingness, and action outcomes. Attach deployment, schema, traffic, and upstream metadata for diagnosis while protecting sensitive series. Use maintenance suppression only with audit logs. Provide a safe manual path when detector state is lost and avoid silently adapting the baseline after an unreviewed alarm. Shadow and replay changes across long normal and incident histories, and roll back detector, baseline, and response rules together when false alarms, delay, missed shifts, or automated-action harm exceed bounds.
lessons.description: Change-point detection locates times where the data-generating regime changes, such as a shift in mean, variance, trend, covariance, or event rate. It is different from point anomaly detection: one extreme observation is transient, while a change point marks a boundary after which many observations follow a new pattern. This chapter develops offline segmentation as penalized cost minimization, cumulative-sum evidence, exact dynamic programming, PELT pruning, binary segmentation, online detection delay, minimum segment length, penalty selection, and tolerance-based evaluation. You will learn how seasonality, trend, autocorrelation, missingness, logging changes, and multiple related series can create false boundaries or hide real ones. A worked latency example distinguishes a release-induced persistent shift from a short spike and connects detection to rollback. The lab implements exact penalized mean-shift segmentation, compares its strongest boundary with a vectorized CUSUM statistic, and verifies localization, translation, constant-series, and penalty behavior. Production guidance fixes event-time ordering, baseline and cost assumptions, confirmation windows, reset and cooldown logic, and change ownership; monitors false-alarm run length, delay, duplicate alarms, and post-change stabilization rather than merely counting detected indices.
learningObjectives: Distinguish transient anomalies from persistent regime changes and define offline versus online objectives.
Formulate penalized segmentation and implement exact dynamic programming for mean changes.
Explain PELT, binary segmentation, CUSUM, penalties, minimum segments, and detection-delay trade-offs.
Evaluate and operate change detectors under seasonality, dependence, tolerance windows, and intervention feedback.

deepSections.title: Define the parameter and observation process that may change
deepSections.body: Let y_1,...,y_n be ordered observations and tau_1<...<tau_m unknown boundaries. Within each segment, assume a stable parameter under a chosen cost. Squared deviation from segment mean detects mean changes under a Gaussian-like model; likelihood costs can target variance, count rate, distribution, regression coefficients, covariance, or kernel discrepancy. The cost determines what a change means. A mean cost will misinterpret a smooth trend as many steps unless trend is modeled or removed. Seasonality should be estimated from a training period or with past-only methods, then detection applied to residuals; using future smoothing can leak and shift boundaries. Irregular sampling, missing periods, censoring, and changing aggregation alter the observation process and may require exposure or time weighting. Multivariate detectors can pool weak coordinated shifts but suffer dimensionality and changing covariance. Include metadata for deployments, schema versions, traffic mix, and holidays so detected boundaries can be explained rather than automatically labeled incidents.

deepSections.title: Offline penalized segmentation and search algorithms
deepSections.body: A common objective minimizes sum_{j=0}^m C(y_{tau_j+1:tau_{j+1}})+beta m, with tau_0=0 and tau_{m+1}=n. Without penalty beta or a fixed m, fit improves by adding boundaries. Minimum segment length encodes resolution and prevents tiny segments. Basic exact dynamic programming computes F(t)=min_{s<t}[F(s)+C(y_{s+1:t})+beta], storing the best previous s; with O(1) segment cost from prefix sums, it is O(n^2). Optimal partitioning is exact for the declared additive objective. PELT adds pruning: when one candidate cannot beat another for any future endpoint under a cost condition, discard it. Its expected computation can be linear in settings where changes increase with n, but worst-case and constants depend on data and penalty. Binary segmentation finds the best single split, then recurses; it is fast and intuitive but greedy, so nearby or weak changes can be missed. Window methods compare adjacent windows and localize at their scale. Search method, cost, penalty, and constraints are separate choices and must be versioned together.

deepSections.title: Online evidence, false alarms, and delay
deepSections.body: Online detection observes one point at a time and must alarm before seeing a complete future segment. For a known upward mean shift, one-sided CUSUM updates G_t=max(0,G_{t-1}+z_t-k), where z_t is standardized relative to baseline and k is a reference allowance. Alarm when G_t>h. Persistent positive drift accumulates; negative evidence resets to zero. Page-Hinkley, generalized likelihood ratios, Bayesian online change-point methods, and sequential probability ratios encode different unknown-shift and run-length beliefs. Parameters determine in-control average run length, detection delay, and sensitivity to shift size. Evaluate on long normal histories and simulated or labeled shifts, preserving autocorrelation. After an alarm, define whether to reset statistic immediately, wait for confirmation, adapt the baseline, or pause during remediation. Automatic baseline adaptation can absorb a harmful shift; no adaptation causes permanent alarms after a legitimate change. Confirmation windows and hysteresis reduce noise but add delay. Report distribution of delay and false alarms per time, not only whether one boundary was eventually found.

deepSections.title: Evaluate boundaries with tolerance and connect them to response
deepSections.body: Exact timestamp matching is often inappropriate because labels and detection have granularity. Match predicted and true boundaries within a declared tolerance using one-to-one assignment, then report precision, recall, localization error, and delay. Multiple alarms around one change should not earn multiple true positives. Segment metrics can measure how well pairs of times are grouped into the same regime. Choose tolerance from operational action, not after seeing results. Evaluate across shift sizes, durations, directions, seasonality, missingness, and dependent noise. A detector that finds large shifts but misses gradual or variance changes should say so. In production, attach release, configuration, data schema, and upstream health metadata to alarms; group correlated metrics into incidents; suppress known maintenance windows carefully; and route to an owner. Monitor alarm rate, duplicate rate, confirmation failures, delay, post-alarm persistence, baseline age, and action outcome. Backtest any automated rollback to avoid reacting to benign traffic mix or instrumentation changes.

lessons.math: For boundaries tau, minimize J=sum_j C(tau_j,tau_{j+1})+beta m. For a mean-shift squared-error cost C(s,t)=sum_{i=s}^{t-1}(y_i-ybar_{s:t})^2, prefix sums give C=sum y_i^2-(sum y_i)^2/(t-s). Dynamic programming F(t)=min_{s<=t-L}[F(s)+C(s,t)+beta] with minimum length L returns an exact optimum after backtracking. A one-sided standardized CUSUM G_t=max(0,G_{t-1}+z_t-k) alarms at G_t>h; k and h tune target shift, run length, and delay.

workedExamples.title: Penalty controls segmentation
workedExamples.body: Splitting at t=60 reduces squared-error cost by 180. With penalty beta=30, the change is worthwhile; adding a tiny split that reduces cost by five is not. Raising beta yields fewer broader regimes; lowering it yields more sensitivity and false boundaries. Choose beta under later-window or incident replay evidence.

workedExamples.title: CUSUM accumulates a small persistent shift
workedExamples.body: Standardized observations move from mean zero to mean 0.5. Individual values rarely exceed a three-sigma point threshold, but with k=0.25 the expected CUSUM increment becomes 0.25 per step. The statistic reaches h=5 after roughly 20 post-change observations on average, illustrating the delay-versus-false-alarm trade-off.

exercises.prompt: Why does a minimum segment length reject a one-point spike as a regime?
exercises.solution: A regime must persist for at least the declared length, so a single point cannot form its own segment even if its residual is large.

exercises.prompt: A daily cycle creates two boundaries every day. What is wrong?
exercises.solution: Known seasonality is not represented in the stable-segment model. Residualize or model the cycle using leakage-safe methods before change detection.

exercises.prompt: Why report both boundary recall and delay?
exercises.solution: A detector can eventually match every change but react too late to prevent harm. Delay quantifies timeliness within the tolerance-matching evidence.

lessons.title: Supervised Rare-event Modeling
lessons.interviewAnswer: For rare events, I first protect the label, split, and evaluation design. I can retain all positives and subsample negatives for efficiency, but I store inclusion probabilities and either weight the likelihood or correct and calibrate probabilities on representative data. Class weights and oversampling change the training objective; they may help ranking or optimization but do not automatically produce population probabilities. Duplicating positives adds no new information, and synthetic examples can violate temporal, categorical, or causal constraints. I evaluate PR/AP, recall at review capacity, calibration, and cost on a later untouched population, tune thresholds separately, audit nonalerts, and monitor prevalence, label maturity, hard-negative mix, subgroup support, and queue outcomes.
keyPoints: Event diversity and label quality matter more than raw class ratio alone.
Negative subsampling changes the sample prior and usually the probability intercept.
Weights, resampling, calibration, and thresholding solve different problems.
Validation must preserve deployment prevalence, time, groups, and label maturity.
Selective review and hard-negative mining create feedback that requires audits.
lessons.why: At one event per ten thousand cases, training on every easy negative can be expensive and may contribute little gradient, while only a few event mechanisms determine whether the model generalizes. Sampling and weighting can focus computation, but they also tempt teams to report results on balanced test sets, interpret weighted scores as probabilities, or synthesize impossible positives. Rare labels are often delayed, disputed, and selected by an existing policy. A model may learn investigator behavior rather than event risk. The engineering objective is a trustworthy pipeline from event definition through sampling, training, calibration, threshold, review, and outcome. A simple regularized logistic model with corrected probabilities and honest evaluation can be more useful than a sophisticated imbalance technique whose score is impossible to calibrate or audit.
lessons.intuition: Suppose the real population contains one positive in one hundred cases, but training keeps every positive and only enough negatives to make one positive in four sampled rows. The feature relationship within positives and negatives may remain informative, so score ordering can be good. Yet the sample tells the model that positives are far more common than reality, shifting its intercept upward. Subtracting the difference between sample and population prior log-odds restores the base-rate level under random case-control sampling and a correctly specified logistic model; an independent calibration set can handle additional misspecification. Class weighting creates a similar objective change. Thresholding then asks which calibrated risks justify action under cost or capacity. These are separate knobs. Copying a rare positive many times increases its gradient weight but does not reveal another kind of positive, and can make one mislabeled event dominate.
lessons.deepDive: Rare-event modeling is a distribution and feedback problem, not a request to mechanically balance a table. Sampling and weighting decide which likelihood is optimized; calibration restores probability meaning under a representative population; thresholding converts risk to action. Honest time/group splits, mature labels, event diversity, inclusion probabilities, audits, and operational costs determine whether the score can be trusted.
lessons.workedExample: Fraud prevalence is 0.5 percent. Training retains all 5,000 frauds and samples 15,000 nonfrauds, creating sample prevalence 25 percent. An unweighted logistic model can rank well but predicts probabilities near the sample prior. The log-odds correction is logit(0.005)-logit(0.25), about -4.20. Add it to every fitted logit, then validate and recalibrate on a later untouched population. Operations reviews the top 2,000 expected-value cases, not every probability above 0.5.

commonMistakes.misconception: Balancing the classes is always required.
commonMistakes.correction: Many models learn useful rankings from imbalanced data. Sampling or weighting should address compute, optimization, or cost for a stated reason and preserve honest evaluation.

commonMistakes.misconception: Class weights automatically make probabilities better.
commonMistakes.correction: Weights change the target loss and effective prior. Validate and usually calibrate probabilities on a representative independent population.

commonMistakes.misconception: SMOTE creates more real positive information.
commonMistakes.correction: It interpolates training representations under strong validity assumptions. It does not create independent event mechanisms and can generate impossible mixed or temporal cases.

commonMistakes.misconception: Loss weighting and lowering the alert threshold are equivalent.
commonMistakes.correction: They act at training and decision stages and can change rankings, calibration, and regularization differently. Tune and validate each layer explicitly.

followUps.question: When is negative subsampling safe for logistic slopes?
followUps.answer: Under random sampling within outcome class, correct specification, and appropriate estimation, slopes can be preserved while the intercept shifts. Feature-dependent selection needs weights or explicit modeling.

followUps.question: Why calibrate on independent predictions?
followUps.answer: Training predictions are optimistically fit and can make a calibrator too extreme. Use held-out or cross-validated predictions that represent deployment sampling.

followUps.question: What is the biggest limit with ten positives?
followUps.answer: The event diversity and uncertainty are fundamentally small. Complex resampling cannot replace independent positive evidence; simplify, report wide uncertainty, and collect or transfer defensible information.

lessons.production: Version event, entity, horizon and maturity definitions, extraction timestamps, split rules, incident grouping, class and stratum inclusion probabilities, resampling seed, sample and class weights, feature pipeline, estimator, calibration cohort, prevalence assumption, and threshold or top-k policy. Test prior correction and weighted metrics on golden populations. Monitor true and sampled prevalence, label maturity, event diversity, hard-negative source mix, score and calibration drift, AP and recall at capacity when mature, alert and incident yield, audit misses, intervention outcomes, and subgroup support. Keep nonalert exploration to reduce selective-label blindness. Secure event data and avoid exposing rare cases through explanations. Define queue overflow and model-failure fallbacks. Canary the complete model-calibration-policy bundle on later traffic and roll back all stages together when probability, workload, detection, fairness, or net-value limits fail.
lessons.description: Supervised rare-event modeling uses labeled positives and negatives to learn a ranking or event probability when positives are scarce. The central problem is not that algorithms cannot see a minority class; it is that effective information is limited by the number, diversity, and labeling quality of events, while naive sampling and weighting can distort probabilities and validation. This chapter develops rare-event logistic behavior, case-control and negative subsampling, inverse-probability weighting, prior or intercept correction, class weights, hard-negative mining, resampling, calibration, cost-sensitive thresholds, and temporal or grouped evaluation. You will understand why oversampling duplicates does not create new positive information, why synthetic interpolation can be invalid for mixed or temporal data, and why weighting the training loss is different from choosing a decision threshold. A worked fraud example shows how a model trained on all positives and sampled negatives can preserve ranking yet overstate prevalence until corrected or calibrated. The lab reproduces that intercept shift with scikit-learn, applies a log-odds prior correction, and verifies prevalence, ranking, and cost-policy invariants. Production guidance versions inclusion probabilities, label maturity, calibration and policy separately; audits nonalerts; monitors prevalence, hard-negative mix, calibration, queue yield, and subgroup event support.
learningObjectives: Design case-control, weighted, or resampled training data without corrupting evaluation or probability interpretation.
Apply and explain prior-log-odds correction after random negative subsampling.
Separate representation, ranking objective, probability calibration, and cost-sensitive threshold policy.
Diagnose label delay, leakage, hard-negative feedback, subgroup scarcity, and prevalence drift in production.

deepSections.title: Protect event information before changing class balance
deepSections.body: Define the event, prediction time, horizon, entity, maturity, and action. Ensure every feature is available before the prediction timestamp; post-investigation status, future aggregates, and resolution codes are common leakage. Split chronologically when prevalence, policy, or behavior changes, and keep related entities or incidents together. The effective positive sample size is the number of independent and diverse event mechanisms, not the number of duplicated rows. Inspect positive coverage across time, source, severity, subgroup, and acquisition process. Negatives may be unlabeled future positives or unreviewed unknowns. Label delay requires matured cohorts; selective investigation requires random audits or exploration. Deduplicate events and decide whether repeated positive rows represent separate prediction opportunities or one incident. Start with regularized logistic and tree baselines, stable features, and PR plus capacity evaluation. If a fold contains too few positives for tuning or calibration, reduce complexity, aggregate carefully, use repeated grouped windows, or collect more evidence rather than hiding the problem with resampling.

deepSections.title: Sampling and weighting change the fitted distribution
deepSections.body: Keeping all positives and randomly sampling negatives can reduce training cost. Record inclusion probability for every class and stratum. Unweighted case-control logistic regression can estimate slopes consistently under ideal random sampling and correct specification, while the intercept reflects sample prevalence. If population prevalence pi and sampled prevalence pi_s are known, add logit(pi)-logit(pi_s) to the fitted sample logit. More generally use inverse-probability weights or calibrate on a representative independent set. Stratified, time-dependent, or hard-negative sampling needs corresponding weights and may alter slopes if selection depends on features given class. Class weights multiply loss contributions and can emphasize events or approximate costs, but the resulting probability scores target a weighted distribution unless corrected. Weight normalization and library regularization conventions matter. Negative sampling should happen after split boundaries; sampling first can duplicate entities across train and test. Preserve a representative untouched evaluation set even if training is sampled. Track sampling changes as model-version changes.

deepSections.title: Use resampling and specialized objectives for a stated purpose
deepSections.body: Random oversampling repeats positive rows. It can help minibatch composition or solver gradients but adds no independent information and increases overfitting to mislabeled or atypical events. Random undersampling saves compute but may discard informative hard negatives and distort probability estimates. Synthetic interpolation methods such as SMOTE assume that interpolating minority neighbors creates valid events. That can fail with one-hot categories, sequences, graph identities, time, constraints, or disconnected event mechanisms; synthetic rows must be generated inside training folds and validated mechanistically. Focal loss downweights easy examples in some high-capacity models, changing optimization toward difficult cases; its scores still need representative calibration. Hard-negative mining can improve boundaries by adding confusing negatives, but feedback from a deployed model changes the training distribution and can neglect unseen regions. Separate the representation and ranking objective from probability calibration. Fit Platt-style logistic or isotonic calibration on independent representative predictions with enough events, and assess reliability uncertainty. Calibration cannot rescue leakage or absent event modes.

deepSections.title: Select decisions and learn from a selective feedback loop
deepSections.body: After estimating or calibrating probabilities, choose a threshold from coherent intervention costs, severity, constraints, and capacity. Weighting the loss is not equivalent to selecting the final threshold in every model, especially under regularization, misspecification, and heterogeneous costs. A top-k policy can fit a fixed review queue; severity-aware expected value can prioritize different event types. Evaluate the locked end-to-end policy on a later population with real prevalence using AP, recall and precision at capacity, calibration, raw counts, incident grouping, delay, and net outcomes. Report confidence intervals driven by rare positive support. In production, only selected alerts may receive high-quality labels, creating selective labels and self-fulfilling hard-negative pools. Randomly audit nonalerts and explore score bands. Monitor population and sampled prevalence, inclusion rates, event support, score and calibration drift, queue yield, audit misses, label age, intervention effects, and subgroup recall. Retain examples before intervention when evaluating natural outcomes, or define policy-value estimands explicitly.

lessons.math: For population prevalence pi and case-control sample prevalence pi_s, a fitted sample logit eta_s(x) can be corrected under ideal random within-class sampling by eta_pop(x)=eta_s(x)+log[pi/(1-pi)]-log[pi_s/(1-pi_s)]. The sigmoid of eta_pop estimates population probability under the model assumptions. Inverse-probability weighted loss uses weight 1/q_i for inclusion probability q_i. With calibrated p and costs C_FP,C_FN, the simple action threshold is C_FP/(C_FP+C_FN), modified when intervention cost, benefit, capacity, or heterogeneous severity enters.

workedExamples.title: Why duplicated positives do not create evidence
workedExamples.body: Repeating one confirmed attack 100 times makes the optimizer see 100 identical gradients, but uncertainty about unseen attack types has not fallen as if 100 independent attacks occurred. Group duplicates, weight deliberately, and evaluate on distinct incidents.

workedExamples.title: Hard-negative mining changes the sample
workedExamples.body: After deployment, investigators label many high-score false positives. Adding them improves that boundary, but low-score nonalerts remain mostly unlabeled. Keep inclusion metadata, audit low-score regions, and evaluate on a representative cohort so the next model does not overfit yesterday's alert policy.

lab.goal: Demonstrate probability distortion from negative subsampling, apply prior-log-odds correction, and verify ranking, prevalence, and cost-policy invariants.
lab.useIt:
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import average_precision_score
model=LogisticRegression(C=1e6,max_iter=2000).fit(X[keep],y[keep])
raw=model.predict_proba(X)[:,1]
corrected=prior_correct(raw,prevalence,sample_prevalence)
raw_ap=average_precision_score(y,raw); corrected_ap=average_precision_score(y,corrected)
lab.verifyIt:
assert sample_prevalence>5*prevalence
assert raw.mean()>3*prevalence
assert abs(corrected.mean()-prevalence)<0.01
assert abs(raw_ap-corrected_ap)<1e-12
assert np.array_equal(np.argsort(raw),np.argsort(corrected))
# Correction changes probability policy even though ranking is fixed.
assert np.sum(raw>=0.1)>np.sum(corrected>=0.1)
# Perfect prior-only sample predictions map back to the population prior.
assert abs(prior_correct(np.array([sample_prevalence]),prevalence,sample_prevalence)[0]-prevalence)<1e-12
lab.shipIt: Persist event and maturity definitions, splits, inclusion probabilities, weights, model, calibration and threshold separately; audit nonalerts, monitor population/sample prevalence and queue outcomes, and roll back the entire sampled-training-to-policy bundle.

exercises.prompt: Training prevalence is 0.5 but population prevalence is 0.01. What happens to uncorrected probabilities?
exercises.solution: They generally reflect the sampled prior and are too high for the population. Apply a justified prior or weighting correction and validate calibration on representative data.

exercises.prompt: Why must synthetic oversampling happen inside each training fold?
exercises.solution: Creating synthetic rows before splitting lets validation information and neighbors influence training and can place related synthetic points across folds, causing leakage.

exercises.prompt: A weighted model improves recall but doubles false-alert cost. Is it better?
exercises.solution: Not under the declared operational objective unless recovered event benefit exceeds the extra cost. Compare a locked threshold or capacity policy and net value on later representative data.

lessons.title: Accelerated Failure Time Models
lessons.interviewAnswer: An AFT model writes log T=x beta+sigma epsilon, so exp(beta_j) is a time ratio when other covariates are fixed. A positive coefficient stretches every modeled time quantile; for example exp(0.2)=1.22 means about 22 percent longer time under the model. The error distribution determines survival and hazard shape: Weibull, log-normal, and log-logistic are common choices. For an observed event the likelihood contributes the density f(t|x); for right censoring it contributes S(t|x), because only survival past the censor time is known. I compare distributions with residuals, calibration, likelihood-based criteria and held-out horizon scores, inspect nonlinear and time-varying acceleration, and avoid unsupported tail extrapolation. Time ratios are not automatically causal, and a convenient parametric curve does not replace censoring, entry, or competing-risk design.
keyPoints: AFT coefficients multiply the event-time scale rather than the instantaneous hazard.
Censored rows contribute survival probabilities, not event densities or negative labels.
The chosen error distribution determines hazard shape and extrapolated tails.
Weibull is both AFT and PH; log-normal and log-logistic generally are not PH.
Communicable time ratios remain conditional, model-based, and noncausal without identification.
lessons.why: Stakeholders often ask how long an intervention, device state, or customer characteristic delays an event. AFT models answer on that duration scale: covariates expand or contract the time axis. They can estimate medians and other quantiles even when proportional hazards is awkward, and a parametric distribution supports smooth survival curves and carefully bounded extrapolation. The cost is stronger structure. A log-normal model permits hazards that rise and then fall; a Weibull hazard is monotone; a log-logistic distribution can have a heavy tail. Choosing by convenience can create persuasive but false late-horizon predictions. Censoring also changes the likelihood, and delayed or interval observation needs additional terms. A rigorous AFT workflow uses substantive hazard expectations, graphical and residual checks, temporal validation, and sensitivity across plausible families before translating coefficients into operational claims.
lessons.intuition: Imagine every subject follows the same underlying event-time movie, but a covariate changes playback speed. A time ratio of two makes landmarks such as the median and 90th percentile occur twice as late. Taking logs turns multiplicative time changes into an additive regression. Random variation around that regression follows a chosen error distribution, which induces a distribution for positive T. When an event is observed at t, the model must place density near t. When observation stops at c without an event, the model only needs to assign probability to T>c, so the contribution is survival S(c). Subjects censored late can be more informative about long duration than subjects censored early. The fitted distribution fills gaps and extends beyond observations, which is helpful inside support and dangerous in an unsupported tail.
lessons.deepDive: AFT modeling is positive-duration regression with censoring-aware likelihood. Its distinctive payoff is the time ratio, a direct statement about how modeled quantiles stretch or contract. That interpretation is stronger than a generic risk score and therefore demands stronger checks: common acceleration, distribution and tail shape, correct censoring and entry contributions, covariate timing, and validation where follow-up exists. Parametric smoothness can improve estimation and enable carefully bounded forecasts, but it cannot create evidence beyond the observed population and time range.
lessons.workedExample: A binary maintenance feature has fitted beta=0.30 in an AFT model. exp(0.30)=1.35, so conditional event-time quantiles are estimated to be 35 percent longer for maintained units under the common-acceleration model. If the reference median is 100 days with the same other covariates, the fitted maintained median is about 135 days. This is not a 35-point survival-probability increase, and it is not causal unless maintenance assignment and censoring are identified appropriately.

commonMistakes.misconception: exp(beta) is a hazard ratio in every AFT model.
commonMistakes.correction: It is a time ratio under the AFT parameterization. Only special families such as Weibull also admit a PH representation with transformed coefficients.

commonMistakes.misconception: Censored observations contribute zero to the likelihood.
commonMistakes.correction: They contribute the probability of surviving beyond their censor time, which can strongly constrain the tail.

commonMistakes.misconception: The best in-sample distribution criterion guarantees reliable long-range forecasts.
commonMistakes.correction: Tail extrapolation is assumption driven and needs domain checks, temporal validation, and sensitivity across plausible families.

commonMistakes.misconception: A treatment time ratio from observational data is automatically causal.
commonMistakes.correction: Assignment, timing, confounding, censoring, competing events, and the target estimand require an explicit causal design.

followUps.question: Why is Weibull both PH and AFT?
followUps.answer: Its scale transformation and power-form cumulative hazard allow covariates to be expressed either as constant time acceleration or as a constant hazard multiplier, with related coefficients.

followUps.question: How do you choose among log-normal and log-logistic?
followUps.answer: Use plausible hazard and tail behavior, residual and nonparametric comparisons, held-out calibration and Brier scores, and sensitivity rather than one fit statistic alone.

followUps.question: What changes for interval-censored outcomes?
followUps.answer: If the event is known only between L and R, its likelihood contribution is F(R)-F(L), or equivalently S(L)-S(R), computed stably.

lessons.production: Publish a model card with time origin and unit, event and censor definitions, entry and interval rules, target population, distribution parameterization, link, feature transformations, optimizer tolerances, uncertainty method, maximum supported horizon, and tail fallback. Persist parameters and preprocessing as one versioned artifact. Validate convergence from multiple starts, gradient size, plausible parameter bounds, KM overlays, residuals, temporal Brier and calibration curves, quantile coverage, and operational utility. Monitor event and censoring latency, time distributions, covariate support, fitted shape, tail mass, calibration, subgroup errors, and numerical failures. Never silently extrapolate beyond the declared horizon; return an abstention or conservative policy. Shadow distribution or extraction changes and compare subject-level likelihood and predictions. Roll back event logic, preprocessing, parameters, and serving code together.
lessons.description: Accelerated failure-time models place covariate effects directly on event time rather than on instantaneous hazard. In a log-linear AFT model, log T=x^T beta+sigma epsilon, so exp(beta_j) is a time ratio: values above one stretch the event-time distribution and values below one accelerate failure. This chapter derives censored likelihood contributions, compares Weibull, exponential, log-normal, and log-logistic assumptions, and explains when Weibull AFT is simultaneously a proportional-hazards model. It covers quantiles, survival and hazard recovery, residual and distributional diagnostics, nonlinearities, heterogeneity, delayed and interval censoring, extrapolation risk, and causal limits. A worked example translates a coefficient into median-time change. The lab implements a censored Weibull AFT likelihood, fits it with SciPy, verifies parameter recovery and time-unit invariance, and turns fitted parameters into survival predictions. Production guidance versions the time unit, distribution, censoring contribution, feature encoding, optimizer, supported horizon, and tail policy. AFT models provide unusually communicable duration effects, but that clarity depends on an adequate distribution and common acceleration structure.
learningObjectives: Interpret AFT coefficients as multiplicative changes in event-time quantiles under a common acceleration model.
Construct right-censored likelihoods from event densities and censoring survival contributions.
Compare Weibull, log-normal, and log-logistic tail and hazard assumptions using diagnostics and validation.
Recognize extrapolation, interval censoring, heterogeneity, time-varying effects, and causal limitations in deployment.

deepSections.title: Log-time regression creates a common acceleration factor
deepSections.body: The generic AFT form is log T=x^T beta+sigma epsilon, with sigma>0 and a specified standardized error distribution. Increasing x_j by one shifts log time by beta_j and multiplies every conditional quantile by exp(beta_j), assuming no interaction changes the scale or shape. An intercept sets baseline duration in the chosen time unit. The error distribution supplies a standard survival function, from which conditional survival, density, hazard, mean where finite, and quantiles follow. For Weibull AFT it is convenient to write scale lambda(x)=exp(x beta) and shape rho; S(t|x)=exp[-(t/lambda)^rho]. The pth event-time quantile is lambda[-log(1-p)]^(1/rho). Covariate effects may be modeled with splines and interactions, but the basic model still imposes common acceleration across quantiles. Quantile ratios that vary strongly by p indicate this restriction or distribution may be inadequate. Centering and scaling aid optimization but must be reversed consistently for interpretation.

deepSections.title: Likelihood contributions encode exactly what observation reveals
deepSections.body: Let y_i=min(T_i,C_i) and delta_i indicate an observed event. Under independent right censoring conditional on modeled information, the event-time likelihood contribution is f(y_i|x_i)^delta_i S(y_i|x_i)^(1-delta_i), ignoring censoring-distribution factors that do not involve event parameters. On the log scale, sum delta_i log f plus (1-delta_i)log S. For Weibull, log f=log rho-rho log lambda+(rho-1)log y-(y/lambda)^rho, while log S=-(y/lambda)^rho. Left truncation conditions the contribution on surviving past entry and divides by S(entry). Interval censoring contributes S(L)-S(R), requiring stable log-difference calculations. Left censoring contributes F(R). Treating all non-events as ordinary negatives discards their follow-up time and biases estimates. Extreme times, overflow in exp(x beta), and nearly zero interval probabilities require transformed parameters, scaling, bounds, stable logarithms, gradients, and convergence checks. Standard errors can come from the observed information or robust sandwich methods when appropriate.

deepSections.title: Distribution choice controls hazard shape and tail claims
deepSections.body: An exponential AFT model fixes constant hazard and is often too rigid. Weibull allows monotonically increasing hazard when rho>1 and decreasing hazard when rho<1; it is special because it also satisfies proportional hazards, with a sign-and-scale relationship between AFT and PH coefficients. Log-normal hazards typically rise and then decline, while log-logistic hazards can be nonmonotone and have heavier tails; their moments may not all exist. Compare plausible families using domain knowledge, nonparametric KM overlays, transformed survival plots, Cox-Snell or randomized quantile residuals, held-out Brier scores, calibration, and likelihood criteria used on the same observations. A lower AIC is not proof of reliable extrapolation. Examine event-time quantile residuals by covariate and calendar cohort. Flexible spline-based parametric survival can reduce shape bias but increases tuning and extrapolation sensitivity. Mixtures, frailty, cure fractions, and competing causes can mimic heavy tails or nonmonotone hazards, so distributional failure may point to omitted structure rather than a different named family alone.

deepSections.title: Time ratios support decisions only inside an identified, supported target
deepSections.body: A time ratio is conditional on covariates and the assumed common acceleration structure. It does not mean every individual's event is literally delayed by that factor, and an observational treatment coefficient is not causal without exchangeability, positivity, consistency, timing, and censoring assumptions. Time-dependent treatment can create immortal-time bias if encoded as a baseline exposure. Competing events alter the estimand: modeling cause-specific time while censoring competing causes does not estimate the real-world probability of the cause in isolation. For prediction, choose horizons within mature follow-up, validate probabilities and quantiles on later cohorts, and compare against KM and Cox baselines. For operations, translate distributions into quantities such as probability of failure before warranty, expected workload by week, or a supported quantile. Define behavior for out-of-range covariates and tails, including truncation, abstention, or conservative fallback. Re-estimate or recalibrate when the time origin, event process, population, or intervention policy changes.

lessons.math: log T=x^T beta+sigma epsilon. In Weibull parameterization lambda_i=exp(x_i^T beta), rho>0, S_i(t)=exp[-(t/lambda_i)^rho], and f_i(t)=(rho/lambda_i)(t/lambda_i)^(rho-1)exp[-(t/lambda_i)^rho]. The right-censored log likelihood is sum_i delta_i log f_i(y_i)+(1-delta_i)log S_i(y_i). A one-unit covariate change multiplies every modeled quantile by exp(beta_j). Weibull median is lambda(log 2)^(1/rho). With delayed entry a_i, subtract log S_i(a_i) from the contribution.

workedExamples.title: Event and censor contributions
workedExamples.body: Two otherwise identical subjects are observed to day 10. One fails at day 10 and contributes f(10); the other is censored at day 10 and contributes S(10). The second tells us only that its latent event time exceeds 10.

workedExamples.title: Weibull median
workedExamples.body: With scale lambda=12 and shape rho=2, median time is 12*sqrt(log 2), about 9.99. Doubling lambda doubles that and every other quantile while leaving rho unchanged.

lab.goal: Implement a right-censored Weibull AFT likelihood, fit it with SciPy, verify parameter recovery and time-unit invariance, and produce monotone survival curves.
lab.buildIt:
import numpy as np
rng=np.random.default_rng(17); n=900; x=rng.uniform(-1,1,n); X=np.c_[np.ones(n),x]
beta_true=np.array([2.0,0.55]); rho_true=1.7; scale=np.exp(X@beta_true)
latent=scale*(-np.log(rng.uniform(size=n)))**(1/rho_true); censor=rng.exponential(12.0,n)
time=np.minimum(latent,censor); event=(latent<=censor).astype(int)
def weibull_aft_nll(params,X,time,event):
    beta=np.asarray(params[:-1]); rho=np.exp(params[-1]); logt=np.log(np.asarray(time)); logscale=X@beta; z=np.exp(rho*(logt-logscale))
    logf=np.log(rho)-rho*logscale+(rho-1)*logt-z; logs=-z
    return -np.sum(event*logf+(1-event)*logs)
def survival_curve(params,row,grid):
    rho=np.exp(params[-1]); lam=np.exp(np.asarray(row)@params[:-1]); return np.exp(-(np.asarray(grid)/lam)**rho)
lab.useIt:
from scipy.optimize import minimize
start=np.array([np.log(np.median(time)),0.0,0.0])
fit=minimize(weibull_aft_nll,start,args=(X,time,event),method='L-BFGS-B',bounds=[(None,None),(None,None),(-3,3)])
params=fit.x; beta_hat=params[:-1]; rho_hat=np.exp(params[-1])
fit_days2=minimize(weibull_aft_nll,start+np.array([np.log(2),0,0]),args=(X,2*time,event),method='L-BFGS-B',bounds=[(None,None),(None,None),(-3,3)])
grid=np.linspace(.1,20,100); s_low=survival_curve(params,[1,-1],grid); s_high=survival_curve(params,[1,1],grid)
lab.verifyIt:
assert fit.success and fit_days2.success
assert .2<event.mean()<.9
assert np.allclose(beta_hat,beta_true,atol=.13)
assert abs(rho_hat-rho_true)<.18
# Changing days to two-day units shifts only the log-time intercept by log(2).
assert abs((fit_days2.x[0]-params[0])-np.log(2))<2e-4
assert abs(fit_days2.x[1]-params[1])<2e-4 and abs(fit_days2.x[2]-params[2])<2e-4
assert np.all(np.diff(s_low)<=0) and np.all(np.diff(s_high)<=0)
assert np.all(s_high>=s_low)
assert np.isfinite(weibull_aft_nll(params,X,time,event))
lab.shipIt: Version time unit, distribution, event, censoring and entry likelihood, preprocessing, optimizer and tail policy; validate temporal calibration and quantiles, monitor support and convergence, and roll back the full compatible artifact.

exercises.prompt: An AFT coefficient is log(0.8). What does it mean?
exercises.solution: A one-unit increase multiplies modeled event-time quantiles by 0.8, representing about 20 percent shorter times under the model.

exercises.prompt: Write the likelihood contribution for a subject censored at c.
exercises.solution: S(c|x), the probability their latent event time exceeds c; on the log scale it contributes log S(c|x).

exercises.prompt: Why might a log-normal model fit where Weibull fails?
exercises.solution: Log-normal permits a hazard that rises and then falls, whereas Weibull hazard is monotone. The choice still needs tail and validation checks.

lessons.title: Competing Risks
lessons.interviewAnswer: With competing risks, an event of one cause prevents a different cause from being the first event. The cause-specific hazard is the instantaneous rate of cause k among subjects still free of every event. The cumulative incidence F_k(t)=P(T<=t,J=k) is the actual probability of cause k by t. Aalen-Johansen estimates it by adding S(t-)d_k/n at each event time while updating event-free survival by all-cause events. Treating competing events as censored and plotting 1-KM overestimates cause probability because it imagines those subjects could later experience the cause. Cause-specific Cox models the rate among event-free subjects; Fine-Gray models a subdistribution risk set to connect covariates directly to CIF. I select by estimand, report cause-specific calibrated probabilities, account for censoring and cause adjudication, and avoid causal claims without an intervention framework.
keyPoints: A competing event removes the possibility of another event being the first outcome; it is not ordinary loss to follow-up.
CIF accumulates cause-specific events weighted by probability of still being event-free from every cause.
One minus cause-specific Kaplan-Meier is generally not the real-world cause probability.
Cause-specific and subdistribution hazard ratios use different risk sets and answer different questions.
All cause probabilities plus event-free survival must reconcile within one coherent state system.
lessons.why: A platform may want the probability a customer churns before upgrading, a reliability team may distinguish electrical from mechanical first failure, and a clinician may predict relapse before death. If the alternative event is simply censored, ordinary Kaplan-Meier acts as if that person remains exchangeably capable of the target event later. The resulting hypothetical net risk can exceed the probability actually observable in a world with competing causes. Correct analysis distinguishes rate questions from probability questions. Cause-specific hazards help study mechanisms and build transition models, while cumulative incidence directly supports forecasting and resource allocation. Fine-Gray regression can target covariate associations with cumulative incidence but has a less intuitive risk set. These quantities can move in different directions because a covariate may change the competing cause. Explicit estimands and probability accounting prevent attractive but contradictory dashboards.
lessons.intuition: Picture probability mass beginning in an event-free state. At each time, some mass flows to cause A and some to cause B. Once mass enters either absorbing state, it cannot later enter the other as its first event. The cause-A cumulative incidence is every flow into A added over time. The amount available to flow is the probability still event-free from all causes just before that time. Aalen-Johansen mirrors this accounting in observed risk sets: add S_prev times the fraction d_A/n to cause A, add S_prev*d_B/n to cause B, then reduce S by all events. Censoring removes observation but does not receive event probability. A cause-specific hazard asks about the current flow rate among mass still in the origin. Fine-Gray constructs a different comparison set to model the accumulated probability for one cause.
lessons.deepDive: Competing-risk analysis is probability flow over mutually exclusive first-event states. Cause-specific hazards govern instantaneous exits from the event-free state; cumulative incidence integrates each exit while accounting for depletion by every other cause. Aalen-Johansen provides nonparametric probability accounting, cause-specific regression models transition rates, and Fine-Gray models a quantity tied to a chosen CIF. None is universally best because the estimands differ. Correct cause taxonomy, censoring, entry, intervention logic, horizon support, and joint calibration are essential to useful interpretation.
lessons.workedExample: One hundred devices are initially event-free. At month one, 10 fail mechanically and 5 fail electrically. Aalen-Johansen adds 0.10 to mechanical CIF and 0.05 to electrical CIF, leaving survival 0.85. If 10 of the 85 still at risk fail mechanically at month two, add 0.85*(10/85)=0.10, so mechanical CIF becomes 0.20 and survival falls to 0.75. The month-two increment uses only probability mass that survived every cause through month one.

commonMistakes.misconception: A competing event is just another independent censoring time.
commonMistakes.correction: It makes the alternative first event impossible and must receive probability mass in the competing-risk system.

commonMistakes.misconception: One minus cause-specific KM estimates the observed probability of that cause.
commonMistakes.correction: It estimates a hypothetical net risk after treating competing events as removable censoring and generally overstates real-world CIF.

commonMistakes.misconception: Fine-Gray and cause-specific hazard ratios should match.
commonMistakes.correction: They use different risk sets and estimands; competing-cause effects can make their coefficients differ legitimately.

commonMistakes.misconception: Reducing a competing event must reduce every other cause's incidence.
commonMistakes.correction: Keeping subjects event-free longer can increase opportunities for another cause even when its instantaneous rate is unchanged.

followUps.question: When is censoring competing events acceptable?
followUps.answer: It is part of estimating a cause-specific hazard. It is not acceptable to interpret one minus that cause-specific KM as the actual cumulative incidence.

followUps.question: Which regression should be used for prediction?
followUps.answer: Either can contribute, but validate the final cause-specific CIFs. Combining models for all cause-specific hazards is coherent and flexible; Fine-Gray directly targets one CIF.

followUps.question: How does competing-risk analysis extend to recovery or later transitions?
followUps.answer: Use a multi-state model with transition-specific hazards and Aalen-Johansen transition probabilities rather than stopping at the first absorbing event.

lessons.production: Define an immutable event ontology with mutually exclusive first-event codes, hierarchy, source systems, precedence for simultaneous records, adjudication states, unknown-cause handling, backfill policy, origin, entry, and cutoff. Reconcile counts from raw events to risk sets and require event-free survival plus every CIF to sum to one within tolerance. Version cause-specific models, baselines, Fine-Gray components if used, preprocessing, and horizon grid. Validate temporal discrimination, Brier score, calibration, and decision utility separately for every cause, with event and censoring support. Monitor cause mix, unknown and pending rates, adjudication delay, taxonomy drift, all-cause incidence, probability-sum errors, tail support, subgroup calibration, and action outcomes. Protect sensitive causes and small cells. Shadow ontology or model changes on identical cutoffs, compare subject-level state paths, and roll back taxonomy, extraction, models, and serving schema as one bundle.
lessons.description: Competing risks arise when one subject can experience several mutually exclusive first events and one event prevents the others from occurring first. Churn, upgrade, and account closure; failure from different components; or death from different causes are not ordinary independent censoring categories. This chapter separates overall survival, cause-specific hazard, cumulative incidence, and subdistribution hazard; derives the Aalen-Johansen cumulative-incidence update; and shows why one minus Kaplan-Meier overestimates a cause's real-world probability when competing events are censored. It compares cause-specific Cox regression with Fine-Gray regression, emphasizing that their coefficients answer different questions and need not agree. It covers censoring assumptions, delayed entry, ties, multi-state extensions, recurrent outcomes, composite endpoints, intervention interpretation, evaluation, and calibration by cause. A worked example follows probability mass from event-free survival into two causes. The lab implements Aalen-Johansen and verifies probability conservation, monotonicity, cause-label symmetry, and the naive Kaplan-Meier bias direction. Production guidance versions cause taxonomy and adjudication, reconciles all cause probabilities, monitors unknown and late-coded outcomes, and reports supported horizons rather than hazard ratios alone.
learningObjectives: Distinguish cause-specific hazards, cumulative incidence functions, and subdistribution hazards by estimand and risk set.
Compute Aalen-Johansen cumulative incidence while conserving probability across event-free and cause states.
Choose cause-specific or Fine-Gray regression according to etiologic, prediction, or policy questions.
Handle censoring, cause coding, evaluation, interventions, and multi-state extensions without probability contradictions.

deepSections.title: Hazards and cumulative incidence describe different parts of the process
deepSections.body: Let J identify the first-event cause. The cause-specific hazard h_k(t) is the limiting instantaneous rate of cause k conditional on remaining free of every event just before t. Overall survival is S(t)=P(T>t), governed by the sum of cause-specific hazards: S(t)=exp[-sum_k H_k(t)] under continuous time. The cumulative incidence F_k(t)=P(T<=t,J=k)=integral_0^t S(u-)dH_k(u). Therefore F_k depends on both the target cause hazard and all competing hazards through S. A covariate can lower h_k yet raise F_k if it strongly suppresses a competing event and leaves more subjects available for cause k; the reverse can also occur. A subdistribution hazard is a mathematical transformation linked directly to F_k and keeps subjects with competing events in a modified risk set. It is not the instantaneous biological or operational rate among currently event-free subjects. State the target before fitting: mechanism, real-world first-event probability, intervention policy, or multi-state transition.

deepSections.title: Aalen-Johansen moves probability mass without double counting
deepSections.body: At distinct event time t_j, let n_j be subjects at risk of any first event, d_kj events of cause k, and d_j=sum_k d_kj. Starting with Shat(0)=1 and Fhat_k(0)=0, update Fhat_k(t_j)=Fhat_k(t_j-)+Shat(t_j-)d_kj/n_j for every cause, then Shat(t_j)=Shat(t_j-)(1-d_j/n_j). Thus Shat+sum_k Fhat_k remains one at each event time in a complete first-event state system. Censoring changes later n_j without receiving probability mass. Delayed entry changes risk membership. With no competing causes, the target CIF reduces to one minus Kaplan-Meier. When competing events exist, censoring them and computing one minus a cause-specific KM treats their removed risk as if it represented people still susceptible, producing a hypothetical net-risk curve that generally exceeds the observed-world CIF. Confidence intervals and simultaneous comparisons require appropriate variance or resampling; clustered subjects require cluster-level methods.

deepSections.title: Cause-specific Cox and Fine-Gray regression answer different questions
deepSections.body: For cause-specific Cox regression, events from other causes end the subject's cause-k risk interval and are treated as censored for estimating beta_k. This is valid for the cause-specific hazard estimand under its assumptions, even though one minus the resulting KM-style curve is not a CIF. To predict CIFs, combine estimated hazards for every cause with overall survival. Cause-specific models are natural for etiologic rate questions and multi-state simulation. Fine-Gray regression models a proportional subdistribution hazard associated with F_k; its modified risk sets retain or reweight subjects after competing events. It can summarize covariate association with cumulative incidence and support direct CIF prediction, but its hazard ratio is not a cause-specific rate ratio and proportionality may fail. A covariate's coefficients can differ in sign or magnitude across the two approaches without contradiction. Evaluate predictions on CIF calibration and cause-specific Brier or discrimination metrics, not on coefficient significance alone.

deepSections.title: Cause definitions, interventions, and richer state paths determine validity
deepSections.body: Competing causes must be mutually exclusive as first-event labels, collectively adequate for the target, and adjudicated consistently. Unknown or pending cause is not harmless censoring when its probability depends on the true cause; use adjudication, multiple imputation, sensitivity analysis, or an explicit category as appropriate. Composite endpoints answer whether any component occurs but can hide opposing cause effects. Recurrent events and transitions after the first event require multi-state or recurrent-event models rather than a first-event competing-risk shortcut. Interpreting treatment effects is especially delicate: eliminating a competing cause can increase observed incidence of the target simply by keeping people at risk longer. Separable, controlled direct, and total effects require distinct counterfactual assumptions. Prediction validation should use temporal splits, mature cause labels, common horizons, and cause-specific calibration. For deployment, output a coherent vector of CIFs and event-free probability, enforce nonnegativity and sum constraints, and define actions when the most likely cause is uncertain.

lessons.math: For cause k, h_k(t)=lim_{dt->0}P(t<=T<t+dt,J=k | T>=t)/dt. Overall S(t)=exp[-sum_k H_k(t)] and F_k(t)=integral_0^t S(u-)dH_k(u). Aalen-Johansen updates Delta Fhat_k(t_j)=Shat(t_j-)d_kj/n_j and Shat(t_j)=Shat(t_j-)(1-sum_k d_kj/n_j), giving Shat(t)+sum_k Fhat_k(t)=1. The Fine-Gray subdistribution hazard satisfies alpha_k*(t)=dF_k(t)/[1-F_k(t-)] but uses a modified risk concept distinct from subjects currently free of every event.

workedExamples.title: Why naive one-minus-KM is too high
workedExamples.body: If half a cohort experiences a competing event early, censoring those subjects in a cause-A KM calculation acts as though comparable cause-A-susceptible subjects remain. The hypothetical net risk can keep climbing toward one even though half the cohort can no longer have A first.

workedExamples.title: Opposite-looking effects without contradiction
workedExamples.body: A treatment can leave the target cause-specific hazard unchanged but sharply reduce a competing death. More subjects then survive long enough to experience the target, increasing its CIF. Rate and probability estimands differ.

lab.goal: Implement Aalen-Johansen cumulative incidence, contrast it with naive cause-specific one-minus-KM, and verify probability conservation, monotonicity, and cause-label symmetry.
lab.useIt:
# NumPy indexing produces a coherent fixed-horizon report from the step functions.
horizon=6.0
row=np.searchsorted(ts,horizon,side='right')-1
report={'event_free':float(s[row]),'cause_1':float(cif[row,0]),'cause_2':float(cif[row,1])}
lab.verifyIt:

lessons.title: Multi-objective Optimization & Pareto Trade-offs
lessons.interviewAnswer: In multi-objective optimization, a feasible point dominates another if it is no worse on every objective and strictly better on at least one. Pareto-optimal points are not dominated, so the result is generally a frontier rather than one answer. Weighted sums are simple and can recover supported points on convex fronts, but may miss nonconvex regions and hide stakeholder preferences. Epsilon constraints or lexicographic rules are often clearer for hard limits and priorities; evolutionary algorithms such as NSGA-II approximate broader fronts. I normalize only with declared meaning, include uncertainty and feasibility, evaluate coverage/diversity, and treat selection from the frontier as a separate governed decision.
keyPoints: Pareto optimal means not dominated, not universally best
Decision space and objective space are different
Scalarization embeds preferences and can miss parts of a front
Front quality requires convergence and diversity evidence
Choosing one point is a policy decision after optimization
lessons.why: A model can improve accuracy by adding latency, a supply plan can cut cost by increasing risk, and a ranking system can increase engagement while worsening fairness or user welfare. Collapsing these outcomes into one unreviewed score hides value judgments and enables compensation that stakeholders may reject. Multi-objective methods expose feasible alternatives and marginal trade-offs. They are also useful for architecture search and engineering design. Yet a giant approximate frontier can overwhelm decision makers, and poorly normalized metrics or noisy evaluations can manufacture dominance. Interviews test whether candidates can distinguish optimization mechanics from stakeholder choice. Production systems need a stable metric contract and explicit guardrails before a frontier is trusted.
lessons.intuition: Plot two objectives to minimize. Points toward the lower-left are better. A point is dominated when another lies no higher and no farther right, with at least one strict improvement. The nondominated boundary is the Pareto front: moving along it improves one objective only by sacrificing another. A weighted sum rolls a straight contour line toward the feasible objective set and touches a supported point; concave inward portions may never be touched. Epsilon constraints instead cap one objective and optimize the other, making limits explicit. After computing alternatives, humans or a policy still choose a point based on budgets, thresholds, risk, and accountability.
lessons.deepDive: Multi-objective optimization preserves conflict until preferences are declared. It produces an evidence-backed set of efficient alternatives; decision analysis then maps that set to one action under values and uncertainty.
lessons.workedExample: Four classifiers have (error, latency ms): A=(0.12,20), B=(0.10,35), C=(0.09,70), D=(0.13,50). D is dominated by A because A has lower error and latency. A, B, and C form a front. If production requires latency<=40, C is infeasible and B has the lowest error among allowed models. A weighted sum could choose differently depending on scaling and weight, but the latency constraint expresses the policy more clearly. Fairness and memory can be added as guardrails or objectives; uncertainty intervals from repeated evaluation may make A and B statistically indistinguishable, motivating a simpler or cheaper selection.

commonMistakes.mistake: Calling every nondominated point equally good
commonMistakes.correction: They are efficient under modeled objectives, but feasibility, uncertainty, stakeholder preferences, and risk still determine suitability.

commonMistakes.correction: Weights and normalization encode units and values; document them and test sensitivity.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming weighted sums recover the whole front
commonMistakes.correction: Linear scalarization can miss unsupported points on nonconvex fronts; use epsilon constraints or suitable front methods.

commonMistakes.mistake: Optimizing many redundant objectives
commonMistakes.correction: Dominance loses discrimination; remove redundancy or turn nonnegotiable measures into explicit constraints.

lessons.description: Multi-objective optimization handles decisions where several criteria conflict and no single scalar score is scientifically or organizationally sufficient. Rather than pretending one configuration is universally best, it identifies feasible trade-offs through dominance, Pareto optimality, fronts, scalarization, epsilon constraints, lexicographic priorities, evolutionary methods, hypervolume, and multi-criteria decision analysis. This chapter develops decision space versus objective space, weak and strict dominance, supported and unsupported Pareto points, normalization, preference elicitation, constraints, uncertainty, many-objective difficulties, and post-optimization selection. You will learn why weighted sums expose only part of a nonconvex front, why objectives should preserve units until preferences are explicit, how NSGA-II uses nondominated sorting and crowding distance, and why optimizing a frontier is separate from choosing a policy. A worked model-selection example balances error, latency, cost, and fairness guardrails. The lab implements nondominated filtering and hypervolume in two dimensions, uses a SciPy epsilon-constraint sweep, and verifies invariance and known fronts. Production guidance covers stakeholder governance, metric drift, robust feasibility, monitoring, rollback, and transparent decision records.

deepSections.title: Dominance, Pareto sets, and objective direction
deepSections.body: Let F(x)=(f_1(x),...,f_m(x)) for feasible x, with all objectives converted consistently to minimization or maximization. For minimization, a dominates b if f_j(a)<=f_j(b) for every j and strict inequality holds for at least one. A Pareto-optimal decision is not dominated by another feasible decision. The Pareto set lives in decision space; its image is the Pareto front in objective space. Weak dominance, strict dominance, and epsilon-dominance differ and should be named. Constraints determine feasibility before dominance. Duplicate objective vectors, ties, missing values, and stochastic estimates need explicit handling.

deepSections.title: Weighted sums, epsilon constraints, and priorities
deepSections.body: A weighted sum minimizes sum_j w_j f_j(x) with nonnegative weights, after any necessary scaling. Weights encode both units and preference; they are not objective facts. For convex achievable objective sets, varying positive weights finds supported Pareto points, but nonconvex fronts can contain efficient unsupported points never optimal for any linear weight. The epsilon-constraint method optimizes one objective while bounding others and can trace such regions. Lexicographic optimization enforces strict priority by optimizing objectives sequentially while preserving earlier optima within tolerances. Goal programming minimizes deviations from targets. Each method should match how stakeholders actually express trade-offs.

deepSections.title: Front construction and NSGA-II intuition
deepSections.body: Exact scalarization sweeps suit tractable mathematical programs. Population-based evolutionary algorithms are useful for nonconvex, discontinuous, mixed, or black-box problems but yield approximations, not proof by default. NSGA-II combines parent and offspring populations, sorts candidates into nondomination ranks, and fills the next generation front by front. When a front must be split, crowding distance favors isolated points to preserve spread, while extreme points receive priority. Selection compares rank then crowding; crossover and mutation explore decisions. Results depend on population, operators, budget, constraints, seed, and representation, so repeated runs and baseline fronts are essential.

deepSections.title: Measuring a front and choosing one point
deepSections.body: Convergence asks whether candidates approach the true or best-known front; diversity asks whether useful regions are covered. Hypervolume measures objective-space volume dominated by a front relative to a stated worse reference point, rewarding both convergence and spread but becoming expensive and reference-sensitive in many objectives. Generational distance, epsilon indicators, and coverage add other views. A knee point may offer a favorable marginal trade-off but is not automatically the stakeholder choice. Post-optimization decision methods should expose normalized values, hard constraints, uncertainty, dominated alternatives removed, and how the selected point changes under plausible weights or thresholds.

deepSections.title: Uncertainty, many objectives, and governance
deepSections.body: Estimated objectives have sampling, simulation, or model uncertainty. Point-estimate dominance can flip under noise, so use replication, posterior/interval comparisons, robust or chance constraints, and sensitivity analysis. With many objectives, most points become nondominated and visualization plus selection degrade; reduce redundant metrics, promote nonnegotiable outcomes to guardrails, or use reference directions and preference-guided search. Objectives are vulnerable to gaming and distribution shift. Define owners, populations, time horizons, denominators, floors, and refresh cadence. Preserve the frontier considered, stakeholder input, rejected alternatives, and revisit triggers so optimization does not launder an opaque value choice into mathematics.

lessons.math: For minimization, x dominates y when f_j(x)<=f_j(y) for all j and f_k(x)<f_k(y) for some k. The Pareto set P={x in X: no feasible y dominates x}; front is F(P). Weighted sum minimizes w^T F(x), w>=0. Epsilon constraint minimizes f_1(x) subject to f_j(x)<=epsilon_j for j>1. In two dimensions with worse reference r, hypervolume is the area of the union of rectangles [f_1(x),r_1]x[f_2(x),r_2] for nondominated feasible x, after consistent minimization orientation.

lab.useIt:
from math import sqrt
from scipy.optimize import minimize
# Trace f1=x^2 versus f2=(x-1)^2 by bounding f2 at several epsilons.
library_front=[]
for epsilon in (0.04,0.16,0.36,0.64,1.0):
    result=minimize(lambda z:z[0]**2,[max(0.0,1-sqrt(epsilon))],bounds=[(0,1)],constraints=[{'type':'ineq','fun':lambda z,e=epsilon:e-(z[0]-1)**2}],method='SLSQP')
    assert result.success
    x=float(result.x[0]); library_front.append((x*x,(x-1)**2))
lab.verifyIt:
assert set(front)=={(0.12,0.20),(0.10,0.35),(0.09,0.70)}
assert (0.13,0.50) not in front
assert pareto(list(reversed(points)))==list(reversed(front))
assert hv>0
assert len(library_front)==5
assert all(not dominates(a,b) for i,a in enumerate(library_front) for j,b in enumerate(library_front) if i!=j)
assert all(0<=a<=1 and 0<=b<=1 for a,b in library_front)
assert hypervolume_2d(front,(0.25,1.1))>hv
