lessons.title: Locality-Sensitive Hashing (LSH)
lessons.interviewAnswer: Locality-sensitive hashing is a candidate-generation framework in which nearby objects collide more often than far objects. For MinHash signatures, divide k=br rows into b bands of r rows; a pair is a candidate if every row matches in at least one band. If row agreement is s and independence is a useful approximation, candidate probability is 1−(1−s^r)^b. Larger r demands stronger within-band agreement and improves precision; more bands create more chances and improve recall. The S-curve is not a hard threshold, and candidates still require full scoring or exact verification. I tune b and r on labeled pairs, report candidate recall and candidate volume separately from final ranking metrics, version the hash family, handle hot buckets, and never describe LSH as universally optimal across metrics.
keyPoints: An LSH family is metric-specific: close pairs have higher collision probability than far pairs.
MinHash banding performs an OR over bands of ANDs within a band.
The probability 1−(1−s^r)^b produces a soft S-curve, not deterministic thresholding.
LSH generates candidates; a second stage computes or learns the final similarity and decision.
Measure candidate recall, bucket skew, memory and latency before downstream ranking quality.
lessons.why: Even a compact signature does not solve quadratic search: comparing every pair among n objects still needs Θ(n²) comparisons, and querying against all n still needs linear work. LSH spends extra memory to index randomized collisions so that likely neighbors are examined and most far objects are skipped. It is valuable when exact indexing structures deteriorate in high dimensions and approximation is acceptable. The deeper lesson is system decomposition: a recall-oriented retrieval stage deliberately admits false positives, then a more expensive scorer restores precision. Understanding the probability curve, independence assumptions and bucket distribution is essential because poor parameters can either miss true neighbors or recreate an all-pairs workload through giant buckets.
lessons.intuition: Suppose each MinHash row agrees with probability s. Requiring r rows in one band to all agree has probability s^r—an AND that suppresses weak pairs. Giving the pair b independent bands creates b chances—an OR that rescues strong pairs. It fails to become a candidate only if every band fails, giving (1−s^r)^b, so success is one minus that. For s near zero the probability stays low; near one it rises sharply. Changing r and b moves and sharpens this transition, but no finite setting turns it into a perfect step.
lessons.deepDive: LSH organizes approximate retrieval around collision probabilities rather than exact metric partitions. MinHash banding illustrates amplification through AND and OR operations, while other metrics need other families. Correct evaluation separates the candidate generator from the downstream scorer and treats index versioning, hot buckets, updates and adversarial inputs as first-class concerns.
lessons.math: A family H is (R,cR,p1,p2)-sensitive for a distance when points at distance at most R collide with probability at least p1 and points beyond cR collide with probability at most p2, with p1>p2. Concatenating r hashes maps collision p to p^r; using b independent tables maps it to 1−(1−p^r)^b. For MinHash p=s=Jaccard. A rough transition location solves s^r≈1/b, so s≈(1/b)^(1/r), but operating characteristics must use the full curve. Classical query exponents are summarized by ρ=log(1/p1)/log(1/p2) under framework assumptions.

commonMistakes.misconception: LSH returns the nearest neighbor exactly.
commonMistakes.correction: It probabilistically generates candidates and may miss neighbors; score candidates and quantify recall.

commonMistakes.misconception: The S-curve threshold is deterministic.
commonMistakes.correction: Every similarity has a nonzero candidate probability except special endpoints; the curve is soft.

commonMistakes.misconception: Any hash family works for any similarity.
commonMistakes.correction: Collision behavior must correspond to the chosen geometry.

commonMistakes.misconception: Final ranking precision is enough to evaluate the index.
commonMistakes.correction: Measure candidate recall and volume separately because missed candidates cannot be repaired downstream.

followUps.question: What do more bands do?
followUps.answer: They increase the number of chances for a collision, raising recall and candidate volume.

followUps.question: What do more rows per band do?
followUps.answer: They require stronger agreement within each band, reducing false candidates but also recall.

followUps.question: Why exact-score candidates after LSH?
followUps.answer: Bucket collisions are deliberately noisy; exact or richer scoring restores ordering and supports calibrated decisions.

lessons.production: Freeze representation, signature and band schemas into an index version. Build immutable snapshots or dual-write compatible online indexes, validate counts and checksums, and promote through canary queries. Tune from labeled candidate recall versus unique candidates, bytes, latency and memory—not from the S-curve alone. Track bucket-size quantiles, hot partitions, duplicate candidates, empty queries, write lag, deletion debt and fallback use. Cap or split hot buckets with measured recall impact. Exact-score or rerank candidates, and preserve a brute-force audit slice. Protect index writes and query rates against collision flooding; restrict access to signatures and membership. Keep previous snapshots and routing configuration so index, threshold and reranker can be rolled back independently.
lessons.workedExample: With b=20 bands and r=5 rows, similarity 0.8 yields candidate probability 1−(1−0.8^5)^20≈0.9996, while similarity 0.3 yields about 0.047. This looks attractive, yet a corpus with a billion unrelated pairs can still create many candidates, and correlated signature rows or template-heavy documents distort the calculation. The expected candidate volume and empirical labeled recall matter more than the apparent threshold alone.
lessons.description: Locality-sensitive hashing is a family of randomized indexes for approximate near-neighbor retrieval. This chapter defines locality sensitivity through collision probabilities, explains why an LSH family must match the target distance or similarity, and derives MinHash banding as an OR-of-AND amplification scheme. It works through the candidate probability 1−(1−s^r)^b, the resulting S-curve, the effects of bands and rows, and the difference between an approximate transition and a guaranteed threshold. It connects the construction to the Indyk–Motwani near-neighbor framework and distinguishes MinHash LSH for Jaccard from random-hyperplane hashing for angular similarity and p-stable methods for certain Lp distances. The chapter treats multi-probe lookup, multiple tables, candidate deduplication, exact rescoring, recall–latency trade-offs and the limitations of correlated hashes. The lab builds band buckets over deterministic MinHash signatures, verifies theoretical monotonicity and retrieves similar sets while excluding a disjoint set. Production guidance covers labeled tuning, candidate recall, bucket skew, memory, hot keys, online updates, backfills, hash versioning, adversarial flooding, privacy and rollback. LSH is positioned as a retrieval component, not a final similarity metric or universal nearest-neighbor solution.
learningObjectives: Derive MinHash banding's candidate probability and explain the roles of b and r.
Match an LSH family to Jaccard, angular or Lp geometry without conflating their collision laws.
Tune and evaluate candidate generation independently from exact scoring or downstream ranking.
Design a versioned, observable index that handles hot buckets, updates, abuse and rollback.

deepSections.title: Locality sensitivity is a probabilistic property tied to a geometry
deepSections.body: An ordinary hash tries to distribute keys uniformly and makes similar inputs unrelated. An LSH family deliberately gives near objects a higher collision probability. The definition is relative to a distance, near radius R, approximation factor c and probabilities p1>p2. MinHash supplies collision probability equal to Jaccard similarity. Random hyperplanes produce a collision law related to the angle between vectors, making them suitable for cosine or angular search. P-stable projections support certain Lp distances. Binary Hamming distance has bit-sampling constructions. Using the wrong family destroys the proximity promise even if the code still returns buckets. Feature normalization and representation determine the geometry before indexing. LSH is most compelling where exact scans are too costly and approximate misses are acceptable; low-dimensional trees, graph indexes, inverted indexes or product quantization may be better under other workloads.

deepSections.title: Banding amplifies a modest row collision gap into an S-curve
deepSections.body: Arrange a k-row MinHash signature into b bands of r rows, k=br. Hash each complete band tuple into a bucket. Two objects become candidates when at least one band tuple matches. Under independent rows, one band matches with probability s^r and all b bands fail with probability (1−s^r)^b. Increasing r is a stricter AND: it lowers candidate probability, especially for moderate similarities. Increasing b is a broader OR: it raises probability at every nonzero similarity. Holding k fixed forces a trade-off rather than allowing both improvements. The popular approximation (1/b)^(1/r) locates the bend but is not a guarantee. Hash rows can be correlated, finite-hash collisions add noise, and objects with templated shingles violate simple corpus assumptions, so empirical curves are necessary.

deepSections.title: Candidate recall and candidate volume expose retrieval-stage quality
deepSections.body: Offline evaluation starts with labeled or exact-computed relevant neighbors for representative queries. Candidate recall is the fraction that appear anywhere in the union of buckets. Candidates per query, unique bucket probes, bytes read and tail latency measure cost. The downstream exact Jaccard or learned reranker then has its own precision, recall, NDCG and decision threshold. Reporting only final precision hides relevant pairs that the candidate stage made impossible to recover; reporting only theoretical collision probability hides corpus skew. Tune b, r, table count and multi-probe radius against the complete recall–cost curve. Include short and long sets, languages, templates, new items and sparse segments. Compare with a brute-force subset during monitoring. A gray zone can probe extra buckets or use a fallback index for high-value queries.

deepSections.title: Index mechanics and failure behavior determine production reliability
deepSections.body: Persist the preprocessing version, hash family, row order, band layout and bucket encoding. A changed seed requires a parallel index or rebuild; mixing versions silently eliminates legitimate collisions. Online insertion writes every band, while deletion needs reverse mappings, tombstones or compaction. Deduplicate candidates returned by multiple bands and cap pathological buckets, but measure the recall lost by caps. Common shingles can create hot buckets that overload partitions; salting, stop-shingle policy, frequency-aware filtering and secondary partitioning trade recall for stability. Adversaries may craft collisions or flood popular bands, so authenticate writes, rate-limit queries and use keyed or robust hashes where the threat model warrants it. Snapshot manifests, checksums and canary queries support atomic promotion and rollback. Signatures and shared buckets can leak similarity or membership, requiring access control and retention policy.

workedExamples.title: Parameter trade-off at fixed signature size
workedExamples.body: For 120 rows, 30×4 banding is recall-heavy, while 12×10 is precision-heavy. Both consume the same signature rows but yield radically different candidate curves.

workedExamples.title: Hot-template bucket
workedExamples.body: A legal footer contributes many identical shingles across otherwise unrelated pages. Buckets explode, so boilerplate removal or frequency-aware shingles may improve both cost and relevance.

lessons.title: Bloom Filters
lessons.interviewAnswer: A Bloom filter is an insert-only approximate-membership structure with an m-bit array and k hash locations per key. Insert sets all k bits; lookup returns definitely absent if any bit is zero and possibly present if all are one. Under the model of independent uniform hashes after n distinct insertions, the false-positive probability is approximately (1−e^(−kn/m))^k and the optimal integer k is near (m/n)ln2. A correct ordinary filter has no false negatives only while its hash and bit-state contract is preserved and bits are never cleared. I size from expected cardinality and target error, version hashing and capacity, rebuild before saturation, verify positives against an authoritative store, and monitor fill ratio and empirical false positives. Deletion needs a counting or deletion-capable alternative, not clearing shared bits.
keyPoints: Negative answers are definitive; positive answers require confirmation when correctness matters.
False positives arise because unrelated keys can collectively set every queried bit.
Capacity, bit count and hash count jointly determine error; overfilling invalidates the target rate.
The no-false-negative claim assumes stable hashing, completed writes, intact bits and no unsupported deletion.
Filters can reduce expensive negative I/O, but they are not key-value stores and cannot enumerate members.
lessons.why: Many storage and network workloads ask about keys that are absent. Checking an authoritative database, disk block, remote service or large denylist for every miss is expensive. A Bloom filter uses a small memory-resident precheck to reject most nonmembers cheaply while allowing configurable false positives. Its value comes from asymmetric costs: a false positive merely performs the slower authoritative lookup, whereas a false negative could incorrectly skip real data and is therefore forbidden by the ordinary contract. The structure teaches how probabilistic error, capacity planning, hashing and operational consistency combine; a mathematically sized filter can still fail if it is overfilled, partially written, rebuilt under different seeds or used to authorize destructive actions without confirmation.
lessons.intuition: Think of m lamps initially off. Each inserted key chooses k lamps and switches them on. A query checks the same positions. If one lamp is off, that key could never have been inserted under the current contract. If every lamp is on, the key may have set them—or other keys may have set them coincidentally. More hash locations initially reduce accidental agreement, but too many rapidly fill the array. The best k balances those forces for the planned number of distinct insertions.
lessons.deepDive: Bloom filters exploit a one-sided error contract to avoid expensive negative work. Their textbook formula assumes a planned load and ideal hashes, while reliable deployments must preserve bit and hash versions, coordinate writes, avoid unsupported deletion and rebuild before saturation. The filter is an optimization layer whose positives are verified by an authoritative source.
lessons.math: After kn independent bit assignments into m positions, a particular bit remains zero with probability (1−1/m)^(kn)≈e^(−kn/m). A query's k positions are all one with approximate probability p=(1−e^(−kn/m))^k. Minimizing p for fixed m,n gives k*=(m/n)ln2 and p*≈(0.6185)^(m/n). Rearranging gives m≈−n ln p/(ln2)^2 bits. These are model-based approximations: duplicate hashes, finite m, nonuniform inputs and dependent hash derivation affect exact behavior. Union by bitwise OR is valid only for identical m, k and hash family and corresponds to the union's larger load.

commonMistakes.misconception: A positive means the key exists.
commonMistakes.correction: It means possibly present; confirm against the authoritative set when correctness matters.

commonMistakes.misconception: Bloom filters never have false negatives under any deployment.
commonMistakes.correction: The claim depends on stable hashes, completed writes, intact state and no unsupported clearing.

commonMistakes.misconception: More hash functions always reduce errors.
commonMistakes.correction: Past the load-dependent optimum they fill the array faster and increase both CPU and false positives.

commonMistakes.misconception: Deleting means clearing the key's bits.
commonMistakes.correction: Bits are shared; clearing creates false negatives for other keys.

followUps.question: How do you choose m and k?
followUps.answer: Use expected distinct n and target p: m≈−n ln p/(ln2)^2 and k≈(m/n)ln2, then round and test.

followUps.question: Can two Bloom filters be unioned?
followUps.answer: Bitwise OR represents a union only when dimensions and every hash choice match; the resulting load determines its new error rate.

followUps.question: When is a Bloom filter a bad choice?
followUps.answer: When exact positives are required without a backing check, members must be enumerated, deletions are ordinary, or the exact set already fits cheaply.

lessons.production: Document n, target p, m, k, hash algorithm and seeds, key encoding, duplicate semantics and rebuild trigger. Put the filter only on a path where a negative safely skips work and a positive can consult authority. Build immutable checksummed snapshots from a known source watermark; overlay concurrent writes or dual-write, canary the snapshot, then atomically promote. During missing or stale state, bypass optimization instead of claiming absence. Monitor bit occupancy, estimated distinct load, negative rate, confirmed positives, empirical false-positive rate, hash CPU, snapshot age and rebuild duration. Alert before saturation. Use counting or another structure for deletion, and guard against counter errors. Keep the last good snapshot and configuration for independent rollback, with rate limiting or keyed hashes for hostile keys.
lessons.workedExample: For one million expected distinct keys and target p=1%, m≈9.59 million bits, about 1.20 MB, and k≈6.64, so choose 7 hashes and evaluate the integer result. If two million keys are inserted without resizing, the false-positive rate rises dramatically even though lookups still execute. Fill ratio is therefore an operational signal, not just an implementation detail. A reported positive must still check the underlying store before returning a value or denying access.
lessons.description: Bloom filters provide compact approximate membership with one-sided error. This chapter develops the bit-array and multi-hash mechanism, proves why a zero bit certifies absence, derives expected occupancy and the standard false-positive approximation, and obtains the near-optimal number of hashes and memory-sizing formula. It distinguishes planned distinct insertions from events, explains why overcapacity raises error, and examines finite-hash collisions, double hashing, stable serialization and adversarial keys. The no-false-negative guarantee is stated with its real assumptions: identical hash configuration, durable completed insertion, uncorrupted state and no clearing of shared bits. Variants include counting, scalable, blocked, partitioned and stable Bloom filters, plus Cuckoo and quotient filters, with attention to deletion and cache locality. The lab implements deterministic double hashing, checks every inserted key, measures empirical false positives against theory and verifies serialization-relevant determinism. Production design treats the filter as a negative cache in front of an authoritative store, monitors fill and observed error, rebuilds through versioned snapshots, coordinates updates, handles warmup and rollback, and protects against collision flooding. It also explains when a plain set, sorted structure or exact database index is a better choice.
learningObjectives: Derive Bloom-filter occupancy, false-positive probability, memory sizing and optimal hash count.
Explain the precise assumptions behind one-sided error and why ordinary deletion is unsafe.
Choose among ordinary, counting, scalable, blocked, Cuckoo or exact membership structures.
Operate a versioned filter with empirical error monitoring, authoritative confirmation and safe rebuilds.

deepSections.title: One-sided error follows from monotone bit updates
deepSections.body: An ordinary filter initializes every bit to zero. Insertion deterministically maps a key to k positions and changes those bits only from zero to one. Therefore, if a later lookup under the identical hash configuration finds a zero at any required position, that exact insertion could not have completed in the represented state. When all positions are one, membership remains uncertain because assignments from many other keys overlap. The often-repeated no-false-negative guarantee is conditional: a reader that uses different seeds, observes a stale replica before insertion, reads a corrupt snapshot, loses a write or clears a shared bit can return false negatives. The filter also cannot recover keys, store associated values or count exact frequency. It is an optimization for membership questions with asymmetric consequences, not a replacement for the authoritative set.

deepSections.title: Sizing balances occupancy, hash work and the expected distinct load
deepSections.body: Each of kn assignments misses a chosen bit with probability 1−1/m, producing expected zero fraction near exp(−kn/m). Assuming query locations behave independently, the false-positive rate is the kth power of the occupied fraction. For fixed bits per inserted key, too few hashes leave weak fingerprints and too many saturate the array; differentiating the approximation yields k=(m/n)ln2. Round to a practical positive integer and compute the achieved rate rather than blindly rounding. Capacity n refers to distinct inserted identities, although duplicates repeat work without changing bits. The model presumes uniform hashes and a planned load. Monitor actual fraction of one bits, infer effective load if useful, and benchmark with representative negative keys. If growth is uncertain, use scalable layers or rebuild; merely accepting arbitrary overfill abandons the service-level error target.

deepSections.title: Deletion, locality and unbounded streams require different structures
deepSections.body: Clearing an ordinary bit during deletion can erase evidence shared by other keys and create false negatives. A counting Bloom filter replaces bits with small counters, increments and decrements positions, but needs more memory and must prevent overflow, underflow and duplicate-delete errors. Scalable Bloom filters append new layers as capacity grows and query all layers, allocating per-layer error so total false-positive probability remains bounded. Blocked filters map a key to a cache-line-sized region, improving locality with a different error profile. Stable filters intentionally forget old items for sliding streams and therefore allow false negatives relative to all history. Cuckoo filters store compact fingerprints in candidate buckets and support deletion under occupancy constraints; quotient filters offer other locality and resizing properties. Choose from update semantics, error asymmetry, enumeration needs, concurrency and hardware behavior—not name recognition.

deepSections.title: Production correctness belongs to the filter-plus-store protocol
deepSections.body: A safe read path asks the filter first; negative skips the expensive store, while positive queries the authoritative store. Never use a positive alone to grant access, claim existence, bill a user or delete data. Define how writes update store and filter. Store-first then filter can temporarily cause extra I/O but preserves correctness; filter-first can advertise an uncommitted key. Rebuild into an immutable snapshot with configuration, expected count, actual count, fill ratio, checksum and source watermark, then atomically swap readers. During rebuild, overlay recent writes or dual-write to avoid false negatives. Replication lag and process restarts need explicit behavior, often bypassing the filter until ready. Monitor negative bypass rate, positive confirmation rate, empirical false positives, fill ratio, hash latency, snapshot age and authoritative misses. Rate-limit adversarial probes and consider keyed hashing where inputs are hostile.

workedExamples.title: SSTable negative lookup
workedExamples.body: A storage engine checks each file's filter before touching its index and data blocks. A false positive costs an unnecessary read; a false negative would lose a real key and is unacceptable.

workedExamples.title: Unsafe deletion
workedExamples.body: Keys A and B share one bit. Clearing A's positions also clears B's evidence, so B can appear absent; a counting or deletion-capable structure is required.

lab.goal: Implement a deterministic Bloom filter, size it from an error target, and test one-sided membership and empirical false positives.

# Positive answers are checked against the authoritative set.
def lookup(key):
    if key not in bf: return 'definitely absent'
    return 'present' if key in inserted else 'false positive'

exercises.prompt: Why is a zero bit definitive?
exercises.solution: Insertion would have set every deterministic position; an intact zero proves that insertion is not represented.

exercises.prompt: What happens when n doubles without resizing?

exercises.prompt: Why is store-first writing often safer?
exercises.solution: A lagging filter causes extra authoritative reads, while a filter that advertises an uncommitted key can violate the protocol.

lessons.title: Count-Min Sketch & Heavy Hitters
lessons.interviewAnswer: A Count-Min sketch summarizes a nonnegative frequency vector in a d×w counter table. Each update adds its amount to one bucket per hash row; a point query returns the minimum of those counters. In a cash-register stream the estimate never undercounts, because each chosen counter contains the target frequency plus collision mass. With width about e/ε and depth about ln(1/δ), the overestimate is at most ε times total stream mass with probability at least 1−δ under the standard hash assumptions. Rows reduce failure probability; width reduces collision error. Sketches with identical dimensions and hashes merge by elementwise addition. I distinguish this contract from signed turnstile streams, version the hashes, prevent overflow, validate heavy hitters against exact samples, and monitor error as distribution and total mass change.
keyPoints: The minimum removes rows with unusually large positive collision noise.
Nonnegative updates give one-sided overestimation; signed updates need a different analysis or sketch.
Width controls additive error and depth controls the probability that every row is bad.
Linearity enables merge only when counter shape, hash family, encoding and update semantics match.
Heavy-hitter discovery also needs a candidate mechanism because the sketch cannot enumerate original keys.
lessons.why: High-rate streams often contain too many distinct keys to maintain an exact counter map on every worker. Operators still need approximate frequencies, heavy hitters, join-size signals or anomaly features with fixed memory and mergeable state. Count-Min offers constant update and query time relative to the key universe and a clear additive-error guarantee. Its simplicity can be deceptive: it does not retain keys, small frequencies can have terrible relative error, signed deletions alter the guarantee, and incompatible sketches cannot be merged. Learning the exact model—frequency vector, update semantics, total mass and hash assumptions—prevents a useful sketch from becoming an undocumented approximate database.
lessons.intuition: Each row is a row of shared counting bins. An event increments one bin in every row. Querying a key finds counters that contain its true count plus counts from keys that collided there. All are too high in a nonnegative stream, but different rows have different collisions; taking the minimum chooses the least contaminated view. Wider rows give keys more space, while additional independent rows give more chances to find a clean-ish bucket.
lessons.deepDive: Count-Min is a linear randomized summary of a frequency vector. Its one-sided point estimate and epsilon-delta bound belong to nonnegative updates and compatible hashes, not every stream imaginable. Successful systems pair it with candidate tracking, explicit merge schemas, overflow protection, exact audit samples and capacity choices based on absolute error.
lessons.math: Let f_i≥0 and total mass ||f||_1=Σ_i f_i. Row j stores C[j,h_j(i)] plus collisions. Query f_hat_i=min_j C[j,h_j(i)], so f_hat_i≥f_i. With w=ceil(e/ε), one row's expected collision mass is at most ||f||_1/w and Markov bounds a row as bad with probability at most 1/e; d=ceil(ln(1/δ)) independent rows make all rows bad with probability at most δ. Thus f_hat_i≤f_i+ε||f||_1 with probability at least 1−δ. Constants vary by convention. Pairwise-independent hashing suffices for the common proof; merge is elementwise addition for identical hash mappings.

commonMistakes.misconception: The sketch returns an unbiased exact-like count.
commonMistakes.correction: In nonnegative streams the minimum is generally upward biased by collisions and has an additive probabilistic bound.

commonMistakes.misconception: Depth improves numerical precision.
commonMistakes.correction: Depth mainly lowers failure probability; width reduces collision magnitude.

commonMistakes.misconception: The sketch can return all heavy hitters by itself.
commonMistakes.correction: It stores counters but no keys, so pair it with candidate tracking.

commonMistakes.misconception: Any same-sized sketches can be added.
commonMistakes.correction: Every hash, encoding, counter and epoch parameter must match.

followUps.question: Why take the minimum rather than the mean?
followUps.answer: Every row has nonnegative collision noise; the minimum selects the least contaminated row.

followUps.question: What does ε control?
followUps.answer: An additive error scale relative to total stream L1 mass, primarily through width.

followUps.question: Count-Min or Count Sketch for signed updates?
followUps.answer: Count Sketch is usually the principled choice for general signed turnstile streams and L2-style error; state the stream model first.

lessons.production: Define the stream model, unit and deduplication contract; set ε, δ, counter width, hash algorithm and seeds from the allowed absolute error and traffic horizon. Include these in an immutable merge schema and reject mismatches. Pair the sketch with a bounded candidate tracker and exact confirmation for alerts, billing or blocking. Monitor total mass, update rate, candidate churn, table occupancy proxy, maximum counters, overflow headroom, sampled exact error, merge lag and replay rates. Rotate by time bucket for windows and rebuild when schemas change. Use keyed hashing and rate limits for hostile keys. Snapshot with checksums and source watermarks, retain a previous epoch, and fall back to exact or degraded aggregation if state is corrupt rather than serving unqualified estimates.
lessons.workedExample: A stream has one million events and ε=0.001. The guarantee allows additive error up to 1,000 with high probability. That may be excellent for a key occurring 100,000 times but useless for a key occurring 5 times. The bound is additive in total mass, not relative to each key. A top-k system can use the sketch to score candidates tracked by a heap or sampled dictionary, then verify promoted keys exactly when action costs are high.
lessons.description: The Count-Min sketch is a fixed-memory streaming summary for approximate point frequencies and related aggregate queries. This chapter models a stream as updates to a frequency vector, constructs the depth-by-width counter array, and explains why querying the minimum yields a one-sided estimate under nonnegative updates. It derives the standard width and depth choices from ε additive error and δ failure probability, clarifies constants and hash-independence assumptions, and interprets error relative to total L1 mass rather than individual count. It covers weighted updates, conservative update, inner-product and merge operations, and distinguishes the cash-register model from strict and general turnstile streams. It explains why a sketch cannot enumerate keys, so heavy-hitter systems need a candidate structure, and why negative updates, counter overflow and incompatible hash versions can invalidate expectations. The lab implements deterministic rows, compares estimates with exact Counter values, verifies non-underestimation and merge equivalence, and checks a practical error envelope. Production guidance addresses parameter budgets, key encoding, distributed merge manifests, skew, candidate tracking, exact audits, saturation, concurrency, adversarial hashes, privacy and rollback. Comparisons with Bloom filters, Count Sketch, Misra–Gries and HyperLogLog reinforce that each structure answers a different query.
learningObjectives: Implement Count-Min updates, point queries and compatible merges from the frequency-vector model.
Derive and correctly interpret the ε||f||1 additive-error and δ failure guarantee.
Distinguish nonnegative, strict-turnstile and signed-stream behavior and select alternatives when needed.
Build a heavy-hitter service with candidate tracking, exact audits, versioned schemas and safe failure behavior.

deepSections.title: Every counter is truth plus collision noise
deepSections.body: Choose d hash functions mapping the key universe into w columns. An update (i,Δ) adds Δ to C[j,h_j(i)] for every row. In a nonnegative cash-register stream, the queried cell equals f_i plus frequencies of other keys mapped to the same column. It cannot be below f_i, and the minimum across rows chooses the smallest collision sum. Update and query take O(d), memory is O(dw), independent of universe size, and the sketch stores no key identities. Weighted positive updates work naturally. Conservative update increments only counters at the current minimum level and often reduces practical overestimation, but its merge and signed-update properties need separate care. Keys must have canonical byte encoding, and persistent services need deterministic, domain-separated hashes rather than runtime-randomized language hashes.

deepSections.title: Width bounds collision magnitude while depth suppresses bad luck
deepSections.body: For a target key in one row, each other key collides with probability about 1/w, so expected collision mass is at most ||f||1/w. With w=e/ε, Markov's inequality says the probability this row's noise exceeds ε||f||1 is at most 1/e. The estimate fails only if every independent row has excessive noise, yielding e^(−d) and d≈ln(1/δ). This is a per-query probabilistic statement under the hash model; simultaneous guarantees over many adaptive queries require adjusted reasoning. The bound includes target mass in some presentations or uses residual mass in tighter forms, but remains additive. Large total volume raises absolute error even at fixed key frequency. More depth does not shrink typical collision size; more width does. Empirical errors can be far smaller than the worst-case bound, yet parameter selection must match the consequence of error.

deepSections.title: Update semantics determine which estimator and guarantee apply
deepSections.body: Cash-register streams only add nonnegative mass. Strict turnstile streams permit negative updates while every true frequency remains nonnegative; individual counters can change in complex ways, and the simple never-underestimate argument is not automatically preserved for arbitrary operational mistakes. General turnstile vectors may have negative frequencies and often use Count Sketch, which applies random signs and a median estimator to obtain different L2-style guarantees. Count-Min can represent signed updates algebraically, but users must not quote the cash-register one-sided claim unchanged. Counter width must handle total increments without overflow; saturating silently biases results, while wrapping is catastrophic. Deduplication and exactly-once semantics matter because replayed events legitimately increase the sketch. Sliding windows require bucketed sketches, decay or another time-aware design rather than deleting events casually.

deepSections.title: Heavy hitters need identities, compatible merges and exact audit paths
deepSections.body: The table cannot list which keys generated its counters. A heavy-hitter service therefore tracks candidates through Misra–Gries, Space-Saving, a bounded heap updated from observed keys, or upstream sampling, then queries the sketch for scores. Distributed sketches merge by elementwise addition only when width, depth, seed order, key encoding, counter type and epoch match. A manifest should reject incompatible state instead of producing plausible nonsense. Compare candidate estimates with exact counts on sampled partitions or a promoted shortlist and report upper-biased uncertainty. Monitor total mass, distinct-candidate rate, collision error, table saturation, counter maxima, merge rejection and distribution shifts. Hash-flooding attackers can force collisions if mappings are predictable, so threat models may require keyed hashing and rate limits. Sketches can leak approximate activity and should inherit data access and retention controls.

workedExamples.title: Good absolute, poor relative accuracy
workedExamples.body: An error ceiling of 500 is negligible for a million-count key but overwhelms a ten-count key; report the guarantee in the scale of the decision.

workedExamples.title: Invalid merge
workedExamples.body: Two workers use different seeds. Adding their corresponding cells mixes unrelated buckets, so every resulting query is undefined despite matching array dimensions.

lab.goal: Implement Count-Min frequency estimates, verify their one-sided behavior, and prove compatible distributed merge equivalence.
lab.shipIt: Version the stream and hash schema, reject incompatible merges, track candidates separately, audit estimates against exact samples, protect counters from overflow, and rotate or roll back complete epochs.

exercises.prompt: Sketch the ε–δ proof for a point query.
exercises.solution: Expected one-row collision is bounded by total mass over width; Markov bounds one row, and independent depth exponentially reduces all-rows failure.

exercises.prompt: Why can a rare key have poor relative error?
exercises.solution: The guarantee is additive in total stream mass, not proportional to that key's true count.

exercises.prompt: What metadata must match before merge?
exercises.solution: Width, depth, ordered hash seeds and algorithm, key encoding, counter semantics and time or source epoch.

lessons.title: HyperLogLog & Distinct Counting
lessons.interviewAnswer: HyperLogLog estimates the number of distinct elements using a uniform hash and m=2^p registers. The first p hash bits select a register; the remaining bits provide a rank equal to the position of the first one. Each register stores its maximum observed rank. Rare long zero prefixes imply many distinct trials. HLL combines registers with a bias-corrected harmonic-mean estimator, applies small-range correction such as linear counting when many registers are zero, and has standard error roughly 1.04/√m in its classical regime. Compatible sketches merge by register-wise maximum, so duplicates and partitions do not double count. I version precision, hash and encoding, monitor zero registers and saturation, validate against exact samples, and rebuild rather than merge incompatible sketches. It estimates cardinality, not identities, membership, frequency, intersections without extra machinery, or deletions.
keyPoints: Hash prefixes assign independent-looking substreams; suffix ranks encode rare-event evidence.
Register maxima are duplicate-insensitive and merge through elementwise maximum.
The harmonic mean limits domination by exceptionally large registers.
Precision p sets m=2^p, relative error near 1.04/√m, and memory that grows linearly in m.
Small-range, bias and large-range corrections are part of a practical implementation, not optional decoration.
lessons.why: Counting distinct users, devices, queries, products or flows exactly can require a distributed set whose memory and shuffle costs scale with cardinality. HyperLogLog summarizes the same question in fixed memory, tolerates duplicates and merges naturally across workers and time partitions. It is one of the clearest demonstrations that a carefully chosen random statistic can retain useful global information while discarding identities. The price is controlled uncertainty and a strict compatibility contract. A robust service must understand hashing, corrections, precision, small cardinalities, merge semantics and privacy—not merely call an estimate method and assume that every cardinality-related query is now solved.
lessons.intuition: A fair binary hash begins with one zero half the time, two zeros one quarter, ten zeros roughly once in 1,024 trials. Seeing a very long zero run suggests that many distinct hashes were tried. One maximum is volatile, so HLL splits the stream into many registers using prefix bits. Each register observes its own suffix-rank maximum. Combining many substream estimates with a harmonic-mean form reduces variance and prevents one freak register from dominating. Repeated elements reproduce the same register and rank, leaving state unchanged.
lessons.deepDive: HyperLogLog performs stochastic averaging over hash-partitioned substreams and encodes each substream by a maximum geometric rank. Its estimator, range corrections and constants form one algorithmic contract. Compatibility and hash quality are essential to mergeability, while exact audits and uncertainty are essential to decisions.
lessons.math: Let m=2^p registers M_j. A uniform L-bit hash chooses j with p bits and rank ρ from the remaining q=L−p bits, where P(ρ≥r)=2^{-(r-1)}. Update M_j=max(M_j,ρ). The raw estimate is E=α_m m² /(Σ_j 2^{-M_j}), with α_m approaching about 0.7213/(1+1.079/m) for common m. When V registers are zero and the range is small, linear counting uses m ln(m/V). Classical relative standard error is approximately 1.04/√m. Register-wise max computes set union for compatible sketches. Inclusion–exclusion estimates intersections by |A|+|B|−|A∪B| but can be extremely noisy when overlap is small.

commonMistakes.misconception: HLL estimates event volume.
commonMistakes.correction: It estimates distinct canonical hashes; use counters for total events or frequencies.

commonMistakes.misconception: Sketch estimates can be added across partitions.
commonMistakes.correction: Merge registers by maximum; adding estimates double counts overlap.

commonMistakes.misconception: Any precisions or hash seeds can merge.
commonMistakes.correction: Compatibility is part of the data schema; reject or use a mathematically supported conversion.

commonMistakes.misconception: Inclusion–exclusion makes every intersection accurate.
commonMistakes.correction: Subtracting noisy large estimates is unstable for small overlaps.

followUps.question: Why use a harmonic mean?
followUps.answer: It aggregates reciprocal register scales and limits domination by unusually large maximum ranks.

followUps.question: What does increasing p do?
followUps.answer: It doubles registers and memory per bit while reducing standard error by roughly √2.

followUps.question: How do HLL sketches merge?
followUps.answer: For identical schemas, take the elementwise maximum register because each register stores a union-compatible maximum.

lessons.production: Treat identity definition and sketch format as a versioned metric contract. Persist precision, register width, full hash and seed, byte encoding, rank and correction conventions, source window and checksum. Reject incompatible merges and validate any downsampling path. Handle late data and time windows through explicit bucket policy rather than deleting from a monolithic sketch. Monitor zero-register fraction, register histogram, maximum rank, sparse/dense transitions, merge rejections, snapshot age and relative error against exact audit slices. Attach uncertainty to alerts and confirm financially or legally consequential thresholds exactly. Restrict access because hashes and sketches can leak membership. Retain a prior snapshot and exact fallback for bounded cohorts so a bad hash rollout or serialization change can be rolled back.
lessons.workedExample: With p=10 there are 1,024 registers and classical relative standard error about 3.25%. A true cardinality of one million therefore has a typical error scale of tens of thousands, not an exact last digit. Increasing to p=14 uses sixteen times as many registers and reduces standard error by four. Two daily sketches with the same hash contract merge by maximum to estimate distinct users across both days, automatically deduplicating users present on both days.
lessons.description: HyperLogLog is a fixed-memory probabilistic algorithm for distinct counting. This chapter builds from the probability of leading-zero runs in uniform hashes to stochastic averaging across 2^p registers. It specifies register selection and rank calculation, explains maximum updates and duplicate invariance, derives the raw harmonic-mean estimator and interprets its normalization constant. It covers linear-counting correction for small ranges, empirical bias correction in modern variants, finite hash-width behavior and the classical relative standard error near 1.04/√m. It proves union merge as register-wise maximum and explains why differences, deletions and small intersections are not directly supported. Comparisons with exact sets, bitmaps, linear counting and bottom-k sketches clarify when HLL is appropriate. The lab implements a deterministic 64-bit version with small-range correction, verifies duplicate invariance and partition merge equality, and compares estimates with exact cardinality. Production guidance covers precision and hash versioning, sparse-to-dense storage, serialization, distributed aggregation, register saturation, exact audits, uncertainty-aware thresholds, privacy, corrupted state and rollback. The emphasis is on the full sketch contract: cardinality semantics, canonical identities, uniform hashes, compatible registers and corrections must all align.
learningObjectives: Implement register indexing, leading-zero rank updates, raw estimation and small-range correction.
Explain the 1.04/√m precision law and choose p from memory and decision uncertainty.
Prove duplicate invariance and compatible union merge while recognizing unsupported deletion and difference queries.
Operate versioned sketches with exact audits, serialization checks, privacy controls and rollback.

deepSections.title: Leading-zero ranks turn uniform hashes into cardinality evidence
deepSections.body: A uniformly distributed binary hash behaves like repeated fair coin flips. The probability that its suffix begins with r−1 zeros is 2^{-(r-1)}, so the largest observed rank grows logarithmically with the number of distinct trials. Duplicate keys reproduce the same full hash and cannot increase a maximum twice. A single global maximum has large variance. Earlier algorithms averaged multiple estimators; HLL uses stochastic averaging by dedicating p hash bits to one of m registers and computing a rank from the remaining bits. Each register summarizes a random substream. Uniformity and sufficient hash width are fundamental. Sequential IDs must be hashed, key encodings must be canonical, and domain separation prevents unintended reuse. A poor hash that clusters prefixes or suffixes biases register assignment or ranks and defeats the statistical model.

deepSections.title: The harmonic-mean estimator and corrections cover different cardinality regimes
deepSections.body: Each register M_j corresponds roughly to a substream cardinality proportional to 2^{M_j}. HLL aggregates through the reciprocal sum Σ2^{-M_j}, a harmonic-mean-like construction less sensitive than an arithmetic mean to a few extreme ranks. Multiplying by α_m m² corrects systematic bias in the asymptotic model. At small cardinalities many registers remain zero and the raw estimate is biased; linear counting m ln(m/V), where V is the zero-register count, uses occupancy information more effectively. Production variants such as HyperLogLog++ add empirically calibrated bias tables, sparse representations and refined range logic. At enormous cardinalities finite hash spaces cause collisions and registers can saturate, requiring large-range correction or a wider hash. Corrections must match implementation constants and serialization version; mixing formulas from different variants produces subtle drift.

deepSections.title: Precision is predictable, but not every set query is stable
deepSections.body: In the classical operating range the standard error is about 1.04/√m, and m doubles in the exponent p. One extra precision bit doubles memory but reduces standard error by only √2. Choose p from the uncertainty tolerable for the decision, and use replicated experiments or implementation guidance for tails and small ranges. HLL returns cardinality, not a confidence guarantee for every adversarial stream. Union is natural: each union register is the maximum of component registers. Intersection via inclusion–exclusion subtracts three noisy large estimates; when overlap is small, error can be comparable to or larger than the result, even producing negative raw differences. Direct joint estimators or other sketches may be necessary. Set difference and deletion cannot undo maxima without retaining more state or time-bucketed sketches.

deepSections.title: Distributed distinct counting is a schema-governed aggregation service
deepSections.body: Define the counted identity, event eligibility, time boundary, late-data policy and canonical byte encoding before sketching. Persist p, register width, hash algorithm and seed, rank convention, correction version, format version and source epoch. Merge only exact matches; downsampling higher precision may be possible with a proven implementation, while upsampling cannot recreate lost information. Use sparse storage for low cardinalities and switch deterministically to dense state. Snapshot checksums and register histograms reveal corruption and saturation. Audit against exact sets on sampled tenants or bounded windows and track signed relative error, not only average absolute error. Thresholds for billing, privacy release or capacity decisions should include uncertainty or exact confirmation. Hashing identifiers does not anonymize them against membership inference, so restrict sketches and apply retention and aggregation policy.

workedExamples.title: Union without double counting
workedExamples.body: Worker sketches share a user seen on both partitions. Max-merge preserves the same register evidence, whereas summing daily cardinality estimates would count the user twice.

workedExamples.title: Unstable small intersection
workedExamples.body: Two sets each near one million have union 1.99 million. Subtracting noisy HLL estimates to infer a ten-thousand overlap can have error comparable to the overlap.

lab.goal: Implement a 64-bit HyperLogLog with small-range correction, then verify duplicates, accuracy and max-merge semantics.
lab.verifyIt:
assert np.array_equal(combined.registers,whole.registers)
assert abs(estimate-exact)/exact<.10
before=whole.registers.copy(); [whole.add(v) for v in values[:1000]]; assert np.array_equal(before,whole.registers)
empty=HyperLogLog(10); assert empty.estimate()==0.0
small=HyperLogLog(10); [small.add(i) for i in range(100)]; assert abs(small.estimate()-100)/100<.15
try: left.merge(HyperLogLog(11))
except AssertionError: pass
else: raise AssertionError('precision mismatch must not merge')
lab.shipIt: Freeze identity, hash and estimator versions, reject incompatible state, monitor register distributions and exact audit error, and attach uncertainty or exact confirmation to consequential thresholds.

exercises.prompt: Why do duplicates not change a sketch?
exercises.solution: The same key selects the same register and rank, and max with the stored value is idempotent.

exercises.prompt: How does memory scale with precision p?
exercises.solution: Registers m=2^p, so each extra bit doubles memory and improves standard error only by about √2.

exercises.prompt: Why is subtraction unsupported?
exercises.solution: A maximum does not retain which element created it or the next-largest rank, so removing an element cannot reconstruct prior state.

lessons.title: PageRank & Link Analysis
lessons.interviewAnswer: PageRank is the stationary distribution of a random-surfer Markov chain. From page j, follow one of its outgoing links with probability α and teleport according to distribution v with probability 1−α. Dangling pages need an explicit transition, commonly v. With a column-stochastic matrix P, r=αPr+(1−α)v; teleportation makes the usual finite chain well behaved and power iteration converges. I normalize orientation, deduplicate or weight edges deliberately, handle dangling mass, iterate until a residual or rank-change tolerance, and compare with an independent solve on small graphs. PageRank measures recursive prominence under this browsing model—not relevance, truth, causality or safety. Production systems combine it with content and quality signals, defend against link farms, version graph snapshots, monitor convergence and slices, and keep rollback and explanation paths.
keyPoints: PageRank is an eigenvector or stationary-distribution problem on a normalized directed graph.
Teleportation prevents rank traps and usually supplies uniqueness and convergence under standard conditions.
Dangling nodes must redistribute their probability mass rather than leaking it.
Row-versus-column conventions are equivalent only when equations and multiplication match.
Recursive link prominence is one signal and is vulnerable to graph construction choices and manipulation.
lessons.why: Many networks contain no direct feature called importance. PageRank defines importance recursively: a node receives more credit when it is linked by nodes that themselves have credit, with each source distributing its vote across outgoing links. The construction influenced web search and remains useful for citation, trust, recommendation, entity and dependency graphs. Its lasting value is broader: it connects graph modeling, Markov chains, eigenvectors, sparse iteration and large-scale system operation. Yet every score is conditional on how nodes, edges, weights, teleportation and time were defined. Without that context, a precise-looking rank can legitimize popularity bias, spam or data-quality artifacts.
lessons.intuition: Imagine a browser who repeatedly flips a biased coin. Usually it clicks a uniformly selected outgoing link; sometimes it jumps to a page drawn from a teleport distribution. The long-run fraction of time spent on each page is PageRank. A page gains score from incoming neighbors, but each neighbor divides its contribution across its outgoing choices. Teleportation lets the surfer escape cycles and reach components that links alone cannot reach. A page with no outgoing links must also teleport, or probability disappears from the model.
lessons.deepDive: PageRank converts a directed graph into an ergodic-style random-surfer process and solves its stationary distribution with sparse iterative linear algebra. Correctness depends on stochastic orientation, dangling handling, teleportation and convergence evidence. Interpretation and production safety depend on graph provenance, temporal and spam controls, fairness analysis and combining the score with task-specific signals.
lessons.math: Let P be column-stochastic, P_ij=P(move to i | currently at j). Replace dangling columns with v. For damping α∈(0,1) and probability vector v, r satisfies r=αPr+(1−α)v, equivalently (I−αP)r=(1−α)v. Power iteration r_{t+1}=αPr_t+(1−α)v preserves nonnegativity and unit sum. Stop using ||r_{t+1}−r_t||_1 and verify fixed-point residual ||r−αPr−(1−α)v||_1. Personalized PageRank changes v. With row-stochastic convention, distributions multiply on the left or P is transposed; mixing conventions creates wrong results that may still sum to one.

commonMistakes.misconception: PageRank is the number of inbound links.
commonMistakes.correction: It recursively weights sources and divides each source's contribution across outgoing probability.

commonMistakes.misconception: Normalize the final vector and dangling bugs disappear.
commonMistakes.correction: Post-hoc normalization hides leaked mass but does not implement the intended Markov chain.

commonMistakes.misconception: α=0.85 is universally optimal.
commonMistakes.correction: It is a modeling and convergence choice that should be evaluated for the graph and task.

commonMistakes.misconception: High PageRank means trustworthy or relevant.
commonMistakes.correction: It means prominence under the defined graph and teleport model; combine with task-specific evidence.

followUps.question: Why is teleportation necessary?
followUps.answer: It escapes traps, connects components through the preference distribution and typically ensures a unique convergent stationary score.

followUps.question: How do you handle dangling nodes?
followUps.answer: Redistribute their mass according to the teleport distribution or another explicit probability vector during every iteration.

followUps.question: How would you validate an implementation?
followUps.answer: Check stochastic columns, mass conservation, nonnegativity, convergence change, fixed-point residual, motifs and an independent small-graph solve.

lessons.production: Version node identity and canonicalization, edge semantics and window, weights, duplicate and self-link policy, dangling treatment, α, teleport vector, solver tolerance and graph watermark. Validate stochasticity and graph counts before iteration. Use sparse partitioned multiplication, record mass, residual, iterations and top-k stability, and compare selected motifs with an independent implementation. Promote snapshots atomically after spam, cohort and downstream ranking checks. Monitor graph volume, dangling fraction, component changes, score concentration, top-k churn, residual, latency and manipulation signals. Combine PageRank with relevance, freshness, safety and quality rather than treating it as authority. Restrict private-edge access and retain the prior graph, vector and routing configuration for independent rollback.
lessons.workedExample: Pages A and B link to each other, C links to A, and D is dangling. Without teleportation, the A–B component traps mass and D leaks it if mishandled. With α=0.85, uniform v and D's column replaced by v, every iteration preserves total probability and all nodes receive some base mass. A ranks strongly because it receives from B and C, but the exact order depends on outgoing normalization and teleport choice.
lessons.description: PageRank is a graph-centrality algorithm defined by the stationary distribution of a damped random-surfer process. This chapter constructs a directed transition matrix from links, makes row and column conventions explicit, distributes each source's vote over outgoing edges, and handles self-links, duplicates, weights and dangling nodes. It derives the fixed-point and linear-system forms, explains teleportation, irreducibility, aperiodicity and convergence, and implements sparse-style power iteration with change and residual checks. Personalized PageRank, topic-sensitive teleportation and incremental or approximate computation extend the basic method. The chapter distinguishes PageRank from HITS, degree, shortest-path centralities, content relevance and causal authority. It examines link farms, sybil structures, temporal staleness, popularity feedback, graph incompleteness and fairness across cohorts. The lab builds a stochastic matrix, compares power iteration with a direct linear solve, verifies probability conservation, residual and permutation invariance, and exercises dangling behavior. Production guidance covers graph contracts, snapshot manifests, distributed sparse multiplication, convergence diagnostics, spam defenses, canaries, feature combination, explanations, monitoring, privacy and rollback. The central message is that PageRank is mathematically precise about one browsing model, not universally authoritative about page quality or truth.
learningObjectives: Construct a valid transition matrix with explicit orientation, edge weighting and dangling policy.
Derive PageRank's fixed point and compute it with converged power iteration and residual checks.
Explain how damping, teleportation and personalization change reachability and interpretation.
Design a scalable, manipulation-aware graph-ranking pipeline with reproducible snapshots and rollback.

deepSections.title: Graph construction determines the random surfer's choices
deepSections.body: Choose what a node represents, which directed events become edges, the time window and whether multiple edges encode weight or are deduplicated. Under a column-stochastic convention, column j contains probabilities of moving from j to destinations i; an unweighted page divides one across unique outgoing neighbors. Weighted links divide normalized positive weight. Self-links may be retained or removed by policy. A dangling node with zero outdegree has no valid column, so redirect its mass—commonly according to teleport vector v or uniformly. Failing to do so causes rank mass to vanish. Graph extraction errors, redirects, duplicate URLs, bots and missing private links change the chain. Before ranking, verify every column sum, nonnegative entries, node count, edge count, dangling share and provenance. The mathematics is conditional on this constructed graph, not on an abstract true network.

deepSections.title: Teleportation creates a solvable fixed point and controls mixing
deepSections.body: Pure link following can become trapped in a closed component or oscillate in a periodic graph, and stationary distributions may not be unique. At each step, the damped surfer follows P with probability α and teleports via v otherwise. For positive v and α<1, the resulting transition has broad reachability and a unique positive stationary distribution in the usual finite setting. Rearranging yields a nonsingular linear system because the spectral radius of αP is below one. α near one emphasizes long link paths but slows convergence and increases sensitivity to graph structure; lower α emphasizes teleportation. The historical default near 0.85 is not a law. Personalized PageRank concentrates v on users, topics or seeds and must be interpreted as proximity to that preference, with privacy and filter-bubble implications.

deepSections.title: Sparse power iteration needs conservation and residual diagnostics
deepSections.body: Initialize a probability vector and repeatedly compute link contribution, dangling redistribution and teleportation. Sparse matrix-vector multiplication costs O(E) per iteration rather than materializing an N×N matrix. Partitioning by source or destination changes communication; dangling mass is a global scalar reduction. Stop when L1 change or a norm-scaled criterion reaches tolerance, but also compute the fixed-point residual because a coding error can appear stable. Record iteration count, mass before normalization, residual, top-k stability and rank distribution. A direct solve or eigenvector on small sampled graphs is an excellent independent test. Warm starts help related snapshots but can mask incomplete updates, so compare cold-start canaries. Monte Carlo walks and local push algorithms are alternatives for massive or personalized workloads, each with approximation and latency trade-offs.

deepSections.title: Prominence is not truth, and graph incentives invite manipulation
deepSections.body: PageRank rewards incoming mass under the chosen link behavior. It does not evaluate textual relevance, factuality, recency, safety, creator quality or causal influence. Link farms and sybil clusters manufacture endorsement; dangling and redirect policies can shift credit. Spam-resistant systems detect suspicious topology, discount untrusted edges, incorporate seed trust and combine rank with content, freshness and quality features. Evaluate ranking utility and harms by query, language, site size and new-versus-established nodes. Popularity signals can create feedback that entrenches incumbents. Version graph snapshot, extraction code, node mapping, edge policy, α, v, tolerance and output checksum. Canary on known motifs and business slices before promotion. Monitor graph and rank drift, residual, concentration, top-k turnover, spam indicators and downstream outcomes. Preserve explanations such as major contributing neighborhoods without exposing private edges, and roll back the feature independently from the rest of ranking.

workedExamples.title: Outgoing dilution
workedExamples.body: Two pages with equal rank link to A, but one has one outgoing edge and the other has ten. Their contributions are rank and rank/10 respectively under uniform link choice.

workedExamples.title: Personalized teleportation
workedExamples.body: Putting most teleport mass on trusted research seeds turns the score into proximity to that trust context, not a global statement of importance.

assert np.allclose(P.sum(axis=0),1) and np.all(P>=0)
assert np.all(rank>0) and abs(rank.sum()-1)<1e-12
assert residual<1e-11 and np.allclose(rank,direct,atol=1e-11) and iterations<1000

exercises.prompt: What happens as α approaches one?

exercises.prompt: Why can PageRank reinforce popularity?
exercises.solution: Visibility and links can feed future visibility, so a prominence feature may create a self-reinforcing exposure loop.

lessons.title: Vector vs Raster Spatial Data
lessons.interviewAnswer: Vector data represents discrete features as points, lines and polygons with attributes; raster data represents a regularly sampled field as cells in one or more bands. I choose from the phenomenon and operations, not from file extension. Boundaries, networks and identifiable objects often fit vector topology; imagery, elevation, temperature and continuous surfaces fit rasters. Resolution is a measurement and aggregation choice: a pixel records support over an area, not an infinitely precise point. Conversions are lossy—rasterization depends on grid alignment and inclusion rules, while polygonization inherits pixel stair-steps. In production I preserve CRS, extent, affine transform, resolution, nodata mask, band units, geometry validity and lineage; tile and window large rasters, spatially index vectors, and test mass or class conservation across transformations.
keyPoints: Vector geometries model discrete objects; rasters model sampled fields on a grid, though many phenomena admit both views.
A raster cell has spatial support, resolution, alignment, CRS, bands, datatype and nodata semantics.
Vector validity and topology distinguish mere coordinate arrays from trustworthy spatial features.
Rasterization, resampling and polygonization introduce scale- and rule-dependent information loss.
Cloud-efficient processing depends on spatial windows, tiles, overviews, chunk alignment and metadata contracts.
lessons.why: Spatial analysis starts with a representation choice that silently defines what can be measured. A coastline stored as a line supports length and adjacency reasoning; the same coast in a land-cover grid supports neighborhood filters and image models but its length changes with resolution. Treating a raster as a normal table loses cell footprint, alignment and nodata meaning. Treating polygons as arbitrary lists loses holes, rings, topology and validity. Understanding both models prevents invalid joins, biased zonal statistics, memory explosions and conversions that appear visually plausible while changing totals. It also guides system design: vectors favor feature and spatial-index access, while rasters favor tiled array operations and multiresolution reads.
lessons.intuition: A vector map is like a collection of named cut-outs: a city point, a road path, a parcel boundary. A raster is like graph paper laid over the world, with each square storing a value such as elevation or reflectance. Finer graph paper shows smaller patterns but costs more storage and does not create information that the sensor never observed. Converting cut-outs to cells asks which cells count as covered; converting cells to polygons traces blocky boundaries. Neither is a neutral serialization change.
lessons.deepDive: Vector and raster are data models with different error, topology and access patterns. Reliable work defines geometry or grid semantics, validates metadata and masks, chooses scale from the decision, and treats every conversion as an explicit measurement operation. Hybrid pipelines are normal, but alignment and lineage must remain visible.
lessons.math: A raster geotransform maps pixel column c and row r to coordinates with an affine map: x=a c+b r+c0 and y=d c+e r+f0, commonly with b=d=0 and e<0 for north-up grids. Pixel-center and pixel-corner conventions differ by half a cell. A zonal total for density z_i over equal-area cells is Σ_i z_i A_i over included support, not merely Σ_i z_i. Vector polygon area and length are meaningful only in an appropriate metric CRS or geodesic calculation. Rasterization approximates indicator 1_G(x) over cells using center, all-touched or fractional coverage rules.

commonMistakes.misconception: A GeoTIFF is spatial because it has pixels.
commonMistakes.correction: Spatial meaning also requires a valid transform, CRS, band semantics and nodata contract.

commonMistakes.misconception: Higher raster resolution always means higher accuracy.
commonMistakes.correction: It can oversample uncertain source data and increase cost without adding information.

commonMistakes.misconception: Rasterization is reversible.
commonMistakes.correction: Grid alignment and inclusion discard boundary detail; polygonization cannot recover the original geometry.

commonMistakes.misconception: Zero and nodata are interchangeable.
commonMistakes.correction: Zero may be a valid measurement; use explicit masks and variable semantics.

followUps.question: When would you choose raster over vector?
followUps.answer: For regularly sampled continuous fields, imagery and neighborhood array operations, especially when tiled window access dominates.

followUps.question: What is the difference between pixel center and pixel area?
followUps.answer: A center convention treats the value as located at one point; an area-support convention summarizes the entire cell footprint.

followUps.question: How do you validate a vector-to-raster conversion?
followUps.answer: Check CRS and alignment, compare area or mass under the chosen rule, inspect boundary cases and quantify resolution sensitivity.

lessons.production: Publish a dataset contract containing feature or band semantics, CRS, bounds, geometry type or affine transform, resolution, dtype, units, scale, nodata and time. Reject missing or contradictory spatial metadata. For vectors, validate geometry and IDs and build a versioned index. For rasters, use tiled windows, masks, compression and overviews matched to access patterns. Every conversion records source checksum, target grid, inclusion or resampling rule and conservation tests. Monitor invalid or empty geometry, bounds drift, nodata share, pixel distributions, tile read amplification, file counts and lineage completeness. Restrict precise sensitive locations, aggregate with privacy review, and keep immutable source plus previous derived manifests for rollback.
lessons.workedExample: A one-kilometer land-cover raster and a parcel polygon overlap at the parcel edge. Center-in-cell rasterization may assign zero boundary cells; all-touched includes every intersected cell and overstates small parcels; fractional coverage weights each cell by intersected area. For categorical labels, majority or mode may be appropriate. For population counts, area weighting can still be wrong if people are concentrated within cells, so ancillary dasymetric information may be required.
